## [](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12837995)Abstract

With the rise of generative artificial intelligence, the application of AI in learning environments has received widespread attention. Although empirical studies have explored the effect of AI on self-efficacy, the results have not been consistent. This study conducted a meta-analysis on the results from 23 empirical studies on the impact of AI use on self-efficacy. These studies were published between January 2005 and February 2025 and indexed in one or more of the three major educational research databases: Web of Science, Scopus, and ERIC. The results indicated that AI had a significant positive impact on self-efficacy in learning contexts (effect size of 0.758). Specifically, discipline (Q = 10.348, _p_< 0.05) and the specific role played by AI (Q = 3.991, _p_< 0.05) significantly moderated the effect of AI on self-efficacy. In our discussion, suggestions are provided for enhancing learner self-efficacy and improving the effectiveness of AI in the learning contexts.

**Keywords:**artificial intelligence, self-efficacy, meta-analysis, AIED

## [](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12837995)1. Background

Artificial intelligence (AI) is an influential technology that is impacting students and educators in all fields at every level ([Morales-García et al., 2024](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12837995#B32-behavsci-16-00158)). With its potential to improve learning, teaching, and management, AI is sparking widespread attention among scholars interested in its application to education ([Ng et al., 2023](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12837995#B34-behavsci-16-00158)). When compared to traditional learning contexts, AI-enabled learning environments provide the opportunity to bring richer learning experiences to students ([Ren et al., 2025](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12837995#B40-behavsci-16-00158)), such as personalized learning support and intelligent learning assistance, which are believed to help improve students’ criticality and creativity ([Volante et al., 2023](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12837995#B49-behavsci-16-00158)).

Meanwhile, AI has become an increasingly favorable tool for analyzing complicated data ([Talaei Khoei et al., 2023](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12837995#B47-behavsci-16-00158)) to comprehensively explore students’ learning behavioral patterns ([Raihan et al., 2024](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12837995#B39-behavsci-16-00158)). In a study conducted by [Cerezo et al.](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12837995#B6-behavsci-16-00158) ([2020](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12837995#B6-behavsci-16-00158)), an AI system was used to observe students’ self-regulated learning (SRL) process and collect the research data. AI has been shown to significantly improve students’ self-efficacy through its unique features, such as providing an adaptable learning environment and personalized learning experience ([Massaty et al., 2024](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12837995#B31-behavsci-16-00158)). In this way, AI has the potential to have an impact on psychological factors that affect students’ learning ([J. Wang et al., 2025](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12837995#B52-behavsci-16-00158); [Salah et al., 2024](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12837995#B42-behavsci-16-00158)).

Self-efficacy refers to an individual’s beliefs about their ability to perform a specific task and plays an important role in influencing human performance ([Bandura, 1997](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12837995#B4-behavsci-16-00158); [Jeong & Jeong, 2024](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12837995#B23-behavsci-16-00158)). Research has shown self-efficacy to be a positive predictor of academic achievement ([Shen et al., 2013](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12837995#B44-behavsci-16-00158)). Students who hold high self-efficacy exert greater effort and display more persistence than students who doubt their abilities and have low self-efficacy ([Schunk, 1990](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12837995#B43-behavsci-16-00158)).

In addition, self-efficacy is affected by many elements, such as feedback and rewards, communication and interactions, and motivation and attitude ([Peechapol et al., 2018](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12837995#B37-behavsci-16-00158)). Numerous AI technologies have the potential to enhance self-efficacy through one or more of these elements. Generative AI (capable of creating new content such as text, images, or code), such as ChatGPT and DeepSeek, can interact with individuals by voice or text in a human manner, enhancing students’ one-on-one communication, engagement, and learning experiences ([Labadze et al., 2023](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12837995#B26-behavsci-16-00158)). AI-mediated language learning platforms support personalized lessons, which can give real-time feedback to students ([Wei, 2023](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12837995#B55-behavsci-16-00158)). Studies have already shown the ability of AI to develop self-efficacy. For example, AI adoption in organizations shown to boost creative self-efficacy ([Jeong & Jeong, 2024](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12837995#B23-behavsci-16-00158)), whilst generative AI has been shown to enhance the self-efficacy and higher-order thinking of preservice teachers ([Lu et al., 2024](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12837995#B30-behavsci-16-00158)).

A comprehensive understanding of the impact of AI on learners’ self-efficacy in educational contexts is crucial for enhancing students’ learning effectiveness in AI-enabled learning contexts, but there are few reviews that comprehensively explore this area. Although the systematic review of [Massaty et al.](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12837995#B31-behavsci-16-00158) ([2024](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12837995#B31-behavsci-16-00158)) explored the impact of AI on self-efficacy, it mainly focused on the aspect of computational thinking. To fill this gap, this study conducts a meta-analysis of the impact of AI on learners’ self-efficacy in educational contexts, aiming to address the following questions:(1)How effective is AI in promoting learners’ self-efficacy in learning contexts?(2)How do characteristics such as learner levels, disciplines, the type of AI utilized, research settings, the role of AI, and the duration of the study moderate the influencing effect?

## [](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12837995)2. Methods

### 2.1. Data Sources and Search Strategy

This study employed a meta-analytic methodology to address the inconsistent conclusions regarding the effects of AI on self-efficacy. Specifically, this study adopted a search strategy using three databases, well-known in the field of education (Web of Science, Scopus, and ERIC), to retrieve and download relevant studies from academic journals and conference papers. The inclusion criteria for this study are shown in [Table 1](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12837995#behavsci-16-00158-t001).

### 2.2. Literature Search and Screening

In this study, we used Boolean operators (AND, OR and NOT) in these three databases, and the specific search string was (“AI” OR “Artificial intelligence” OR “Machine intelligence” OR “Machine learning” OR “Neural network” OR “Intelligence virtual reality” OR “Intelligent agent” OR “Natural language processing” OR “Recommendation system” OR “Intelligent tutoring system” OR “Expert system” OR “Chatbot”) AND (“self-efficacy”) AND (“education” OR “learning” OR “educational” OR “pedagogical”). All articles were imported into the application Rayyan ([Ouzzani et al., 2016](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12837995#B35-behavsci-16-00158)) for screening. To ensure strict adherence to the inclusion criteria, the first coder reviewed the screening of all the collected articles, with a second coder screening 25% of all articles. The screening inter-coder consistency was 94.23%, and consensus was reached to resolve any discrepancies.

We used a 2021 PRISMA diagram format to describe the search strategy (see [Figure 1](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12837995#behavsci-16-00158-f001)). We screened for year and study type and downloaded 1433 articles. Duplicates were removed, and then the titles and abstracts were reviewed, which reduced the number of articles down to 101. The articles were reviewed to ensure they met all the established inclusion criteria, and the remaining 96 studies underwent full-text screening. Finally, 23 eligible articles were identified for the meta-analysis.

### 2.3. Coding

In this study, we referred to existing coding strategies ([Y. Wang et al., 2024](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12837995#B54-behavsci-16-00158); [L. Zheng et al., 2023](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12837995#B63-behavsci-16-00158)) to create current coding for the moderating variables; these are, specifically, (1) learner levels: K-12, university, and others; (2) research settings: classroom, online learning, mixed, and others; (3) disciplines: natural sciences, social sciences, engineering, medical, and humanities; (4) type of AI utilized: learning prediction, intelligent tutoring system, student behavior detection, intelligent learning environment, educational robot, and others; (5) the role of AI: intelligent tutor, intelligent learning tool, mixed, and others; and (6) durations of the experiment: <1 month, 1–3 months, >3 months, or not clearly defined. Two coders independently analyzed all 23 articles, and 20 documents had the same coding results. Using the average mutual agreement and reliability formulas, the K value was calculated to be 86.96%, while the reliability coefficient was determined to be 0.93, which indicated that the coding framework demonstrated high reliability ([Gaur & Kumar, 2018](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12837995#B16-behavsci-16-00158)). Finally, the discrepancies were solved by face-to-face discussion.

### 2.4. Research Quality Assessment

Criteria to assess research quality were derived from previous methodologies ([Kmet et al., 2004](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12837995#B25-behavsci-16-00158); [Y. Wang et al., 2024](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12837995#B54-behavsci-16-00158)). The specific quality assessment criteria for this study are as follows: (1) The question is sufficiently described. (2) Sample characteristics are clearly described. (3) The study design is evident and appropriate. (4) Measurement tools are clearly described. (5) Analytic methods are described and appropriate. Each criterion was ranked according to whether it was deemed clear, relatively clear, and not clear, and was assigned 3 points, 2 points, and 1 point, respectively. Two coders evaluated the articles with a consistency of 91.30%. Each article scored between 11 and 15 points, representing the quality of the literature included in current meta-analysis, which met the requirements.

### 2.5. Statistical Analyses

#### 2.5.1. Effect Size Calculations

Most of our studies had small sample sizes, and for this reason we used Hedges’ g to estimate effect sizes ([Hedges & Olkin, 2014](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12837995#B18-behavsci-16-00158)). Hedges’ g is a primary measure for the standardized mean difference for studies with small sample sizes ([Borenstein et al., 2021](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12837995#B5-behavsci-16-00158)). To describe the effect size of this study, we utilized [Cohen](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12837995#B12-behavsci-16-00158)’s ([2013](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12837995#B12-behavsci-16-00158)) definitions represented as small (≤0.20), medium (0.20~0.80), and large (≥0.80).

#### 2.5.2. Analyses of Heterogeneity

This study utilized a comprehensive meta-analysis 3.0 (CMA 3.0) approach ([J. Chen et al., 2022](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12837995#B9-behavsci-16-00158)). We used the Q-test with the I 2-test to calculate heterogeneity, and the results showed that Q = 213.115, _p_< 0.05, I 2 = 89.677 (see first table in [Section 3](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12837995#sec3-behavsci-16-00158)), and the I 2 values were greater than 75%, indicating strong heterogeneity between studies ([Higgins et al., 2003](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12837995#B19-behavsci-16-00158)). Therefore, the random-effects model was used for the meta-analysis of this study. This indicates that there may be potential moderating variables for the effect of AI on self-efficacy; thus, we conducted a moderating variable analysis.

#### 2.5.3. Publication Bias and Sensitive Analysis

This study adopted a funnel plot, classic fail-safe N and Egger’s test to assess the publication bias. The effect sizes shown in the funnel plot are evenly distributed on either side of the summed effect size, which provides a preliminary indication that there is no serious publication bias in the selected studies ([J. Chen et al., 2022](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12837995#B9-behavsci-16-00158)); see [Figure 2](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12837995#behavsci-16-00158-f002). The results of the classic fail-safe N provided a Z-value = 13.606, _p_< 0.001, which indicated we needed to include over 1086 unpublished articles to decease the overall effect. The number of articles (i.e., 1086) was over 125, based on the test standard 5k + 10, where k represents the 23 studies included in this meta-analysis ([Rosenthal, 1995](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12837995#B41-behavsci-16-00158)). This indicates the results of the meta-analysis of this study are robust and are not affected by a substantial publication bias. The result of an Egger’s test did not attain statistical significance (_p_ = 0.073 > 0.05) ([Egger et al., 1997](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12837995#B14-behavsci-16-00158)), also suggesting the absence of substantial publication bias ([F. Wang et al., 2024](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12837995#B51-behavsci-16-00158)). The above multiple validation results indicated that there is no substantial publication bias in this paper, and the validity of the sample included in the meta-analysis was high.

We also used the one-study-removed method ([J. Chen et al., 2022](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12837995#B9-behavsci-16-00158)) to perform sensitivity analysis to test anomalous data and robustness. The result showed that effect sizes were relatively stable regardless of which study was deleted. Specifically, a random effects model was used, with effects values biased in the range [0.598, 0.815], indicating that the result is reliable (see [Figure 3](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12837995#behavsci-16-00158-f003)).

## [](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12837995)3. Results

### 3.1. Overall Effect Size of AI on Self-Efficacy

[Table 2](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12837995#behavsci-16-00158-t002) shows the meta-analysis results for the overall effect size of AI on self-efficacy; specifically, the total effect size is 0.758, and the 95% confidence intervals range from 0.470 to 1.045, revealing a medium effect size according to [Cohen](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12837995#B12-behavsci-16-00158)’s ([2013](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12837995#B12-behavsci-16-00158)) suggestion (i.e., medium effect range from 0.20 to 0.80).

In [Figure 4](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12837995#behavsci-16-00158-f004), the forest plot shows the effect sizes versus weights for each study separately. Among the selected studies, 16 effect values have positive and significant effects, 2 items have negative and significant effects, and the other 5 effect values were not significant.

### 3.2. Moderator Analysis

#### 3.2.1. Learner Levels

As shown in [Table 3](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12837995#behavsci-16-00158-t003), the overall composite effect size for learner levels was 0.745, _p_< 0.05. The effect size for university students was 0.813, _p_< 0.05, while the effects for K-12 and other learners were not significant. Overall, there was no significant difference in the effect of AI on the self-efficacy of learners at different levels of study by the results measured of the group effect (Q = 2.740, _p_ = 0.254).

#### 3.2.2. Research Settings

As shown in [Table 4](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12837995#behavsci-16-00158-t004), the overall composite effect size for different research settings was 0.715, _p_< 0.05. However, there was no significant difference in the effect of AI on learners’ self-efficacy in different research settings, as shown by the results of the test of group effect (Q = 0.289, _p_ = 0.591).

#### 3.2.3. Disciplines

There was a significant difference in the effect of AI on self-efficacy across disciplines (Q = 10.348, _p_ = 0.035) (see [Table 5](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12837995#behavsci-16-00158-t005)). Specifically, AI had a high effect value on learner self-efficacy in natural science subjects (1.310, _p_< 0.05) as well as medicine subjects (1.013, _p_< 0.05), while it was not significant for learner self-efficacy in engineering subjects (_p_ = 0.894).

#### 3.2.4. Type of AI Utilized

The overall composite effect size for type of AI utilized reached 0.574 (_p_< 0.05), and the effect sizes for each type within the group were significant. However, as can be seen in [Table 6](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12837995#behavsci-16-00158-t006), there was no significant difference between AI on learners’ self-efficacy in terms of type of AI utilized (Q = 5.392, _p_ = 0.067).

#### 3.2.5. The Role of AI

As shown in [Table 7](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12837995#behavsci-16-00158-t007), the overall composite effect size for the role of AI was 0.544, _p_< 0.05, while different AI application roles were found to have significant differences on learners’ self-efficacy (Q = 3.991, _p_< 0.05). The role of AI as an intelligent learning tool had the highest effect value on learner self-efficacy (0.883, _p_< 0.05), while as a mixed tool (i.e., both for intelligent learning tools and intelligent tutors) it had a relatively low effect value on learner self-efficacy (0.450, _p_< 0.05).

#### 3.2.6. Duration of Studies

The overall composite effect size for the duration of the studies reached 0.667 (_p_< 0.05), with medium and significant effect sizes for the time taken for the studies. However, as can be seen in [Table 8](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12837995#behavsci-16-00158-t008), there was no significant difference in the effect of AI on learners’ self-efficacy across different durations of the studies (Q = 1.872, _p_> 0.05).

## [](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12837995)4. Discussion

### 4.1. AI Can Effectively Promote Learners’ Self-Efficacy in Learning Contexts

In this study, we conducted a meta-analysis of 23 studies to analyze the effects of AI on learners’ self-efficacy in learning contexts; overall, we found that AI had a medium and significant positive effect on learners’ self-efficacy (0.758, _p_< 0.05). This finding is similar to a systematic literature review by [Massaty et al.](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12837995#B31-behavsci-16-00158) ([2024](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12837995#B31-behavsci-16-00158)), who found that AI can enhance students’ self-efficacy through multiple elements (e.g., interactive activities). Self-efficacy refers to the explicit beliefs or self-confidence that individuals hold about their abilities, namely, the expectations and judgments they make about their abilities during the learning process ([Bandura, 1986](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12837995#B3-behavsci-16-00158)). Prior learning experiences and curricular or instructional strategies are recognized as important factors influencing individual self-efficacy ([Van Dinther et al., 2011](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12837995#B48-behavsci-16-00158)). AI has been shown to have multiple roles in education, such as providing a personalized learning environment and timely feedback ([Crompton & Burke, 2023](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12837995#B13-behavsci-16-00158)). And these might further enhance students’ learning confidence whilst promoting their self-efficacy.

According to this result, the integration of AI into classroom can enhance students’ self-efficacy, which would contribute to their success in learning. Therefore, the role of AI to enhance a learner’s self-efficacy in learning contexts should not be underestimated. AI-related learning activities could help improve students’ self-efficacy and promote learning effectiveness. It is recommended that educators enhance the integration of AI in classrooms and design additional activities that promote student–AI interaction. Furthermore, due to the low numbers of experimental studies on the effects of AI on self-efficacy in learning contexts, the need for more experimental research in this domain is highlighted.

### 4.2. Moderating Effects of AI on Learners’ Self-Efficacy in Learning Contexts

#### 4.2.1. Learner Levels

In this study, analysis results revealed the impact of AI on the self-efficacy of learners at different levels (as shown in [Table 2](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12837995#behavsci-16-00158-t002)). AI had a significant positive impact regarding the self-efficacy of university students. Although AI also showed a positive impact on K-12, as well as other level learners, it was not significant. Meanwhile, statistical analysis (Q = 2.740, _p_> 0.05) did not show a significant difference in AI impact on self-efficacy at different learners’ levels, suggesting that the effect of AI on self-efficacy remains relatively consistent across different learners’ levels. Similarly to previous systematic review studies, AI was found to be mostly used in university education ([Ng et al., 2023](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12837995#B34-behavsci-16-00158); [Zhai et al., 2021](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12837995#B62-behavsci-16-00158)). This suggests that although AI is effective at improving learner self-efficacy in university education, it might not be extensively utilized in K-12 education. This may be related to the numerous implementation issues of using AI at the K-12 level, such as age-appropriate educational content and infrastructure ([Felix & Webb, 2024](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12837995#B15-behavsci-16-00158)). More research needs to be undertaken to identify if and how educational material can be designed and used at the K-12 level to further facilitate students’ interactive learning with AI to enhance self-efficacy.

#### 4.2.2. Research Settings

The results showed that AI had a positive and significant effect on the self-efficacy of learners in the online context, as well as in the classroom context (as shown in [Table 3](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12837995#behavsci-16-00158-t003)). However, statistical analysis (Q = 0.289, _p_> 0.05) showed that there was no significant difference in the effect of AI on learners’ self-efficacy between the different research settings. This result suggests that the effect of AI on college students’ self-efficacy is relatively consistent across research settings. Our study also found that, among the articles included in this meta-analysis, most of the research contexts were based in a classroom, with only one research context set in an online context. This may be related to students’ trust and preference for people as teachers rather than AI agents in online courses ([Spence et al., 2024](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12837995#B45-behavsci-16-00158)); few courses have developed strategies to enable robust AI-integrated teaching and learning, few lecturers are willing to share their courses whilst still trialing, developing, and refining AI-focused coursework, and few lecturers are open to sharing course work that is unable to be formally assessed as true student work. With all these possibilities there is still much research to be undertaken in this area.

#### 4.2.3. Disciplines

The results of this study showed that the application of AI in four different disciplines—social sciences, medicine, humanities, and natural sciences—significantly increased learners’ self-efficacy (as shown in [Table 4](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12837995#behavsci-16-00158-t004)). But the effect value for learners of the engineering discipline was small and non-significant. Additionally, the statistical analysis (Q = 10.348, _p_< 0.05) showed that the effect of AI application on self-efficacy in different disciplines was significant, which indicated that it had the highest effect on self-efficacy for students of natural sciences and medical disciplines, and it had less of an effect on self-efficacy for humanities students. The results from the engineering disciplines was inconsistent with previous research findings. The study by [Yilmaz and Karaoglan Yilmaz](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12837995#B60-behavsci-16-00158) ([2023](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12837995#B60-behavsci-16-00158)) showed that ChatGPT significantly increased computer science students’ programming self-efficacy. This inconsistency may be due to the numerous interpretations of the term engineering or the plausibility that engineering disciplines may require students to utilize their personal understanding and practical experience, and, as AI gives direct answers, this may hinder the internalization process and thus deprive students of a source of self-efficacy ([Yang et al., 2025](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12837995#B59-behavsci-16-00158)).

We also found that of the 23 studies included in this meta-analysis, most of the articles conducted experimental research in the social disciplines, and the effect of AI on learners in these fields was large and significant. This may be due to the abundant learning resources and personalized learning aids available for AI integration ([Ansari et al., 2024](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12837995#B2-behavsci-16-00158)). This suggests AI may also enhance students’ self-confidence in accomplishing social discipline tasks, such as writing and speaking ([A. Chen et al., 2025](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12837995#B8-behavsci-16-00158)), whilst strengthening their self-efficacy. A previous study which investigated the use of AI in English language education found that student self-efficacy and speaking was significantly improved ([Yıldız, 2024](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12837995#B61-behavsci-16-00158)). This study found that the effect of AI on learners’ self-efficacy in different disciplines is differentiated, and it is suggested that educators need to consider the differences between disciplines when developing AI-integrated material.

#### 4.2.4. Type of AI Utilized

For the type of AI utilized in this study, the results have identified a significant positive impact on learners’ self-efficacy when the AI types utilized were intelligent learning environments and learning robots (as shown in [Table 5](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12837995#behavsci-16-00158-t005)). However, there was no significant effect on learners’ self-efficacy when the AI type utilized was an intelligent tutoring system. Statistical analysis showed (Q = 5.392, _p_> 0.05) that the difference between different AI application types on learners’ self-efficacy was not significant, which means that the effect of different AI application types on learners’ self-efficacy is relatively consistent. In this study, we summarized three types of applications of AI, namely, intelligent learning environments, educational robots, and intelligent tutoring systems from the included studies. Since AI is in its early stages and the full extent of AI types has not yet been developed and utilized to support education, educators need to consider the fit between AI types and teaching design. This is yet another research area for researchers.

#### 4.2.5. The Role of AI

The analysis of this study revealed a significant difference in the effect of the roles of different AI applications on learners’ self-efficacy (Q = 3.991, _p_< 0.05) (as shown in [Table 6](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12837995#behavsci-16-00158-t006)). Specifically, the highest effect value was found when the role of AI was as an intelligent learning tool, while the lowest effect value was found when the role of AI was multi-purpose and used as a mixed tool (i.e., both as an intelligent learning tool and an intelligent tutor). AI as an intelligent learning tool is mainly used by students, possibly to support their self-learning. The self-regulated learning of students is based on their thoughts, feelings, and behaviors that students then develop to achieve their personal goals ([Alonso-Mencía et al., 2020](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12837995#B1-behavsci-16-00158); [Zimmerman, 2000](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12837995#B65-behavsci-16-00158)). Therefore, students can use AI to personalize their learning according to their own learning progress, which may enhance their self-confidence and self-efficacy in the process of task solving. Educators could give more consideration to students’ use of AI tools to promote greater self-confidence in the actual educational process.

#### 4.2.6. Length of Experimental Research Design

Initially, the study results revealed that all different time spans of the experiments have significant and positive effects as concerns AI, with regard to improving students’ self-efficacy (as shown in [Table 7](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12837995#behavsci-16-00158-t007)). This encourages educators to try to use AI and integrate AI into their learning classrooms, which may be able to help students increase their self-efficacy and self-confidence in learning. However, through further statistical analysis (Q = 1.872, _p_> 0.05), it was found that the difference in AI improving students’ self-efficacy across a range of time spans was not significant, indicating the effects were relatively consistent. Longer periods of technology learning can reduce the novelty effect and students’ interests ([Sun & Zhou, 2024](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12837995#B46-behavsci-16-00158)), while shorter periods of AI use may limit the time available to evaluate and identify change in student effectiveness or the time to develop skills and confidence with the new technology and delivery methods ([Sun & Zhou, 2024](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12837995#B46-behavsci-16-00158)).

### 4.3. Limitation and Future Studies

Although the present study provides valuable insights, and recommended future research was reported throughout the Discussion section, it has several limitations that should be acknowledged. Due to the inclusion criteria, only 23 papers were included in this study; these papers in the meta-analysis had relatively small sample sizes. And some relevant but not fully compliant papers may have been excluded. In addition, some subgroups in this study included fewer than five observations (N < 5), which may limit the precision of estimates in these categories. Although this study proposed relevant moderating variables based on existing studies, other potential moderating variables may have been overlooked. It is recommended that future studies incorporate more potential moderator variables to achieve more comprehensive and in-depth analyses. Meanwhile, the heterogeneity of this study is very high; the potential for unmeasured factors might account for a great deal of variation between included studies. Furthermore, although several approaches were used to evaluate publication bias in the present study, it remains essential for future research to implement more comprehensive methods to enhance the rigor of the assessment.

## [](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12837995)5. Conclusions

This study employed meta-analysis to answer two questions about the effects of AI on learners’ self-efficacy in educational contexts. In doing so, we found that (1) AI had a significant positive, medium-sized impact on learners’ self-efficacy, and (2) increases in learner self-efficacy were moderated by the context and purpose of AI use. Overall, this study revealed the effects of AI on self-efficacy in educational contexts. It analyzed the reasons that may influence the changes in the effects of AI on self-efficacy from the perspective of multiple moderating variables. This provides insights into the relationship between AI and self-efficacy and suggests ways to enhance the use of AI in education from the perspective of self-efficacy.

args.summary:
This is a meta-analysis study published in Behavioral Sciences (2026) by Ren, Stephens, and Lee from the University of Auckland, examining the impact of AI on learners' self-efficacy in educational contexts. The study analyzed 23 empirical studies published between January 2005 and February 2025, indexed in Web of Science, Scopus, and ERIC databases.

**Key Findings:**
- AI had a significant positive impact on self-efficacy in learning contexts, with a medium effect size of 0.758 (Hedges' g).
- Two moderating variables were significant: discipline (Q = 10.348, p < 0.05) and the role played by AI (Q = 3.991, p < 0.05).
- AI had the highest effect on self-efficacy in natural sciences (1.310) and medicine (1.013), while the effect was not significant for engineering.
- AI as an intelligent learning tool produced the highest effect on self-efficacy (0.883), while mixed roles (tool + tutor) had lower effects (0.450).
- No significant moderating effects were found for learner levels, research settings, type of AI utilized, or duration of studies.

**Methodology:** The study used a random-effects model due to high heterogeneity (I² = 89.677). Hedges' g was used for effect size calculations. Publication bias was assessed via funnel plot, classic fail-safe N, and Egger's test, all indicating no substantial bias. Sensitivity analysis confirmed robustness of results.

**Conclusion:** AI effectively promotes learners' self-efficacy, particularly in natural sciences and medicine, and when used as an intelligent learning tool. The study recommends integrating AI in classrooms and designing activities that promote student-AI interaction, while noting the need for more experimental research in this domain.

## SYSTEMATIC REVIEW article

Front. Educ., 13 March 2026

Sec. Digital Education

Volume 11 - 2026 | <https://doi.org/10.3389/feduc.2026.1782626>

# Artificial intelligence in education: a systematic review of personalized learning trends and future directions

Maryam Ikram 1

Shamsiah Banu Mohamed Hanefar 1

Syed Muhammad Umer Saleem 2\*

Fariha Zulfiqar 3

1. Faculty of Education and Liberal Arts, INTI International University, Nilai, Negeri Sembilan, Malaysia

2. Department of Business Administration, Faculty of Management Sciences, ILMA University, Karachi, Pakistan

3. Institute of Computer Science and Information Technology, The Women University Multan, Multan, Pakistan

Article metrics

## Abstract

**Purpose:**

The objective of this research is to compile a thorough review of existing literature, highlighting how artificial intelligence and personalized learning have shaped emerging research opportunities.

**Research methodology:**

This study employs the PRISMA review protocol alongside a meta-literature review to analyze pertinent works sourced from the Scopus database, spanning the years 2013 to 2025.

**Findings:**

The study examines the progress and deficiencies in the integration of artificial intelligence and personalized learning in education. It underscores a transition in global research priorities from dominant regions such as China, USA and Europe to broader Asia, signaling new opportunities for educational improvement. However, the findings reveal that the swift expansion of AI, combined with persistent concerns about educational standards in developing countries, may create additional institutional pressures that influence the effectiveness of education.

**Implications:**

The findings from this review present significant implications for research, practice, and policy. For educators and academic institutions, the results highlight the necessity of professional development that goes beyond technical proficiency, emphasizing pedagogical integration and digital literacy. Furthermore, policymakers are urged to develop ethical frameworks for AI implementation in education, addressing critical issues such as data privacy, algorithmic bias, and unequal access.

**Originality:**

The significance of this study lies in its effort to bridge a gap in the existing literature by systematically analyzing and reviewing research on Artificial Intelligence and Personalized Learning using PRISMA and meta-literature review methodologies. This comprehensive analysis offers researchers a clearer understanding of key developments and emerging trends within the field. Moreover, it identifies promising avenues for future inquiry and serves as a foundational reference for subsequent investigations.

## 1 Introduction and literature review

The rapid advancement of artificial intelligence (AI) technologies has fundamentally transformed the landscape of educational research and practice, with personalized learning emerging as one of the most promising applications of AI in educational settings. Recent comprehensive analyses of the artificial intelligence in education (AIED) field demonstrate the exponential growth and diversification of research priorities, with systematic reviews mapping over 10 literature reviews that collectively illustrate the field’s evolution toward more sophisticated, data-driven approaches to individualized instruction ([Mustafa et al., 2024](#ref27)). As educational institutions worldwide grapple with the challenge of accommodating diverse learner needs, backgrounds, and learning preferences within increasingly heterogeneous student populations, AI-driven personalized learning systems have gained substantial attention as a potential solution to enhance learning outcomes while maintaining educational scalability and accessibility ([Zhang et al., 2024](#ref45)). The convergence of machine learning algorithms, educational data analytics, and adaptive instructional design has created unprecedented opportunities to tailor educational experiences to individual learners, including students with disabilities and those requiring specialized support, with recent meta-analytic evidence demonstrating medium positive effects of AI interventions across diverse learner populations ([Zhang et al., 2024](#ref45)). Contemporary developments in AI-enabled assessment systems and dialogic tutoring platforms exemplify how advanced technologies such as sequence mining, natural language processing, and automated feedback generation are enabling truly personalized educational experiences that adapt to individual learning patterns and preferences in real-time ([Chen et al., 2020](#ref9); [Wang et al., 2025](#ref42)).

The conceptual foundation of AI-enabled personalized learning rests on the premise that effective education must account for individual differences in cognitive abilities, learning styles, prior knowledge, motivation and contextual factors that influence learning processes. Traditional educational approaches constrained by practical limitations of classroom instruction and resource availability have historically struggled to provide truly individualized learning experiences on a scale. However, the emergence of sophisticated AI technologies, including machine learning algorithms, natural language processing, computer vision, and adaptive systems has enabled the development of intelligent educational platforms capable of analyzing vast amounts of learner data in real-time and making dynamic adjustments to instructional content, pacing and delivery methods based on individual learner characteristics and performance patterns.

The historical evolution of AI in personalized learning can be traced through several distinct phases, each characterized by technological innovations and pedagogical insights that have progressively enhanced the sophistication and effectiveness of personalized learning systems. The earliest implementations emerged from rule-based intelligent tutoring systems (ITS) developed in the 1970s and 1980s, which utilized expert systems and predetermined decision trees to provide basic adaptive feedback and content sequencing. These foundational systems established the core architectural components that continue to underpin contemporary AI-driven educational technologies: student models for tracking learner progress and characteristics, domain models for organizing educational content and learning objectives and tutoring models for determining appropriate instructional strategies and interventions.

The subsequent evolution in the 1990s and early 2000s witnessed the integration of more sophisticated data collection mechanisms and statistical modeling approaches, enabling systems to capture and analyze learner interactions with greater granularity and precision. This period coincided with the emergence of learning analytics as a distinct research discipline, focusing on the systematic collection, analysis and interpretation of educational data to improve learning outcomes and institutional effectiveness. The proliferation of online learning platforms and digital educational resources during this era generated unprecedented volumes of learner data, creating both opportunities and challenges for personalizing educational experiences through computational methods.

Contemporary AI-driven personalized learning systems, which have emerged and rapidly evolved since the 2010s, are characterized by the adoption of advanced machine learning techniques, including deep learning, neural networks, reinforcement learning and ensemble methods, which have dramatically enhanced the predictive accuracy and adaptive capabilities of educational technologies ([Figure 1](#fig1)). Modern personalized learning platforms leverage sophisticated algorithms, such as collaborative filtering, content-based recommendation systems, and hybrid approaches, to analyze multiple data streams simultaneously. These data streams include clickstream data, assessment results, time-on-task metrics, physiological indicators, and social interaction patterns, enabling the creation of comprehensive learner profiles that inform personalized instructional decisions.

Figure 1

![Bar chart showing publication trends from 2013 to 2025, with a gradual increase until 2023, then a sharp rise to 68 publications in 2024 and 122 in 2025.](https://www.frontiersin.org/files/Articles/1782626/xml-images/feduc-11-1782626-g001.webp)

Growth of artificial intelligence and personalized learning publications from 2013 to 2025. Source: Scopus database.

Recent developments in generative artificial intelligence and large language models have further revolutionized the personalized learning landscape, enabling systems to provide contextually appropriate feedback, generate customized learning materials and engage in sophisticated natural language interactions with learners. These technologies have demonstrated remarkable capabilities in understanding learner queries, providing explanations tailored to individual comprehension levels, adapting communication styles to match learner preferences, and creating personalized educational content across diverse subject domains and learning contexts. The integration of conversational AI agents and intelligent tutoring capabilities has made it possible to create virtual mentors and educational assistants that can provide personalized support at scale, addressing one of the fundamental challenges in traditional educational settings. In this review, generative AI is operationalized as AI systems capable of producing novel, context-sensitive outputs (e.g., text, feedback, learning materials, or dialogue) based on probabilistic language and content models, including large language models and related generative architectures, that support adaptive and interactive learning processes ([Chen et al., 2020](#ref9); [Guettala et al., 2024](#ref15); [Shen et al., 2025](#ref35)).

Despite the substantial technological advances and promising applications of AI in personalized learning, the current research landscape reveals significant gaps in understanding of the effectiveness, implementation challenges and broader implications of these technologies. Existing literature demonstrates considerable heterogeneity in research methodologies, outcome measures, implementation contexts and theoretical frameworks employed to study AI-driven personalized learning systems. This methodological diversity, while reflecting the multidisciplinary nature of the field has resulted in fragmented evidence that limits ability to draw definitive conclusions about the effectiveness of different AI approaches for personalized learning across various educational contexts and learner populations.

Meta-analytic evidence suggests that AI-enabled adaptive learning systems can produce medium to large positive effects on learner cognitive outcomes, with reported effect sizes ranging from *g* = 0.50 to *g* = 0.70 across different studies and contexts. However, these aggregated effects are moderated by numerous factors, including study design quality, implementation duration, adaptive system features, educational domain, learner characteristics and geographic context, indicating that the effectiveness of AI-driven personalized learning is highly dependent on specific implementation conditions and contextual factors.

The current body of research also reveals significant gaps in understanding of the mechanisms through which AI-driven personalization affects learning processes and outcomes. While numerous studies document positive effects of personalized learning interventions, fewer investigations have examined the underlying cognitive, motivational and social processes that mediate these effects. This limitation is particularly important given the complexity of learning processes and the potential for AI systems to influence multiple aspects of the learning experience simultaneously, including cognitive load, motivation, engagement, self-regulation and social interaction patterns.

Methodologically, the field is characterized by considerable diversity in research approaches, ranging from randomized controlled trials and quasi-experimental designs to case studies, design-based research and mixed-methods investigations. While this methodological pluralism reflects the complexity of educational phenomena and the need for multiple perspectives, it also creates challenges for synthesizing evidence and establishing robust conclusions about the effectiveness of AI-driven personalized learning approaches.

The geographic and contextual distribution of research in AI-driven personalized learning reveals significant disparities, with most high-quality studies conducted in developed countries with advanced technological infrastructure and well-established educational research traditions. This geographic concentration raises important questions about the applicability of research findings to diverse cultural, linguistic, and socioeconomic contexts, particularly in developing countries where educational challenges are more acute and technological resources are more limited. Furthermore, most existing research has focused on specific educational domains, such as mathematics, computer science, and language learning, with limited attention to other subject areas and interdisciplinary applications.

Ethical considerations surrounding AI-driven personalized learning have received increasing attention in recent literature, with researchers highlighting concerns related to data privacy, algorithmic bias, transparency, accountability and the potential for AI systems to perpetuate or exacerbate existing educational inequalities. Studies have documented instances of algorithmic bias in educational AI systems, particularly affecting students from underrepresented groups or those with diverse learning needs. Privacy concerns have been raised regarding the extensive data collection required for effective personalization, including sensitive information about learning difficulties, socioeconomic status and personal characteristics that may be inferred from behavioral data.

The implementation of AI-driven personalized learning systems in real-world educational contexts faces numerous practical challenges that have been inadequately addressed in existing research. These challenges include technical infrastructure requirements, teacher training and support needs, integration with existing educational systems and curricula, cost considerations and institutional change management processes. Research has identified teacher acceptance and trust as critical factors influencing the successful implementation of AI-driven educational technologies. However, few studies have systematically examined the factors that promote or inhibit teacher adoption of these systems.

Current literature reviews and systematic syntheses in the field of AI and personalized learning have made important contributions to understanding but also reveal significant limitations that justify the need for additional comprehensive reviews. Existing meta-analyses have typically focused on specific types of AI systems or educational domains, limiting their scope and generalizability. Many reviews have included studies of varying methodological quality without implementing rigorous quality assessment criteria, which may compromise the reliability of their conclusions. Furthermore, most existing reviews have not adequately addressed implementation factors, contextual moderators, and ethical considerations that are crucial for understanding the broader implications of AI-driven personalized learning.

The rapid pace of technological development in AI has also created challenges for maintaining a current and comprehensive understanding of the field. Many existing reviews were conducted several years ago. They may not adequately reflect recent advances in AI technologies, particularly in areas such as deep learning, natural language processing, and generative AI. The emergence of large language models and conversational AI systems has created new possibilities for personalized learning that are not well-represented in existing systematic reviews, highlighting the need for updated syntheses that incorporate these technological developments.

The theoretical foundations underlying AI-driven personalized learning research also reveal important gaps and inconsistencies. While numerous studies reference established learning theories and educational frameworks, there is often a limited explicit connection between theoretical principles and the design and evaluation of AI systems. This disconnect between theory and practice limits the ability to understand why certain AI approaches are effective and under what conditions, hindering the development of more robust and generalizable personalized learning systems.

To address this theory practice gap, emerging studies increasingly emphasize the need to explicitly align AI-driven personalized learning features with established pedagogical theories. For instance, adaptive content sequencing, learner-controlled pacing, and feedback personalization commonly implemented in AI systems are conceptually grounded in constructivist learning theory, which views learning as an active process of knowledge construction shaped by prior experience and contextual interaction ([Chen et al., 2020](#ref9); [Castro et al., 2024](#ref8)). Similarly, AI-supported dialogic tutoring systems, collaborative recommendation engines, and social feedback mechanisms reflect principles of social learning theory by facilitating observation, interaction, and knowledge co-construction within digitally mediated learning environments ([Wang et al., 2025](#ref42); [Mustafa et al., 2024](#ref27)). Explicitly mapping AI functionalities to such pedagogical foundations is essential for ensuring that technological innovation meaningfully supports learning processes rather than operating as a purely technical intervention.

The measurement and evaluation of personalized learning outcomes present additional challenges that have been inadequately addressed in existing research. Many studies rely on traditional academic achievement measures that may not fully capture the benefits of personalized learning, such as improved motivation, self-regulation, metacognitive awareness, and long-term retention. Furthermore, the complexity of customized learning systems makes it difficult to isolate the effects of specific AI components or features, limiting the understanding of which aspects of personalization are most important for different learners and learning contexts.

Given these identified gaps and limitations in the current research landscape, there is a compelling need for a comprehensive systematic literature review that synthesizes high-quality evidence on AI-driven personalized learning from peer-reviewed sources indexed in major academic databases. Such a review would provide valuable insights into the current state of knowledge, identify robust evidence for the effectiveness of different AI approaches, examine moderating factors that influence outcomes, and highlight priority areas for future research and development.

The proposed systematic literature review aims to address these gaps by focusing specifically on high-quality peer-reviewed articles published in journals indexed in Scopus that meet rigorous peer-review standards. This approach will ensure that the review synthesizes the most reliable and methodologically sound evidence available, providing a solid foundation for evidence-based recommendations regarding the implementation and further development of AI-driven personalized learning systems.

The systematic approach will enable comprehensive identification and synthesis of relevant studies while maintaining transparency and reproducibility throughout the review process. By implementing rigorous inclusion and exclusion criteria, quality assessment procedures, and systematic data extraction protocols, the review will provide a more robust and reliable synthesis of evidence than has been available in previous reviews. The focus on both quantitative outcomes and qualitative implementation factors will provide a comprehensive understanding of not only whether AI-driven personalized learning is effective, but also how and under what conditions it works best.

This systematic literature review will contribute to the field by providing educational researchers, practitioners, policymakers, and technology developers with evidence-based guidance for implementing AI-driven personalized learning systems effectively and ethically. The review findings will inform future research priorities, guide the development of more effective AI technologies for education, and support evidence-based decision-making regarding the adoption and implementation of personalized learning systems in diverse educational contexts. Furthermore, the systematic identification of research gaps and methodological limitations will help establish priorities for future investigations and contribute to the continued advancement of the field.

The urgency of this systematic review is underscored by the rapid adoption of AI technologies in educational settings worldwide, often without sufficient empirical evidence to guide implementation decisions. Educational institutions are increasingly investing in AI-driven, personalized learning platforms; however, the lack of comprehensive, high-quality evidence synthesis limits their ability to make informed choices about which technologies to adopt and how to implement them effectively. This review will address this critical need by providing a rigorous, evidence-based foundation for decision-making in the implementation of AI-driven personalized learning.

## 2 Methodology

The methodology is divided into two main parts: the review protocol and the meta-literature review. The systematic approach incorporates four elements: the review protocol (PRISMA), the development of research questions using the PICo framework, a comprehensive, inclusive search strategy and the analysis of findings.

### 2.1 The review protocol—PRISMA

The Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) framework was adopted for conducting the systematic review of literature ([Ikram and Kenayathulla, 2023](#ref18); [Rethlefsen et al., 2021](#ref32); [Saleem et al., 2024](#ref34)). PRISMA provides structured guidelines that support authors in determining inclusion and exclusion criteria while also enhancing the transparency and quality assessment of reviews. Although originally developed for systematic reviews of randomized controlled trials, it has been widely recognized as applicable to other types of systematic reviews ([Moher et al., 2009](#ref24)). According to [Sierra-Correa and Cantera Kintz (2015)](#ref37), PRISMA offers distinct advantages: it refines research focus, sets clear boundaries for study selection, and facilitates efficient analysis of large datasets. More recently, [Page et al. (2021)](#ref28) emphasized that PRISMA enables a comprehensive and systematic exploration of terms and concepts, including those related to policies on artificial intelligence in higher education. Given these strengths, the PRISMA methodology is particularly well-suited for investigating the intersection of Artificial Intelligence and Personalized Learning in this study.

In line with PRISMA 2020 guidance, the framework was applied to guide study identification, screening, eligibility assessment, and transparent reporting of the search process, while quality appraisal was conducted separately using the Mixed Methods Appraisal Tool (MMAT). This approach is consistent with prior systematic reviews that employ PRISMA for reporting structure and MMAT for methodological rigor in heterogeneous evidence bases ([Moher et al., 2009](#ref24); [Page et al., 2021](#ref28); [Mustafa et al., 2024](#ref27)).

### 2.2 Formulation of research question

This study employed the PICo framework to construct its research question, as it is a widely recognized approach for generating systematic review queries ([Dhir and Gupta, 2021](#ref12)). The framework incorporates three main components: Population, Interest, and Context. Accordingly, this research identified existing literature as the Population, personalized learning as the Interest, and artificial intelligence as the Context, thereby framing the research question effectively.

### 2.3 Systematic search strategies

This study employed a three-step systematic search comprising identification, screening, and evaluation of eligibility.

#### 2.3.1 Identification

For this research, a substantial number of potentially relevant documents were identified through a systematic process carried out in three stages. The first stage involved identifying keywords, followed by the inclusion of analogous terms and synonyms drawn from various sources and existing literature. These keywords were then used to construct a comprehensive search query within the Scopus database, recognized for its high-quality standards and suitability for systematic literature reviews ([Mehmood et al., 2022a](#ref21),[b](#ref22); [Wider et al., 2025](#ref44)). Scopus was selected as the sole database due to its broad multidisciplinary coverage and strong representation of peer-reviewed journals in education and computer science, making it suitable for trend-focused systematic reviews ([Rethlefsen et al., 2021](#ref32)). The final search string (see [Table 1](#tab1)) targeted document titles containing the most relevant keywords. In this initial step, the Scopus search yielded a total of 219 documents.

| Scopus | [TITLE (artificial intelligence) OR TITLE (AI) AND TITLE (“personalized learning”) OR TITLE (“personalized learning”)] |

The search string.

The search was restricted to title fields to ensure high conceptual relevance and to capture studies with an explicit primary focus on artificial intelligence and personalized learning, a strategy commonly used to enhance thematic precision in systematic reviews ([Rethlefsen et al., 2021](#ref32)).

#### 2.3.2 Screening

The purpose of the screening phase was to remove irrelevant publications and ensure consistency in the dataset ([Ikram et al., 2025](#ref17); [Mehmood et al., 2022a](#ref21),[b](#ref22)). Screening focused on two main criteria: document type and language. Specifically, the study included only research articles and excluded all documents not written in English language. Following this step, 149 documents were excluded from the dataset ([Table 2](#tab2)).

Table 2

| Criterion | Eligibility | Exclusion |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Document type | Articles | Conference paper, book, book chapter, review, and note |
| Language | English | Non-English |

#### 2.3.3 Eligibility

The third step involved an eligibility review of the 70 studies that had passed the initial screening. This stage required a close examination of each article’s title, abstract, and main content to verify their relevance to the research objectives. As a result, 31 studies met the inclusion criteria and were included in the final analysis ([Figure 2](#fig2)).

Data retrieval process. Source: [Ikram et al. (2025)](#ref17).

In addition to eligibility screening, a structured quality appraisal was conducted using the Mixed Methods Appraisal Tool (MMAT, 2018 version). The MMAT was selected because it allows consistent appraisal across qualitative, quantitative, and mixed-methods study designs, which aligns with the methodological diversity of the included studies. Each article was assessed against the relevant MMAT criteria based on its research design to ensure minimum methodological rigor and transparency. The quality appraisal was used as a screening and interpretive safeguard rather than as a basis for quantitative weighting, in line with the descriptive and thematic objectives of this systematic review.

[Figures 3](#fig3)–[6](#fig6) collectively provide a descriptive overview of the methodological distribution, geographical spread, leading contributors, and disciplinary focus of the reviewed literature. ### 3.1 The method used by the reviewed articles

[Figure 3](#fig3) illustrates the methodological distribution of the reviewed literature. Qualitative research was used in 14 papers, compared with 13 that relied on quantitative designs and four that applied mixed methods. The preference for qualitative approaches highlights the field’s emphasis on exploring complex experiences and perceptions surrounding AI and personalized learning.

### 3.2 The research setting used by the reviewed articles

The analysis of publications by country highlights the truly global scope of research into artificial intelligence and personalized learning ([Figure 4](#fig4)). With six papers, China is the leading contributor, reflecting both its policy-driven investment in AI and its emphasis on educational digitalization. India follows with four contributions, demonstrating active application of AI across diverse areas, including engineering, adaptive learning, and language education. The USA, Saudi Arabia, Colombia, and Kazakhstan each added two papers, indicating steady engagement, particularly with the USA’s established EdTech landscape and Saudi Arabia’s Vision 2030 reforms. A range of countries, including Pakistan, UAE, Bangladesh, Morocco, Serbia, Iran, Oman, UK, Germany, South Africa, Russia, Thailand, and Australia, contributed one paper each, showing that research interest extends beyond traditional centers of AI development. While China and India emerge as leaders, the overall pattern reveals a wide geographical spread, affirming the global relevance of this field and its potential for future cross-national collaboration.

### 3.3 Top authors of the reviewed articles

Exploring opportunities for collaboration in artificial intelligence and personalized learning begins with recognizing the leading voices in the field. According to Scopus, 160 different authors from multiple institutions have published on this subject. Chiappe, A., emerges with three contributions, while Liu M., Sajja R., Sermet Y., Wu L., and Zhou X., follow with two publications each. In addition, Aboraya W., Abrar M., Abualkishik A. Z., and Agatova, A., have each made a single contribution to the body of research ([Figure 5](#fig5)).

### 3.4 The subject area of the reviewed articles

According to Scopus classifications, 30.2% of the publications were in Social Sciences journals, 26.2% in Computer Science journals, and 11.1% in Engineering journals (see [Figure 6](#fig6)). This distribution highlights the interdisciplinary nature of research on artificial intelligence and personalized learning. Within the Social Sciences, most studies addressing this topic were published, while only 33 articles appeared in Computer Science and 16 in Engineering. These figures suggest that artificial intelligence and personalized learning have gained greater traction in Social Sciences and Computer Science than in Engineering.

Taken together, [Figures 3](#fig3)–[6](#fig6) illustrate complementary dimensions of the reviewed studies, enabling a concise synthesis of research design preferences, geographic concentration, authorship patterns, and disciplinary emphasis within AI-driven personalized learning research.

## 4 Discussion on research topics in artificial intelligence and personalized learning

Across the reviewed studies, notable methodological variation was observed in research design, outcome measures, and implementation contexts, contributing to differences in reported effectiveness of AI-driven personalized learning. While several quantitative and mixed-methods studies reported positive learning gains, others highlighted contextual constraints, ethical risks, and inconsistent outcomes, underscoring the need to interpret findings in light of methodological quality and study context ([Mustafa et al., 2024](#ref27); [Zhang et al., 2024](#ref45); [Castro et al., 2024](#ref8)) as reflected in the descriptive patterns summarized in [Figures 3](#fig3)–[6](#fig6).

### 4.1 Personalized learning pathways and student engagement

Across the literature, one of the most prominent themes is the capacity of AI to construct personalized learning experiences tailored to students’ needs. Research highlights how AI facilitates real-time feedback, adjusts content flexibly, and encourages both creativity and motivation ([Abrar et al., 2025](#ref1); [Baba et al., 2024](#ref6); [Baltezarević and Baltezarević, 2024](#ref7); [Rajesh et al., 2024](#ref31); [Tapalova and Zhiyenbayeva, 2022](#ref41)). Reported outcomes include increased vocabulary retention, more accurate syntax, a deeper understanding of complex concepts, and heightened student engagement ([Aravind et al., 2025](#ref5)). Furthermore, AI-driven gamification and continuous evaluation enhance learner-focused approaches, resulting in better academic outcomes than traditional instruction. Overall, the findings imply that AI-enabled personalization benefits both academic performance and students’ motivation to take an active role in their learning journey.

### 4.2 Predictive analytics, assessment, and early intervention

A second major theme concerns the role of AI in predictive analytics and customized assessment. Evidence suggests that AI systems are capable of projecting students’ academic progress, grouping them according to risk levels, and enabling early intervention strategies ([Huang et al., 2025](#ref16); [Shoaib et al., 2024](#ref36)). Innovations such as AI-supported oral assessments ([Dong et al., 2024](#ref13)) and simulation-based instruction ([Rajesh et al., 2024](#ref31)) illustrate how these tools improve both assessment validity and inclusivity. Predictive algorithms and recommendation models not only enhance accuracy and engagement but also equip educators to develop targeted strategies that reduce dropout rates and support struggling learners. Collectively, these findings signal a movement toward data-driven and preventative approaches in education.

### 4.3 Teacher training, digital competence, and pedagogical innovation

Another theme concerns the need for teacher readiness and digital competence to ensure AI is integrated effectively into teaching and learning. According to [Castro et al. (2024)](#ref8), [Moslemi and Arani (2024)](#ref25), and [Wang et al. (2024)](#ref43) both pre-service and practicing teachers require adequate preparation to adopt AI for personalized education. Similarly, [Rajesh et al. (2024)](#ref31) and [Junruang and Kanjug (2025)](#ref19) argue that teachers must scaffold computational and active learning approaches to cultivate problem-solving and creativity among students. The evidence indicates that although AI tools provide substantial opportunities, their effectiveness relies heavily on pedagogical alignment. Consequently, teacher agency and digital literacy emerge as pivotal factors in realizing equitable and impactful AI integration.

These findings further indicate that effective AI integration depends on making pedagogical assumptions explicit, particularly by aligning system design features with constructivist and social learning principles that guide how learners actively engage, collaborate and regulate their learning processes ([Castro et al., 2024](#ref8); [Wang et al., 2024](#ref43)).

### 4.4 Ethical, governance, and data privacy concerns

The prominent cross-cutting theme identified is the importance of ethics and governance in AI adoption. Concerns frequently cited include data privacy, bias in algorithms, unequal access, and questions of epistemic trust ([Al-Omari et al., 2025](#ref4); [Castro et al., 2024](#ref8); [Mulaudzi and Hamilton, 2025](#ref26); [Sunmboye et al., 2025](#ref38)). Learners have voiced apprehension about inaccuracies and the misuse of AI-generated information, particularly within fields such as medicine, where errors carry serious consequences ([Shen et al., 2025](#ref35)). Scholars propose measures such as robust governance structures, transparency protocols, and regular audits to manage these risks. In addition, educators favor hybrid models that integrate AI with conventional methods instead of fully replacing them ([Agatova and Latipova, 2025](#ref2)). Overall, these studies emphasize that ethical and transparent AI practices are essential for equitable and trustworthy educational outcomes.

### 4.5 Generative AI and education 5.0 transformation

Within this review, Education 5.0 is operationalized as a learner-centered educational paradigm that integrates advanced digital technologies, including generative AI, with humanistic values, inclusivity, and societal relevance, emphasizing personalized learning, ethical governance, and human-AI collaboration rather than automation alone ([Castro et al., 2024](#ref8); [Ronksley-Pavia et al., 2025](#ref33); [Guettala et al., 2024](#ref15)). The role of generative AI is widely recognized as pivotal in advancing education toward the vision of Education 5.0. Research points to its ability to deliver adaptive instruction, personalize content creation, and cater to learners with unique needs ([Guettala et al., 2024](#ref15); [Ronksley-Pavia et al., 2025](#ref33); [Shen et al., 2025](#ref35)). In professional disciplines such as nursing and medicine, prompt engineering and AI tutoring have proven effective in strengthening both analytical and clinical skills ([Tao and Pan, 2025](#ref40)). Similarly, its integration into inclusive pedagogies supports twice-exceptional and neurodivergent learners through tailored, strengths-based approaches ([Ronksley-Pavia et al., 2025](#ref33)). These insights underline that generative AI represents more than a supportive tool; it is a catalyst transforming educational inclusivity and learning design.
