") [Versions Notes](https://www.mdpi.com/2078-2489/16/10/895/notes) ## Abstract In the era of artificial intelligence, higher education is embracing new opportunities for pedagogical innovation. This study investigates the impact of integrating AI into college English teaching, focusing on its role in enhancing students’ critical thinking and academic engagement. A controlled experiment compared AI-assisted instruction with traditional teaching, revealing that AI-supported learning improved overall English proficiency, especially in writing skills and among lower- and intermediate-level learners. Behavioral analysis showed that the quality of AI interaction—such as meaningful feedback adoption and autonomous revision—was more influential than mere usage frequency. Student feedback further suggested that AI-enhanced teaching stimulated motivation and self-efficacy while also raising concerns about potential overreliance and shallow engagement. These findings highlight both the promise and the limitations of AI in language education, underscoring the importance of teacher facilitation and thoughtful design of human–AI interaction to support deep and sustainable learning. Keywords: [artificial intelligence](https://www.mdpi.com/search?q=artificial+intelligence); [college english](https://www.mdpi.com/search?q=college+english); [instructional control experiment](https://www.mdpi.com/search?q=instructional+control+experiment); [learning behavior analysis](https://www.mdpi.com/search?q=learning+behavior+analysis); [teaching effectiveness evaluation](https://www.mdpi.com/search?q=teaching+effectiveness+evaluation) ## 1. Introduction In the second decade of the 21st century, artificial intelligence (AI) technologies entered a phase of large-scale practical application. In particular, the rapid breakthroughs of Generative Artificial Intelligence (Generative AI) in natural language processing and human–computer interaction have profoundly disrupted traditional educational models and created opportunities for deep structural transformation [[1](https://www.mdpi.com/2078-2489/16/10/895#B1-information-16-00895),[2](https://www.mdpi.com/2078-2489/16/10/895#B2-information-16-00895),[3](https://www.mdpi.com/2078-2489/16/10/895#B3-information-16-00895)]. With the increasingly widespread use of large language models such as ChatGPT and DeepSeek, the educational field is undergoing a paradigm shift from “tool-assisted” instruction to “intelligent symbiosis” [[4](https://www.mdpi.com/2078-2489/16/10/895#B4-information-16-00895),[5](https://www.mdpi.com/2078-2489/16/10/895#B5-information-16-00895),[6](https://www.mdpi.com/2078-2489/16/10/895#B6-information-16-00895)]. In the context of college English teaching, Generative AI not only provides language generation and knowledge supplementation but also reshapes learners’ cognitive pathways and linguistic thinking through contextual simulation, interactive guidance, and personalized feedback. Traditional college English instruction in China [[7](https://www.mdpi.com/2078-2489/16/10/895#B7-information-16-00895)] is typically teacher-centered, focusing on systematic input of vocabulary, grammar, and reading, often assessed through standardized tests. While this approach ensures efficiency in knowledge transmission, its limitations have become increasingly evident. Students have limited opportunities for language output, which restricts the development of communicative competence. In addition, the highly homogenized nature of instruction fails to meet the diverse needs and cognitive rhythms of learners [[8](https://www.mdpi.com/2078-2489/16/10/895#B8-information-16-00895)]. In an era where emerging engineering disciplines, intercultural communication, and global competence are gaining prominence, the educational role of college English urgently needs to shift—from knowledge transmission to competency building and from uniform instruction to intelligent adaptation. The rise of Generative AI [[9](https://www.mdpi.com/2078-2489/16/10/895#B9-information-16-00895)] offers a timely opportunity for deep reform in college English instruction. First, AI systems possess robust language generation and adaptive response capabilities that can simulate authentic communicative contexts through task-based learning, enhancing the realism and immersion of language practice [[10](https://www.mdpi.com/2078-2489/16/10/895#B10-information-16-00895)]. Second, AI systems can record and analyze learners’ behavioral data, enabling dynamic learner profiling and real-time interventions, thereby shifting pedagogical decision-making from experience-driven to data-driven processes. Third, AI systems are inherently scalable, connecting individual learners with global resources and thus providing boundless learning spaces and diversified language input [[11](https://www.mdpi.com/2078-2489/16/10/895#B11-information-16-00895)]. In this context, the integration of Generative AI into college English education has become a key breakthrough point for the intelligent transformation of higher education. International debates and risk landscape: While the affordances of Generative AI are promising, international scholarship has highlighted critical risks that must be integrated into any conceptual framework. Cognitive offloading may lead to the accumulation of “cognitive debt,” reducing opportunities for retrieval practice and executive control [[12](https://www.mdpi.com/2078-2489/16/10/895#B12-information-16-00895)]. Overconfidence in AI outputs correlates with reduced critical-thinking effort and miscalibrated metacognition [[13](https://www.mdpi.com/2078-2489/16/10/895#B13-information-16-00895)]. Scholars have also described a “cognitive paradox” in which efficiency gains may paradoxically suppress deep processing if not properly scaffolded [[14](https://www.mdpi.com/2078-2489/16/10/895#B14-information-16-00895)]. Policy-level guidance (UNESCO, 2023/2025; OECD, 2025) further cautions that current AI systems lack metacognition and self-evaluation, underscoring the importance of human oversight and ethical guardrails [[15](https://www.mdpi.com/2078-2489/16/10/895#B15-information-16-00895)]. Taken together, these debates indicate that the same affordances (simulation, adaptive feedback, and scalability) must be weighed against corresponding risks (cognitive offloading, shallow engagement, and dependency). Any research design should, therefore, explicitly model these tensions. From generic “challenges” to testable tensions: To address these debates, we reconceptualize the challenges of AI-supported instruction as a set of testable tensions: (1) quality of AI interaction versus frequency of use; (2) teacher facilitation versus tool autonomy; and (3) feedback adoption versus cognitive passivity. These tensions motivate our central hypotheses: (a) the quality of AI-mediated interactions will be a stronger predictor of learning gains than frequency of use; and (b) learners who maintain calibrated self-monitoring will benefit more than those who rely uncritically on AI assistance. These hypotheses align with international debates while operationalizing the conceptual framework for empirical testing. Existing studies have primarily focused on the technological functions of AI and the construction of teaching platforms, with limited attention to how AI operates within authentic classrooms and reshapes learner behavior. Empirical comparative studies targeting language courses remain scarce. Therefore, this study seeks to bridge domestic implementation with international debates by explicitly modeling both the affordances and risks of AI in college English instruction. Specifically, we take the integration of a Generative AI platform into authentic classrooms as our starting point, aiming to connect instructional design with learner behavior and outcomes and to provide both empirical evidence and theoretical insight for AI-driven educational innovation. Globally, AI in education has undergone extensive exploration. From early Intelligent Tutoring Systems [[16](https://www.mdpi.com/2078-2489/16/10/895#B16-information-16-00895)] to learning analytics platforms grounded in cognitive science, AI has evolved from a teaching assistant to an active participant in learning processes [[17](https://www.mdpi.com/2078-2489/16/10/895#B17-information-16-00895)]. In recent years, the rise of Generative AI has transformed the nature of linguistic interaction in educational contexts. Hwang et al. [[18](https://www.mdpi.com/2078-2489/16/10/895#B18-information-16-00895)] found that ChatGPT provides high-quality feedback, language modeling, and text reconstruction in English writing instruction, significantly enhancing learners’ expressive abilities and writing confidence. Lin [[19](https://www.mdpi.com/2078-2489/16/10/895#B19-information-16-00895)] further emphasized that Generative AI enables “collaborative writing,” helping learners internalize linguistic structures and discourse logic through interaction. In China, the development of smart education systems has accelerated in recent years. Research has primarily focused on platform construction (e.g., “smart classrooms” [[20](https://www.mdpi.com/2078-2489/16/10/895#B20-information-16-00895)]), instructional model design, and AI-based assessment systems. For example, Zheng et al. [[21](https://www.mdpi.com/2078-2489/16/10/895#B21-information-16-00895)] proposed a “teacher-led + AI-supported” collaborative teaching framework for college English, using knowledge graphs and corpora to facilitate precision instruction. However, domestic research still faces several limitations: (1) much of the work remains at the level of technological application, lacking classroom-based behavioral data; (2) most studies rely on theoretical construction or survey interviews, with limited empirical control studies and behavioral modeling; and (3) classroom integration of Generative AI remains exploratory, with little systematic research on instructional models, outcome evaluation, or learner behavior mechanisms. This study addresses these gaps by centering on the integration of Generative AI into college English instruction. We implement a six-week comparative experiment with three core components: (1) Construction of a hybrid human–AI collaborative teaching model. (2) Integration of multi-source data for instructional evaluation. (3) Development of a replicable intelligent instructional pathway model. The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. [Section 2](https://www.mdpi.com/2078-2489/16/10/895#sec2-information-16-00895) elaborates on the research motivation. [Section 3](https://www.mdpi.com/2078-2489/16/10/895#sec3-information-16-00895) develops the theoretical and conceptual framework for integrating Generative AI into college English instruction, drawing upon constructivist learning theory and international critiques of AI affordances. [Section 4](https://www.mdpi.com/2078-2489/16/10/895#sec4-information-16-00895) details the experimental design and methodology. [Section 5](https://www.mdpi.com/2078-2489/16/10/895#sec5-information-16-00895) presents the results across instructional effectiveness, behavioral patterns, and subjective learner feedback. [Section 6](https://www.mdpi.com/2078-2489/16/10/895#sec6-information-16-00895) explores pedagogical implications and reflects on limitations. [Section 7](https://www.mdpi.com/2078-2489/16/10/895#sec7-information-16-00895) concludes with recommendations for future work. ## 2. Motivation Driven by both theoretical inquiry and practical demands, this study conducts an in-depth investigation into the implementation effects and operational mechanisms of Generative-AI-assisted instruction in college English classrooms. Specifically, the research addresses three core questions: Is Generative-AI-assisted instruction more effective than traditional teaching in terms of learning outcomes? This question is examined through a quasi-experimental pretest–posttest design comparing students’ scores across Generative-AI-assisted and traditional instruction groups, with the aim of evaluating the relative impact of the two teaching models on language learning effectiveness. What are the behavioral characteristics of students in a Generative-AI-supported learning environment? Drawing on platform log data (e.g., question frequency, interaction content, and dwell time) and behavioral pathway modeling techniques, the study analyzes the structure and evolution of student learning behaviors within AI-enhanced instructional settings. What are the instructional advantages and potential challenges of Generative-AI-assisted teaching? By synthesizing data from student questionnaires, teacher interviews, and classroom observations, the study systematically identifies the benefits of Generative AI instruction in areas such as motivation, engagement, and competence development while also highlighting practical challenges such as cognitive dependency and uneven interaction quality. Based on these research questions, the study aims to construct a task-driven, human–AI collaborative instructional model for college English teaching. A comprehensive evaluation is conducted across three key dimensions: instructional effectiveness, learning behavior, and teaching satisfaction. On this basis, the study proposes optimized instructional strategies and practical recommendations for Generative-AI-supported pedagogy while acknowledging current limitations (e.g., short intervention duration and single-institution sampling) and pointing to directions for future refinement. ## 3. Constructing a Logical Framework for AI–Education Integration With the accelerated integration of artificial intelligence into education, constructing a scientific and systematic framework for AI–education fusion has become both a theoretical prerequisite and a practical guide for promoting the intelligent transformation of higher education curricula. This study proposes a logical pathway for the deep integration of Generative AI and college English instruction from three interrelated dimensions: educational philosophy, technological mechanisms, and instructional processes. Rather than serving as a purely descriptive taxonomy, the framework is explicitly anchored in established theories of constructivism, distributed cognition, scaffolding, and human–AI collaboration. As shown in [Figure 1](https://www.mdpi.com/2078-2489/16/10/895#fig_body_display_information-16-00895-f001), the framework provides the theoretical foundation for both the empirical design and the pedagogical transformation of AI-assisted teaching. ![Image 7: Information 16 00895 g001](https://www.mdpi.com/information/information-16-00895/article_deploy/html/images/information-16-00895-g001-550.jpg)[](https://www.mdpi.com/2078-2489/16/10/895#fig_body_display_information-16-00895-f001) **Figure 1.** The framework for AI–education fusion. ### 3.1. Theoretical Foundation: From Constructivism to Distributed Cognition The integration of AI and education can be understood as a process of co-constructing cognition between human learners and artificial intelligence systems. Its theoretical basis can be traced to Constructivist Learning Theory, which emphasizes that knowledge should be actively constructed by learners through interaction with their environment rather than passively received from teachers [[22](https://www.mdpi.com/2078-2489/16/10/895#B22-information-16-00895)]. From this perspective, Generative AI is not merely a “language generator” but functions as an “interactive learner” with semantic understanding capabilities. It dynamically responds to student input by providing feedback, corrections, and guidance, thereby creating a socially constructed learning environment [[23](https://www.mdpi.com/2078-2489/16/10/895#B23-information-16-00895)]. Beyond constructivism, the framework also draws on scaffolding theory and distributed cognition. Scaffolding theory emphasizes temporary supports provided by more capable others—teachers, peers, or intelligent systems—that enable learners to accomplish tasks beyond their current ability. Generative AI can serve as a dynamic scaffold, gradually reducing assistance as learners gain independence. Distributed cognition theory [[24](https://www.mdpi.com/2078-2489/16/10/895#B24-information-16-00895)] highlights that cognitive processes are not confined to the individual mind but are distributed across people, artifacts, and environments. From this perspective, AI platforms become part of the learner’s cognitive ecology, extending working memory, externalizing representations, and enabling collaborative problem solving. These theoretical lenses ensure that the proposed framework is not merely descriptive but also conceptually grounded. Building on these perspectives, the emerging Smart Learning Theory [[25](https://www.mdpi.com/2078-2489/16/10/895#B25-information-16-00895)] further emphasizes that data sensing, contextual adaptation, and system intelligence are key elements for achieving a ubiquitous–personalized–optimized learning cycle [[26](https://www.mdpi.com/2078-2489/16/10/895#B26-information-16-00895)]. The language generation and interactive functions of Generative AI make it an ideal vehicle for implementing a hybrid of constructivist, scaffolding, and adaptive learning paradigms. As such, it represents a critical component of cognition-driven instruction in the future. ### 3.2. Integration Mechanism: A Three-Tiered Human–AI Collaboration Model This study proposes a Three-Tiered Logical Mechanism Model for integrating Generative AI into college English instruction, explicitly informed by human–AI collaboration frameworks [[27](https://www.mdpi.com/2078-2489/16/10/895#B27-information-16-00895)]. It comprises three layers: Tool Layer: At this level, AI functions as an external instructional aid, performing tasks such as language generation, grammar checking, and text expansion. Its role is comparable to that of an enhanced dictionary and corpus-like resource, primarily aimed at improving students’ expression efficiency and assisting teachers in lesson preparation. Process Layer: AI begins to contribute to classroom task design and interaction management. Through task-driven learning, students engage with AI in contextual dialogues, role simulations, and text continuation, forming a cyclical feedback loop of “practice–revision–repractice.” Meanwhile, teachers use behavioral data to dynamically adjust instructional strategies. In this layer, human–AI collaboration theory positions AI as a “collaborative partner” rather than a passive tool, enabling distributed task management and adaptive co-regulation of learning. Cognitive Layer: AI progresses from a language supporter to a facilitator of cognitive development. Through interactive revision, semantic comparison, and logical reasoning, students form a cognitive chain of “reflective questioning → language reconstruction → expressive transfer.” Here, AI serves simultaneously as a cognitive scaffold and an externalized representation system, fostering the development of critical thinking, metacognition, and multimodal communicative competence. ### 3.3. Application Pathway: From Tool Insertion to Paradigm Evolution Based on the structural characteristics of college English tasks and the functional attributes of Generative AI, this study further proposes a Four-Stage Evolutionary Pathway for AI-integrated instruction, as shown in [Table 1](https://www.mdpi.com/2078-2489/16/10/895#table_body_display_information-16-00895-t001). Rather than a simple linear progression, these stages are mapped onto constructivist learning cycles (input → construction → reflection → transfer), thereby clarifying the theoretical grounding of each step. **Table 1.** Four-stage evolutionary pathway of AI integration in college English instruction. ![Image 8](https://pub.mdpi-res.com/img/table.png)[](https://www.mdpi.com/2078-2489/16/10/895#table_body_display_information-16-00895-t001) By explicitly linking each stage to constructivist and distributed cognition principles, the pathway emphasizes not only practical progression but also theoretical justification, thereby transforming the framework from a descriptive taxonomy into a theory-informed model. ## 4. Research Design and Methodology Before examining the impact of Generative Artificial Intelligence (Generative AI) on college English teaching outcomes and learning behaviors, it is essential to establish a systematic and rigorous research design framework. This study adopts a mixed-methods design to address three core questions: whether AI-based instruction is effective, why it is effective, and for whom it is most effective. Specifically, this chapter outlines the implementation pathway across three components: experimental design, data sources, and analytical methods. It includes participant selection, instructional strategies, multi-source data collection, and the construction of multi-level statistical models. By integrating quantitative performance evaluation, behavioral modeling, and subjective pathway analysis, this study not only verifies the effectiveness of AI-assisted instruction but also explores its underlying mechanisms and key influencing factors. The overall research logic and methodological process are illustrated in [Figure 2](https://www.mdpi.com/2078-2489/16/10/895#fig_body_display_information-16-00895-f002). ![Image 9: Information 16 00895 g002](https://www.mdpi.com/information/information-16-00895/article_deploy/html/images/information-16-00895-g002-550.jpg)[](https://www.mdpi.com/2078-2489/16/10/895#fig_body_display_information-16-00895-f002) **Figure 2.** Research design and methodological framework of the study. ### 4.1. Experimental Design and Data Sources This study systematically evaluates the instructional effectiveness and behavioral impacts of Generative AI in college English classrooms. A non-equivalent pretest–posttest control group design, a type of quasi-experimental method, was employed to approximate causal inference in authentic classroom settings while maintaining control over instructional variables. Participants were 2023 undergraduates (non-English majors) from a key provincial university in China, spanning science and engineering, economics and management, and humanities. A total of 150 students were randomly assigned to the experimental or control group ($n = 75$ each) using stratified randomization based on gender and English pretest scores to enhance baseline comparability. Baseline equivalence was checked via independent-samples tests and standardized mean differences; no material imbalance was detected, and balance diagnostics are reported in [Table 2](https://www.mdpi.com/2078-2489/16/10/895#table_body_display_information-16-00895-t002). The experiment lasted six weeks, with two sessions per week (two class hours per session; 24 h total). Course content, instructional objectives, and assessment structures were held constant across groups to minimize extraneous interference. All procedures received approval from the institutional ethics committee and written informed consent was obtained from all participants. **Table 2.** Baseline equivalence diagnostics between experimental and control groups. ![Image 10](https://pub.mdpi-res.com/img/table.png)[](https://www.mdpi.com/2078-2489/16/10/895#table_body_display_information-16-00895-t002) In terms of instructional strategy, the experimental group utilized a dual-platform Generative AI environment (ChatGPT 4.0 and DeepSeek 3.2, accessed via institutional accounts with official web interfaces; no third-party plug-ins or external model add-ons were used) embedded with task-driven modules (e.g., AI-guided writing and discourse extension), real-time feedback mechanisms, and behavioral tracking systems. AI implementation details: Students engaged in a structured “draft → feedback → revision” loop: (i) submit a task-specific prompt and generate a first draft; (ii) request and document AI feedback on content, organization, and language form; (iii) revise the draft and append a short reflection note explaining which recommendations were adopted or rejected and why. To support consistent use, a prompt template library was provided (e.g., genre-audience-purpose specification, style constraints, and content boundaries). Instructors received a short instructional facilitation protocol (pre-brief, live monitoring dashboard, and post-task debrief) to standardize coaching across classes. Responsible-use guidelines were communicated prior to the experiment: AI could be used for idea generation, language polishing, and structural suggestions; full outsourcing of assignments to AI was prohibited. Students were required to attach AI interaction summaries (prompt snapshots or paraphrased logs) to submissions, ensuring auditability and accountability. In contrast, the control group followed a traditional teacher-centered approach combining PPT lectures and paper-based exercises, with feedback provided via manual grading and periodic assessments. All classes were delivered by instructors with comparable qualifications to minimize style bias. To monitor treatment fidelity, periodic classroom observations were conducted using a standardized checklist, with adherence notes summarized in [Table 3](https://www.mdpi.com/2078-2489/16/10/895#table_body_display_information-16-00895-t003). **Table 3.** Classroom observation checklist and fidelity adherence summary. ![Image 11](https://pub.mdpi-res.com/img/table.png)[](https://www.mdpi.com/2078-2489/16/10/895#table_body_display_information-16-00895-t003) To comprehensively assess the effects of AI instruction, a multi-source data collection system was implemented, integrating quantitative and qualitative, process and outcome, and objective and subjective dimensions. In terms of data collection, this study employed a multi-source design to comprehensively capture the outcomes and mechanisms of Generative-AI-assisted instruction. First, cognitive outcome data were obtained from pretest and posttest English proficiency assessments, which covered reading comprehension, language usage, and writing. All items and rubrics were developed by a professional test design team, aligned with CEFR B1–B2 levels and the Chinese Standards of English Language Ability (CSE Levels 4–5). Inter-rater calibration was conducted prior to scoring, and the final scores were averaged from three independent raters under double-blind conditions to ensure reliability and validity. Second, AI platform log data (experimental group only) recorded the full process of student–AI interaction. Key indicators included weekly interaction frequency, average output length per task, revision count, and feedback adoption rate (defined as the proportion of actionable AI suggestions incorporated into the revised draft). Additional measures included weekly usage time, self-revision rate (operationalized by edit-distance between drafts), pathway completeness index (whether the full cycle “draft–feedback–revision–resubmission” was completed), BLEU score, and a lexico–syntactic features index (type–token ratio and clause complexity). All raw logs were anonymized before export, with personal identifiers such as names, IDs, and IPs removed. Data were stored on secure institutional servers with restricted access and daily backups in accordance with university data protection policies. Third, in-class behavioral observations were conducted using structured observation sheets to record behaviors such as question frequency, participation, and engagement. Observers rotated across sessions and cross-reviewed notes. Observation prompts were aligned with the facilitation protocol (e.g., evidence of feedback uptake and quality of revision planning) to ensure consistency between intended pedagogy and enacted practices. Fourth, motivation and perception surveys were administered in Weeks 3 and 6 using a 5-point Likert-scale instrument titled “Generative AI Learning Experience and Motivation,” measuring five dimensions. Scale items, factor structure, and reliability coefficients are reported in [Table 4](https://www.mdpi.com/2078-2489/16/10/895#table_body_display_information-16-00895-t004). Administration procedures were identical across groups to minimize measurement bias. **Table 4.** Scale items, factor structure, and reliability coefficients. ![Image 12](https://pub.mdpi-res.com/img/table.png)[](https://www.mdpi.com/2078-2489/16/10/895#table_body_display_information-16-00895-t004) Finally, teacher and student interviews were conducted in a semi-structured format with instructors and a purposive subsample of students, selected via maximum-variation sampling across behavioral clusters. The interview protocol covered four domains: (i) usefulness and limitations of AI feedback; (ii) changes in writing process and self-regulation; (iii) experiences with the draft–feedback–revision cycle; and (iv) responsible AI use and academic integrity. Interviews lasted approximately 20–30 min, were audio-recorded with participant consent, and were subsequently transcribed. **Academic integrity and ethical safeguards.** Students signed an acceptable-use statement clarifying permitted and prohibited AI uses, and instructors verified consistency across drafts, AI summaries, and final submissions. Any concerns were addressed through formative feedback rather than punitive measures during the study. Informed consent was obtained prior to participation, and privacy safeguards for log data were strictly enforced, in line with COPE/APA ethical guidelines. This five-dimensional framework enabled a comprehensive assessment of both cognitive outcomes and behavioral–cognitive mechanisms under AI-supported learning while ensuring transparency regarding platform implementation, task design, interview protocols, and ethical compliance. ### 4.2. Analysis Methods To evaluate the effectiveness of Generative-AI-assisted instruction, this study employed a mixed-methods approach that integrated statistical inference, behavioral modeling, and structural modeling. #### 4.2.1. Quantitative Assessment of Instructional Effectiveness The English proficiency test was developed and standardized by a professional language testing team. Items were aligned with the Common European Framework of Reference for Languages (CEFR, B1–B2 levels) and the Chinese Standards of English Language Ability (CSE Levels 4–5), ensuring both international and national comparability. Reliability and validity were confirmed through a pilot test ($n = 80$), yielding Cronbach’s $\alpha = 0.89$ for the overall scale and inter-rater reliability of $r = 0.92$ for writing tasks. Individual learning gains were computed as $$ Gain_{i} = Post_{i} - Pre_{i} $$ (1) Group differences were first examined with an independent samples t-test: $$ t = \frac{\left(\bar{X}\right)_{AI} - \left(\bar{X}\right)_{TR}}{\sqrt{\frac{s_{AI}^{2}}{n_{AI}} + \frac{s_{TR}^{2}}{n_{TR}}}} $$ (2) If normality assumptions were violated, the non-parametric Mann–Whitney U test was applied. To control for baseline bias, ANCOVA was performed: $$ Y_{i j} = \mu + \tau_{i} + \beta X_{i j} + \epsilon_{i j} $$ (3) where $Y_{i j}$ denotes the posttest score, $\tau_{i}$ the treatment effect (AI vs. control), and $X_{i j}$ the pretest covariate. #### 4.2.2. Modeling of Learning Behavior Data The following behavioral indicators were defined, as shown in [Table 5](https://www.mdpi.com/2078-2489/16/10/895#table_body_display_information-16-00895-t005). **Table 5.** Behavioral feature definitions. ![Image 13](https://pub.mdpi-res.com/img/table.png)[](https://www.mdpi.com/2078-2489/16/10/895#table_body_display_information-16-00895-t005) The use of BLEU scores and linguistic feature indices was theoretically justified as they provide objective measures of revision quality and language complexity. This hybrid metric complements human ratings, reducing subjectivity and capturing both surface-level edits and deeper structural improvements in student writing. To model learning processes, a Markov Chain was employed with the following state set: S: Start Task; Q: Ask Question; F: Receive Feedback; R: Revise and Retry; C: Submit Task. The transition probabilities were defined by the matrix: $$ P = \left[\right. p_{i j} \left]\right. $$ (4) Finally, to examine how behaviors predicted learning outcomes, a multiple regression model was constructed: $$ Gain_{i} = \beta_{0} + \beta_{1} F_{1} + \beta_{2} F_{2} + \beta_{3} F_{3} + \beta_{4} F_{4} + \beta_{5} F_{5} + \beta_{6} F_{6} + \epsilon $$ (5) Significance tests of $\beta_{i}$ coefficients identified the most influential behavioral predictors of student learning gains. #### 4.2.3. Subjective Perception and Structural Modeling The motivation and perception survey was adapted from validated instruments in second-language acquisition research. Items measured five dimensions: AI usefulness, ease of use, engagement, self-efficacy, and satisfaction. args.summary:
This is an open-access research article published in the journal **Information** (MDPI, 2025, Volume 16, Issue 10, Article 895) titled "Comparing AI-Assisted and Traditional Teaching in College English: Pedagogical Benefits and Learning Behaviors," authored by Changyi Li (Harbin University of Science and Technology) and Jiang Long (Jilin University). The study investigates the impact of integrating Generative AI (ChatGPT 4.0 and DeepSeek 3.2) into college English instruction in China.

**Methodology:** A six-week quasi-experiment was conducted with 150 non-English major undergraduates randomly assigned to an AI-assisted group and a traditional teaching group (75 each). The AI group used a structured "draft → feedback → revision" loop with prompt templates and responsible-use guidelines. Data sources included pretest/posttest English proficiency assessments, AI platform log data, classroom observations, motivation surveys, and semi-structured interviews.

**Key Findings:**
1. AI-assisted instruction improved overall English proficiency, particularly in writing skills and among lower- and intermediate-level learners.
2. The quality of AI interaction (meaningful feedback adoption and autonomous revision) was more influential than mere usage frequency.
3. AI-enhanced teaching stimulated motivation and self-efficacy but raised concerns about potential overreliance and shallow engagement.
4. Behavioral analysis using Markov chain modeling identified distinct student interaction patterns.

**Theoretical Framework:** The study proposes a Three-Tiered Human–AI Collaboration Model (Tool Layer, Process Layer, Cognitive Layer) and a Four-Stage Evolutionary Pathway, grounded in constructivist learning theory, scaffolding theory, and distributed cognition theory.

**Conclusions:** The findings highlight both the promise and limitations of AI in language education, emphasizing the importance of teacher facilitation and thoughtful human–AI interaction design to support deep and sustainable learning.

## CURRICULUM, INSTRUCTION, AND PEDAGOGY article

# Evaluating the impact of an AI-integrated learning platform on student performance: a quasi-experimental study

Madina Yermaganbetova 1

Arailym Ashimbekova 1\*

Dinara Kaibassova 2\*

Riza Akhitova 3

Elmira Dyussembina 4

1. Department of Computer Science, L.N. Gumilyov Eurasian National University, Astana, Kazakhstan

2. School of Software Engineering, Astana IT University, Astana, Kazakhstan

3. School of Creative Industries, Astana IT University, Astana, Kazakhstan

4. Department of Automation and Information Technologies, Shakarim University, Semey, Kazakhstan

Article metrics

## Abstract

The integration of artificial intelligence (AI) into higher education has intensified interest in adaptive learning environments that support personalized instruction and self-regulated learning. However, empirical evidence regarding the pedagogical effectiveness of fully integrated AI-based platforms in practice-oriented, skill-intensive university courses remains limited. This study examines the effect of an AI-integrated learning platform on academic performance, cognitive engagement, and self-regulated learning, employing a quasi-experimental design. In this study, cognitive engagement is conceptualized as a key behavioral and cognitive manifestation of self-regulated learning within an AI-supported instructional environment. 120 undergraduate students enrolled in a university-level 3D modeling course participated in the study, forming an experimental group (*n* = 62) and a control group (*n* = 58). The intervention lasted 8 weeks. Data were collected through pre- and post-tests, rubric-based practical assignments, final course grades, and a mixed-format satisfaction questionnaire. Quantitative analyses included paired *t*-tests, Bowker’s test of symmetry, effect size calculations, and confidence intervals. Qualitative data were examined using thematic analysis. The results reveal statistically significant improvements in post-test performance and practical task proficiency in the experimental group (*p* < 0.05), accompanied by higher levels of perceived autonomy, adaptive support, and self-regulated learning. The findings suggest that a fully integrated AI learning ecosystem can function as a metacognitive scaffold, enhancing strategic learning behaviors and cognitive engagement in applied digital skills education. The study contributes empirical evidence to ongoing discussions on the pedagogical role of AI in higher education and outlines implications for instructional design and future research.

## 1 Introduction

In recent years, the integration of artificial intelligence (AI) into higher education has become a central topic of academic discourse, driven by the rapid expansion of adaptive learning systems, automated assessment tools, and intelligent tutoring technologies. These tools have been shown to personalize learning trajectories, enhance instructional efficiency, and improve student engagement by providing real-time analytics and individualized feedback (Alotaibi, 2024; Mojolou et al., 2024). AI-powered systems can process large volumes of educational data to predict learning difficulties, optimize task sequencing, and adapt the complexity of instructional materials to students’ cognitive needs. Such mechanisms align with key principles of self-regulated learning theory, which emphasizes goal-setting, progress monitoring, and metacognitive control (Peng et al., 2019). At the same time, recent research also highlights several challenges associated with AI implementation in education. Some studies report potential negative consequences, such as a decline in educational quality when AI tools are misused or poorly integrated (Zawacki-Richter et al., 2019). A review of over 150 publications reveals that many AI tools prioritize technical capabilities over pedagogical or ethical considerations, leaving questions of instructional value underexplored (Holmes et al., 2019). Systems such as AIIA illustrate that while AI tools can enhance personalization, they must be implemented within a clear pedagogical framework to avoid unintended consequences (Sajja et al., 2024). Despite growing interest in AI-enhanced learning, a clear research gap remains: relatively few empirical studies have evaluated the pedagogical effectiveness of AI-integrated platforms in practical, skill-oriented university courses, particularly in fields that require hands-on digital competencies, such as 3D modeling. Existing studies often focus on technical aspects rather than measurable learning outcomes, student autonomy, or user experience in real academic environments. Within this theoretical context, cognitive engagement is conceptualized as a key behavioral and cognitive manifestation of self-regulated learning, reflecting learners’ active involvement in planning, monitoring, and regulating their learning processes in AI-supported instructional environments.

Recent years have witnessed an unprecedented expansion of research on AI-integrated learning environments, particularly with the emergence of generative AI and large language models in higher education. Recent studies highlight the growing role of AI in supporting personalized learning, automated feedback, and adaptive instructional design in university contexts (Kasneci et al., 2023; Zawacki-Richter et al., 2024; Crompton and Burke, 2023). These developments indicate a shift toward fully integrated AI-supported learning ecosystems rather than isolated digital tools.

The AI-integrated platform examined in this study was designed as a supplementary instructional module intended to support instructors, provide students with opportunities for self-paced practice, enhance time-management flexibility, and foster autonomous learning through adaptive feedback and personalized task sequencing. These design principles guided both the implementation of the platform and the evaluation framework adopted in the study.

### 1.1 Research problem, research questions, and hypotheses

Despite growing interest in AI-enhanced learning environments, current research lacks empirical evidence on the pedagogical effectiveness of AI-integrated platforms in practice-oriented courses. Existing studies predominantly focus on technical capabilities, while the impact of adaptive algorithms, automated assessment, and intelligent feedback on measurable academic performance, student motivation, and self-regulated learning remains insufficiently explored. This gap is especially evident in disciplines requiring complex cognitive processing and hands-on mastery, such as 3D modeling.

Research problem: There is insufficient empirical understanding of how AI-integrated educational platforms influence academic performance, motivation, and self-regulated learning in practice-oriented higher education courses. Therefore, an AI-integrated educational platform was developed to enhance students’ academic performance, learning motivation, engagement, and self-regulation skills.

Research objective: to evaluate the effectiveness of an AI-integrated educational platform in improving academic performance, motivation, engagement, and self-regulated learning skills in a university-level 3D modeling course.

Research questions (RQs):

*RQ1*: Does the use of an AI-integrated educational platform significantly improve students’ academic performance compared to traditional instruction?

*RQ2*: How does the platform affect students’ motivation and engagement in learning?

*RQ3*: Does the platform support the development of self-regulated learning skills (goal-setting, progress monitoring, metacognition)?

*RQ4*: How do students perceive the usability, adaptive, and overall learning experience of the AI-enhanced platform?

Research hypotheses (H):

*H1*: Students using the AI-integrated platform will demonstrate significantly higher post-test performance than students in the control group.

*H2*: The AI-integrated platform will have a positive effect on students’ learning motivation and engagement.

*H3*: The platform will enhance students’ self-regulated learning skills.

*H4*: Students in the experimental group will report higher satisfaction and more positive perceptions of usability and adaptivity.

These research questions and hypotheses provide a clear analytical direction and are aligned with the theoretical foundation discussed in the Introduction, namely, self-regulated learning theory, with cognitive engagement considered as its central operational component.

The educational activity examined in this study is grounded in self-regulated learning (SRL) theory, which provides the primary conceptual framework for the platform’s design. The platform emphasizes goal-setting, progress monitoring, adaptive feedback, and metacognitive reflection, which are operationalized through AI-driven recommendations and learning analytics. Within this framework, cognitive engagement is treated as an observable indicator of learners’ self-regulatory processes in practice-oriented digital learning tasks. Self-regulated learning provides the conceptual foundation for the platform’s emphasis on goal-setting, progress monitoring, adaptive feedback, and metacognitive reflection, which are operationalized through AI-driven recommendations and learning analytics. Cognitive load theory informs the adaptive sequencing and personalization of learning tasks, ensuring that instructional complexity is dynamically aligned with learners’ prior knowledge to support effective cognitive processing. Activity-based learning principles guide the integration of practice-oriented tasks that require active engagement and the application of knowledge in authentic digital contexts.

## 2 Literature review

### 2.1 AI-integrated learning platforms: global developments

Several large-scale adaptive learning platforms have been introduced worldwide. Smart Sparrow and Squirrel AI provide adaptive feedback and analytics dashboards; however, research indicates that the effectiveness of adaptive learning technologies is strongly influenced by factors such as teacher preparation, instructional design quality, and implementation facilitators (Simon and Zeng, 2024). These studies demonstrate that AI platforms can support differentiated instruction but require alignment with pedagogical models and learner characteristics.

Recent studies also highlight the pedagogical effectiveness of intelligent educational systems in higher education. AI-powered learning platforms have been shown to enhance student engagement, personalize learning paths, and support instructors in monitoring academic progress, thereby improving learning outcomes (Ashimbekova and Bondarenko, 2025). These studies underscore the potential of AI-driven educational technologies to improve teaching and learning processes while aligning academic content with professional requirements.

Recent research also emphasizes the transformative impact of generative AI and large language models on higher education. Studies published in 2023–2025 demonstrate that AI-supported learning platforms can enhance personalization, automate feedback processes, and support data-driven

instructional decision-making (Kasneci et al., 2023; Zawacki-Richter et al., 2019). These findings suggest that AI-integrated ecosystems are increasingly viewed as comprehensive pedagogical infrastructures rather than supplementary technological tools.

### 2.2 AI for assessment and feedback

Recent studies explore the use of large language models (LLMs) such as GPT-4 and related models for evaluating open-ended student responses and programming tasks; research has also highlighted concerns about consistency, bias, and explainability in these automated assessments (Jauhiainen and Garagorry Guerra, 2024). Automated essay scoring systems, including those based on large language models, have been shown in multiple studies to achieve high agreement with human raters, but their effectiveness varies across contexts and highlights ongoing challenges such as consistency, bias, and the need for domain-specific adaptation (Emirtekin, 2025). This study investigates the impact of AI in educational settings on academic outcomes, including changes in grades, engagement, and personalized learning assessments as measurable results of AI implementation in learning environments (Ateeq et al., 2024). Overall, existing systems effectively reduce grading workload but vary in precision, transparency, and contextual understanding.

### 2.3 AI-enhanced personalized learning and student behavior modeling

Research indicates that adaptive algorithms can enhance motivation and engagement when aligned with cognitive and motivational learning principles; adaptive learning platform features have been shown to influence self-regulated learning and engagement, supporting overall educational quality (Ouyang, 2025). The research also considers how artificial intelligence can be used to transform assessment methods and personalize learning paths through adaptive learning, with implications for student performance and the analysis of large student data sets, emphasizing enhancements in academic outcomes via AI-driven adaptive systems (Arwa, 2025). However, most studies emphasize technical performance rather than pedagogical value, leaving questions about student agency, metacognition, and long-term learning habits underexplored. Emerging literature further highlights the pedagogical potential of generative AI systems for supporting metacognition, adaptive feedback, and student engagement in higher education contexts. However, empirical research examining the implementation of fully integrated AI learning environments in practice-oriented courses remains limited, particularly in applied digital skills education.

### 2.4 Gaps identified in previous research

A critical examination of the existing literature reveals several unresolved issues that limit the generalizability and practical relevance of current research on AI-driven educational platforms. First, empirical evidence from practice-oriented and skill-based courses remains limited. Most studies concentrate on domains such as mathematics, language learning, and other theoretical subjects, while creative and applied fields-including 3D modeling, engineering design, and other hands-on disciplines- are still underrepresented. This imbalance constrains our understanding of how adaptive and AI-based systems function in learning contexts that require procedural knowledge, creativity, and iterative problem-solving.

In addition, the influence of AI-supported personalization on self-regulated learning remains insufficiently explored. Although personalization is frequently cited as a key advantage of adaptive learning technologies, relatively few studies systematically examine its effects on learners’ metacognitive processes, such as planning, monitoring, and self-evaluation. As a result, it remains unclear whether adaptive systems genuinely foster self-regulation or merely optimize short-term performance outcomes. Methodological limitations further compound these gaps. Moreover, mixed-methods approaches that combine objective performance data with qualitative insights into user experience remain relatively rare, limiting a comprehensive understanding of learning processes and outcomes.

Finally, current research often provides insufficient attention to students’ subjective perceptions and experiences. While system efficiency and performance gains are frequently emphasized, learners’ perceptions of usability, adaptivity, motivation, and trust in AI-driven systems receive comparatively less scrutiny. Contexts where learners and instructors need to understand and trust adaptive interventions. Although the body of research on AI in education is rapidly expanding, many studies remain conceptual or exploratory, focusing on perceptions, technical capabilities, or ethical considerations. Empirical evaluations of fully integrated AI learning ecosystems embedded within authentic university courses are still relatively scarce. Addressing this gap is therefore essential for advancing evidence-based implementation of AI in higher education.

### 2.5 Contribution of the present study

This study addresses the identified gaps by: conducting a controlled experiment (experimental vs. control group) in a practice-oriented 3D modeling course; evaluating both quantitative outcomes and qualitative perceptions of adaptivity, usability, and motivation; analyzing the effects of AI-generated feedback, automated assessment, and personalized recommendations on self-regulation; applying a mixed-methods design, strengthening methodological rigor; situating the results within established theoretical frameworks, primarily self-regulated learning theory, while using cognitive load theory as a complementary lens to interpret how adaptive learning design supports cognitive engagement and effective task performance.. Thus, this work contributes new empirical evidence on the pedagogical value of AI-integrated educational platforms in applied digital disciplines.

## 3 Research design and methods

The study employed a mixed-methods pretest-posttest design with experimental and control groups. This approach enabled the integration of quantitative measures of learning outcomes with qualitative insights into students’ perceptions of the AI-integrated learning environment (Peng et al., 2019).

The experimental component of the study analyzes the organizational features, implementation methodology, and key outcomes of piloting the AI-integrated educational platform, which was embedded into the academic process at Astana IT University. The platform is designed to support the development of a personalized, adaptive digital learning environment that enhances instruction quality and improves student performance. Employing multiple AI models with differentiated roles allowed the study to align specific model capabilities with distinct pedagogical and assessment objectives, thereby strengthening methodological rigor.

### 3.1 Educational platform overview

The developed platform is designed to host digital courses, interactive assignments, assessment materials, and tools for monitoring learning outcomes. Its structure includes two access levels: one for teachers and one for students. Each has differentiated permissions to ensure flexibility in managing the learning process and protecting personal data.

Once authorized, students gain access to courses, individual assignments, performance records, and a personalized dashboard displaying their academic progress and learning recommendations.

Teachers have access to tools for course creation and editing, uploading content, monitoring student activity, and using automated assessment and monitoring statistical reports.

A key feature of the platform is the integration of artificial intelligence algorithms to:

automatically analyze assignment results;

recommend adaptive courses based on learner profiles;

generate recommendations for further learning.

### 3.2 Integration of artificial intelligence functionality

The educational platform incorporates several modules based on artificial intelligence (AI), each designed to address specific problems within the learning process.

The platform leverages state-of-the-art language models, including GPT-3.5, GPT-4, and Gemini, to generate content and assess learner responses. Each model is configured with specific parameters, including temperature, max token length, and response diversity, to balance creativity and accuracy. The use of two different large language models was a deliberate design choice aimed at functional specialization rather than redundancy. ChatGPT (GPT-3.5/GPT-4) was selected for tasks requiring natural language generation, formative feedback, and interactive question generation due to its strengths in dialogic interaction and pedagogical explainability. In contrast, the Gemini model was employed for rubric-based assessment and final grading, where consistency, structured output, and alignment with predefined evaluation criteria were prioritized. This separation of functions reduced the risk of systematic bias associated with relying on a single model and increased the robustness of the AI-supported instructional workflow.

Assessments are automatically generated based on predefined learning objectives and evaluation criteria, ensuring consistency and alignment with educational standards. Protecting learner privacy is a core principle. Personal data is safeguarded through encryption and secure access protocols. The subsequent section examines the integration of artificial intelligence across the platform’s various functional modules.

#### 3.2.1 Automatic question generation

To improve the effectiveness of formative assessment and active knowledge retrieval, the platform employs the large-scale GPT-3.5 language model (OpenAI). ChatGPT was selected for this functionality due to its demonstrated effectiveness in generating pedagogically coherent open-ended questions and providing adaptive, context-sensitive feedback in educational settings. The model processes lecture materials and automatically generates randomized open-ended questions, except for the option to rewind lecture content. Learners answer the given question in the designated window; if the answer is incorrect, the model allows multiple attempts and, in some cases, provides hints to guide them toward the correct answer. This functionality prevents mechanical memorization of fixed test banks and promotes a deeper understanding of the learning material ([Figure 2](#F2)).

### 3.3 Experimental setup

As part of the research, a comprehensive set of activities was conducted, including an analysis of relevant national and international academic and methodological literature, testing, monitoring, registering academic performance, and conducting both pilot and pedagogical experiments.

A quasi-experimental, non-randomized pretest-posttest control-group design was used. The sample included 120 second-year undergraduate students enrolled in the “3D modeling” course within the “Media Technologies” program at the School of Creative Industries of Astana IT University. Inclusion criteria:

enrolment in the program;

no prior professional experience with Blender (exclusion: portfolio or professional courses). Sampling followed a cluster allocation based on existing academic cohorts.

Two intact cohorts were assigned as follows: one control group (*n* = 58) and one experimental group (*n* = 62). Although randomization was not feasible, the groups were equivalent in terms of gender and age. and pretest performance. The experimental group completed the “3D Modeling” course using the AI-integrated educational platform, while the control group followed the standard curriculum, including:

lecture-based instruction;

supervised practical exercises;

a final LMS-based test.

The control group did not complete additional applied or scenario-based assignments, but total classroom time was identical across groups.

To ensure methodological consistency, both groups used the same lecture materials, course structure, and baseline practical tasks. The only difference was the AI-enhanced adaptive practice available exclusively to the experimental group.

The pedagogical experiment lasted for one academic module (8 weeks). Each week consisted of a 90-min lecture and a 120-min practical session. Students in the experimental group additionally completed 2–3 AI-enhanced tasks per week.

#### 3.3.1 Measurement instructions

A comprehensive set of measurement instruments was employed to assess the effectiveness of the instructional intervention, including:

pre-and post-tests comprising 40 items designed to measure competencies in navigation, modeling, texturing, animation, and rendering in Blender;

practical assignments evaluated using standardized analytic rubrics;

the final course grade represents an aggregate indicator of students’ theoretical and practical performance.

To ensure fairness and comparability between groups, the final performance evaluation followed identical rubric-based criteria. AI-assisted grading served as a decision-support mechanism, while final validation of results remained under instructor supervision.

#### 3.3.2 Validity and reliability

To ensure the psychometric soundness of the instruments, the following procedures were undertaken:

content validation of test items by two domain experts specializing in 3D modeling;

departmental approval of the rubrics used to evaluate practical assignments, ensuring standardized assessment criteria.

assessment of internal consistency of the questionnaire, which demonstrated high reliability (Cronbach’s α = 0.87).

To maintain comparability between groups, the final performance evaluation was conducted using the same rubric-based criteria. AI-assisted grading served as a structured support tool, while final validation and approval of grades remained under instructor supervision.

#### 3.3.3 Statistical analysis

The statistical analysis involved:

assumption checks for parametric testing, including the Shapiro—Wilk test for normality and Levene’s test for homogeneity of variances;

paired *t*-tests to compare pre- and post-test performance;

Bowker’s test of symmetry to examine transitions between categorical proficiency levels.

computation of effect sizes (Cohen’s *d*) and 95% confidence intervals;

qualitative analysis of open-ended questionnaire responses using thematic analysis (Braun & Clarke).

### 3.4 Data collection and evaluation

The purpose of the testing phase was to assess students’ initial knowledge in the “3D Modeling” course, with a particular focus on their proficiency with Blender. A diagnostic pre-test consisting of 40 questions was administered, covering core thematic areas: navigation and interface, 3D object modeling, texturing, basic animation, and rendering processes.

To interpret the results, a performance scale was used to categorize the level of skill proficiency:

High level (75–100%)—demonstrates a strong understanding of Blender’s principles, confident use of both basic and advanced features, and practical experience in 3D modeling.

Above average (60–74%)—indicates confident use of core tools, though some difficulties may arise with advanced or non-standard tasks.

Average level (40–59%) — reflects familiarity with the interface and basic functions, but lacks consistent and structured use of the software at a more advanced level.

Low level (20–39%)—suggests a limited understanding of the software’s functionality and difficulty performing even standard operations.

Very low level (0–19%)—points to minimal or no prior knowledge or experience with Blender.

The analysis of the initial test results provided insight into the students’ baseline preparedness, forming a reference point for comparison with post-course performance indicators following completion of the adaptive AI-integrated program.

### 3.5 Data analysis

The results of pre- and post-course testing, assignment completion, final course grades, and student feedback collected via questionnaires were analyzed to assess the effectiveness of the implemented AI-integrated educational platform. The combination of rubric-based automated assessment and instructor verification ensured reliability and transparency of the evaluation process.

Quantitative analysis enabled comparison of the academic progress of students in the experimental group, who used the platform, with that of students in the control group, who followed a traditional instructional format.

Qualitative data from both open- and closed-ended questionnaire responses were analyzed to understand student satisfaction, level of their motivation, perceived ease of use of the platform’s interface, accessibility of materials, and perceptions of the personalization of the learning process.

This comprehensive approach to data collection and interpretation enabled a well-rounded evaluation of the platform’s impact on the learning process.

## 4 Results

The effectiveness of the personalized and adaptive 3D modeling course delivered via the AI-integrated educational platform was assessed through a detailed analysis of students’ academic performance and engagement in the experimental group, compared with those following a traditional learning format.

This section presents a detailed analysis of empirical data, including results from pre- and post-course testing, success rates in completing assignments, frequency and activity of student interactions with the platform, and final assessments. Particular emphasis is placed on the qualitative feedback from student surveys, which provided insights into their perceptions of the platform’s functionality, user interface, and overall satisfaction with the digital learning tool.

### 4.1 Pre- and post-course test results comparison

The test results were processed using Python, enabling automated data analysis and visualization. To more accurately reflect students’ mastery of content, scores were grouped into five performance categories: high, above average, average, low, and very low. This approach allowed for the distribution of results within each group.

Analysis of the academic performance indicates a significant positive impact of the personalized adaptive learning platform on students’ academic performance. The initial results revealed that the majority of students had low (33.87%) or very low (40.32%) levels of knowledge, and no students were classified as having a high level of proficiency.

### 4.4 Analysis of students’ subjective evaluations regarding the usability and impact of the platform on the learning process

To obtain qualitative feedback from students in the experimental group, a survey was conducted to assess key aspects of the educational platform developed using artificial intelligence technologies. All 62 students from the experimental group participated in the survey.

The evaluation criteria included the following:

Usability and navigation of the interface

Clarity and accessibility of learning materials

Effectiveness, adaptability to students’ level of knowledge

Quality of automated feedback and assignment assessment

Impact on learning motivation

Overall satisfaction with the learning process

The analysis of student responses revealed the following results:

Interface usability: 87% of students reported that the platform’s interface was intuitive and easy to navigate. Most participants positively noted the logical structure of the sections and the ease of access to course materials.

Content accessibility: 82% of respondents indicated that the 3D modeling course materials were clearly presented, included illustrative examples, and were accompanied by helpful video instructions.

Platform adaptability: 76% of students stated that the system’s ability to adjust to their individual knowledge levels, through task customization, recommendations, and hints, contributed to a deeper understanding of complex topics.

AI-based feedback: 79% of students emphasized the usefulness of automated comments and prompt grading of assignments, which enabled them to address mistakes promptly.

Motivation: 74% of students reported that the platform encouraged more active engagement in the learning process compared to traditional methods.

Overall satisfaction: 85% of students expressed satisfaction with the platform’s learning experience and would recommend it for other courses.

A comparison of objective learning outcomes and students’ subjective evaluations reveals a consistent pattern. The observed improvement in post-course performance and knowledge distribution corresponds with students’ positive perceptions of platform usability, adaptive support, and feedback quality. In particular, students who reported higher levels of perceived adaptivity and timely feedback also demonstrated notable progress in practical and theoretical performance. Although the study

did not aim to establish direct causal correlations between individual survey responses and performance scores, the convergence of objective and subjective indicators strengthens the overall interpretation of the platform’s effectiveness.

Thus, the AI-integrated platform demonstrated its effectiveness not only in improving academic outcomes but also in enhancing the quality of educational interaction, personalizing the learning experience, and increasing student motivation.

## 5 Findings and discussion

This study examined the effectiveness of an AI-integrated educational platform in terms of students’ academic performance, learning motivation and engagement, development of self-regulated learning skills, and learners’ perceptions of usability and overall learning experience.

In response to RQ1, the findings indicate that the use of the AI-integrated educational platform had a statistically significant positive effect on students’ academic performance compared to traditional instruction. Students in the experimental group achieved higher post-test scores than those in the control group. These findings are consistent with previous research indicating that

AI-supported adaptive learning environments can improve academic performance through personalized feedback and task sequencing (Peng et al., 2019; Ashimbekova and Bondarenko, 2025). Similar positive effects of AI-integrated platforms on measurable learning outcomes have been reported in recent higher education studies (Ateeq et al., 2024), supporting the interpretation that adaptive AI tools can enhance both instructional efficiency and student achievement. This improvement can be attributed to adaptive task sequencing, automated feedback, and personalized learning support provided by the platform’s AI components. From the perspective of cognitive load theory, these adaptive mechanisms may have reduced extraneous cognitive load by aligning task complexity with learners’ prior knowledge. This likely enabled students to devote greater cognitive resources to meaningful learning activities, thereby supporting improved performance. Therefore, Hypothesis H1 is supported.

Regarding RQ2, the results demonstrate that the platform positively influenced students’ learning motivation and engagement. Interactive learning activities, timely AI-generated feedback, and personalized recommendations encouraged more active participation and sustained interest in the learning process. This result aligns with studies demonstrating that AI-driven adaptive learning systems can strengthen student engagement and motivation when feedback is timely and personalized (Ouyang, 2025). Previous research has shown that intelligent tutoring and adaptive recommendation systems can foster sustained learner involvement by supporting autonomy and self-monitoring, which is consistent with the patterns observed in the present study. These findings confirm that Hypothesis H2 is supported.

With respect to RQ3, the study shows that the AI-enhanced platform supported the development of self-regulated learning skills, including goal-setting, progress monitoring, and metacognitive awareness. Learning analytics dashboards and continuous performance feedback enabled students to better reflect on their learning progress and adjust their learning strategies accordingly. The observed development of self-regulated learning skills corresponds with existing literature emphasizing the role of adaptive learning analytics and AI-generated feedback in supporting metacognitive processes (Ouyang, 2025; Peng et al., 2019). These studies highlight that personalized feedback and progress monitoring tools can function as scaffolds for planning, monitoring, and self-evaluation, reinforcing the interpretation of the current findings. Thus, Hypothesis H3 is confirmed.

In answer to RQ4, students in the experimental group reported generally positive perceptions of the platform’s usability, adaptivity, and overall learning experience. The platform was perceived as user-friendly, adaptive to individual learning needs, and supportive of effective learning. Positive student perceptions of usability and adaptive support are also consistent with prior research on AI-enhanced learning environments, which indicates that perceived usefulness and ease of use are critical factors influencing acceptance of educational technologies (Holmes et al., 2019; Simon and Zeng, 2024). The present findings support these conclusions by demonstrating that students not only benefited academically but also reported a favorable learning experience. These results indicate higher student satisfaction with the AI-integrated platform, thereby supporting Hypothesis H4.

Overall, the findings suggest that AI-integrated educational platforms have the potential to support learning outcomes, student engagement, and self-regulated learning when implemented as supplementary instructional tools within an existing course structure. These results correspond with a growing body of research demonstrating the pedagogical effectiveness of AI-supported adaptive learning environments in higher education (Holmes et al., 2019; Ateeq et al., 2024). Previous studies have shown that personalized feedback, learning analytics, and intelligent tutoring systems can significantly improve student performance, engagement, and self- regulated learning, which aligns with the patterns observed in the present study.

Key features included automatic question generation during lectures, AI-powered assessment of practical assignments, personalized learning recommendations, and adaptive task sequencing.

**Key Findings:**
- **Academic Performance (RQ1):** The experimental group showed statistically significant improvements in post-test performance compared to the control group (p < 0.05). Bowker's test of symmetry confirmed significant differences in knowledge level distributions before and after training.
- **Knowledge Distribution:** Post-test results showed the experimental group had 8.06% high-level, 27.42% above average, 38.71% average, 19.35% low, and 6.45% very low proficiency, compared to the control group's 3.45% high, 12.07% above average, 24.14% average, 43.10% low, and 17.24% very low.
- **Motivation and Engagement (RQ2):** 74% of students reported increased motivation and active engagement with the platform.
- **Self-Regulated Learning (RQ3):** The platform supported development of goal-setting, progress monitoring, and metacognitive awareness through learning analytics dashboards and continuous feedback.
- **Student Perceptions (RQ4):** 87% found the interface intuitive, 82% rated content accessibility positively, 76% appreciated adaptability, 79% valued AI feedback, and 85% expressed overall satisfaction.

The study concludes that AI-integrated platforms can function as metacognitive scaffolds, enhancing strategic learning behaviors and cognitive engagement in applied digital skills education. The authors frame their findings within self-regulated learning theory and cognitive load theory.

# Artificial intelligence vs traditional teaching methods on student performance: Effectiveness and challenges

Dawulung Judith Onyefu (1) ,   Dakogol Evelyn Toedat (1)

(1)  Department of French, Federal University of Education Pankshin Plateau State, Nigeria

Artificial intelligence, Education, Traditional teaching methods, Student performance, Adaptive learning, Personalized learning

* [Abstract](#abstract)
* [Authors](#authors)
* [How to Cite](#citation)
* [License](#licensing)

## Abstract

The increasing need to achieve better results in students, individualized learning, and scalable educational services has made the argument of artificial intelligence in education versus conventional teaching techniques more intense. Even though traditional teacher-centered training is necessary to ensure social interaction, emotional support, and contextual understanding, AI-based learning, generative AI, intelligent tutoring systems, and adaptive learning platforms have reshaped the educational environment. The proposed PRISMA-based literature review research problem is to examine the comparative efficacy and limitations of artificial intelligence versus conventional teaching procedures on student performance in higher education, K-12 education, and STEM education settings. The systematic review analyzed academic achievement, student engagement, learning analytics, automated assessment, educational chatbots, personalized feedback, and technology-enhanced learning. Recent trends related to ChatGPT, multimodal learning, predictive analytics, AI-based assessment, and human-centered AI were used as the focus of the selection process. The results show that AI-based learning systems tend to be more effective in enhancing academic motivation, self-regulated learning, adaptive learning, and personalized learning results than conventional teaching strategies. The conventional approaches to teaching are more efficient in promoting collaborative learning, emotional intelligence, critical thinking, and teacher-student relationship. Other significant issues associated with ethical AI, algorithmic bias, data privacy, academic integrity, teacher preparedness, and the digital divide are also noted in the review. Blended learning, Education 4.0, and Education 5.0 models are expected to be integrated into future educational models with the aim of maximizing the performance and equity of students and education, by applying AI-facilitated personalization in combination with human pedagogical skills.
