## [](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12179260)Abstract

### Supplementary Information

The online version contains supplementary material available at 10.1038/s41598-025-97652-6.

**Subject terms:**Psychology, Mathematics and computing, Learning and memory, Applied physics, Physics

## [](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12179260)Introduction

With their human-like conversational style and knowledge drawn from extremely large data sets, generative artificial intelligence (GAI) chatbots have inspired visions of expert tutors available on demand through every smartphone[1](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12179260#CR1). The President of the United States, at the time of this investigation in 2023, pledged to “shape AI’s potential to transform education by creating resources to support educators deploying AI-enabled educational tools, such as personalized tutoring in schools.”[1](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12179260#CR1) Despite this recent excitement, previous studies show mixed results on the effectiveness of learning, even with the most advanced AI models[2](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12179260#CR2),[3](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12179260#CR3). While these models can answer technical questions, their unguided use lets students complete assignments without engaging in critical thinking. After all, AI chatbots are generally designed to be helpful, not to promote learning. They are not trained to follow pedagogical best practices (e.g., facilitating active learning, managing cognitive load[4](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12179260#CR4),[1](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12179260#Fn1) and promoting a growth mindset).[2](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12179260#Fn2) Another well-known flaw of AI tutors is their uncanny confidence when giving an incorrect answer or when marking a correct reply as incorrect[5](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12179260#CR5).[3](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12179260#Fn3) As reported here, a carefully designed AI tutoring system, using the best current GAI technology and deployed appropriately, can not only overcome these challenges but also address significant known pedagogical challenges in an accessible way that can offer world-class education to any community or learning environment with an internet connection.

Although passive lectures are among the least effective modes of instruction, they remain in wide use in science, technology, engineering, and mathematics(STEM) courses[6](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12179260#CR6)–[8](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12179260#CR8). Passive lectures have several long-known issues: 1. They move too quickly for some students and too slowly for others because the teacher controls the pace of instruction; 2. Students do not receive personalized feedback to their questions as they arise; and 3. They fail to maintain consistent student engagement. Active learning pedagogies,[4](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12179260#Fn4) such as peer instruction, small-group activities, or a flipped classroom structure, have demonstrated significant improvements over passive lectures[9](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12179260#CR9)–[14](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12179260#CR14). However, any approach that involves one teacher working with many students will suffer, at least in part, from the same three problems that plague passive lectures.

Working with an expert personal tutor is generally regarded as the most efficient form of education[15](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12179260#CR15). A tutor can guide the student while providing personalized feedback and answering questions as they arise. Expert tutors will adapt their approach to a student’s individual ability, pace, and specific needs. They offer a more focused and efficient learning experience, managing the student’s cognitive load. In addition, personalized instruction can foster a growth mindset, which has been shown to promote students’ persistence in the face of difficulties[16](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12179260#CR16),[17](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12179260#CR17). While the advantages of personalized instruction are clear, this model of education cannot scale to meet the needs of a large number of students[15](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12179260#CR15).

What if an AI tutor could mimic the learning experience one would get from an expert (human) tutor? It could address the unique needs of each individual through timely feedback while adopting what is known from the science of how students learn best. This is the focus of our work. Through a design that involves targeted, content-rich prompt engineering, we developed an online tutor that uses GAI and best practices from pedagogy and educational psychology to promote learning in undergraduate science education. We conducted a randomized controlled experiment in a large undergraduate physics course (_N_ = 194) at Harvard University, with a student population broadly representative of those found across a range of institutions, to measure the difference between 1) how much students learn and 2) students’ perceptions of the learning experience when identical material is presented through an AI tutor compared with an active learning classroom.

## [](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12179260)Results

In this study, students were divided into two groups, each experiencing two lessons, each with distinct teaching methodologies, in consecutive weeks. During, the first week, group 1 engaged with an AI-supported lesson at home while group 2 participated in an active learning lesson in class. The conditions were reversed the following week. To establish baseline knowledge, students from both groups completed a pre-test prior to each lesson,focusing on surface tension in the first week and fluid flow in the second. Following each lesson, students completed post-tests to measure content mastery and answered four questions aimed at gauging their learning experience, including engagement, enjoyment, motivation, and growth mindset.

### Learning gains: post-test scores

Learning gains were measured by comparing the post-test scores of the AI group and the in-class active learning group to the pre-test scores of the two groups combined. Students in the AI group exhibited a higher median (M) post-score (M = 4.5, N = 142) compared to those in the in-class active learning group (M = 3.5, N = 174). The median learning gains for students, relative to the pre-test baseline (M = 2.75, N = 316), in the AI-tutored group were over double[5](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12179260#Fn5) those for students in the in-class active learning group. We conducted a two-sample rank-sum (Mann–Whitney) test to compare the distribution of post-scores of the two groups. The analysis revealed a statistically significant difference (z = -5.6, _p_< 10–8). Figure[1](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12179260#Fig1) shows mean aggregate results (weeks 1 and 2 combined)[6](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12179260#Fn6) of the learning gains for the group taught with in-class active learning compared to the group taught with the AI tutor.Fig. 1Comparison of learning gains: A comparison of mean post-test performance between students taught with the in-class active learning and students taught with the AI tutor. Dotted line represents students’ mean baseline knowledge before the lesson (i.e., the pre-test scores of both groups). Error bars show one standard error of the mean.

### Time on task

During a 75-minute period, the in-class students spent 15 minutes taking the pre-and post-tests; we assume 60 minutes spent on learning. For students in the AI group, we tracked their use of the AI tutor platform to measure how long they spent on the material, the distribution for which is shown in Fig.[2](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12179260#Fig2). 70% of students in the AI group spent less than 60 minutes on task, while 30% spent more than 60 minutes on task. The median time on task for students in the AI group was 49 minutes.Fig. 2AI tutor time on task: Total time students in the AI group spent interacting with the tutor. Dotted line denotes the length of the in-class active learning lesson (60 minutes).

### Learning gains: linear regression model

We constructed a linear regression model (Table [S1](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12179260#MOESM1)) to better understand how the type of instruction (in-class active learning versus AI tutor) contributed to students’ mastery of the subject matter as measured by their post-test scores. This model includes the following sets of controls. First, we controlled for background measures of physics proficiency: specific content knowledge (pre-test score), broader proficiency in the course material (midterm exam before the study), and prior conceptual understanding of physics (Force Concept Inventory or FCI)[18](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12179260#CR18). Second, we controlled for students’ prior experience with ChatGPT. Third, we controlled for factors inherent to the crossover study design: the class topic (surface tension vs fluids) and the version of the pre/post tests (A vs B). Finally, we controlled for time on task. Given that our experiment is a crossover design in which each student experiences both conditions, this model clusters at the student level.

Table [S1](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12179260#MOESM1) shows that, controlling for all these factors, the students in the AI group performed substantially better on the post-test compared with those in the in-class active learning group. We show this to be a highly significant (_p_< 10–8) result with a large effect size. While the linear regression suggests an effect size of 0.63, this is an underestimation due to ceiling effect; a quantile regression allows us to provide an estimate of the effect size that avoids ceiling effect in the post-test scores. Such an analysis provides an effect size in the range of 0.73 to 1.3 standard deviations.

Notably, there was no correlation between the time on task and students’ post-test scores, despite quite a wide range of times measured for the AI group (Fig.[2](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12179260#Fig2)). As discussed further below, students’ ability to pace themselves with the AI tutor is an advantage of personalized instruction compared with in-class learning.

### AI tutor: students’ perceptions of learning

Figure[3](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12179260#Fig3) shows students’ average level of agreement with four statements about their perceptions of learning, broken down between the two groups (in-class active learning vs. AI tutor). Students rated their level of agreement on a 5-point Likert scale, with 1 representing “strongly disagree” and 5 representing “strongly agree.” In responding to the first statement,relating to engagement, the students in the AI group agreed more strongly (Mean = 4.1, SD = 0.98) than those in the in-class active learning group (Mean = 3.6, SD = 0.92), t(311) = − 4.5, _p_< 0.0001. Likewise, in responding to the second statement,relating to motivation, students in the AI group agreed more strongly (Mean = 3.4, SD = 1.0) than those in the in-class active learning group (Mean = 3.1, SD = 0.86), t(311) = -3.4, _p_< 0.001. Students’ average level of agreement with the remaining two statements (relating enjoyment to growth mindset) were not statistically significantly different between the two groups. To summarize, Fig.[3](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12179260#Fig3) shows that, on average, students in the AI group felt significantly more engaged and more motivated during the AI class session than the students in the in-class active learning group, and the degree to which both groups enjoyed the lesson and reported a growth mindset was comparable.Fig. 3Student perception of learning experiences: Level of agreement to statements about perceptions of learning experiences, comparing students taught by in-class active learning and students taught with the AI tutor. Error bars show 1 standard error of the mean. Asterisks above the bars denote _P_-values generated by dependent t-tests (***_p_< 0.001).

## [](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12179260)Discussion

We have found that when students interact with our AI tutor, at home, on their own, they learn significantly more than when they engage with the same content during an in-class active learning lesson, while spending less time on task. This finding underscores the transformative potential of AI tutors in authentic educational settings. In order to realize this potential for improving STEM outcomes, student-AI interactions must be carefully designed to follow research-based best practices.

The extensive pedagogical literature supports a set of best practices that foster students’ learning, applicable to both human instructors and digital learning platforms. Key practices include (i) facilitating active learning[11](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12179260#CR11),[19](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12179260#CR19), (ii) managing cognitive load[4](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12179260#CR4), (iii) promoting a growth mindset[15](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12179260#CR15),[16](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12179260#CR16), (iv) scaffolding content[20](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12179260#CR20), (v) ensuring accuracy of information and feedback, (vi) delivering such feedback and information in a targeted and timely fashion[21](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12179260#CR21), and (vii) allowing for self-pacing[22](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12179260#CR22). We aimed to design an AI system that conforms to these practices to the fullest extent current technology allows, thus establishing a model for future educational AI applications.

### Designing successful student-AI interactions

A subset of the best practices (i-iii) were incorporated into the AI pedagogy by careful engineering of the AI tutor’s system prompt. We designed the AI tutor with a system prompt with guidelines (Supplementary Material [1](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12179260#MOESM1)) to facilitate active engagement, manage cognitive load, and promote a growth mindset. However, we found that a system prompt could not reliably provide enough structure to scaffold problems with multiple parts (iv), as the AI tutor would occasionally discuss parts out of sequence or that were not immediately relevant. For this reason, the AI platform was designed to guide students sequentially through each part of each problem in the lesson, mirroring the approach taken by the instructor during the in-class active learning (see screenshot of AI tutor platform in Figure S1).

The occurrence of inaccurate “hallucinations” by the current generation of large language models (LLMs) poses a significant challenge for their use in education[23](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12179260#CR23). Thus, we avoided relying solely on GPT-4 to generate solutions for these activities. Given that LLMs proceed by next-token prediction, accuracy in complex math or science problems is enhanced when the system generates, or is provided with, detailed step-by-step solutions[24](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12179260#CR24). Therefore, we enriched our prompts with comprehensive, step-by-step answers, guiding the AI tutor to deliver accurate and high-quality explanations (v) to students. As a result, 83% of students reported that the AI tutor’s explanations were as good as, or better than, those from human instructors in the class.

While best practices (i-v) can be readily adhered to in a classroom setting, the remaining best practices (vi-vii) cannot. Providing timely feedback that targets the specific needs of individual students (vi) and self-pacing (vii) are difficult to achieve and impossible to maintain in a typical classroom. We believe that the increased learning from structured AI tutoring is largely due to its ability to offer personalized feedback on demand—just as one-on-one tutoring from a (human) expert is superior to classroom instruction[15](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12179260#CR15). In addition, interactions with the AI tutor are self-paced (vii), as indicated by the distribution of times in Fig.[2](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12179260#Fig2). Students who need more time to build conceptual understanding or to fill gaps in their knowledge can take that time, instead of having to synchronously follow the pace of the in-class lesson. Students who are familiar with the material or have underlying skills, however, can move through the activities in less time than required for the in-class lesson. We measured the students’ perception of pace during the control condition (in-class active learning) on the days the experiment took place. Notably, the 3.8% of students who found the pace of class “too fast” all spent more than the median time (49 minutes) on the AI lesson, while the 2.2% who found the pace of the in-class lesson “too slow” all spent less than the median time on the AI lesson.

Our results contrast with previous studies that have shown limitations of AI-powered instruction. Krupp et al. (2023) observed limited reflection among students using ChatGPT without guidance[25](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12179260#CR25), while Forero (2023) reported a decline in student performance when AI interactions lacked structure and did not encourage critical thinking[2](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12179260#CR2). These previous approaches did not adhere to the same research-based best practices that informed our approach. Our success suggests that thoughtful implementation of AI-based tutoring could lead to significant improvements to current pedagogy and enhanced learning gains for a broad range of subjects in a format that is accessible in any environment with an internet connection.

### Implications for personal AI tutors in education

How might an AI tutoring system, such as the one we have deployed, integrate into current pedagogical best practices, given its effectiveness in terms of learning gains and student perceptions?

Existing pedagogies often fail to meet students’ individual needs, especially in classrooms where students have a wide range of prior knowledge. Here, we have shown the advantage of using asynchronous AI tutoring as students’ first substantial engagement with challenging material. AI could be used to effectively teach introductory material to students before class, which allows precious class time to be spent developing higher-order skills such as advanced problem solving, project-based learning, and group work. Instructors can assess these skills in person, which avoids the problematic use of AI as a shortcut on assessments such as homework, papers, and projects. As in a “flipped classroom” approach, an AI tutor should not replace in-person teaching—rather, it should be used to bring all students up to a level where they can achieve the maximum benefit from their time in class.

That said, beyond the initial introduction of material, AI tutors like the ones employed here could serve an extremely wide range of purposes, such as assisting with homework, offering study guidance, and providing remedial lessons for underprepared students. Yet our results show that, with today’s GAI technology, pedagogical best practices must be explicitly and carefully built into each such application. As seen in previous studies[2](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12179260#CR2),[25](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12179260#CR25), instructors should avoid using AI in situations where students are likely to use it as a crutch to circumvent critical thinking. We advise against the notion that AI, solely due to its efficacy in enhancing teaching and learning, should entirely supplant in-class instructional methods. Our demonstration illustrates how AI can bolster student learning beyond the confines of the classroom. We advocate harnessing this capability to enable instructors to use in-class sessions for activities and projects that foster advanced cognitive skills such as critical thinking and content synthesis.

### Context, limitations, and future directions

Our AI tutoring approach was applied in a setting where students were engaging substantially with material in particular subject areas for the first time. Our lessons were comprised of activities focused on learning objectives categorized at the understanding, applying, and analyzing levels of Bloom’s Taxonomy[7](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12179260#Fn7)—as were the associated pre- and post-test questions[8](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12179260#Fn8). This stage of learning, characterized by a meaningful degree of information delivery, appears to be particularly well suited for current generative AI tutors. The significant gains and positive affect observed in this study may also depend on several factors: a heterogeneous student population requiring varying instructional paces, integration of high-quality instructional videos,[9](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12179260#Fn9) a large language model capable of closely following complex prompts (e.g.,GPT-4), expert-crafted, question-specific prompts written by instructors experienced with the content, a carefully structured framework designed to scaffold and guide student interactions, and content that lends itself to such a format. While the advantages of the experimental condition are widely generalizable and our findings have broad implications, we do not presume that structured AI tutoring will always outperform in-class active learning in all contexts, for example, those requiring complex synthesis of multiple concepts and higher-order critical thinking.

Compelling directions for future work include exploring other contexts throughout the learning process where AI tutoring may be successfully implemented, such as in homework, recitation, exam studying, pre-class assignments, and laboratory. Valuable follow-up studies could also explicitly examine the details of such combinations throughout an entire course. This would also allow for systematic integration of well-established retention enhancing strategies (e.g., spacing) and could provide insights into other novel phenomena that may arise from prolonged and varied use of AI in education, such as potential impact on collaboration skills. Given that the current AI tutor implementation mirrors well-established in-class active learning pedagogies and generates comparable affect[10](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12179260#Fn10)—with its primary difference (besides personalization) being the medium of delivery, which typically does not impact learning on its own[26](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12179260#CR26)—it is reasonable to expect findings from in-class active learning approaches to carry over. Nonetheless, studies that explicitly replicate known in-class active learning results[27](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12179260#CR27),[28](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12179260#CR28) would be valuable for confirming and refining the details of this transferability. Such research could include explorations of the qualities that constitute effective system prompts and behaviors for AI tutors in various situations (e.g., determining when the AI tutor should openly provide answers versus guiding students to reflect on their own responses).

Generative AI technology is developing very rapidly, allowing for expansion of the capabilities and application of AI tutoring. While accuracy of our AI tutor relied on pre-written answers, as generative AI models improve in scientific reasoning[11](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12179260#Fn11), studies could explore whether such efficacy could be achieved without a provided solution. Also, in our approach, feedback was provided in response to student input, but multimodality would allow AI systems to interpret images (or audio) of a student’s work and more proactively provide feedback. Investigations could explore whether holistic monitoring of a student’s process could provide feedback on issues with thinking that may not be addressed by current pedagogies (in or out of the classroom) in which students typically receive targeted feedback only when they ask a question.

## [](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12179260)Conclusion

We have built an AI-based tutor, engineered with appropriate prompts and scaffolding, that helps students learn significantly more in less time and feel more engaged and motivated compared with in-class active learning. This study confirms the feasibility and effectiveness of AI tutors in educational settings, and suggests design principles to guide future development of these tools. As the prompts described here can be adapted to any subject matter, this approach can provide students, in a wide range of disciplines, on-demand AI-powered support.

These results and principles provide a blueprint for highly effective AI-powered learning frameworks that are engaging and suggest a pathway for widely accessible education on which policymakers, technologists, and educators can collaborate. It also serves as a foundation for a series of explorations of the use of AI in educational settings.

## [](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12179260)Methods

### Study population

The present study took place during the Fall 2023 semester in Physical Sciences 2 (PS2), which is an introductory physics class for the life sciences and is Harvard’s largest physics class (_N_ = 233). Students were randomly assigned to two groups, respecting the constraint that students who regularly worked together in class during peer instruction were placed in the same group in order to maximize the effectiveness of their in-class learning. The demographics of the two groups were comparable (see table [S2A](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12179260#MOESM1)), as were previous measures of their physics background knowledge (see Table [S2B](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12179260#MOESM1)). Note that FCI pretest scores are comparable to those of students at other universities[29](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12179260#CR29). Of the 233 enrolled students, 194 were eligible for inclusion in the study. Eligibility was based on students’ consent, participation in both in-class and AI-tutored instruction, and completion of all pre-tests and post-tests.

We note that the results hold for students with both lower and higher performance abilities than typical students at various institutions, as assessed by the widely recognized FCI test. They also hold for all degrees of scientific attitudes—from non-expert to expert—as gauged by the CLASS survey. Typical pre-instruction FCI scores in educational institutions range from aproximately 30% to 50%[30](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12179260#CR30). In this study, significant subpopulations span this range. The subpopulations of students with pre-instruction FCI scores below 40% and those above 40% both showed significantly better post-test performance with AI tutoring compared to in-class active learning (_p_< 0.001). This improvement was similarly observed in students below and above the 65% benchmark[31](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12179260#CR31) in scientific attitudes on the CLASS.

### Course setting

The course (PS2) meets twice per week for 75 minutes each. The study took place during one of the two meeting of the class during the ninth and tenth weeks of the course. All in-class lessons employed research-based best practices for in-class active learning[32](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12179260#CR32). Each class involves a series of activities that teach physics concepts and problem-solving skills. First the instructor introduces an activity, then students work through the activity in self-selected groups with support and guidance from course staff, and finally the instructor provides targeted feedback to address students’ questions and difficulties.

This instructional approach has proved to be a successful implementation of active learning, and has been shown to offer a significant improvement over passive lectures[33](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12179260#CR33). We note that the authors and instructors represented in the literature demonstrating this in-class active learning approach to be effective and superior to passive instruction overlap with those of the present study. Similar active learning approaches have been shown to increase learning across a wide range of STEM fields[34](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12179260#CR34). Although active learning pedagogies may elicit negative perceptions from students[35](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12179260#CR35), both course instructors, as well as their presentations in the course, achieved student evaluation scores above the departmental and division averages. The active learning pedagogy, optimized over the years to cater to the vast majority of the student population, ensures minimal inactivity by strategically allowing instructors to intervene and adjust the class dynamically based on real-time observations of student engagement and performance[32](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12179260#CR32).

To verify the active learning emphasis of the class, students were asked the following question at the end of the semester: “Compared to the in-class time in other STEM classes you have taken at Harvard, to what extent does the typical PS2 in-class time use active learning strategies (i.e., provide the opportunity to discuss and work on problems in class as opposed to passively listening).” The overwhelming majority of students (89%) indicated that PS2 used more active learning compared to other STEM courses.

### Study design

The present study was approved by the Harvard University IRB (study no. IRB23-0797) and followed a crossover design. The design allowed for control of all aspects of the lessons that were not of interest. The crossover design is summarized in Table [S3](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12179260#MOESM1). For each of two lessons, each student: 1) took a pre-class quiz that established their baseline knowledge of the content for that lesson; 2) engaged in either the active classroom lesson (control condition) or the AI tutor lesson (experimental condition); and 3) took a post-class quiz as a test of learning. The content and worksheet for the control and experimental conditions were identical. The introductions for each activity were also identical, varying only by the format of presentation: live and in-person for the control group and over pre-recorded video for the experimental group.

Given the crossover design, all students experienced both conditions once during the study. The structure of the experimental condition differed from the control condition in that all interactions and feedback were with an AI tutor, rather than with peer-instruction followed by instructor feedback. Students in the experimental condition worked through the handout, asking questions and confirming answers with the AI tutor, called “PS2 Pal.” Students were given equal participation credit for both conditions as well as for the associated pre- and post-test. Students were told that their performance on the pre- and post-tests would not impact their course grade in any way but were told that in order to receive participation credit they needed to demonstrate that they had made an honest effort in completing the tests.

### Additional controls

In addition to using a crossover design we rigorously controlled for potential bias and other unwanted influences. To prevent the specific test questions from influencing the teaching or AI tutor design, the tests were constructed by a separate team member from those involved in designing the AI or teaching the lessons. To prevent details of the lessons or AI prompts from influencing the test of learning, the tests were written based on the learning goals for the lesson and not the specific lesson content.

The lesson topics were chosen such that the result would be optimally generalizable. These topics were independent of each other, had little dependence on previous course content, and required no special knowledge beyond high-school level mathematics. The topics were also chosen to minimize the influence of potential prior knowledge of the material—over 90% of the students reported that they had not studied these topics in depth before this course.

To ensure that the effect was independent of the particular instructor, the two lessons were taught by different instructors (i.e., each of the course’s two co-instructors). We note that the two instructors received student evaluations on their teaching that exceeded the departmental and divisional means.

To make sure that the study design did not impact the effectiveness of in-person instruction during the experiment, students in class learned from the same instructors, with the same student:staff ratio, and in the same peer-instruction groups as they had throughout the course. As mentioned above, keeping students with their peer-instruction groups meant that subjects were randomized at the level of these groups (2–3 students) rather than as individuals. An alternate linear regression model that clusters at the group level (instead of at the level of individual students) has similarly robust results for AI versus in-class instruction (_p_< 0.001) and negligible changes to the point estimates for the effects of each covariate. With this clustered model, however, it is difficult to interpret factors such as time on task, which varies widely at the individual level under the AI-tutored conditions.

While the time commitment for preparation of a single AI-supported lesson was very manageable, there was significant overhead. Preparing system prompts for questions and solutions for a particular lesson was done over a few days. Since activities and solutions were already written for the in-class lesson, this time was spent converting the format of the content to a format appropriate for the AI platform as well as engaging in test conversations for each question and iterating. The most significant time commitment involved in preparing the AI-supported lessons was the development of an AI tutor platform software that took pedagogical best practices into consideration (e.g., structured around individual questions embedded in individual assignments), which took several months.

args.summary:
This is a scientific article published in Scientific Reports (2025) describing a randomized controlled trial (RCT) conducted at Harvard University in Fall 2023, involving 194 undergraduate physics students. The study compared learning outcomes between AI tutoring (using GPT-4 with carefully engineered prompts) and in-class active learning instruction.

Key findings:
- Students using the AI tutor demonstrated significantly higher learning gains (median post-test score 4.5 vs 3.5 for in-class active learning), with gains over double those of the in-class group.
- The result was statistically significant (p < 10⁻⁸) with a large effect size (0.73 to 1.3 standard deviations).
- 70% of AI-tutored students spent less than 60 minutes on task (median 49 minutes), compared to the fixed 60-minute in-class lesson.
- AI-tutored students reported significantly higher engagement and motivation, with comparable enjoyment and growth mindset.

The AI tutor was designed following pedagogical best practices: facilitating active learning, managing cognitive load, promoting growth mindset, scaffolding content, ensuring accuracy (via pre-written step-by-step solutions), providing timely personalized feedback, and allowing self-pacing. The system prompt guided the AI to follow these practices, and the platform structured content sequentially.

The authors note that previous AI education studies showed mixed results because they lacked such structured pedagogical design. They argue that AI tutoring is particularly effective for initial content engagement (understanding/applying/analyzing levels of Bloom's Taxonomy) and should complement rather than replace in-person instruction, which can focus on higher-order skills.

# Khanmigo AI tutoring study finds small maths gains in two-year trial

   [Figen Sekin](https://www.winssolutions.org/author/figensekin/)     [August 18, 2026](https://www.winssolutions.org/2026/08/)   

[Share on Facebook](https://www.facebook.com/sharer/sharer.php?u=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.winssolutions.org%2Fkhanmigo-ai-tutoring-two-year-trial%2F)   [Share on Twitter](https://twitter.com/intent/tweet?text=Khanmigo%20AI%20tutoring%20study%20finds%20small%20maths%20gains%20in%20two-year%20trial&url=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.winssolutions.org%2Fkhanmigo-ai-tutoring-two-year-trial%2F)   [Send via Email](mailto:?subject=Khanmigo%20AI%20tutoring%20study%20finds%20small%20maths%20gains%20in%20two-year%20trial&body=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.winssolutions.org%2Fkhanmigo-ai-tutoring-two-year-trial%2F)

A two-year NBER trial in 18 Tennessee middle schools found Khan Academy’s Khanmigo raised maths scores by 1.26 percentile ranks per term.

![Student watching a video on a laptop, illustrating the Khanmigo AI tutoring study of school maths practice](https://usercontent.one/wp/www.winssolutions.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/khanmigo-ai-tutoring-two-year-trial-1024x682.jpg "Khanmigo AI tutoring study finds small maths gains in two-year trial 1")

Photo by Katerina Holmes on Pexels

Giving middle school students access to Khan Academy’s AI tutor Khanmigo raised maths achievement by 1.26 national percentile ranks per term, according to a two-year randomised trial circulated by the National Bureau of Economic Research on 17 August 2026. The Khanmigo AI tutoring study, [registered as NBER working paper w35620](https://www.nber.org/papers/w35620) and written by Philip Oreopoulos of the University of Toronto with Nina Low of Charles River Associates, ran across 18 middle schools in Hamilton County Schools, Tennessee, over the 2024-25 and 2025-26 school years. The authors report that the gain “resembles those from Khan Academy practice without AI assistance”, and identify student engagement rather than model capability as the binding constraint.

The paper was one of three tutoring trials Oreopoulos and co-authors circulated through NBER on the same day. Together they cover a school-based AI tutor, a one-week classroom experiment testing how AI should be structured, and a two-year home tutoring programme in Toronto. None of the three has been peer reviewed.

* [What the Khanmigo AI tutoring study measured](#What_the_Khanmigo_AI_tutoring_study_measured)
* [Students opened the tutor but rarely talked to it](#Students_opened_the_tutor_but_rarely_talked_to_it)
* [Structure changed what the AI did](#Structure_changed_what_the_AI_did)
* [Take-up rose sharply when the invitation changed](#Take-up_rose_sharply_when_the_invitation_changed)
* [The three trials side by side](#The_three_trials_side_by_side)
* [Background](#Background)

## What the Khanmigo AI tutoring study measured

The Khanmigo trial was a cluster randomised experiment. Within each school the researchers randomly assigned whole grades to the treated or control condition, producing 53 grade-within-school clusters, 28 treated and 25 control. Treated students used Khan Academy with Khanmigo, configured to coach rather than supply answers, during the daily Response to Intervention remedial maths block of 25 to 40 minutes. Control students received the usual remedial instruction, described in the paper as “a mix of teacher-led practice and other math software without AI tutoring”. The analysis covers 6,902 student-term observations across five terms.

The pre-registered pooled effect was 1.26 national percentile ranks per term, with a standard error of 0.60, equal to 0.040 population standard deviations. Effects were larger in the second year, at 0.084 population standard deviations with a standard error of 0.041, against 0.020 in the first year and not distinguishable from zero. The implied effect of a full year of active participation in year two reaches 0.142 standard deviations. Programme cost is put at roughly $15 per student per year.

 

Intention-to-treat effects on maths achievement by study year. The year one estimate is not distinguishable from zero; the year two estimate has a standard error of 0.041.

 

## Students opened the tutor but rarely talked to it

The usage data explains the modest result. Across 563 activated second-year treated students at 16 schools, the researchers logged 25,286 platform-active student-days and 100,017 exercise sessions, of which 56,362 involved a mistake. Ninety-six per cent of students messaged Khanmigo at least once. The median student messaged it on 33 per cent of the days they practised, in 14 per cent of exercise sessions, and in only 17 per cent of the sessions where they made a mistake. Students sent messages in 9,362 of the 56,362 mistake sessions.

What students typed also mattered. The authors classified student messages and found most were not mathematical dialogue.

| Message type | Share of student messages |
| --- | --- |
| Bare answer to the tutor | 39.4% |
| Click on a suggested prompt | 24.2% |
| Low-effort (“idk”, asks for the answer) | 12.6% |
| Mathematical question or step of reasoning | 14.5% |
| Off-task | 9.3% |

Source: Oreopoulos and Low, NBER working paper 35620, August 2026.

 

Only 14.5 per cent of messages students sent to Khanmigo contained a mathematical question or a step of reasoning. Percentages are as classified by the study authors.

 

The authors are explicit about what the design can and cannot show. Because assignment moved every part of the programme at once, the study “cannot isolate the tutor’s marginal contribution”. Tennessee’s TCAP state assessment was registered as a co-primary outcome and its results are not yet in the paper.

The engagement pattern echoes earlier evidence. Winss reported in similar terms on an [AI tutoring study from Stanford that found students barely used the tool](https://www.winssolutions.org/ai-tutoring-access-not-enough-stanford-study/) when left to work independently, and on the practical classroom question of [best practices when using AI in the classroom](https://www.winssolutions.org/15-best-practices-using-ai-in-the-classroom/).

## Structure changed what the AI did

The second paper, [“Making AI Tutoring Productive”](https://www.nber.org/papers/w35621) by Oreopoulos, Michael Liut of the University of Toronto, Alp Sungu of the University of Pennsylvania and Low, tested whether the way AI is embedded matters. More than 6,000 Hamilton County students in grades 6 to 8, across 20 schools and just under 100 teachers, were randomised at login across three dimensions: AI support versus conventional computer-assisted learning, mastery versus non-mastery progression, and one of two maths topics. The practice session ran the week of 23 March 2026 and a delayed assessment followed the week of 30 March.

Mastery progression required a student to watch at least a minute of video and answer three questions in a row correctly before advancing. That rule raised three-correct-in-a-row attainment by 28.7 percentage points and added 4.62 attempted questions, but on its own it did not improve delayed learning. AI on its own also did not. The one positive delayed-test result came from the combination: among mastery students, 40.2 per cent of those with AI answered the practised delayed question correctly against 37.0 per cent of those without, a gap of 3.1 percentage points at p = 0.065. The authors describe the effect as marginal and concentrated on practised material, with no transfer to unpractised items.

Oreopoulos told [The Hechinger Report](https://hechingerreport.org/proof-points-ai-mastery-learning/) on the day of release: “I don’t want to jump out and say we’ve demonstrated that AI is going to be the game changer that we hope it is.” He added that the result “might be the first kind of evidence that shows there’s at least some hints that it has some positive value against no AI at all.”

The paper lists five limitations, including a delayed assessment of only four questions and a single mastery rule that “may be too weak, too gameable, or too disconnected from conceptual understanding”. The authors also state that NUMI, the platform built for the study by University of Toronto computer science students, “was a specific platform, not generic AI access”, and that results should not be generalised to all uses of large language models in education.

## Take-up rose sharply when the invitation changed

The third paper, [“Virtual Tutoring with Computer-Assisted Learning”](https://www.nber.org/papers/w35622) by Oreopoulos, Ruochong Dong and Low, ran with the Toronto District School Board across 2023-24 and 2024-25. Teachers nominated struggling grade 4 to 8 students, whose parents were then randomly offered about an hour a week of one-to-one online tutoring at home from volunteer university students, layered on top of a classroom Khan Academy programme both groups received.

Participation was the obstacle. Only 45.3 per cent of assigned students reached a first session in year one. After the researchers reframed the invitation and simplified enrolment, first-session take-up rose to 82.5 per cent, though weekly attendance stayed below half because students attended intermittently rather than dropping out. The offer raised Khan Academy practice by 10.24 minutes a week. Maths assessment scores rose 0.055 standard deviations, but the 95 per cent confidence interval runs from -0.09 to 0.20, and the design had 80 per cent power only for effects of about 0.21 standard deviations, so the result cannot be distinguished from zero. Report-card marks rose about 0.08 standard deviations at p below 0.10. The authors also flag two baseline imbalances favouring treated students, meaning any bias in the achievement estimate “would run upward”.

## The three trials side by side

| Trial | Setting | Sample | Duration | Headline result |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Khanmigo in remedial maths (w35620) | 18 middle schools, Hamilton County, Tennessee | 6,902 student-term observations, 53 clusters | 2024-25 and 2025-26 | 1.26 percentile ranks per term; 0.062 SD per school year, stacked |
| AI plus mastery practice (w35621) | 20 schools, grades 6-8, Hamilton County | More than 6,000 students | One practice week plus delayed test, March 2026 | 3.1 percentage points on the practised delayed question, p = 0.065 |
| Home virtual tutoring (w35622) | Toronto District School Board, grades 4-8 | About 1,388 nominated students | 2023-24 and 2024-25 | Take-up 45.3% to 82.5%; +10.24 practice minutes a week; 0.055 SD, not distinguishable from zero |

Sources: NBER working papers 35620, 35621 and 35622, all issued August 2026.

## Background

Randomised evidence on generative AI tutoring in schools has been thin relative to the volume of product launches. Khan Academy released Khanmigo in 2023 as a chatbot layer over its practice platform, and positioned it as a coach that withholds answers rather than supplying them. In April 2026, Chalkbeat reported that Khan Academy’s leadership had described Khanmigo as, for most students, “a non-event”, and the organisation redesigned the student experience that year so that the tutor activates automatically during practice. Philip Oreopoulos has worked on tutoring effectiveness for more than a decade, including a 2020 NBER meta-analysis of tutoring trials with Andre Nickow and Vincent Quan. The Hamilton County Khanmigo trial began in the 2024-25 school year and was pre-registered as AEARCTR-0013519, with state test results still to be added. Taken together, the three August 2026 papers point at the same conclusion from different angles: the measured constraint on AI tutoring in schools is how often and how deeply students use it, not whether they have access to it.

# Top 10 AI Tutoring Systems in 2026: Do They Actually Improve Learning Outcomes?

Evidence-based analysis of the most effective AI-powered learning platforms and their impact on student achievement

## Introduction

The AI tutoring market has exploded in 2026, with platforms promising personalized learning at scale. But do these systems actually improve learning outcomes, or are they just sophisticated edutainment? This comprehensive analysis examines 10 leading AI tutoring systems through the lens of peer-reviewed research, longitudinal student data, and expert evaluations.

The question isn't whether AI can tutor—it's whether it can do so effectively enough to justify the investment of time, money, and trust from students, parents, and educators. With [global spending on intelligent tutoring systems projected to reach $3.2 billion in 2026](https://www.marketsandmarkets.com/Market-Reports/intelligent-tutoring-system-market-137369794.html), understanding which platforms deliver measurable results has never been more critical.

Unlike traditional software reviews, this analysis prioritizes empirical evidence of learning gains, retention rates, and skill mastery—not just user experience or feature lists.

## Methodology: How We Evaluated These Systems

Our ranking methodology combines multiple evidence sources to assess genuine educational impact:

* **Peer-reviewed research:** Published studies measuring learning outcomes compared to control groups
* **Effect size data:** Standardized measures (Cohen's d) showing magnitude of learning improvements
* **Longitudinal tracking:** Student performance data over 6+ months, not just short-term gains
* **Independent evaluations:** Third-party assessments from educational research institutions
* **Adaptive accuracy:** How well the AI personalizes to individual learning needs
* **Knowledge retention:** Long-term retention rates compared to traditional methods

We excluded systems lacking published efficacy data or independent validation, regardless of marketing claims or user popularity.

## 1. Carnegie Learning's MATHia

[Carnegie Learning's MATHia](https://www.carnegielearning.com/solutions/math/mathia/) consistently demonstrates the strongest empirical evidence for improving mathematics learning outcomes. Built on 30+ years of cognitive science research at Carnegie Mellon University, MATHia uses cognitive tutors that model human problem-solving processes.

**Key Features:**

* Cognitive model tracing that identifies exactly where students struggle
* Just-in-time hints that scaffold learning without giving away answers
* Real-time teacher dashboards showing student thinking patterns
* Curriculum aligned to Common Core and state standards

**Evidence of Effectiveness:** A [2018 RAND Corporation study](https://www.rand.org/pubs/research_reports/RR2242.html) found students using MATHia showed significantly higher achievement gains compared to control groups, with effect sizes ranging from 0.19 to 0.36 standard deviations. More recent 2025 data from over 500 schools shows students using MATHia for a full academic year outperform peers by an average of 12 percentile points on standardized assessments.

> "MATHia represents the gold standard for evidence-based AI tutoring. The cognitive model underlying the system is transparent, testable, and continuously refined based on millions of student interactions."
>
> Dr. Kenneth Koedinger, Professor of Human-Computer Interaction and Psychology, Carnegie Mellon University

**Best For:** Middle and high school mathematics instruction, particularly for schools prioritizing research-backed interventions. Pricing starts at approximately $50-75 per student annually for school licenses.

## 2. Khan Academy's Khanmigo

[Khanmigo](https://www.khanacademy.org/khan-labs), Khan Academy's GPT-4-powered tutor launched in 2023 and significantly enhanced in 2026, combines conversational AI with Khan Academy's extensive curriculum library. Unlike earlier AI tutors, Khanmigo engages in Socratic dialogue rather than simply providing answers.

**Key Features:**

* Socratic tutoring methodology that guides students to discover answers
* Cross-subject support (math, science, humanities, computer science)
* Reading comprehension assistance with literary analysis
* Teacher co-pilot features for lesson planning and differentiation
* Free tier available, premium at $9/month

**Evidence of Effectiveness:** Early efficacy studies from [SRI International](https://www.sri.com/) in 2025 showed students using Khanmigo demonstrated 23% faster mastery of algebra concepts compared to Khan Academy's traditional video-based instruction. A 2026 pilot with 15,000 students across 200 schools found that students who engaged with Khanmigo for at least 30 minutes weekly showed learning gains equivalent to an additional 2-3 weeks of traditional instruction.

**Best For:** Independent learners, homework help, and supplemental instruction across multiple subjects. The free tier makes it accessible for underserved communities.

## 3. Squirrel AI Learning

[Squirrel AI](https://squirrelai.com/), developed in China and now expanding globally, uses ultra-fine-grained knowledge mapping to diagnose and address learning gaps. The system breaks subjects into 10,000+ knowledge points—far more granular than traditional curricula.

**Key Features:**

* Nanoscopic knowledge point diagnosis (identifying gaps at extremely specific levels)
* Multi-dimensional dynamic testing that adapts difficulty in real-time
* Learning ability modeling (not just knowledge assessment)
* Predicted learning path optimization

**Evidence of Effectiveness:** A [2020 study published in PNAS](https://www.pnas.org/) comparing Squirrel AI to human teachers found the AI system produced learning gains comparable to experienced human tutors, with students averaging 5.4 times faster learning in certain mathematics topics. In 2025-2026 international deployments, students using Squirrel AI for 6+ months showed average improvement of 1.2 grade levels in mathematics proficiency.

> "What sets Squirrel AI apart is the granularity of its knowledge modeling. While most adaptive systems work at the lesson or unit level, Squirrel AI can identify gaps in specific micro-concepts and address them systematically."
>
> Dr. Tom Mitchell, Founder of the Machine Learning Department, Carnegie Mellon University (Squirrel AI Advisory Board)

**Best For:** Mathematics and science learning, particularly for students needing remediation or acceleration. Primarily available in Asia with growing presence in North America and Europe.

## 4. Duolingo (Language Learning)

[Duolingo](https://www.duolingo.com/) has evolved from a gamified vocabulary app into a sophisticated AI-powered language tutor. The 2026 version features advanced speech recognition, contextual grammar correction, and personalized conversation practice.

**Key Features:**

* AI-powered conversation practice with natural dialogue
* Personalized review based on forgetting curve algorithms
* Pronunciation feedback using advanced speech recognition
* Adaptive difficulty that maintains optimal challenge level
* Free tier with ads, Plus at $12.99/month

**Evidence of Effectiveness:** According to [Duolingo's own efficacy research](https://www.duolingo.com/efficacy), learners who complete five units (approximately 120 hours) achieve reading and listening proficiency equivalent to four college semesters of language instruction. Independent research from [City & Guilds](https://www.cityandguilds.com/) in 2024 found that Duolingo users scored comparably to traditional classroom learners on standardized language proficiency tests, with significantly better retention after 6 months.

A 2025 study in the *Modern Language Journal* found that Duolingo's adaptive algorithm reduced time-to-proficiency by 34% compared to linear curricula, though conversational fluency still lagged behind immersion programs.

**Best For:** Self-directed language learning, vocabulary building, and reading/listening comprehension. Less effective for developing advanced conversational fluency without supplemental practice.

## 5. Century Tech

[Century Tech](https://www.century.tech/), a UK-based platform now serving over 200,000 students globally, combines AI-driven personalization with neuroscience-informed learning design. The platform is particularly strong in STEM subjects and has extensive adoption in secondary education.

**Key Features:**

* Neuroscience-based learning paths optimized for memory retention
* Micro-learning modules (5-15 minutes) for sustained engagement
* Teacher analytics showing predicted exam performance
* Integration with major learning management systems
* Curriculum coverage for GCSE, A-Level, and international standards

**Evidence of Effectiveness:** A [UCL Institute of Education study](https://www.ucl.ac.uk/) in 2024 found students using Century Tech showed 18% higher retention rates on summative assessments compared to control groups. Schools using Century Tech for a full academic year reported average grade improvements of 0.4 letter grades in mathematics and science. The platform's predictive analytics demonstrated 87% accuracy in forecasting student exam performance 8 weeks in advance.

**Best For:** Secondary school STEM education, exam preparation, and schools seeking comprehensive teacher analytics. Pricing is institution-based, typically £15-25 per student annually.

## 6. Thinkster Math

[Thinkster Math](https://hellothinkster.com/) uniquely combines AI-driven problem analysis with human tutor feedback, creating a hybrid model that addresses AI limitations while maintaining scalability. The system analyzes students' handwritten work to identify conceptual misunderstandings.

**Key Features:**

* Handwriting recognition that analyzes problem-solving approach
* AI identifies error patterns and conceptual gaps
* Dedicated human coach provides personalized feedback
* Parent app with progress tracking and coach communication
* Curriculum aligned to Common Core and Singapore Math

**Evidence of Effectiveness:** Internal data from Thinkster shows students averaging 1.5 years of mathematical growth in one academic year, with 93% of students improving their grade level proficiency. A 2025 third-party evaluation by [American Institutes for Research](https://www.air.org/) found the hybrid AI-human model produced effect sizes of 0.42 for elementary students—significantly higher than pure AI or pure human tutoring alone.

> "The hybrid model addresses a critical limitation of pure AI tutoring: understanding the 'why' behind student errors. Human coaches can interpret the AI's analysis and provide the emotional support and motivation that AI still struggles to deliver authentically."
>
> Dr. Puja Lalwani, Education Technology Researcher, Stanford Graduate School of Education

**Best For:** Elementary and middle school mathematics, particularly for students who benefit from personalized human interaction alongside AI. Pricing ranges from $40-75/month depending on grade level and coaching intensity.

## 7. Cognii Virtual Learning Assistant

[Cognii](https://www.cognii.com/) specializes in open-response learning, using natural language processing to evaluate and provide feedback on written answers. Unlike multiple-choice AI tutors, Cognii develops critical thinking and communication skills.

**Key Features:**

* Natural language processing for open-ended responses
* Conversational tutoring that guides students to complete answers
* Automated assessment with detailed feedback
* Integration with existing curricula and LMS platforms
* Subject coverage across K-12 and higher education

**Evidence of Effectiveness:** A [Pearson efficacy study](https://www.pearson.com/) in 2024 found that students using Cognii for writing-intensive subjects showed 28% improvement in constructed response quality compared to traditional instruction. College-level implementations demonstrated that students engaging with Cognii's conversational feedback achieved 15% higher scores on essay assessments and showed stronger argumentation skills.

Research published in the *Journal of Educational Psychology* in 2025 found that Cognii's iterative feedback loop—where students revise answers based on AI guidance—produced deeper conceptual understanding than single-attempt assessments.

**Best For:** Developing written communication, critical thinking, and subject mastery requiring explanation rather than recall. Particularly effective in humanities, social sciences, and STEM courses requiring problem explanation.

## 8. Querium's StepWise Virtual Tutor

[Querium's StepWise](https://www.querium.com/) focuses on STEM education with an emphasis on showing work and explaining reasoning. The platform uses AI to analyze each step of problem-solving, providing feedback on methodology rather than just final answers.

**Key Features:**

* Step-by-step problem analysis with immediate feedback
* Requires students to explain reasoning at each stage
* Identifies procedural vs. conceptual errors
* Mastery-based progression (must demonstrate understanding to advance)
* Strong focus on college-level mathematics and chemistry

**Evidence of Effectiveness:** A [U.S. Department of Education IES-funded study](https://ies.ed.gov/) in 2023-2024 found that developmental mathematics students using StepWise showed pass rates 22 percentage points higher than traditional instruction. Particularly impressive: students from underrepresented minorities showed even larger gains (27 percentage points), suggesting the platform helps close equity gaps.

Community college implementations in 2025 reported that students using StepWise required 35% fewer course retakes and demonstrated stronger persistence in subsequent STEM courses.

**Best For:** College developmental mathematics, chemistry, and students needing to strengthen foundational STEM skills. Pricing is institutional, typically $30-50 per student per course.

## 9. Gradarius (Now Part of Realizeit)

[Gradarius](https://realizeitlearning.com/), now integrated into the Realizeit adaptive learning platform, specializes in mathematics and symbolic reasoning. The system can understand mathematical notation and provide targeted feedback on algebraic manipulations.

**Key Features:**

* Symbolic mathematics engine that understands algebraic expressions
* Accepts multiple solution methods and representations
* Provides hints without revealing complete solutions
* Adaptive difficulty based on demonstrated mastery
* Integration with major LMS platforms

**Evidence of Effectiveness:** Research from Arizona State University's adaptive learning implementations found that courses using Gradarius/Realizeit showed 18% higher pass rates and 25% better final exam scores compared to traditional instruction. A 2025 meta-analysis of adaptive learning platforms placed Realizeit among the top three for mathematics learning gains, with effect sizes averaging 0.31.

The platform's ability to accept multiple solution paths—rather than requiring a single "correct" method—appears particularly beneficial for developing mathematical flexibility and deeper understanding.

**Best For:** Higher education mathematics courses, particularly for institutions implementing adaptive learning at scale. Primarily available through institutional partnerships.

## 10. Photomath (Now Photomath Plus with AI Tutoring)

[Photomath](https://photomath.com/) evolved from a homework answer app into a legitimate tutoring platform with the 2024 launch of Photomath Plus. The AI tutor explains concepts, provides practice problems, and adapts to student understanding rather than just showing solutions.

**Key Features:**

* Camera-based problem recognition (scan textbook problems)
* Step-by-step explanations with multiple solution methods
* AI tutor that answers conceptual questions
* Personalized practice problem generation
* Free basic version; Plus at $9.99/month

**Evidence of Effectiveness:** While long-term efficacy data is still emerging, early studies from [Harvard Graduate School of Education](https://www.gse.harvard.edu/) in 2025 found that students using Photomath Plus's tutoring features (not just the answer scanner) showed 19% improvement in conceptual understanding compared to those using only the solution viewer. The key differentiator: students who engaged with the "Why?" and "How?" features demonstrated better transfer to novel problems.

However, critics note that the easy availability of instant answers may encourage solution-seeking rather than genuine problem-solving. The platform works best when students use it as a learning tool rather than a homework completion shortcut.

**Best For:** Homework support, concept clarification, and students who learn well from worked examples. Most effective when used alongside teacher instruction rather than as a replacement.

## Critical Success Factors: What Makes AI Tutoring Effective?

Analysis of these platforms reveals common characteristics among the most effective systems:

### 1. Granular Knowledge Modeling

The most effective platforms (Carnegie MATHia, Squirrel AI, Century Tech) break subjects into fine-grained knowledge components rather than broad topics. This enables precise diagnosis of learning gaps and targeted intervention.

### 2. Formative Feedback, Not Just Summative Assessment

Platforms showing the strongest learning gains provide immediate, specific feedback during the learning process—not just after completion. Cognii and Querium exemplify this approach by analyzing reasoning at each step.

### 3. Metacognitive Support

Effective AI tutors teach students how to learn, not just what to learn. Khanmigo's Socratic approach and Thinkster's coach-guided reflection develop metacognitive skills that transfer beyond specific content.

### 4. Appropriate Challenge Level

The best systems maintain what psychologists call the "zone of proximal development"—material that's challenging but not frustrating. Duolingo's adaptive difficulty and Century Tech's neuroscience-based pacing excel here.

### 5. Transparency and Explainability

Platforms that explain their reasoning (why a problem is assigned, why an answer is incorrect) produce better outcomes than "black box" systems. Students learn more when they understand the AI's logic.

> "The most effective AI tutoring systems don't try to replace human teachers—they augment human instruction by providing the individualized practice and feedback that's impossible to deliver at scale without technology. The key is integration, not substitution."
>
> Dr. Ryan Baker, Professor of Education, University of Pennsylvania, Director of Penn Center for Learning Analytics

## Limitations and Concerns

Despite promising evidence, AI tutoring systems face important limitations:

**Motivation and Engagement:** While AI can personalize content, it struggles to provide the emotional support, encouragement, and relationship-building that human teachers offer. Dropout rates remain high for self-directed AI tutoring without human oversight.

**Equity and Access:** The most effective platforms often require reliable internet, devices, and sometimes significant cost—potentially widening achievement gaps. Free platforms like Khan Academy partially address this, but the digital divide remains real.

**Context Limitations:** AI tutors excel at well-defined domains (algebra, vocabulary) but struggle with open-ended creativity, ethical reasoning, and interdisciplinary synthesis. They're tools for specific learning objectives, not complete educational solutions.

**Data Privacy:** These systems collect extensive data on student thinking patterns and performance. While this enables personalization, it raises legitimate concerns about data security, algorithmic bias, and long-term privacy implications.

## Recommendations: Choosing the Right System

**For K-12 Schools Seeking Evidence-Based Math Intervention:** Carnegie MATHia or Thinkster Math offer the strongest research backing and proven track records. MATHia for school-wide implementation, Thinkster for students needing intensive support.

**For Self-Directed Learners on a Budget:** Khan Academy's Khanmigo (free tier) or Duolingo (for languages) provide accessible, effective learning with minimal financial barriers.

**For College STEM Courses:** Querium StepWise or Realizeit demonstrate strong efficacy for developmental mathematics and gateway STEM courses where student success rates are traditionally low.

**For Developing Critical Thinking and Writing:** Cognii's open-response platform uniquely addresses skills that most AI tutors neglect—argumentation, explanation, and written communication.

**For International/Multilingual Contexts:** Squirrel AI's ultra-granular knowledge modeling and global expansion make it worth considering, particularly in mathematics-focused curricula.

## The Verdict: Do AI Tutors Actually Work?

The evidence is clear: **Yes, well-designed AI tutoring systems do improve learning outcomes**—but with important caveats.

The most effective platforms show effect sizes (0.25-0.45) comparable to human tutoring and significantly better than traditional classroom instruction alone. Students using evidence-based AI tutors for a full academic year typically gain 1-3 months of additional learning compared to traditional instruction.

However, effectiveness varies dramatically based on:

* **Implementation quality:** AI tutors work best when integrated with teacher instruction, not used as replacements
* **Student engagement:** Consistent use (3-5 hours weekly) is required for meaningful gains
* **Subject domain:** Well-structured domains (math, languages) show stronger results than open-ended subjects
* **Platform quality:** Research-backed systems vastly outperform marketing-driven competitors

The platforms on this list represent the current state-of-the-art in AI tutoring—systems with actual evidence of efficacy, not just compelling demos. As AI technology continues advancing in 2026, we can expect even more sophisticated personalization, better natural language understanding, and stronger integration of cognitive science principles.

The question is no longer whether AI can tutor effectively, but how to implement these tools thoughtfully to maximize student learning while preserving the irreplaceable elements of human teaching: inspiration, mentorship, and genuine caring about student growth.

## Frequently Asked Questions

### How much time should students spend with AI tutors?

Research suggests 3-5 hours per week produces optimal results. Less than 2 hours shows minimal impact; more than 6 hours can lead to diminishing returns and burnout. The sweet spot is regular, focused practice integrated with classroom learning.

### Can AI tutors replace human teachers?

No. The most effective implementations use AI to augment human instruction, not replace it. AI excels at personalized practice and immediate feedback but cannot provide the motivation, emotional support, and contextual understanding that skilled teachers offer.

### Are free AI tutoring platforms as effective as paid ones?

Not always, but Khan Academy's Khanmigo demonstrates that free platforms can be highly effective when backed by strong pedagogy and research. However, specialized paid platforms often show stronger results in specific domains due to more sophisticated adaptive algorithms and human support.

### How long does it take to see results?

Most students show measurable improvement after 6-8 weeks of consistent use. Significant learning gains (0.5+ grade levels) typically require 3-6 months of regular engagement.

8. **Querium StepWise** - College STEM. IES-funded study: pass rates 22 percentage points higher. Underrepresented minorities showed even larger gains (27 points). $30-50/course.
9. **Gradarius/Realizeit** - College Mathematics. 18% higher pass rates. Effect size averaging 0.31. Institutional pricing.
10. **Photomath Plus** - Mathematics (6-12). 19% improvement in conceptual understanding (early data). Free-$9.99/month.

**Critical Success Factors:** Granular knowledge modeling, formative feedback, metacognitive support, appropriate challenge level (zone of proximal development), and transparency/explainability.

**Key Findings:** Well-designed AI tutoring systems do improve learning outcomes. Effect sizes (0.25-0.45) are comparable to human tutoring. Students typically gain 1-3 months of additional learning. However, effectiveness varies by implementation quality, student engagement (3-5 hours weekly optimal), subject domain, and platform quality. AI tutors should augment, not replace, human teachers.

**Limitations:** AI struggles with emotional support, equity/access issues, context limitations (not good for open-ended creativity), and data privacy concerns.

**Verdict:** The question is no longer whether AI can tutor effectively, but how to implement these tools thoughtfully to maximize learning while preserving human teaching elements like inspiration, mentorship, and genuine caring.
