### PUBLIC INTEREST STATEMENT

A recent study conducted in Indonesian universities revealed the positive influence of Artificial Intelligence (AI) writing tools on English as a Foreign Language (EFL) student writing. Interviews with four EFL teachers across three universities highlighted the diverse range of AI writing tools, including Quillbot, WordTune, Jenni, Chat-GPT, Paperpal, Copy.ai, and Essay Writer. Teachers unanimously agreed that these tools improved students' writing quality, particularly in terms of content and organization. The study's implications suggest that integrating AI writing tools can elevate the quality of EFL student writing, enhancing language learning outcomes. These findings have broader implications for educators, students, and policymakers interested in optimizing language instruction through technology.

## 1. Introduction

The use of Artificial Intelligent (AI)-powered writing tools in English as a foreign language (EFL) classroom is increasing rapidly. These tools include grammar checks, writing aids, and programs that can create written works like essays without human help. They are easy to use and effective, saving students and educators time and effort (T. S. Chang et al., [Citation 2021](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/2331186X.2023.2236469#); Gayed et al., [Citation 2022](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/2331186X.2023.2236469#); Jeanjaroonsri, [Citation 2023](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/2331186X.2023.2236469#); Zhao, [Citation 2022](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/2331186X.2023.2236469#)). Additionally, AI writing tools have been used particularly for EFL learners with low English proficiency. By using these tools, students can receive immediate feedback and assistance, improving their writing skills faster.

In general, AI writing tools are intended to analyze written materials and provide comments on many parts of the writing, such as grammar, vocabulary, syntax, content, and structure (Hosseini et al., [Citation 2023](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/2331186X.2023.2236469#); Strobl et al., [Citation 2019](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/2331186X.2023.2236469#); Thorp, [Citation 2023](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/2331186X.2023.2236469#)). Such feedback is created by machine-learning algorithms that compare the written text to a big database of correct and incorrect instances of writing. In other words, EFL students can obtain instant and tailored feedback on their writing, which can assist them in identifying and correcting faults more rapidly. This real-time feedback can also assist students in comprehending the fundamental concepts of successful writing and offer them with direction for enhancing their writing abilities (Akgun & Greenhow, [Citation 2022](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/2331186X.2023.2236469#); Nazari et al., [Citation 2021](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/2331186X.2023.2236469#); Rudolph et al., [Citation 2023](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/2331186X.2023.2236469#)).

Recently, there is a growing amount of research on how AI writing tools affect student writing skills, and this research is relevant to the TEFL enterprise. Some research suggests that adopting AI-powered writing tools can help students improve their writing (e.g., Kurniati & Fithriani, [Citation 2022](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/2331186X.2023.2236469#); Wang, [Citation 2022](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/2331186X.2023.2236469#); Zhao, [Citation 2022](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/2331186X.2023.2236469#)), while others have voiced concerns about the side effect of these tools (e.g., Y. Liu et al., [Citation 2022](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/2331186X.2023.2236469#); Lund & Wang, [Citation 2023](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/2331186X.2023.2236469#); Qadir, [Citation 2022](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/2331186X.2023.2236469#)). Nevertheless, the literature presented focuses solely on the role of AI writing tools in improving grammar and syntax. While this is undeniably a crucial aspect, it does not address the full spectrum of what contributes to effective writing. The content and organization of a piece of writing are equally significant components that profoundly affect the reader’s understanding and engagement (I. Lee & Yuan, [Citation 2021](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/2331186X.2023.2236469#)). Content is the core of any piece of writing. It carries the ideas, thoughts, and messages that the writer wants to convey. It is the “what” of the writing—the substance. High-quality content is relevant, informative, original, and meaningful, resonating with the audience and fulfilling its purpose—whether that be to inform, persuade, entertain, or provoke thought (Molina et al., [Citation 2021](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/2331186X.2023.2236469#)). Organization, on the other hand, is the “how” of the writing—the structure. It involves how the content is arranged, connecting ideas in a logical, coherent manner that guides the reader through the piece. The organization can significantly affect how well the reader understands the content, how persuasively an argument is presented, or how engaging a narrative is. Good organization ensures a smooth flow of ideas, making the writing easier to follow and more impactful (Awada et al., [Citation 2020](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/2331186X.2023.2236469#)). Therefore, the focus on just grammar and syntax overlooks the critical roles of content and organization in writing. While getting the words right is essential, what those words express and how they are structured are just as vital to effective communication. Thus, it is crucial to explore what the types of AI writing tools and how the tools address these other key aspects of writing from the perspective of EFL educators.

A similar situation holds true in the Indonesian context. To the best of our knowledge, there is almost no research in the Indonesian context that has been reported in journal articles examining the impact of AI writing tools on the content and organization from either students’ or teachers’ perspective. The present authors are aware of the seminal work of Miranty and Widiati ([Citation 2021](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/2331186X.2023.2236469#)) and Fahmi and Cahyono ([Citation 2021](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/2331186X.2023.2236469#)), which, to some degree of details, examine the use of Automated Writing Evaluation (AWE) as one of the AI writing tools employed by Indonesian EFL students in their writing. Miranty and Widiati ([Citation 2021](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/2331186X.2023.2236469#)) explored students’ perceptions of the merits and drawbacks of AWE (i.e., Grammarly), while Fahmi and Cahyono ([Citation 2021](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/2331186X.2023.2236469#)) aimed to investigate differences in students’ perceptions towards the use of AWE based on their proficiency levels. Their research findings suggest that using AWE can provide students with positive benefits, which were consistent across their studies. Despite these insightful findings, more research on the impact of AI writing tools is necessary. It is true the previous studies have provided information regarding the influence of these tools on student writing. However, it is still unclear how AI writing tools affect the quality of student writing particularly on the aspects of content and organization. Consequently, this study has been meticulously designed to fill the prevailing knowledge gap, thereby delivering a more comprehensive understanding of AI writing tools’ utility in EFL classrooms. The primary objective of this research is to explore the variety of AI writing tools and evaluate their impact on student writing, particularly focusing on content and organization, through the lens of EFL teachers. To this end, we posed the following critical research questions:

1.   What types of AI writing tools are used by EFL teachers to improve students’ writing quality, particularly in terms of content and organization?

2.   How do EFL teachers perceive the impact of AI writing tools on the content and organization aspects of students’ writing?

The urgency in answering these research questions stems from two primary reasons. Firstly, understanding the types of AI writing tools used by teachers and their methods of integration could provide a blueprint for other educators looking to implement similar technologies in their teaching practices. This insight can ultimately contribute to the broader and more effective use of AI in EFL instruction. Secondly, investigating teachers’ perceptions of AI writing tools is crucial. If teachers view these tools as beneficial, this positive perception can lead to more widespread adoption, enriching EFL instruction across the board. However, if teachers are apprehensive or skeptical about these tools, identifying and addressing their concerns becomes paramount. This understanding would allow for modifications in AI tools or teaching strategies to ensure the potential of AI is fully realized and appreciated in language learning settings. By answering these questions, this study hopes to pave the way for more effective AI integration in EFL classrooms.

## 2. Literature review

### 2.1. Teaching writing in the artificial intelligence era

The evolution of teaching writing in the current age of technological proliferation cannot be dissociated from the rapid advancement of digital tools and. As eloquently discussed in Haleem’s et al. ([Citation 2022](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/2331186X.2023.2236469#)) research, this shift is precipitated by an increasing fusion of digital utilities within the educational realm, effectively transforming traditional pen-and-paper methodologies into far more creative and dynamic pedagogical experiences. Garlinska et al. ([Citation 2023](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/2331186X.2023.2236469#)) discuss how virtual classrooms, online workshops, and cloud-based writing tools, for example, are revolutionizing the domain of writing instruction. These platforms offer functionalities such as real-time feedback, collaborative editing, and plagiarism checks. Such features not only enhance the writing acumen of students, as per Nykyporets’s ([Citation 2023](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/2331186X.2023.2236469#)) study, but also inspire them to engage in critical thinking and independent reasoning.

Furthermore, as illustrated by Bhutoria’s ([Citation 2022](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/2331186X.2023.2236469#)) work, AI-driven platforms and applications offer personalized learning opportunities for students, identifying their writing strengths and weaknesses. This empowers educators to tailor their teaching strategies to each student’s unique needs and preferences, leading to more effective learning outcomes (Dogan et al., [Citation 2023](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/2331186X.2023.2236469#)). In the same vein, Cahyono et al. ([Citation 2023](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/2331186X.2023.2236469#)) explored of the workable approach mediated by mobile technology in teaching writing uncovers another layer of tech-enabled pedagogical innovation. Students are emboldened to publish their work in public forums, nurturing their confidence and writing abilities. Such platforms also promote peer review and feedback mechanisms, fostering a sense of community and collaborative learning (Umamah & Cahyono, [Citation 2022](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/2331186X.2023.2236469#)). However, as the literature acknowledges, the digitization of writing instruction is not without its challenges. As Duncan and Joyner ([Citation 2022](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/2331186X.2023.2236469#)) articulated, educators must grapple with issues related to digital equity, privacy, and the potential for distraction. These issues underscore the necessity for an ongoing dialogue and proactive approaches in crafting pedagogical policies and strategies as we continue to navigate the teaching of writing in this artificial intelligence era.

### 2.2. The impact of AI writing tools on students writing quality

There has been burgeoning research on the impact of AI writing tools on students’ writing ability. While several studies indicate positive outcomes, others highlight potential negative impacts. On the positive side, AI writing tools such as Grammarly, QuillBot, Wordtune, and Jenni have been found to significantly improve students’ writing skills. These tools utilize advanced algorithms to identify common errors in grammar, punctuation, and syntax and provide suggestions to improve clarity and style. They also offer unique capabilities such as paraphrasing and refining sentences for enhanced effectiveness. A study by Tambunan et al. ([Citation 2022](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/2331186X.2023.2236469#)) showed that using Grammarly improved students’ grammar and punctuation. Grammarly’s AI analyzes the user’s text, provides real-time suggestions for enhancing grammar, spelling, punctuation, clarity, engagement, and delivery. This has the effect of turning the process of writing into a learning opportunity. QuillBot, another AI tool, specializes in paraphrasing, helping students avoid plagiarism while maintaining the original meaning of their content. Kurniati and Fithriani ([Citation 2021](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/2331186X.2023.2236469#)) found that QuillBot aided students in developing better paraphrasing skills, which is a critical competency in academic writing. WordTune, on the other hand, focuses on refining and improving the tone and style of the text. A study by Lam and Moorhouse ([Citation 2022](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/2331186X.2023.2236469#)) found that WordTune effectively helped students identify their writing weaknesses, thereby promoting self-assessment and learning. This tool goes beyond simple grammar correction and delves into the stylistic elements of writing. Jenni is another AI-based writing assistant that provides predictive text suggestions to help users compose emails, reports, articles, and other documents more efficiently. Although no specific research was cited in this regard, user feedback suggests a positive impact on writing productivity and creativity. GPT-3, developed by OpenAI, represents a significant advancement in language model technology. Capable of generating coherent and contextually relevant sentences, GPT-3 has been found to stimulate students’ creative and critical thinking (Mhlanga, [Citation 2023](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/2331186X.2023.2236469#)). It can be an excellent tool for students to experiment with different writing styles and ideas. These studies highlight the potential of AI tools in enhancing the writing abilities of students.

In terms of the content and the structure of writing, a number of research has shown that AI writing tools can significantly enhance the efficiency and quality of writing tasks. AI-based tools, like GPT-3 and its successor GPT-4, have been leveraged to suggest the next word or paragraph in a text, aiding authors in creating human-like compositions (Y. Liu et al., [Citation 2023](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/2331186X.2023.2236469#)). This process is facilitated by machine learning algorithms that predict text sequences based on the vast amount of data they have been trained on. Furthermore, there is ongoing research exploring the impact of these tools on different aspects of writing. For instance, a study found that AI writing tools like “AI KAKU”, a popular Japanese-developed English language learning tool, could potentially reduce cognitive barriers for English as a Foreign Language (EFL) learners when producing written text in English (Gayed et al., [Citation 2022](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/2331186X.2023.2236469#)). This is achieved by providing real-time translation and grammar suggestions, making the writing process less daunting. Another important application of AI in writing is its ability to expedite the literature review process, which deals with large volumes of partially structured (meta)data (Wagner et al., [Citation 2022](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/2331186X.2023.2236469#)). This is particularly valuable in fields like healthcare and social sciences, where researchers must often sift through enormous bodies of literature for their studies. In conclusion, the evolution and application of AI writing tools like have undoubtedly marked a significant stride in the world of writing and literature. These advancements hold substantial potential in not only streamlining the writing process but also in improving the quality and efficiency of written output.

Despite these advantages, certain studies have indicated potential drawbacks. For instance, AI writing tools may inadvertently promote over-reliance among students, as they might lean too heavily on these tools for correction without thoroughly understanding their mistakes. This dependency can stunt their natural learning process and development of self-editing skills. Iskender ([Citation 2023](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/2331186X.2023.2236469#)) provided a critical perspective on this matter, arguing that the use of AI writing tools could lead to diminished critical thinking skills if students become overly dependent on them. They expressed concern that students might prioritize quick fixes from AI tools over deeply understanding and learning from their mistakes, which would essentially negate the process of learning, growth, and development in writing. In addition to concerns about over-reliance, the impact of AI writing tools on creativity has also been questioned. Some educators worry that students might use these tools not just for refining their language, but also for generating ideas, potentially curtailing their creative thinking and originality (Johinke et al., [Citation 2023](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/2331186X.2023.2236469#)). Furthermore, Farrokhnia et al. ([Citation 2023](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/2331186X.2023.2236469#)) pointed out that while AI tools can improve certain writing skills, they may not be as effective in addressing higher-order writing elements, such as argument structure and coherence. These aspects require a deep understanding of the topic, logical thinking, and the ability to connect ideas, which are currently beyond the capacity of AI tools. In terms of tone and context, AI tools may also falter. These tools might not fully grasp the subtleties and nuances of human language and emotion, potentially leading to suggestions that may not be appropriate or accurate in a given context (Haleem et al., [Citation 2022](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/2331186X.2023.2236469#)). Finally, issues of digital equity have been raised. Not all students have equal access to these technologies, leading to potential disparities in learning outcomes. In their study, Mozumder et al. ([Citation 2023](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/2331186X.2023.2236469#)) noted that students without access to high-speed internet or modern digital devices might be unable to utilize these AI tools, widening the educational achievement gap. Therefore, while the application of AI in writing instruction has promising benefits, educators need to be mindful of these potential drawbacks and address them proactively in their teaching strategies.

## 3. Method

### 3.1. Research design

To address the research questions, a qualitative approach was employed, specifically utilizing a case study methodology. The case study methodology, which typically involves conducting interviews and/or observations, enables the researcher to uncover important factors that emerge from the open-ended process (Yin, [Citation 2009](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/2331186X.2023.2236469#)). Through this methodology, we were able to explore in-depth the types of AI writing tools used by EFL teachers, as well as their perceptions about the impact of these tools on students’ writing quality, particularly in terms of content and organization.

### 3.2. Research participants

This study focused on gaining insights from EFL teachers experienced with AI writing tools, specifically their views on how these tools affect student’s writing quality, particularly in terms of content and organization. Four writing teachers were recruited from three different universities, one being a public institution and the other two, private. The selection was primarily based on their practical experience with AI writing tools in the classroom, accessibility, willingness to participate, and teaching expertise in advanced courses such as essay writing and argumentative essay writing. These advanced courses often demand a higher level of grammatical knowledge and a deeper understanding of discourse structure.

All the recruited teachers possessed at least three years of experience in teaching EFL and a minimum of one year’s experience in applying AI writing tools in their classrooms. These AI tools served as supplementary teaching resources, aiding in grammar checking, paraphrasing, plagiarism detection, generating content, and offering suggestions to enhance the clarity and coherence of students’ writing. This ensured the teachers’ experiences transcended mere theoretical knowledge, encapsulating practical applications of AI tools in real-life teaching scenarios.

Teachers’ classes varied in size, ranging from intimate, personalized instruction settings to larger, conventional classrooms. This range in teaching environments was intentional, allowing the study to account for various factors potentially impacting the efficacy of AI tools. These factors could include class size, available institutional resources, the composition of the student population, and individual teaching styles. Such a diverse selection of participants enabled a comprehensive understanding of EFL teachers’ experiences and perspectives while using AI writing tools.

Participants were designated as T1, T2, T3, and T4 to maintain confidentiality. The recruitment process began with contacting prospective participants via email, outlining the study’s purpose, their roles, data collection methods, and their rights, including the ability to withdraw from the study at any point without any repercussions. This ensured adherence to ethical research guidelines. They were also provided with an informed consent form to read, comprehend, and sign if they agreed to participate. Through this careful recruitment process, the study maintained the highest ethical standards while ensuring the inclusion of relevant experiences and perspectives. ### 3.3. Instrument

We used interviews as our research instrument to collect the required data for this study. This instrument allowed us to gather rich, qualitative data related to EFL teachers’ use of AI writing tools, and their perspectives on the impact of these tools on students’ writing quality- specifically, in terms of content and organization. Lee et al. ([Citation 2022](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/2331186X.2023.2236469#)), and Zhao ([Citation 2022](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/2331186X.2023.2236469#)) served as valuable references. By undertaking an in-depth review of these sources, we focused on the topics and themes that aligned with our research objectives.

This thorough literature review helped us craft our interview protocol. It included specific questions such as “What AI writing tools have you used in your classroom?” and “In what ways have these tools impacted your students’ writing, specifically with respect to content and organization?” This interview guide allowed us to investigate both the practical applications and theoretical implications of AI writing tools in the EFL teaching context.

### 3.4. Data collection procedure

After designing the interview protocol centered on the types of AI writing tools utilized by EFL teachers and their views on the impact of these tools on student writing quality (specifically, content and organization), we organized interviews with each participant. These were scheduled according to their convenience and availability. Before starting each interview, we briefed the participants about the study’s objectives, the interview process, and our rigorous approach to data protection. We secured their informed consent to proceed, ensuring they comprehended their rights, including the freedom to withdraw from the study at any time. During the interview, we began with general questions about their experiences teaching EFL and using AI writing tools, thus fostering a relaxed environment conducive for open discussions. Gradually, we introduced more specific questions aligned with our interview protocol, delving into the particular AI writing tools they had employed and their impact on students’ writing quality, particularly in terms of content and organization improvements.

To address potential social-desirability bias inherent in self-reported data, we emphasized to the participants that there were no right or wrong answers and encouraged them to be as open and honest as possible. This was done to ensure the reliability and authenticity of the responses gathered. Each interview was recorded with the participant’s permission, to maintain accuracy in capturing their responses, an integral part of reliable transcription and subsequent data analysis. Note-taking during the interviews was also employed as a means to highlight significant points, capture nuanced details, and document immediate observations.

Upon the conclusion of each interview, we expressed our gratitude to the participants for their contributions, also providing them with an opportunity to pose any questions about the study or to add any further comments. Following the interviews, we carefully transcribed the recorded dialogues, transforming verbal insights into textual data. Accuracy during this stage is critical, as the transcribed data underpin our subsequent analysis. All collected data, encompassing the interview recordings, transcriptions, and notes, were securely stored, respecting participant privacy and enabling efficient data management for ensuing stages of data analysis and research reporting. Adhering to these practices ensured a comprehensive, ethical, and effective data collection procedure for our research on AI writing tools’ use and impact in EFL teaching.

### 3.5. Data analysis

We employed a thematic case study to analyze the qualitative data. As outlined by Braun and Clarke ([Citation 2006](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/2331186X.2023.2236469#)), the goal of this thematic analysis was to identify patterns and connections among themes extracted from the qualitative data, thereby addressing our research questions. We divided the analysis into five distinct steps.

In the first step, we thoroughly read the interview transcript multiple times to familiarize ourselves with its content. The second step involved developing preliminary codes that grouped related words and phrases in line with our research criteria. Following a detailed analysis of these codes, we then categorized each one. In this step, we also compared the results to identify any relationships or patterns. Finally, we established a set of categories from these grouped codes.

This is a scholarly article published in Cogent Education (Volume 10, 2023, Issue 2) titled "The impact of AI writing tools on the content and organization of students' writing: EFL teachers' perspective." The study, conducted by Marzuki, Utami Widiati, Diyenti Rusdin, Darwin, and Inda Indrawati from Indonesian universities (Universitas Madako Tolitoli and Universitas Negeri Malang), used a qualitative case study design with semi-structured interviews of four EFL teachers across three Indonesian universities.

The AI tools identified included Quillbot, WordTune, Jenni, Chat-GPT, Paperpal, Copy.ai, and Essay Writer. All four teachers unanimously agreed that AI writing tools positively improved students' writing quality, particularly in content and organization.

The study addresses a gap in existing literature, which has focused primarily on grammar and syntax improvements rather than content and organization. The authors argue that content (the "what" of writing) and organization (the "how" of writing) are equally critical components of effective writing. The paper includes a literature review covering teaching writing in the AI era, discusses both positive impacts (improved grammar, paraphrasing, tone, creativity) and potential drawbacks (over-reliance, diminished critical thinking, digital equity concerns) of AI writing tools.

The findings suggest that integrating AI writing tools can be beneficial in elevating the quality of EFL student writing, and recommendations for future research are provided.

<summary>
This CASRAI guide (last updated 23 July 2026) documents how universities have shifted from blanket bans on generative AI tools toward tiered permission frameworks and disclosure requirements. Between 2023 and 2026, most institutions moved through a common arc: initial prohibition, then a shift toward conditional, task-specific frameworks. Blanket bans proved difficult to enforce due to AI-detection false positives and didn't account for how AI tools are used differently across disciplines.

Tiered policies, exemplified by Carnegie Mellon University's Eberly Center (which offers six sample policy statements ranging from full prohibition to conditional use), specify permission by tool, task, assignment, or course stage. Disclosure requirements mirror research-integrity norms: students must report which tool (including version), what task it was used for, and sometimes the prompts and outputs. Data privacy has emerged as a separate but related policy axis, with institutions restricting sensitive data from consumer AI tools and offering institutionally licensed alternatives.

AI-detection tools remain part of enforcement but are treated cautiously due to false-positive problems, particularly for non-native English writers. Institutional guidance now treats detector results as one input requiring corroboration, not standalone proof. For research administrators, key takeaways include: design tiered frameworks with disclosure and oversight, consider data privacy as a distinct compliance concern, and recognize that AI-detection tools have limitations that should be reflected in policy language.

SUMMARY:

This document, "Assessment Reform for the Age of Artificial Intelligence," authored by Jason M. Lodge and colleagues, was commissioned by TEQSA in November 2023 to guide Australian higher education institutions in reforming assessment practices in response to generative AI. It argues that bans on AI are oversimplified and that assessment must evolve to address both risks (academic integrity) and opportunities (preparing students for an AI-ubiquitous world). The document builds on the foundational "Assessment 2020" propositions and aligns with the Higher Education Standards Framework.

**Guiding Principles:**
1. Assessment should equip students to participate ethically in an AI-ubiquitous society.
2. Trustworthy judgements require multiple, inclusive, and contextualised approaches to assessment.

**Five Key Propositions for Assessment Reform:**
1. **Appropriate, authentic engagement with AI** – Assessment should foster critical, ethical, and productive use of AI aligned with disciplinary values.
2. **Systemic program-level approach** – Assessment design should span entire programs (not just individual units) to allow multiple methods and integrated tasks.
3. **Emphasis on the process of learning** – Assessment should reveal thinking, judgement, and decision-making processes that AI cannot easily simulate.
4. **Collaboration with peers and AI** – Students should work appropriately with each other and AI, with clear boundaries articulated.
5. **Security at meaningful points across a program** – Key assessment moments (e.g., capstones) should be secured to assure learning outcomes, rather than attempting to secure all tasks.

The document emphasizes that reform is not prescriptive but offers a "compass" for direction. It calls for inclusive stakeholder discussions (students, educators, accreditors, First Nations peoples) and acknowledges challenges including workload, capability building, and accreditation barriers. The report was developed through expert collaboration at a TEQSA-hosted forum in August 2023, with additional public consultation.

--- SOURCE 1: Perceptions and Use of AI Chatbots among Students in Higher Education: A Scoping Review of Empirical Studies ---
URL: https://www.mdpi.com/2227-7102/14/8/922

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a scoping review published in Education Sciences (2024) by Schei, Møgelvang, and Ludvigsen from Western Norway University of Applied Sciences. The review analyzes 24 empirical articles published between 1 January 2022 and 5 September 2023 on students' perceptions and use of AI chatbots (like ChatGPT, Copilot, Gemini, Claude) in higher education. The study used a five-stage scoping review methodology.

**Key Findings:**

**Geographic & Disciplinary Distribution:** Research is concentrated in Asia, with STEM disciplines (computer science, programming, engineering) being predominant. Mixed methods were the most common research approach.

**Positive Perceptions:** Students perceive AI chatbots as highly useful, motivating, and easy to use—serving as personal task assistants, providing immediate feedback, and helping with writing, coding, and academic tasks. This aligns with the Technology Acceptance Model (TAM) and Unified Theory of Acceptance and Use of Technology (UTAUT) frameworks.

**Concerns:** Students worry about accuracy and reliability of AI responses, potential negative impacts on learning, critical thinking, creativity, academic integrity, and plagiarism. There is a recognized tension between surface-level use (shortcuts) and deep learning approaches.

**Learning Processes:** Students use AI chatbots for diverse, purpose-driven tasks including brainstorming, summarizing, coding, problem-solving, writing support, and language learning. The review concludes that while positive attitudes and critical use prevail, addressing students' concerns is crucial for responsible AI integration in higher education.
</summary>

**Key Findings:**

- **Modest but real gains:** Late 2024 surveys show U.S. workers using generative AI saved ~5.4% of weekly hours, translating to ~1.1% workforce-wide productivity. For a 40-hour week, this is roughly 2 hours saved.
- **Uneven benefits:** AI productivity gains are strongest for novice/less-experienced workers (e.g., ~14-15% improvement in customer support, largest for juniors). Benefits are significant on well-defined tasks but weaker or adverse on complex, judgment-heavy problems.

- **Requirements beyond tools:** Gains require high-quality data, redesigned workflows, training, and robust safeguards. Integration costs, oversight, and change management consume resources. Hallucination risks, privacy regulations, and curriculum alignment remain challenges.
- **Macro context:** U.S. labor productivity grew ~2.3% in 2024 and 1.5% year-over-year by Q2 2025 — an uptick, but not a dramatic AI-driven shift.

**Practical 18-Month Agenda:**

1. Identify 3 workflows where AI can improve time and quality (e.g., formative feedback on drafts, generating aligned practice items, triaging student services).
2. Establish "gold standard" baselines without AI, then insert AI for repetitive tasks — not to replace human judgment.
3. Use retrieval-augmented generation for course content; require human review for high-stakes decisions (final grades, progression).
4. Procure complementary tools (training, prompt libraries, LMS integration, safe retrieval APIs).
5. Run small cross-functional pilots as mini-randomized controlled trials: define metrics, gather baselines, run for a term, publish methods.
6. Measure net costs (computing, licensing, hidden labor for redesign/review).
7. Track outcomes: hours returned to instruction, grading variability reduction, student support response times, error rates in AI-assisted outputs.

**Conclusion:** The 1.1% productivity boost is modest but sufficient if reinvested into feedback, course clarity, and student support. The key is targeting "upper-junior" levels, routine tasks that free expert time, and aligning incentives for deep use in impactful workflows.

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This webpage presents a systematic review published in npj Science of Learning (Volume 10, Article 29, May 2025) examining AI-driven Intelligent Tutoring Systems (ITS) in K-12 education. Authored by Létourneau et al., the review analyzed 28 studies involving 4,597 students to determine the effects of ITSs on learning outcomes and the experimental designs used to evaluate them.

The introduction highlights the global educational crisis and UNESCO's call to leverage AI for sustainable development. ITSs are defined as software programs equipped with AI that monitor progress, identify difficulties, and adapt instruction to individual learners. Notable prior work includes Kulik & Fletcher's (2016) meta-analysis of 50 controlled assessments, which found no scientific consensus on ITS effectiveness but showed they can be highly effective instructional tools.

Key findings:
- The effects of ITSs on K-12 learning are generally positive but mitigated when compared to non-intelligent tutoring systems.
- 96% of articles were authored by individuals from educational science, computer science, or both; only one article was from an ITS company.
- 54% of studies originated from the USA, 27% from Asia, and 15% from Europe.
- Roughly half (54%) of studies compared school levels and subjects to assess differences.
- None of the included articles mentioned AI ethics considerations, highlighting a gap in addressing ethical implications.
- The review calls for additional research with longer interventions, larger and more diverse sample sizes, and investigation into ethical implications of AI in teaching.

The authors note that ITS effectiveness depends on sound pedagogical features (immediate feedback, guided practice, adaptivity) applied under the right conditions, consistent with Honebein and Reigeluth's (2021) thesis that ITS must be well-aligned with instructional theory to produce positive outcomes.

--- SOURCE 2: The Impact of AI on Learners’ Self-Efficacy: A Meta-Analysis ---
URL: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12837995

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a meta-analysis study published in Behavioral Sciences (2026) by Ren, Stephens, and Lee from the University of Auckland, examining the impact of AI on learners' self-efficacy in educational contexts. The study analyzed 23 empirical studies published between January 2005 and February 2025, indexed in Web of Science, Scopus, and ERIC databases.

**Key Findings:**
- AI had a significant positive impact on self-efficacy in learning contexts, with a medium effect size of 0.758 (Hedges' g).
- Two moderating variables were significant: discipline (Q = 10.348, p < 0.05) and the role played by AI (Q = 3.991, p < 0.05).
- AI had the highest effect on self-efficacy in natural sciences (1.310) and medicine (1.013), while the effect was not significant for engineering.

- No significant moderating effects were found for learner levels, research settings, type of AI utilized, or duration of studies.

**Methodology:** The study used a random-effects model due to high heterogeneity (I² = 89.677). Hedges' g was used for effect size calculations. Publication bias was assessed via funnel plot, classic fail-safe N, and Egger's test, all indicating no substantial bias. Sensitivity analysis confirmed robustness of results.

**Conclusion:** AI effectively promotes learners' self-efficacy, particularly in natural sciences and medicine, and when used as an intelligent learning tool. The study recommends integrating AI in classrooms and designing activities that promote student-AI interaction, while noting the need for more experimental research in this domain.

<summary>
# U.S. Department of Education Report: Artificial Intelligence and the Future of Teaching and Learning (May 2023)

## Overview
This report from the U.S. Department of Education's Office of Educational Technology addresses the need for policy development around AI in education. It defines AI as "automation based on associations" and examines opportunities, risks, and recommendations for integrating AI into teaching and learning.

## Key Definitions
- **AI**: "Automation based on associations" - computers automate reasoning based on patterns in data
- **Two fundamental shifts**: (1) from capturing data to detecting patterns, (2) from providing access to resources to automating instructional decisions

## Three Reasons to Address AI Now
1. **Opportunities**: AI may enable achieving educational priorities at scale (adaptivity, teacher support, customizable resources)
2. **Risks**: Algorithmic bias, surveillance, privacy concerns, potential replacement of teachers (which the Department rejects)
3. **Unintended consequences**: At scale, AI could widen achievement gaps if based on poor data or biased assumptions

## Four Foundations for Ethical AI Policy
1. **Center People** - Keep humans in the loop; AI should augment human decision-making, not replace it
2. **Advance Equity** - Address algorithmic bias and ensure AI doesn't discriminate against underserved communities
3. **Ensure Safety, Ethics, and Effectiveness** - Maintain data privacy/security and require evidence of effectiveness (aligned with ESEA standards)
4. **Promote Transparency** - AI models must be inspectable, explainable, and overridable by educators

## Key Insights by Domain

### Learning
- AI enables adaptivity through intelligent tutoring systems
- Need dual focus: learning *with* AI and learning *about* AI
- Recommendation: Seek AI models aligned to a shared vision for learning

### Teaching
- Always center educators in instructional loops
- AI can improve teaching jobs through automated assistants but must avoid surveillance
- Recommendation: AI must be inspectable, explainable, and overridable by teachers

### Formative Assessment
- AI can enhance feedback loops
- Automated essay scoring is an example application
- Recommendation: Harness assessment expertise to reduce bias

### Research & Development
- Focus on addressing context and the "long tail" of learner variability
- Use design-based research partnerships
- Recommendation: R&D must account for context of teaching and learning

## Seven Recommendations
1. **Emphasize Humans in the Loop** - Require human oversight in educational AI
2. **Align AI Models to a Shared Vision for Education** - Ensure AI supports educational goals
3. **Design Using Modern Learning Principles** - Base AI on sound pedagogy
4. **Prioritize Strengthening Trust** - Build trustworthy systems
5. **Inform and Involve Educators** - Engage teachers in AI adoption
6. **Focus R&D on Addressing Context and Enhancing Trust and Safety** - Research real-world applications
7. **Develop Education-Specific Guidelines and Guardrails** - Create policies for safe AI use

## Key Principles
- "AI in education can only grow at the speed of trust" (Dr. Dale Allen)
- Three perspectives on AI: Human-like reasoning, algorithmic goal pursuit, and intelligence augmentation
- The Department "firmly rejects the idea that AI could replace teachers"
- Policies must address algorithmic discrimination, data privacy, and the need for human checks and balances
</summary>

--- SOURCE 1: AI Tutoring Equity Gap: Why Access Alone Won't Close It ---
URL: https://www.valere.io/ai-tutoring-equity-gap

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This article by Guy Pistone (CEO of Valere) examines the equity problem surrounding AI tutoring in K-12 education. While AI tutoring shows real promise—with a 2020 meta-analysis finding effect sizes equivalent to one-on-one human tutoring in controlled settings—the author warns that the technology risks following the same pattern as other democratizing technologies: benefiting the already-advantaged first and widening the gap before narrowing it.

Key issues identified include:
- **The access gap**: ~15% of U.S. children (9 million students) still lack reliable home broadband, concentrated in low-income, rural, and Tribal communities. As of early 2026, districts report 1 in 5 low-income families still lack reliable home internet.
- **The readiness gap**: The harder problem than access. Schools with the most to gain are often least positioned to close the feedback loop between AI-generated insights and changed instruction, due to fewer teachers per student, less planning time, and less administrative bandwidth.
- **Market failure**: The business incentives point toward well-resourced early adopters. Vendor-funded studies (e.g., Carnegie Learning's own 2022 efficacy study showing 30% improvement on algebra assessments) paint a more optimistic picture than independent research.
- **Teacher training deficit**: A 2022 study found teachers with >10 hours of platform-specific PD were significantly more effective at acting on AI data than those with standard 2-hour onboarding.

The article cites widely deployed platforms including Carnegie Learning's MATHia (3,000+ schools), Khan Academy's Khanmigo (free through OpenAI partnership), DreamBox Learning (5 million+ active students), and Synthesis. District licensing typically runs $15–$30 per student per year.

The author argues that closing the gap requires treating connectivity as infrastructure, designing offline/low-bandwidth AI tools, investing in sustained teacher professional development, and using equity-centered procurement frameworks. State-level AI education policy remains fragmented, with California (AB 2876), Virginia, and North Carolina leading, while most meaningful policy happens at the district level.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"The readiness gap. It is the distance between having access to an AI tool and being able to use it effectively.", "The technology does not distribute itself equitably by default. It never has, nor will.", "The one-size-fits-all classroom is a real problem. A third grader interested in horses who gets a math lesson framed around horses is more engaged, more likely to retain the concept, and more likely to stay curious.", "The companies that get the most out of AI are not necessarily the ones with the most sophisticated models. They are the ones who invested in helping their people understand what the tools are doing and what to do with what they surface.", "The promise is real. So is the gap. And both deserve to be taken seriously."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 2: Frontiers | AI and the digital divide in education ---
URL: https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/computer-science/articles/10.3389/fcomp.2026.1759027/full

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This review article (published February 5, 2026, in Frontiers in Computer Science) by Matjie, Nethavhani, and Matlakala from the University of Limpopo, South Africa, examines how artificial intelligence (AI) contributes to the digital divide in education, focusing on language barriers, cultural mismatches, and algorithmic bias as key factors that create inequities even when access to AI tools exists.

The authors conducted a focused narrative and comparative review of case studies from countries with similar socio-economic statuses and visible urban-rural divides, including South Africa, China, Brazil, Kenya, Mali, and others. Case studies analyzed include: AI4D Maseno University (Kenya) on sign language translation; RobotsMali producing children's books in Bambara; the GPE KIX STEPS project in Benin, Cameroon, and DRC for culturally relevant STEM materials; primary education in urban vs. rural China (revealing a "TPACK divide"); higher education in Latin America during COVID-19; and STEM education in BRICS countries.

The conceptual framework identifies three interconnected digital divides: linguistic divide (limited engagement), cultural divide (reduced relevance), and algorithmic divide (biased feedback and unequal outcomes). The authors argue that even when learners have equal access to AI tools, the tools remain discriminatory due to language dominance (predominantly English), cultural insensitivity, and algorithmic bias from non-representative training datasets.

The article proposes three practical solutions:
1. **Development of AI tools with multilingual and culturally relevant content** (e.g., multilingual intelligent tutoring systems, local-language AI writing assistants, culturally contextualized AI chatbots)
2. **Use of diverse, representative datasets to mitigate algorithmic bias** (e.g., fair adaptive learning algorithms, bias-aware language models, participatory dataset curation)
3. **Capacity-building for educators and learners** (e.g., teacher professional development in AI pedagogy, learner AI literacy workshops, community-based train-the-trainer models)

Key contradictions identified include: participatory vs. top-down AI design approaches; short-term efficiency gains vs. long-term equity outcomes; and the inconsistent emphasis on teacher capacity-building across interventions. The authors conclude that AI's contribution to educational equity depends on participatory design, comprehensive teacher training, and multilingual support, rather than merely providing access to technology.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"AI should change learning for all learners across the globe; however, that is not always the case. AI in higher education brings some concerns with it, specifically the issues of access and such as the algorithmic bias and discrimination.", "According to Van Dijk (2017), the digital divide is the gap between people who do and do not have access to forms of information and communication. This gap appears to be wider for learners from rich countries and regions and those from poor countries and regions in terms of access to AI technologies that enable learning.", "Without deliberate commitments to inclusive design, transparency, and governance, AI risks reproducing and intensifying existing social hierarchies. Algorithmic bias thus constitutes a structural threat to educational equity, requiring systemic intervention if AI is to function as a tool for inclusion rather than exclusion.", "The cases reveal a tension between short-term efficiency gains and long-term equity outcomes. RobotsMali shows that AI-assisted content creation can reduce costs and production time while preserving cultural relevance. However, the BRICS STEM education case demonstrates that policy-driven AI and STEM expansion without parallel investment in access and training leads to skills shortages and labour market exclusion.", "AI does not inherently reduce digital divides. Instead, equitable outcomes depend on participatory design, sustained capacity-building, and institutional readiness."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 3: AI Access Is Creating a New Digital Divide ---
URL: https://edcircuit.com/ai-access-is-creating-a-new-digital-divide

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This article from edCircuit (published in 2026) argues that AI access in K–12 schools is creating a new digital divide, beyond the traditional gaps in internet connectivity and devices. It contrasts "AI-forward" districts, where students learn prompt engineering, AI ethics, and personalized tutoring, with districts that have no AI literacy initiatives, guidance, or professional development. Wealthier suburban districts with dedicated technology coaches, cybersecurity teams, and strong funding can adopt AI quickly, while rural and underfunded districts—often relying on a single tech administrator—struggle to keep pace. The article cites the 2026 State of EdTech District Leadership report by CoSN, which identifies AI, cybersecurity, and staffing as key challenges. Teachers in AI-ready districts receive training on AI-enhanced lesson planning and ethical integration, while others get no guidance, creating instructional and professional inequities. The article acknowledges legitimate concerns about data privacy, cybersecurity, bias, and academic integrity but warns that avoiding AI entirely leaves students unprepared for a workforce increasingly reliant on AI. The author calls for state-level AI guidance, regional collaboration, expanded professional development, public-private partnerships, and AI governance frameworks to ensure equitable access. The central thesis is that the next digital divide will be measured not by devices or bandwidth, but by which students were prepared to shape an AI-driven future and which were left behind.
</summary>

It may ultimately be measured by which students were prepared to shape the future—and which students were left trying to catch up to it."

--- SOURCE 4: AI and the next digital divide in education | Brookings ---
URL: https://www.brookings.edu/articles/ai-and-the-next-digital-divide-in-education

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This Brookings Institution commentary by Michael Trucano (July 10, 2023) examines the evolution of the digital divide in education in the context of emerging AI technologies. The article traces the progression: the first digital divide (rich have technology, poor do not), the second digital divide (rich have technology and skills, poor have technology but lack skills), and a potential third digital divide where the rich have access to both AI technology and human teachers/tutors, while the poor only have access to the technology.

Key context includes the global learning crisis: 70% of 10-year-olds in low- and middle-income countries cannot read basic texts, 244 million children are out of school, and a projected shortage of 70 million teachers by 2030. The article discusses the promise of AI-enabled personalized learning tools like Khan Academy's Khanmigo, while noting that historical efforts at personalized learning technology have had mixed results.

The author raises a critical question: As AI becomes more prevalent in education, could a new divide emerge where wealthy students have access to both AI tools and human support (teachers, tutors, engaged parents), while disadvantaged students only have access to the AI technology? Evidence from COVID-19 remote learning showed that even where technology access was equitable, parental and tutor involvement significantly impacted outcomes. The article concludes that education is fundamentally a human endeavor, and asks what society should do if access to people becomes the new dividing line.
</summary>

Authored by Aarush Tahiliani (2025 Winter Fellow), the piece examines how AI systems in college admissions, financial aid, and hiring processes reinforce systemic biases against marginalized communities. Key points include:

- **Problem**: AI-powered tools in hiring and education replicate societal biases (e.g., a 2019 NBER study found AI resume-screening disproportionately filtered out Black candidates; AI admissions models favor wealthier students).
- **Current Stance**: The U.S. lacks comprehensive AI regulation. The White House's 2022 Blueprint for an AI Bill of Rights outlines principles but lacks enforcement. The EU's AI Act requires audits for high-risk AI systems, but the U.S. has no equivalent.
- **Stakeholders**: Students, job seekers, marginalized communities, educational institutions, employers, policymakers, and AI developers.
- **Tried Policies**: NYC's Local Law 144 (2023) mandates bias audits for hiring AI; Illinois' AI Video Interview Act (2020) requires disclosure but no auditing. No federal regulations govern AI in education.
- **Policy Options Proposed**: (1) Mandatory third-party bias audits with public reporting and penalties; (2) AI model transparency and a "Right to Explanation" policy; (3) An Algorithmic Fairness Certification Program with government incentives.
- **Conclusion**: Collaborative efforts among policymakers, tech developers, and civil rights organizations are needed to ensure AI promotes equity. The paper advocates for mandatory bias audits as a key mechanism.

The piece includes four references and is categorized as a "Capstones Winter 2025" publication.

# Bias in AI: Examples and 6 Ways to Fix it in 2026

This article from AIMultiple (updated August 6, 2026) provides a comprehensive overview of AI bias, including real-world examples, categories, causes, legal frameworks, and mitigation strategies.

## AI Bias Benchmark Results
The author benchmarked 14 leading LLMs on 66 bias evaluation questions across gender, race, age, disability, socioeconomic status, and sexual orientation. Key findings:
- Open-ended questions showed less bias than multiple-choice formats
- GPT-4o cited statistical crime rates for specific races when asked to identify perpetrators

## Recent Real-Life Examples of AI Bias

**Racism:**

**Sexism:**
- A 2024 UNESCO study found LLMs associate women with "home" and "family" four times more often than men
- A 2024 University of Washington study found resume-screening AI favored white male names

- A 2025 University of Melbourne study found AI hiring tools struggled with speech disabilities and non-native accents

- Generative AI depicted autistic individuals using stereotypical imagery

## Types of AI Bias
- **Historical bias**: Training data reflects past prejudices
- **Sample bias**: Training data doesn't represent real-world populations
- **Ontological bias**: Western-centric worldview embedded in AI's fundamental concepts
- **Amplification bias**: AI not only learns but exacerbates human biases
- **Label bias**: Inconsistent or biased data labeling
- **Aggregation bias**: Hiding important differences through data aggregation
- **Confirmation bias**: Favoring information that confirms existing beliefs
- **Cultural & geographic bias**: LLMs trained mostly on Western data
- **Evaluation bias**: Testing on unrepresentative data
- **Politeness bias**: LLMs more likely to comply with harmful requests if asked politely

## Legal Frameworks
- **EU AI Act**: Classifies AI by risk; mandates data governance and bias mitigation for high-risk systems
- **GDPR**: Limits processing of sensitive data; Article 22 grants right to explanation of automated decisions
- **EEOC/U.S. law**: AI vendors can be treated as employers' agents and sued under Title VII, ADA, ADEA
- **South Korea**: AI Framework Act effective January 2026, with fines up to ~$21,000
- **Japan**: AI Basic Act passed May 2025, emphasizing risk-based governance
- **Singapore**: Voluntary, light-touch approach with AI Verify testing tool
- **China**: Binding interim regulations on generative AI since 2023

## Steps to Fix AI Bias
1. **Fathom the algorithm and data**: Examine training datasets, conduct subpopulation analysis, monitor over time
2. **Establish a debiasing strategy**: Technical tools, operational strategies (red teams, third-party auditors), organizational transparency
3. **Improve human-driven processes**: Use model building to identify and address long-standing biases through training and cultural change

The article concludes that while AI can theoretically be unbiased if training data is perfectly clean, in practice AI is unlikely to ever be completely unbiased as it relies on human-created data.

--- SOURCE 13: Bloom's 2 Sigma Problem Debunked: One-to-One Tutoring Isn’t Going to Save Education (Here’s Why) ---
URL: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=IaTk7lHC470

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This video and article by Dr. Luke Rowe (PhD in learning sciences) debunks Benjamin Bloom's famous 1984 '2 Sigma Problem'—the claim that one-to-one tutoring can lift student achievement by two standard deviations (from the 50th to the 98th percentile). 

**Key Arguments & Evidence:**
- Bloom's claim rested heavily on two very small, unpublished studies by his doctoral students (Anania and Burke) in the early 1980s, plus a selectively cherry-picked table of effect sizes from secondary sources.
- Paul von Hippel's (2024) data sleuthing revealed major problems: the famous graph was a hand-drawn caricature, not actual data; Bloom rounded up and fabricated numbers from Walberg's (1984) work; and the doctoral students themselves did not go on to build careers around tutoring research.
- The tutoring condition was heavily confounded: tutors received extra training and coaching, students got frequent formative testing (retrieval practice effect ~0.5 SD), individual feedback, worked examples, Socratic questioning, praise, and extra time on task. These confounds likely inflated the effect.
- The mastery learning condition (which included testing and feedback but no tutoring) already showed over 1 SD gain, meaning about half the 2 sigma effect came from testing and feedback alone.
- Large-scale meta-analyses (Nickow et al., 2020, 2024) show tutoring effects are real but typically around 0.3 to 0.4 standard deviations (moving from 50th to ~64th percentile), not 2.0 SD. Matthew Kraft (2020) found most educational interventions produce effects of about 0.1 SD.
- Replacing classroom instruction with tutoring (as in Bloom's studies) produces inflated effects compared to tutoring as a supplement (the more common real-world scenario).
- Despite the debunking, the 2 sigma claim has become sticky in education and AI circles (e.g., Sal Khan's Khan Academy/Khanmigo citing it as a benchmark for AI tutors).

**Conclusion:** Tutoring is effective but modestly so (~0.3 SD). The 2 sigma claim is highly exaggerated, unreplicable science that has misled educational policy, parental spending on tutoring, and AI tutoring development goals.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"Bloom's two sigma claim had some basis in fact but it also contained elements of fiction like some science fiction" (von Hippel). "The idea that tutoring consistently raises achievement by two standard deviations is exaggerated and oversimplified. About 1/3 of a standard deviation seems to be the typical effect of an intense, well-designed program evaluated against broad tests" (von Hippel). "The two sigma problem is more like a 0.33 problem" (Dr. Luke Rowe). "Most educational interventions produce effect sizes of 0.1 standard deviation... you have a big impact through the aggregation of many small impacts" (Matthew Kraft). "Anania and Burke mixed a potent cocktail of interventions that included tutoring, training, and coaching in effective instructional practices, extra time, and frequent testing, feedback, and retesting" (von Hippel).

--- SOURCE 2: University AI Academic Integrity Policy — CASRAI ---
URL: https://casrai.org/guides/university-ai-academic-integrity-policy-trends

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This CASRAI guide (last updated 23 July 2026) documents how universities have shifted from blanket bans on generative AI tools toward tiered permission frameworks and disclosure requirements. Between 2023 and 2026, most institutions moved through a common arc: initial prohibition, then a shift toward conditional, task-specific frameworks. Blanket bans proved difficult to enforce due to AI-detection false positives and didn't account for how AI tools are used differently across disciplines.

Tiered policies, exemplified by Carnegie Mellon University's Eberly Center (which offers six sample policy statements ranging from full prohibition to conditional use), specify permission by tool, task, assignment, or course stage. The University of Chicago uses a four-tier system (prohibited, permitted with authorization, permitted with citation, broadly allowed), and UCLA treats unauthorized AI use like unauthorized human assistance.

The AI Assessment Scale (AIAS), developed by Leon Furze and Mike Perkins, provides a shared five-level framework from "no AI" to "full AI" for assignment-level communication. Disclosure requirements mirror research-integrity norms: students must report which tool (including version), what task it was used for, and sometimes the prompts and outputs. Data privacy has emerged as a separate but related policy axis, with institutions restricting sensitive data from consumer AI tools and offering institutionally licensed alternatives.

AI-detection tools remain part of enforcement but are treated cautiously due to false-positive problems, particularly for non-native English writers. Institutional guidance now treats detector results as one input requiring corroboration, not standalone proof. For research administrators, key takeaways include: design tiered frameworks with disclosure and oversight, consider data privacy as a distinct compliance concern, and recognize that AI-detection tools have limitations that should be reflected in policy language.
</summary>

<summary>
The University of North America (UoNA) has established a comprehensive Student AI Policy governing the use of Artificial Intelligence tools in academic work. **Core Principles:**
- Academic integrity is paramount; using AI to complete assignments or exams without permission is considered cheating
- Instructors have final authority to set AI rules for their courses; if not explicitly allowed, AI use is prohibited by default
- Any permitted AI use must be transparently disclosed and properly cited

**Prohibited Uses:** Submitting AI-generated work as one's own, using AI on exams or restricted assessments, automating programming assignments, failing to disclose AI use, and violating copyright via AI.

**Consequences of Violations:** Range from failing grade on an assignment to course failure, probation, suspension, or expulsion for serious or repeated offenses.

--- SOURCE 22: Assessment reform for the age of artificial intelligence ---
URL: https://www.teqsa.gov.au/sites/default/files/2023-09/assessment-reform-age-artificial-intelligence-discussion-paper.pdf

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This document, "Assessment Reform for the Age of Artificial Intelligence," authored by Jason M. Lodge and colleagues, was commissioned by TEQSA in November 2023 to guide Australian higher education institutions in reforming assessment practices in response to generative AI. It argues that bans on AI are oversimplified and that assessment must evolve to address both risks (academic integrity) and opportunities (preparing students for an AI-ubiquitous world). The document builds on the foundational "Assessment 2020" propositions and aligns with the Higher Education Standards Framework.

**Guiding Principles:**
1. Assessment should equip students to participate ethically in an AI-ubiquitous society.
2. Trustworthy judgements require multiple, inclusive, and contextualised approaches to assessment.

**Five Key Propositions for Assessment Reform:**
1. **Appropriate, authentic engagement with AI** – Assessment should foster critical, ethical, and productive use of AI aligned with disciplinary values.
2. **Systemic program-level approach** – Assessment design should span entire programs (not just individual units) to allow multiple methods and integrated tasks.
3. **Emphasis on the process of learning** – Assessment should reveal thinking, judgement, and decision-making processes that AI cannot easily simulate.
4. **Collaboration with peers and AI** – Students should work appropriately with each other and AI, with clear boundaries articulated.
5. **Security at meaningful points across a program** – Key assessment moments (e.g., capstones) should be secured to assure learning outcomes, rather than attempting to secure all tasks.

The document emphasizes that reform is not prescriptive but offers a "compass" for direction. It calls for inclusive stakeholder discussions (students, educators, accreditors, First Nations peoples) and acknowledges challenges including workload, capability building, and accreditation barriers. The report was developed through expert collaboration at a TEQSA-hosted forum in August 2023, with additional public consultation.
</summary>

--- SOURCE 1: Perceptions and Use of AI Chatbots among Students in Higher Education: A Scoping Review of Empirical Studies ---
URL: https://www.mdpi.com/2227-7102/14/8/922

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a scoping review published in Education Sciences (2024) by Schei, Møgelvang, and Ludvigsen from Western Norway University of Applied Sciences. The review analyzes 24 empirical articles published between 1 January 2022 and 5 September 2023 on students' perceptions and use of AI chatbots (like ChatGPT, Copilot, Gemini, Claude) in higher education. The study used a five-stage scoping review methodology.

**Key Findings:**

**Geographic & Disciplinary Distribution:** Research is concentrated in Asia, with STEM disciplines (computer science, programming, engineering) being predominant. Mixed methods were the most common research approach.

**Positive Perceptions:** Students perceive AI chatbots as highly useful, motivating, and easy to use—serving as personal task assistants, providing immediate feedback, and helping with writing, coding, and academic tasks. This aligns with the Technology Acceptance Model (TAM) and Unified Theory of Acceptance and Use of Technology (UTAUT) frameworks.

**Concerns:** Students worry about accuracy and reliability of AI responses, potential negative impacts on learning, critical thinking, creativity, academic integrity, and plagiarism. There is a recognized tension between surface-level use (shortcuts) and deep learning approaches.

**Learning Processes:** Students use AI chatbots for diverse, purpose-driven tasks including brainstorming, summarizing, coding, problem-solving, writing support, and language learning. The review concludes that while positive attitudes and critical use prevail, addressing students' concerns is crucial for responsible AI integration in higher education.
</summary>

This article by Professor Keith Lee of SIAI examines the current state of AI productivity in education, arguing that while AI tools produce real efficiency gains, the benefits are uneven, adoption is shallow, and achieving net improvements requires workflow redesign, training, and guardrails.

**Key Findings:**

- **Modest but real gains:** Late 2024 surveys show U.S. workers using generative AI saved ~5.4% of weekly hours, translating to ~1.1% workforce-wide productivity. For a 40-hour week, this is roughly 2 hours saved.
- **Uneven benefits:** AI productivity gains are strongest for novice/less-experienced workers (e.g., ~14-15% improvement in customer support, largest for juniors). Benefits are significant on well-defined tasks but weaker or adverse on complex, judgment-heavy problems.
- **Shallow adoption:** Only 23% of employed U.S. adults used AI for work in the past week; ~30% of ChatGPT usage is work-related. Deep, regular use remains low.
- **Requirements beyond tools:** Gains require high-quality data, redesigned workflows, training, and robust safeguards. Integration costs, oversight, and change management consume resources. Hallucination risks, privacy regulations, and curriculum alignment remain challenges.
- **Macro context:** U.S. labor productivity grew ~2.3% in 2024 and 1.5% year-over-year by Q2 2025 — an uptick, but not a dramatic AI-driven shift.

**Practical 18-Month Agenda:**

1. Identify 3 workflows where AI can improve time and quality (e.g., formative feedback on drafts, generating aligned practice items, triaging student services).
2. Establish "gold standard" baselines without AI, then insert AI for repetitive tasks — not to replace human judgment.
3. Use retrieval-augmented generation for course content; require human review for high-stakes decisions (final grades, progression).
4. Procure complementary tools (training, prompt libraries, LMS integration, safe retrieval APIs).
5. Run small cross-functional pilots as mini-randomized controlled trials: define metrics, gather baselines, run for a term, publish methods.
6. Measure net costs (computing, licensing, hidden labor for redesign/review).
7. Track outcomes: hours returned to instruction, grading variability reduction, student support response times, error rates in AI-assisted outputs.

**Conclusion:** The 1.1% productivity boost is modest but sufficient if reinvested into feedback, course clarity, and student support. The key is targeting "upper-junior" levels, routine tasks that free expert time, and aligning incentives for deep use in impactful workflows.
