# Using AI and technology in education to improve pupil outcomes and reduce staff workload

The Department for Education (DfE), is working with the Department for Science, Innovation and Technology to build the foundations for the safe and effective use of technology and AI to improve outcomes and productivity.

## Our goal

All schools and colleges have the right technology to support pupils and staff, help staff raise standards and tackle the attainment gap to deliver better educational outcomes. This will include AI powered tutoring tools that could support up to 450,000 disadvantaged pupils.

## What this means for you

*This initiative applies in England only.*

If you’re a teacher or leader, you’ll benefit from:

* **Support to make decisions on what works for your pupils**: you’ll be able to access evidence on the quality and impact of technology to guide decisions on what works best.
* **A manageable workload:** safe and reliable technology, including high-speed internet and tools to support administration and planning.
* **Confidence in using new technology:** updated online training materials to use AI safely and effectively.

## Our progress so far

### **************Since 2023: accelerating gigabit internet roll out to schools**************

DfE is working with providers, jointly funded by DSIT and DfE, to accelerate high speed internet rollout to all schools. The programme funds fibre infrastructure for schools who wouldn’t otherwise be connected by commercial rollout.

### **************January 2025: launche**************d pilot of the EdTech Evidence Board

In partnership with the Chartered College of Teaching, DfE launched the EdTech Evidence Board pilot to explore how we effectively build evidence of EdTech products that work well, helping education settings feel confident that they are choosing products that work well for them and for their classrooms.

### **************May 2025: launched DfE ‘test beds’**************

DfE launched the Edtech Impact Testbed programme for schools and colleges. This programme is designed for schools to test technology tools and share real evidence of the impact they have on reducing workload for teachers, improving learner outcomes and inclusivity.

### ****************June 2025: ran hackathons to test impact of content store on AI performance****************

DfE worked with teachers and Edtech providers to test a prototype ‘content store’. This DfE and DSIT joint funded platform stores educational content that can support development of AI applications. The hackathons tested how this content improved performance of AI for education, demonstrating the potential for teachers and schools and providing insights to further improve the content store service.

### ****************June 2025: published training materials on using AI in education****************

School and college staff now have access to guidance and support that helps them understand how to use AI safely and effectively in their classrooms.

### ********************August 2025: set the expectation for schools to meet six core digital and technology standards********************

DfE set out six digital standards schools will need to reach by 2030; broadband internet, wireless network, network switching, digital leadership and governance, filtering and monitoring, and cyber security – driving a safe and reliable technology foundation that will enable all schools to realise the benefits of AI.

### ******************November 2025: published the ‘Technology in Schools’ survey report******************

The Technology in Schools report sets out how schools currently plan, implement, and use technology, including artificial intelligence (AI), to support learning in schools today.

### **************January 2026: hosted the AI in Education Summit************** and published updated generative AI product safety standards

The UK hosted an international high-level summit on generative AI in education in 2026, bringing together education leaders from across the globe to create a collective view on how we will develop effective and responsible AI for use in education.

### ****************Early 2026: launched Schools white paper****************

The Schools White Paper sets out a clear vision to support the safe and effective use of digital technology in schools. This is an important opportunity to ensure that the benefits of AI are realised alongside robust measures to keep learners safe. It also places AI in its wider context, reaffirming that teachers remain at the heart of classroom practice. It will ensure that it is education professionals who determine how and when technology can enhance learning, inclusion and engagement whilst recognising that technology use must be balanced alongside a wider, rich educational experience.

## What we’re planning to do next

### ****************Across 2026, DSIT’s incubator for AI (i.AI) and DfE will:****************

* **Develop sovereign education benchmarks, guided by an educational AI taskforce:**the benchmarks will provide a consistent, trusted framework for evaluating whether AI tools used in the UK education system are grounded in high-quality, curriculum-aligned content and reflect national expectations for pedagogy, safety, accessibility, and inclusion.

* **Co-design and trial AI tutoring tools:** work with educators, experts and developers to co-design and trial AI tutoring tools that support pupils’ learning and strengthen teaching by providing better information about how each pupil is progressing. This will help them focus their expertise where it’s needed most. These tools will be curriculum-aligned, safe-by-design, and tested through in-school trials to ensure they deliver real educational value.

## More information

For more information about this work, read:   
  
[Generative artificial intelligence (AI) in education](https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/generative-artificial-intelligence-in-education)  
[Technology in schools survey report: 2024 to 2025](https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/technology-in-schools-survey-report-2024-to-2025)  
[Meeting digital and technology standards in schools and colleges](https://www.gov.uk/guidance/meeting-digital-and-technology-standards-in-schools-and-colleges)  
  
To find further relevant links to our policy work, read about [using technology in education](https://www.gov.uk/government/collections/using-technology-in-education).

You are tasked with summarizing the raw content of a webpage retrieved from a web search. Your goal is to create a summary that preserves the most important information from the original web page. This summary will be used by a downstream research agent, so it's crucial to maintain the key details without losing essential information.

Here is the raw content of the webpage:

<webpage_content>
![Most Policy Initiative logo](https://mostpolicyinitiative.org/wp-content/uploads/2021/01/Logo-White-400x243.png)

# Preparing Students for AI

![](https://mostpolicyinitiative.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/02/Screenshot-2025-02-28-113506.png)

Four states have passed legislation to pilot AI curriculum, while seven states provide guidance on AI use in the classroom.

People-focused skills, more than technical, are increasingly sought-after by employers in all industries.

Programs exist to teach schoolchildren about peer-to-peer relationships and teamwork, and to encourage creativity and problem-solving.

#### **There is relatively little guidance or training for AI use in classrooms.**

Seventeen states and territories have passed legislation related to AI use in education ([NCSL 2024](https://www.ncsl.org/technology-and-communication/artificial-intelligence-2024-legislation)). [CA](https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billTextClient.xhtml?bill_id=202320240SB1288), [LA](https://legis.la.gov/legis/BillInfo.aspx?i=247280), [NY](https://assembly.state.ny.us/leg/?bn=S08308&term=2023&Summary=Y&Actions=Y), [PR](https://sutra.oslpr.org/medidas/146177), [VA](https://legacylis.virginia.gov/cgi-bin/legp604.exe?241+sum+HB1083), and [WV](https://www.wvlegislature.gov/Bill_Status/bills_text.cfm?billdoc=hb5690%20org.htm&yr=2024&sesstype=RS&i=5690) have created task forces to study the effect and implementation of AI in education, while [IA](https://www.legis.iowa.gov/docs/publications/LGE/90/SF2435.pdf), [MD](https://mgaleg.maryland.gov/mgawebsite/Legislation/Details/sb0360?ys=2024RS), [MI](https://www.legislature.mi.gov/Bills/Bill?ObjectName=2024-HB-5507), [NY](https://assembly.state.ny.us/leg/?bn=S08308&term=2023&Summary=Y&Actions=Y), and [WY](https://wyoleg.gov/Legislation/2024/HB0001) allocate funding for institutions of higher education to develop programs or data centers related to AI. [TN](https://wapp.capitol.tn.gov/apps/BillInfo/default.aspx?BillNumber=SB1711&GA=113) is the only state that has instructed districts to promulgate rules related to the use of AI by educators and students, while [CT](https://www.cga.ct.gov/2024/act/pa/pdf/2024PA-00151-R00HB-05524-PA.pdf), [SC](https://www.scstatehouse.gov/sess125_2023-2024/appropriations2024/gab5100.php), [FL](https://www.flsenate.gov/Session/Bill/2024/1361/?Tab=BillHistory), and [NE](https://nebraskalegislature.gov/bills/view_bill.php?DocumentID=55278) have allocated funds to develop and test programs for high school students relating to AI.

Education and innovation departments in [CA](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1k8kjbLRolKOB7pu5s4wh-4_CufUNJEAI/view), [OH](https://innovateohio.gov/aistrategy), [OR](https://www.oregon.gov/ode/educator-resources/teachingcontent/Documents/ODE_Generative_Artificial_Intelligence_(AI)_in_K-12_Classrooms_2023.pdf), [NC](https://www.dpi.nc.gov/press-release/ncdpi-generative-ai-implementation-recommendations-and-considerations-pk-13-public-schools/download?attachment), [VA](https://www.education.virginia.gov/media/governorvirginiagov/secretary-of-education/pdf/AI-Education-Guidelines.pdf), [WA](https://ospi.k12.wa.us/student-success/resources-subject-area/human-centered-artificial-intelligence-schools), and [WV](https://wvde.us/wp-content/uploads/2024/03/30438-WVDE-AI-Guidance-v1.pdf) have released guidance relating to AI in the classroom, however these vary widely in their focus and audience ([Roschelle et al 2024](https://digitalpromise.dspacedirect.org/server/api/core/bitstreams/654a148a-25c4-4eec-bb8e-2fd1948130a5/content)). The Department of Education developed a federal AI toolkit in response to [Executive Order 14110](https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2023/11/01/2023-24283/safe-secure-and-trustworthy-development-and-use-of-artificial-intelligence), which has since been removed ([U.S. Department of Education 2024](https://tech.ed.gov/files/2024/10/ED-OET-EdLeaders-AI-Toolkit-10.24.24.pdf)). Despite these resources, instruction on AI largely depends on districts, schools, and individual teachers, and teacher training programs are largely not addressing AI instruction and use by teachers or students ([Dusseaul & Lee 2023](https://crpe.org/ai-disrupt-ed-13-states/), [Weiner et al 2024](https://crpe.org/wp-content/uploads/Teacher-Prep-AI-2024.pdf)).

Relatively few teachers use AI in their own work. In the fall of 2023, 18% of teachers reported using AI ([Diliberti et al 2024](https://www.rand.org/pubs/research_reports/RRA956-21.html)). Similarly, school administrators focus more on increasing teachers’ use of AI for grading and lesson plans, rather than teaching students about AI or developing policies for student use ([Court et al 2024](https://pages.eab.com/rs/732-GKV-655/images/2024%20Voice%20of%20the%20Superintendent%20Executive%20Brief.pdf?version=0)). Despite this, 51% of teens and young adults report using generative AI, with 46% using it for help with schoolwork and 55% using it to obtain information generally ([Green et al 2024](https://www.commonsensemedia.org/sites/default/files/research/report/teen-and-young-adult-perspectives-on-generative-ai.pdf)). However, only 4% report being daily users.

#### **Workers need people-focused skills.**

As tasks are increasingly automated, even before the implementation of current Large Language Model (LLM) and generative AI technologies, employers are focusing on workers' ability to navigate human interactions on the job ([Leopold et al 2018](https://www3.weforum.org/docs/WEF_Future_of_Jobs_2018.pdf), [Lyu & Liu 2021](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.apenergy.2021.117307)). Surveys of employers noted that while technical AI skills are useful, the value of “soft skills” has increased, as they are harder or impossible to automate ([America Succeeds 2021](https://americasucceeds.org/wp-content/uploads/2021/04/AmericaSucceeds-DurableSkills-NationalFactSheet-2021.pdf), [Cardon et al 2023](https://doi.org/10.1177/23294906231208166)). Employees who can communicate, manage conflict, work in teams, and who are punctual, creative, problem-solving self-starters are in high demand across industries (**Figure 1**). In MO, the top 5 soft skills were 3.4 times more likely to be requested in job postings than the top 5 hard skills, with 1.2 million jobs demanding soft skills ([America Succeeds 2021](https://americasucceeds.org/wp-content/uploads/2021/04/AmericaSucceeds-DurableSkills-NationalFactSheet-2021.pdf)). Communication skills were the top requested soft skill for MO jobs in 2021.

Recent studies have highlighted how reliance on AI can reduce workers’ creativity and problem-solving capabilities ([Lee HP et al 2025](https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/research/uploads/prod/2025/01/lee_2025_ai_critical_thinking_survey.pdf?ref=404media.co)). Students who used AI were identified as lacking time, curiosity, and interest in a topic ([Al Afnan et al 2024](https://doi.org/10.37965/jait.2024.0496)). However, these outcomes can be mitigated by targeted use of AI in classrooms combined with a focus on soft skill development.

**Schools are equipped to teach both people-focused and technical skills.**

Behavioral management tools are used to teach conflict management and resolution (for more information see [Classroom Management Strategies](https://mostpolicyinitiative.org/science-note/classroom-management-strategies/)). Project based learning (PBL) systems encourage students to work together to solve problems, which fosters the development of soft skills ([Buck Institute for Education 2024](https://www.pblworks.org/what-is-pbl)). PBL has been shown to be effective particularly in science and social studies classrooms, and has been used to teach about AI and digital literacy ([Condliffe et al 2017](https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED578933), [Owens & Hite 2020](https://doi.org/10.1080/02635143.2020.1778663), [Yue Yim & Su 2024](https://doi.org/10.1007/s40692-023-00304-9)).

The social emotional learning (SEL) and related frameworks address people-focused skill development, including maintaining relationships, managing emotions, communication, and empathy ([Committee for Children 2019](https://www.cfchildren.org/wp-content/uploads/policy-advocacy/what-and-why-one-pager.pdf), [Niu et al 2022](https://doi.org/10.3390/su14137947), [Gimbert et al 2023](https://doi.org/10.1177/19427751211014920)). These frameworks are already i to teach technical and people-focused skills simultaneously ([Yue Yim & Su 2024](https://doi.org/10.1007/s40692-023-00304-9)). As with any educational framework, success depends on teacher training and program adherence ([Bailey et al 2019](https://doi.org/10.1177/0031721719827549), [Gimbert et al 2021](https://doi.org/10.1177/19427751211014920))

![](http://mostpolicyinitiative.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/02/Screenshot-2025-02-25-101927-327x400.png)

![](http://mostpolicyinitiative.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/02/Screenshot-2025-02-25-101927-327x400.png)

**Figure 1. Frequency of durable skill requirements in MO and US job postings.** Figure from [America Succeeds 2021](https://americasucceeds.org/wp-content/uploads/2021/04/AmericaSucceeds-DurableSkills-NationalFactSheet-2021.pdf). 92 million national and 2.3 million MO job postings were analyzed from 2019-2020 to assess key skills requested by employers. Durable skills were found in more than half of all MO job postings, with communication as the top required skill.

**References**

Al Afnan MA, Dishari S, MohdZuki SF (2024) Developing Soft Skills in the Artificial Intelligence Era: Communication, Business Writing, and Composition Skills. *Journal of Artificial Intelligence and Technology*. 4(4): 305-317. <https://doi.org/10.37965/jait.2024.0496>

args.summary:
This webpage from the Most Policy Initiative discusses the current state of AI in education, focusing on state legislation, guidance gaps, and the growing importance of "people-focused" (soft) skills over technical AI skills in the workforce.

**Key points:**

- **State AI Legislation:** 17 states/territories have passed AI-related education legislation. Six states (CA, LA, NY, PR, VA, WV) created task forces to study AI in education. Five states (IA, MD, MI, NY, WY) allocated funding for higher education AI programs. TN instructed districts to create rules on AI use by educators and students. Four states (CT, SC, FL, NE) funded AI programs for high school students.

- **Guidance Gap:** Seven states (CA, OH, OR, NC, VA, WA, WV) have released AI classroom guidance, but these vary widely. The U.S. Department of Education's federal AI toolkit (from Executive Order 14110) has since been removed. Teacher training programs largely do not address AI instruction.

- **Teacher and Student AI Use:** In fall 2023, only 18% of teachers reported using AI. School administrators focus more on using AI for grading/lesson plans than teaching students about AI. However, 51% of teens and young adults report using generative AI (46% for schoolwork, 55% for information), but only 4% are daily users.

- **Soft Skills Demand:** Employers increasingly value "people-focused" skills (communication, teamwork, conflict management, creativity, problem-solving) over technical AI skills, as these are harder to automate. In Missouri, the top 5 soft skills were 3.4 times more likely requested than the top 5 hard skills, with 1.2 million jobs demanding soft skills. Communication was the top soft skill.

- **AI's Impact on Skills:** Recent studies show AI reliance can reduce critical thinking, creativity, and problem-solving abilities. However, targeted AI use combined with soft skill development can mitigate these effects.

- **Existing Educational Frameworks:** Schools already have tools to teach both skills—project-based learning (PBL) and social-emotional learning (SEL) frameworks. Success depends on teacher training and program adherence.

# Uneven Adoption of Artificial Intelligence Tools Among U.S. Teachers and Principals in the 2023–2024 School Year

[Julia H. Kaufman](/about/people/k/kaufman_julia_h.html), [Ashley Woo](/about/people/w/woo_ashley.html), [Joshua Eagan](/pubs/authors/e/eagan_joshua.html), [Sabrina Lee](/pubs/authors/l/lee_sohyun.html), [Emma B. Kassan](/about/people/k/kassan_emma_b.html)

![Cover: Uneven Adoption of Artificial Intelligence Tools Among U.S. Teachers and Principals in the 2023–2024 School Year](/content/rand/pubs/research_reports/RRA134-25/_jcr_content/par/product.fit.264x264.jpeg/1742476865831.jpeg)

Using survey data from the RAND American Educator Panels, the authors examine the use of artificial intelligence (AI) tools and products among teachers and principals in kindergarten through grade 12 (K–12) and the provision of school guidance on the use of AI during the 2023–2024 school year. The results indicate that 25 percent of surveyed teachers used AI tools for their instructional planning or teaching. That said, English language arts and science teachers were nearly twice as likely to report using AI tools as mathematics teachers or elementary teachers of all subjects. Nearly 60 percent of U.S. principals reported using AI tools for their work. Teachers and principals in higher-poverty schools were less likely to report using AI tools than those in lower-poverty schools. In addition, principals in high-poverty schools reported providing guidance for use of AI less often than their counterparts in lower-poverty schools. These results have implications for district and school leaders, as well as AI tool developers and researchers.

# The Rising Use of Artificial Intelligence in K-12 Education

On December 13, 2023, the Pennsylvania Advisory Committee to the U.S. Commission on Civil Rights adopted a proposal to study the rising use of [artificial intelligence (AI) in K-12 education](https://conta.cc/3OVK8O5). The focus of the Committee’s inquiry was to examine how AI algorithms are developed, and the impact they can have on either reducing or exacerbating existing disparities (or creating new disparities) in K-12 classrooms based on federally protected classes. The Committee also examined potential solutions and recommendations to remediate identified concerns.

  This AI Policy Template from the Alabama State Department of Education (ALSDE) released in June 2024, provides guidance for Local Education Agencies (LEAs) in Alabama to develop and implement AI policies in K-12 education. The document emerged from the ALSDE AI Summit in November 2023 and subsequent sessions, representing a collaborative effort among various education stakeholders.

  Key Areas Covered:

  1. Eight foundational pillars: Strategy, Governance, Data Privacy and Security, Procurement, Implementation, Competency Development, Risk Management, and Utility and Effectiveness

  2. Clear definitions of AI terminology and systems

  3. Comprehensive guidance on AI usage in educational settings

  4. Data privacy and security compliance requirements

  5. Procurement and implementation guidelines

  6. Risk management framework based on NIST standards

  7. Detailed rules for responsible AI use by all stakeholders

  Unique Aspects:

  1. Alabama-specific context: The template is tailored to Alabama's educational system, with input from diverse stakeholders including the Governor's office, state education associations, and local education agencies.

  2. Strong emphasis on human oversight:

  - Explicitly states that AI systems will supplement, not replace, human instruction

  - Requires human verification of AI-generated content and grading

  - Mandates human-in-the-loop development in AI systems

  3. Detailed data protection measures:

  - Includes specific contract language for AI vendors (Appendix A)

  - Prohibits unauthorized use of school data for training new AI models

  - Requires explicit documentation and approval processes for any AI system training

  4. Implementation accountability:

  - Requires establishment of AI Governance Committees

  - Mandates regular compliance audits

  - Requires corrective action plans for any identified issues

  5. Comprehensive usage guidelines:

  - Clear rules for citing AI use

  - Verification requirements for AI-generated content

  - Process for contesting AI-generated grades

  - Restrictions on AI-powered surveillance and behavioral tracking

  The template stands out for its practical approach to AI integration while maintaining strong protections for student data and emphasizing the primacy of human judgment in education.

  This AI guidance from the Alaska Department of Education & Early Development (AKDEED), developed with the Alaska AI K12 Advisory Group, provides recommendations for districts implementing AI in K-12 education. The framework emphasizes flexible guidance over strict mandates, helping districts move beyond blanket AI bans toward balanced, responsible implementation.

  Key Areas Covered:

  1. Seven guiding principles for AI integration: Human-Centered, Fair Access, Transparency, Oversight, Security, Ethical Use, and Cultural Responsiveness
  2. AI definitions and educational context, including GenAI, LLMs, and popular chatbots
  3. Academic integrity framework addressing plagiarism and citation requirements
  4. Data privacy and security protocols aligned with FERPA and CIPA
  5. Implementation guidance for policy development, vendor vetting, and procurement
  6. AI literacy programs with curated resources for educators and students
  7. Risk management addressing bias, misinformation, and AI limitations

  Unique Aspects:

  1. Alaska-specific context: Addresses remote and rural connectivity challenges, references 2023 DEED survey on student technology access, and links to existing Alaska district policies.
  2. Strong cultural responsiveness emphasis: Aligns with Alaska Standards for Culturally Responsive Schools, requires engagement with diverse stakeholders including elders and community members, addresses algorithmic bias, and mandates that AI tools affirm rather than diminish the diverse cultures of Alaska. Warns against misinterpretation, misappropriation, or exclusion of crucial local context.
  3. Comprehensive digital equity framework: Acknowledges Alaska's significant broadband disparities, emphasizes AI literacy education is as critical as tool access, and provides strategies to actively mitigate the digital divide.
  4. Flexible approach: Designed as "recommendations and considerations" rather than mandates, encourages moving beyond blanket bans, and acknowledges that robust evidence on AI effectiveness is still emerging.
  5. Implementation guidance with external resources: Recommends districts develop key documents, references effective prompting frameworks, provides links to external resources for educators and students, and directs users to a companion resource website for tailored support.
  6. Transparency modeled in practice: Includes AI Use Disclaimer acknowledging the document was drafted with AI assistance while emphasizing extensive human oversight, demonstrating the human-centered principle in action.

  The framework stands out for balancing innovation with protection while addressing Alaska's unique geographic and cultural context through flexible guidance that respects local autonomy.

  This comprehensive guidance document from the Massachusetts Department of Elementary and Secondary Education provides voluntary guidance for districts exploring or implementing artificial intelligence (AI) in K-12 education. It covers key areas such as understanding AI types and capabilities, ethical principles for responsible use, implementation frameworks, equity considerations, legal compliance, AI literacy (teaching both about and with AI), academic integrity, and district operations. The guidance emphasizes that AI integration is a change management process requiring transparency, human oversight, bias mitigation, and data privacy while providing practical tools for educators and school leaders to integrate AI thoughtfully and equitably.

  Includes:

  1. **Five core ethical principles** that serve as the foundation for all AI decisions: data privacy & security, transparency & accountability, bias awareness & mitigation, human oversight & educator judgment, and academic integrity.
  2. **Distinction between teaching ABOUT AI and teaching WITH AI**, with teaching about AI focused on understanding how AI works, its societal impacts, bias, and ethics across all roles (students, educators, families, community partners), while teaching with AI emphasizes using tools to enhance instruction while maintaining human-centered learning.
  3. **Framework addressing three digital divides** identified in the 2024 U.S. National Educational Technology Plan: access divide (devices, internet, assistive technology), use divide (meaningful student and educator engagement with AI), and design divide (teacher capacity to design AI-enhanced learning experiences).
  4. **Action-oriented planning tables** in each section with three columns allowing districts to identify potential action steps aligned with core commitments, document steps already taken for self-assessment, and create plans to move forward.
  5. **Explicit guidance against AI detection tools** due to unreliability and punitive effects, recommending instead trust-based, transparency-focused approaches to academic integrity that create safe spaces for disclosure and emphasize process-oriented assessment and reflection.
  6. **Cross-departmental operational guidance** extending ethical AI principles beyond instruction to district operations including budgeting and financial planning, human resources and hiring systems, data use and dashboards, and procurement and vendor management with consistent oversight.
  7. **Alignment with Massachusetts Digital Literacy and Computer Science (DLCS) Framework** and integration of AI literacy into existing curriculum standards, ensuring AI concepts are embedded across content areas rather than treated as standalone technology skills.
  8. **Collaborative development process** involving DESE's AI Task Force with representatives from 14 Massachusetts districts, partnership with ISTE+ASCD, and acknowledgment that this is living guidance requiring continuous adaptation as AI technology and educational practices evolve.

  This AI Guidance for Local Education Agencies from the Missouri Department of Elementary and Secondary Education, released as Version 1.0 for the 2025-26 school year, provides comprehensive guidance for Missouri's Local Education Agencies (LEAs) in developing and implementing AI policies in K-12 education. The document was developed collaboratively by Missouri's Computer Science Advisory Council, comprising specialists in both education and computer science from across the state.

  What stands out about Missouri's approach is their focus on practical implementation - from detailed prompt engineering guidance using AI for Education's ["Five S" model](/ai-resources/the-five-s-model) to a cyclical seven-step policy development process. They've also integrated AI guidance directly with their existing computer science education initiatives, showing how AI can complement broader digital literacy efforts.

  Like other states, Missouri aligns on core principles of data privacy, academic integrity, and AI literacy. Their guidance emphasizes human oversight and the importance of AI as a tool to enhance rather than replace educators. They've also created strong connections to resources like the Missouri School Boards' Association AI Toolkit.

  In addition to the prompt framework, Missouri has also included a few other AI for Education resources, like our [Uncovering Deepfakes](/ai-resources/uncovering-deepfakes) classroom guide and Gen AI Explainer graphic.

  **Key Areas Covered:**

  1. **Comprehensive AI Framework:**

     + Clear definitions of AI types (reactive, predictive, and generative AI)
     + Focus on AI as a tool to enhance rather than replace human intelligence
     + Emphasis on responsible implementation with human oversight
  2. **Multi-Level Challenges and Benefits Analysis:**

     + Student-level considerations (intellectual property, plagiarism risks vs. personalized learning support)
     + Building-level applications (lesson planning, data analysis vs. educator comfort levels)
     + District-level priorities (data privacy compliance, policy development vs. security concerns)
     + Stakeholder engagement (parent/community concerns vs. accessibility benefits)
  3. **Best Practices Implementation:**

     + Four core principles: Responsible Implementation, Transparency, Rigor, and Curiosity
     + Strong emphasis on human oversight and critical evaluation of AI outputs
     + Guidelines for ensuring human decision-making remains central
  4. **Professional Development and AI Integration:**

     + Eight focus areas for professional development (ethics, access, productivity, pedagogical practices)
     + Detailed prompt engineering guidance with the "Five S" model and "Who, What, Why, Where" framework
     + Emphasis on AI literacy across all grade levels and curriculum areas
  5. **Policy Development Framework:**

     + Cyclical seven-step policy process (Purpose, Compliance, Knowledge, Balance, Integrity, Agency, Evaluation)
     + Comprehensive regulatory compliance (FERPA, COPPA, IDEA, CIPA, Section 504, ADA)
     + Detailed procurement guidelines and vendor evaluation criteria
     + Focus on addressing fairness, bias, and equitable access
  6. **Practical Implementation Tools:**

     + Specific AI use guidelines for different stakeholder groups
     + Academic integrity expectations and honor code recommendations
     + Resource compilation including professional development opportunities through DESE

  **Unique Missouri Elements:**

  + Integration with existing DESE Computer Science Education initiatives
  + State-specific legislative context (Missouri Revised Statutes Section 171.011)
  + Emphasis on local control while providing statewide guidance framework
  + Connection to Missouri School Boards' Association AI Toolkit
  + Reference to DESE Computer Science webpage and listserv for ongoing support

  The document positions Missouri as taking a measured, educationally-focused approach to AI integration, emphasizing local autonomy within a supportive state framework while prioritizing student outcomes and ethical implementation.

This webpage from AI for Education provides a comprehensive compilation of state-level AI guidance for K-12 schools across the United States. As of October 28, 2025, 34 states (and Puerto Rico) have issued official guidance or policy on AI use in K-12 education. The resource includes summaries and links to full guidance documents for each state.

**States Covered (with summary of key elements):**

- **Alabama** (June 2024): AI Policy Template for LEAs with eight foundational pillars, strong emphasis on human oversight, detailed data protection measures, and NIST-based risk management framework.
- **Alaska** (October 2025): Flexible guidance emphasizing cultural responsiveness, digital equity addressing rural/remote connectivity challenges, and AI framework aligned with Alaska Standards for Culturally Responsive Schools.
- **Arizona**: Comprehensive guide from Arizona Institute for Education and the Economy focusing on human agency, AI literacy, and ethical implementation with three-stage recommendations.
- **California** (September 2023): CDE guidance emphasizing AI literacy, equity, and integrating AI skills with computer science standards, including the "5 Big Ideas of AI" framework.
- **Colorado** (August 2024): Roadmap emphasizing local control, equitable access, transparent policies, and inclusion of student voices with tools like the "If and How Checklist."
- **Connecticut**: Guidance from Commission for Educational Technology focusing on responsible AI use, ethical considerations, social/emotional risks, and equity.
- **Delaware**: DOE guidance using SAMR model for AI integration with version tracking and emphasis on continuous review.
- **Georgia** (January 2025, updated June 2025): Framework with "Traffic Light" system (Red/Yellow/Green) for AI use, comprehensive evaluation rubric, and seven core ethical principles.
- **Hawaii**: Concise employee recommendations emphasizing ethical AI use, avoiding AI detection tools, and citing AI-generated content.
- **Indiana**: Guidance emphasizing AI literacy integrated with computer science, personalization, and security compliance.
- **Kentucky**: KDE guidance with "Policy-in-Action Spotlights," three paradigms for AI (directed, supported, empowered), and connection to digital citizenship.
- **Louisiana** (Fall 2024): LDOE framework with four-component cyclical approach, four-tiered AI integration system (Empowered/Enhanced/Assisted/Prohibited), and detailed technical implementation guidance.
- **Maine**: Interactive toolkit organized around "KEEP THE HUMAN IN AI" principle, rejecting technology prohibitions, with ROOTS leadership framework.
- **Massachusetts**: Voluntary guidance with five core ethical principles, distinction between teaching ABOUT and teaching WITH AI, addressing three digital divides, and explicit guidance against AI detection tools.
- **Michigan** (Michigan Virtual, endorsed by MDE): Three-stage maturity framework (Investigating→Implementing→Innovating) across eight domains with planning guide, teacher guide, and parent communication resources.
- **Minnesota**: MDE guidance emphasizing responsible AI use, centering people, advancing equity, and starting with existing guidance.
- **Mississippi**: MDE guidance organized around five digital learning components with emphasis on human oversight.

# Embracing AI in higher education: university policies on generative AI

by [PlagPointer Research Team](https://www.plagiarismchecker.net/author/will/ "View all posts by PlagPointer Research Team")

## Summary:

* Universities like Oxford, Cambridge, Imperial, Harvard, Stanford, and MIT now allow generative AI use but set clear guidelines to protect [academic integrity](https://www.plagiarismchecker.net/articles/why-is-academic-integrity-important/).
* Policies emphasise transparency, responsible use, ethical considerations, and clearly forbid AI [misuse](https://www.plagiarismchecker.net/articles/can-social-networking-promote-plagiarism/) in graded assessments.
* Universities must reflect on educational goals, define precise rules for AI usage, and provide scenarios and clear example clauses in their policies.
* Effective AI policies require ongoing training, transparency, regular reviews, and practical education for students and staff.

Artificial intelligence has quickly become a fixture in education. Tools like ChatGPT and Bard are raising both excitement and concern across campuses. Many universities initially feared that generative AI would fuel plagiarism or undermine learning. However, a growing number of institutions have realised that ***if you can’t beat them, join them*.** Rather than banning these tools, universities in the UK and US are crafting new policies to integrate AI into teaching and learning. At the same time, they are instituting measures to safeguard academic integrity and privacy. These policies generally encourage responsible use of AI and emphasise transparency and [ethics](https://www.plagiarismchecker.net/articles/define-plagiarism/). The goal is to let students and staff benefit from AI’s capabilities without compromising academic standards. We now examine how several universities are approaching generative AI. This overview highlights key guidelines and notable quotes from each institution’s policy.

## Existing University policies

### University of Oxford

The University of Oxford permits students to use generative AI tools to support their learning. It states:

> *“You can make use of generative AI tools (e.g. ChatGPT, Claude, Bing Chat and Google Bard) in developing your academic skills to support your studies. Your ongoing critical appraisal of outputs by reviewing them for accuracy will maximise the potential for AI outputs to be a useful additional tool to support you in your studies.”*

Oxford’s guidance acknowledges that AI can assist with tasks like brainstorming or practice [questions](https://www.plagiarismchecker.net/articles/plagiarism-faqs/) for exams. But it also enforces strict rules to uphold academic integrity. At the same time, it stresses that AI cannot replace human critical thinking. Students must not present AI-generated material as their own work. [The policy warns](https://www.ox.ac.uk/students/academic/guidance/skills/ai-study),

> *“unauthorised use of AI falls under the plagiarism regulations and would be subject to academic penalties in summative assessments.”*

The university will treat any unpermitted use of ChatGPT or similar tools on an exam or final paper as [academic misconduct](https://www.plagiarismchecker.net/articles/academic-misconduct/). If an instructor or department allows AI assistance on an assignment, students should clearly acknowledge how they used the tool. This balanced approach ensures that learners can experiment with AI. They can do so as long as they remain honest and do not undermine their own skill development.

### University of Cambridge

The University of Cambridge has a similar stance that upholds integrity while cautiously embracing AI for learning. Cambridge’s official student guidance makes it plain that students may not use AI-generated content in graded work unless explicitly allowed. The [policy pointedly states](https://blendedlearning.cam.ac.uk/artificial-intelligence-and-education/generative-ai-and-assessment),

> *“A student using any unacknowledged content generated by artificial intelligence within a summative assessment as though it is their own work constitutes academic misconduct, unless explicitly stated otherwise in the assessment brief.”*

That rule means unless an assignment specifically permits AI, students should not rely on it in submitted work. At the same time, Cambridge encourages open discussion about AI use in independent study and formative (ungraded) tasks. The university intentionally worded its new policy to let staff and students engage with these tools more in personal study and practice. This approach invites open dialogue about appropriate use and ethical implications. It helps Cambridge consider what can be gained from AI and what might be lost through over-reliance on such tools. Cambridge is not banning AI outright. Instead, it forbids misuse in coursework but invites students to become informed about AI through guided exploration and discipline-specific norms.

### Imperial College London

Imperial [College](https://www.plagiarismchecker.net/articles/plagiarism-at-college/) London explicitly promotes effective, ethical, and transparent use of AI while drawing a firm line against misconduct. Imperial’s library guidance notes that generative AI can be a helpful starting point for research or idea generation. It advises students to use these tools critically, verify AI outputs against reliable sources, and remain mindful of the technology’s limitations. However, Imperial is unequivocal that AI must not become a shortcut in assessments. The college directs students to disclose any use of AI in coursework. [It also cautions](https://www.imperial.ac.uk/admin-services/library/learning-support/generative-ai-guidance/),

> *“if there is no explicit instruction to use generative AI tools, it would not be considered acceptable to use them to write your assessed work.”*

Using AI to write an assignment without permission is simply not acceptable. The policy equates any such attempt with contract [cheating](https://www.plagiarismchecker.net/articles/essay-cheating/) — essentially the same as paying someone else to do the assignment. Imperial even warns that departments may conduct “authenticity interviews” with students to verify that submitted work reflects the student’s own understanding. Overall, the college’s policy shows a willingness to integrate AI as a learning aid. At the same time, it demonstrates a commitment to ensure fairness and originality in evaluation.

### Harvard University

Harvard University’s approach to AI in the [classroom](https://www.plagiarismchecker.net/articles/how-teachers-can-use-ai-checker-tools-effectively-in-the-classroom/) recognises that one size does not fit all. There is no single university-wide ban or blanket rule; instead, Harvard lets each school and instructor set AI usage policies appropriate to their context. Harvard’s Faculty of Arts and Sciences (FAS) has issued broad guidelines rather than a strict edict. For example, in summer 2023 the FAS released recommendations outlining three possible approaches professors might take regarding AI in their courses.

One option is a *“maximally restrictive”* policy that bans all AI use in coursework. Another is a *“fully encouraging”* policy allowing AI tools with proper attribution. The third approach is a mixed model permitting some uses but not others. “I don’t think there is a one-size-fits-all course policy here,” [one Harvard dean explained](https://www.thecrimson.com/article/2023/9/1/fas-ai-guidance/). He emphasised that faculty should tailor AI rules to their specific learning objectives.

Harvard’s guidance urges instructors to communicate their AI expectations to students clearly and frequently. It also reminds everyone to follow existing academic integrity standards. In addition, it cautions faculty not to input student work into public AI platforms, for privacy [reasons](https://www.plagiarismchecker.net/articles/5-reasons-plagiarism-checker/). Harvard is essentially embracing AI by educating instructors and students about it. Each class can then harness AI’s benefits or impose limits as needed, rather than trying to ignore the [technology](https://www.plagiarismchecker.net/articles/5-innovative-online-learning-companies-that-will-change-education-in-the-next-5-years/).

### Stanford University

Stanford University takes a similar approach. It treats generative AI as an emerging tool to be managed through the Honor Code and course-specific policies. Stanford’s guidance makes it clear that using AI to [cheat](https://www.plagiarismchecker.net/articles/reasons-that-drive-students-to-cheat/) is unacceptable. Yet it stops short of forbidding AI entirely. By default, if a professor hasn’t explicitly said otherwise, Stanford considers AI assistance akin to help from another person. It must not cross the line into doing the student’s work. The [policy states](https://communitystandards.stanford.edu/policies-guidance%23policies-guidance-links/bca-guidance-recommendations#generative-ai-policy-guidance) that:

> *“using generative AI tools to substantially complete an assignment or exam… is not permitted.”*

Students must acknowledge any significant AI help they use, just as they would credit a human tutor. They are also encouraged to disclose it “when in doubt.” At the same time, Stanford explicitly gives individual instructors the freedom to allow or disallow AI tools in their courses. Professors might permit AI for brainstorming or drafting, or ban it for certain [assignments](https://www.plagiarismchecker.net/articles/teachers-make-it-easy-for-students-to-plagiarise/), depending on their learning goals. Stanford’s overall message is to use AI ethically and transparently. In practice, students should not evade learning by having AI produce their answers. They must always follow the specific guidelines set for each class.

### Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT)

MIT has approached AI tool use with an emphasis on responsibility, transparency, and data protection. The institute’s guidance encourages students and faculty to use generative AI in an ethical manner — which includes protecting confidential information and maintaining academic honesty. MIT’s policy urges anyone using AI for academic or research purposes to be upfront about it. [It explicitly advises](https://ist.mit.edu/ai-guidance):

*“You should disclose the use of generative AI tools for all academic, educational, and research-related uses.”*

In other words, students should mention if they use an AI assistant to help write code or a lab report. Likewise, instructors should disclose if they use AI to draft an email or quiz questions. MIT also reiterates that users are responsible for checking the accuracy of AI-generated content and for not misusing it. Furthermore, the institute warns its community not to input sensitive personal or institutional data into AI tools like ChatGPT, because those inputs may be retained externally.

While MIT does not flatly prohibit using AI, it ties its use to existing policies on academic integrity and information security. The overarching goal is to integrate AI into MIT’s environment in a principled way. MIT encourages researchers, teachers, and students to experiment and innovate with AI. But it also urges everyone to keep their eyes open to the ethical and practical implications.

## Guidance on creating AI policies

A well-crafted policy can harness AI’s benefits for teaching and learning, but it must also guard against academic misconduct. The following guide outlines key considerations and actionable steps to help institutions develop their own AI usage policies.

### Key questions to consider

Before drafting an AI policy, university leaders and educators should reflect on fundamental questions about their goals and values. For example:

* **What are our educational objectives, and how might AI support or undermine them?** (e.g. preserving critical thinking and originality versus using AI for efficiency).
* **In which contexts could AI use be beneficial or problematic?** Consider differences between formative exercises and summative assessments, and think about whether AI is appropriate in exams, assignments or research projects.
* **How will we maintain academic integrity and fairness?** Think about what counts as cheating when using AI, and how instructors or tools could detect such misuse.
* **What level of transparency do we expect from students and staff?** Decide if students must disclose any AI assistance they use. Also consider whether instructors should declare their own use of AI in teaching materials.
* **What safeguards are needed for privacy and data security?** Plan guidelines so that no one inadvertently shares personal or confidential information with AI tools.

### Tailored approaches for AI use

Different courses and disciplines may require different approaches to AI. There is no one-size-fits-all solution, so universities can adopt a range of policy stances depending on context. For instance:

* **Prohibit AI in assessments:** Some policies completely ban generative AI in coursework where core skills are at stake. For example, a writing-intensive module might forbid tools like ChatGPT for any writing task. This ensures that students produce 100% of the work themselves.
* **Allow AI with clear limits:** Other policies permit AI as a support tool in specific situations, but with conditions. An instructor might allow students to use AI for brainstorming ideas or for editing drafts. However, students must properly attribute any AI-generated content and refrain from using it in the final submission. (This approach integrates AI as a learning aid while maintaining human oversight.)
* **Embrace AI as a learning tool:** A more permissive approach encourages students and staff to use AI actively, treating it as a skill to develop. In this case, the policy still requires honesty about AI use. It also insists that students verify any AI-generated information and remain accountable for their own work. The emphasis is on teaching how to use AI responsibly, rather than forbidding it.

Whatever approach a university takes, educators should provide a rationale for it. Explaining why a course prohibits or allows AI helps students understand the policy and follow it. For example, you might highlight that the course bans AI in order to protect certain learning outcomes. Conversely, note if the course allows it in order to foster innovation.

### Clear and transparent guidelines

An effective AI policy must be unambiguous so that everyone understands the rules. It should define what counts as “generative AI” and specify which tools or types of assistance fall under its scope. The policy needs to spell out where students may use AI and where they may not. It should also describe what constitutes misuse. For example, the policy can state that presenting AI-generated material as one’s own work is a violation. The document must outline what [consequences](https://www.plagiarismchecker.net/articles/the-consequences-of-plagiarism-an-awakening/) will follow if such misuse occurs.

The policy should also instruct students on how to acknowledge any allowed AI assistance. For example, it could require adding an “AI usage” statement or a citation to note which tool they used. It is also wise to include a note on data privacy. The policy should caution users never to input sensitive personal or institutional data into public AI tools.

To illustrate, a policy document might include statements like:

> “Submitting AI-generated content as your own work will constitute academic misconduct, unless an assessment explicitly permits it.”
>
> “Students may use generative AI tools to support research and drafting. However, they must credit any AI contributions (e.g. in a footnote or appendix), and they remain responsible for the accuracy and integrity of the final submission.”
>
> “If you use AI tools, you are accountable for checking the validity of the AI-generated information. You must ensure it does not contain errors or bias.”

Clear wording like the above leaves little room for confusion. It sets a clear expectation that students use AI only within allowed bounds. This reinforces that honesty and quality are non-negotiable.

### Training and ongoing review

Introducing a new AI policy is only the first step. Universities should also educate their communities about the guidelines and the proper use of AI. This can include workshops or tutorials for both staff and students on how to use generative AI ethically and effectively. Instructors, for example, might demonstrate acceptable versus unacceptable uses of AI in their discipline, so students see practical scenarios. Universities should also remind everyone about the risks of AI, such as false information or inherent biases. Users need to stay critical of AI outputs.

Furthermore, building awareness of data privacy is essential. The policy rollout should highlight that no one should paste exam questions, student assignments, or other confidential data into public AI tools. Doing so could breach privacy or [copyright](https://www.plagiarismchecker.net/articles/plagiarism-and-copyright/). Training users and raising AI literacy ensures that the policy is not just a set of rules. Instead, it becomes part of a broader educational effort.

Finally, universities should treat an AI policy as a living document. University leaders ought to review and update the rules periodically as technology advances and classroom experiences evolve. Gathering feedback from students and faculty can help identify what is working or what needs clarification. With regular re-evaluation, the policy will remain relevant and effective. It will continue to balance innovation in teaching with the fundamental principles of academic integrity.

## Wrapping up…

These examples show that leading universities are moving toward an “embrace with caution” philosophy on generative AI. Across the board, institutions agree that completely outlawing AI is neither practical nor pedagogically sound. Instead, they are developing policies that let students and staff leverage AI tools while upholding honesty, critical thinking, and privacy. Common threads include requiring students to acknowledge AI assistance, forbidding unapproved use of AI on graded work, and providing guidance on using AI productively rather than as a crutch. As [Yale University’s](https://provost.yale.edu/news/guidelines-use-generative-ai-tools) provost put it, the academic community will *“embrace technological tools and harness their power for innovation”* — yet always in a safe, responsible manner. Universities are actively adapting to the AI era. They are doing so not by trying to beat the bots at an impossible game of cat-and-mouse, but by joining them in the service of learning. Each institution’s policy is a work in progress, but collectively they mark a significant shift in higher education. Universities are accepting that generative AI is here to stay. The goal now is to integrate it in ways that enrich – rather than erode – academic integrity and educational quality.

args.summary:
This article examines how leading universities in the UK and US are adopting "embrace with caution" policies on generative AI tools like ChatGPT and Bard. Key institutions profiled include:

- **University of Oxford**: Permits AI for learning support (brainstorming, practice questions) but prohibits unauthorized use in summative assessments, which constitutes plagiarism.
- **University of Cambridge**: Forbids unacknowledged AI-generated content in graded work unless explicitly allowed, but encourages AI use in formative/independent study.
- **Imperial College London**: Promotes ethical, transparent AI use as a research starting point, but equates unauthorized AI use in assessments with contract cheating.
- **Harvard University**: No blanket policy; each school/instructor sets AI rules, with three possible approaches: maximally restrictive, fully encouraging, or mixed.
- **Stanford University**: Treats AI assistance like help from another person; prohibits using AI to substantially complete assignments, with instructors free to set course-specific policies.
- **MIT**: Emphasizes responsibility, transparency, and data protection; requires disclosure of AI use for all academic purposes and warns against inputting sensitive data into public AI tools.

The article also provides guidance for creating AI policies, suggesting universities consider: educational objectives, contexts where AI is beneficial vs. problematic, maintaining academic integrity, transparency expectations, and privacy safeguards. It recommends tailored approaches (prohibit, allow with limits, or embrace AI), clear guidelines defining acceptable use and consequences, and ongoing training and regular policy reviews. The overarching philosophy is that banning AI outright is neither practical nor pedagogically sound; instead, institutions should integrate AI in ways that enrich academic integrity and educational quality.

# AI and ethics: Investigating the first policy responses of higher education institutions to the challenge of generative AI

* [Attila Dabis](#auth-Attila-Dabis-Aff1) 
  [ORCID: orcid.org/0000-0003-4924-7664](https://orcid.org/0000-0003-4924-7664)[1](#Aff1) &

## Abstract

This article addresses the ethical challenges posed by generative artificial intelligence (AI) tools in higher education and explores the first responses of universities to these challenges globally. Drawing on five key international documents from the UN, EU, and OECD, the study used content analysis to identify key ethical dimensions related to the use of generative AI in academia, such as accountability, human oversight, transparency, or inclusiveness. Empirical evidence was compiled from 30 leading universities ranked among the top 500 in the Shanghai Ranking list from May to July 2023, covering those institutions that already had publicly available responses to these dimensions in the form of policy documents or guidelines. The paper identifies the central ethical imperative that student assignments must reflect individual knowledge acquired during their education, with human individuals retaining moral and legal responsibility for AI-related wrongdoings. This top-down requirement aligns with a bottom-up approach, allowing instructors flexibility in determining how they utilize generative AI especially large language models in their own courses. Regarding human oversight, the typical response identified by the study involves a blend of preventive measures (e.g., course assessment modifications) and soft, dialogue-based sanctioning procedures. The challenge of transparency induced the good practice of clear communication of AI use in course syllabi in the first university responses examined by this study.

## Introduction

The competition in generative artificial intelligence (AI) ignited by the arrival of ChatGPT, the conversational platform based on a large language model (LLM) in late November 2022 (OpenAI, [2022](/articles/s41599-024-03526-z#ref-CR61 "OpenAI (2022) Introducing ChatGPT. 
                  https://openai.com/blog/chatgpt
                  
                . Accessed 14 Nov 2022")) had a shocking effect even on those who are not involved in the industry (Rudolph et al. [2023](/articles/s41599-024-03526-z#ref-CR70 "Rudolph J, Tan S, Tan S (2023) War of the chatbots: Bard, Bing Chat, ChatGPT, Ernie and beyond. The new AI gold rush and its impact on higher education. J. Appl Learn Teach. 6(1):364–389. 
                  https://doi.org/10.37074/jalt.2023.6.1.23
                  
                ")). Within four months, on 22 March 2023, an open letter was signed by several hundred IT professionals, corporate stakeholders, and academics calling on all AI labs to immediately pause the training of AI systems more powerful than GPT-4 (i.e., those that may trick a human being into believing it is conversing with a peer rather than a machine) for at least six months (Future of Life Institute, [2023](/articles/s41599-024-03526-z#ref-CR27 "Future of Life Institute (2023) Pause giant AI experiments: An open letter. 
                  https://futureoflife.org/open-letter/pause-giant-ai-experiments/
                  
                . Accessed 15 Nov 2023")).

Despite these concerns, competition in generative AI and LLMs does not seem to lose momentum, forcing various social systems to overcome the existential distress they might feel about the changes and the uncertainty of what the future may bring (Roose, [2023](/articles/s41599-024-03526-z#ref-CR69 "Roose K (2023) GPT-4 is exciting and scary. New York Times, 15 March 2023. 
                  https://www.nytimes.com/2023/03/15/technology/gpt-4-artificial-intelligence-openai.html
                  
                . Accessed 23 Nov 2023")). Organisations and individuals from different sectors of the economy and various industries are looking for adaptive strategies to accommodate the emerging new normal. This includes lawmakers, international organisations, employers, and employees, as well as academic and higher education institutions (Ray, [2023](/articles/s41599-024-03526-z#ref-CR67 "Ray PP (2023) ChatGPT: A comprehensive review on background, applications, key challenges, bias, ethics, limitations and future scope. Internet Things Cyber-Phys. Syst. 3:121–154. 
                  https://doi.org/10.1016/j.iotcps.2023.04.003
                  
                "); Wach et al. [2023](/articles/s41599-024-03526-z#ref-CR94 "Wach K, Duong CD, Ejdys J et al. (2023) The dark side of generative artificial intelligence: A critical analysis of controversies and risks of ChatGPT. Entrep. Bus. Econ. Rev. 11(2):7–24. 
                  https://doi.org/10.15678/eber.2023.110201
                  
                ")). This fierce competition generates gaps in real-time in everyday and academic life, the latter of which is also trying to make sense of the rapid technological advancement and its effects on university-level education (Perkins, [2023](/articles/s41599-024-03526-z#ref-CR63 "Perkins M (2023) Academic Integrity considerations of AI Large Language Models in the post-pandemic era: ChatGPT and beyond. J. Univ. Teach. Learn Pr. 20(2):07. 
                  https://doi.org/10.53761/1.20.02.07
                  
                ")). Naturally, these gaps can only be filled, and relevant questions answered much slower by academia, making AI-related research topics timely.

This article aims to reduce the magnitude of these gaps and is intended to help leaders, administrators, teachers, and students better understand the ramifications of AI tools on higher education institutions. It will do so by providing a non-exhaustive snapshot of how various universities around the world responded to generative AI-induced ethical challenges in their everyday academic lives within six-eights months after the arrival of ChatGPT. Thus, the research had asked what expectations and guidelines the first policies introduced into existing academic structures to ensure the informed, transparent, responsible and ethical use of the new tools of generative AI (henceforth GAI) by students and teachers. Through reviewing and evaluating first responses and related difficulties the paper helps institutional decision-makers to create better policies to address AI issues specific to academia. The research reported here thus addressed actual answers to the question of what happened at the institutional (policy) level as opposed to what should happen with the use of AI in classrooms. Based on such a descriptive overview, one may contemplate normative recommendations and their realistic implementability.

Given the global nature of the study’s subject matter, the paper presents examples from various continents. Even though it was not yet a widespread practice to adopt separate, AI-related guidelines, the research focused on universities that had already done so quite early. Furthermore, as best practices most often accrue from the highest-ranking universities, the analysis only considered higher education institutions that were represented among the top 500 universities in the Shanghai Ranking list (containing 3041 Universities at the time), a commonly used source to rank academic excellence.[Footnote 1](#Fn1) The main sources of this content analysis are internal documents (such as Codes of Ethics, Academic Regulations, Codes of Practice and Procedure, Guidelines for Students and Teachers or similar policy documents) from those institutions whose response to the GAI challenge was publicly accessible.

The investigation is organised around AI-related ethical dilemmas as concluded from relevant international documents, such as the instruments published by the UN, the EU, and the OECD (often considered soft law material). Through these sources, the study inductively identifies the primary aspects that these AI guidelines mention and can be connected to higher education. Thus it only contains concise references to the main ethical implications of the manifold pedagogical practices in which AI tools can be utilised in the classroom. The paper starts with a review of the challenges posed by AI technology to higher education with special focus on ethical dilemmas. Section 3 covers the research objective and the methodology followed. Section 4 presents the analysis of the selected international documents and establishes a list of key ethical principles relevant in HE contexts and in parallel presents the analysis of the examples distilled from the institutional policy documents and guidelines along that dimension. The paper closes with drawing key conclusions as well as listing limitations and ideas for future research.

## Generative AI and higher education: Developments in the literature

### General AI-related challenges in the classroom from a historical perspective

Jacque Ellul fatalistically wrote already in 1954 that the “infusion of some more or less vague sentiment of human welfare” cannot fundamentally alter technology’s “rigorous autonomy”, bringing him to the conclusion that “technology never observes the distinction between moral and immoral use” (Ellul, [1964](/articles/s41599-024-03526-z#ref-CR20 "Ellul J (1964) The technological society. Vintage Books"), p. 97).[Footnote 2](#Fn2) Jumping ahead nearly six decades, the above quote comes to the fore, among others, when evaluating the moral and ethical aspects of the services offered by specific software programs, like ChatGPT. While they might be trained to give ethical answers, these moral barriers can be circumvented by prompt injection (Blalock, [2022](/articles/s41599-024-03526-z#ref-CR8 "Blalock D (2022) Here are all the ways to get around ChatGPT’s safeguards: [1/n]. X Formerly Twitter, 13 December 2022. 
                  https://twitter.com/davisblalock/status/1602600453555961856
                  
                . Accessed 23 Nov 2023")), or manipulated with tricks (Alberti, [2022](/articles/s41599-024-03526-z#ref-CR2 "Alberti S (2022) Silas Alberti on X: ChatGPT is trained to not be evil. X Formerly Twitter, 1 December 2022. 
                  https://t.co/ZMFdqPs17i
                  
                . Accessed 23 Nov 2023")), so generative AI platforms can hardly be held accountable for the inaccuracy of their responses[Footnote 3](#Fn3) or how the physical user who inserted a prompt will make use of the output. Indeed, the AI chatbot is now considered to be a potentially disruptive technology in higher education practices (Farazouli et al. [2024](/articles/s41599-024-03526-z#ref-CR24 "Farazouli A, Cerratto-Pargman T, Bolander-Laksov K, McGrath C (2024) Hello GPT! Goodbye home examination? An exploratory study of AI chatbots impact on university teachers’ assessment practices. Assess. Eval. High. Educ. 49(3):363–375. 
                  https://doi.org/10.1080/02602938.2023.2241676
                  
                ")).

Educators and educational institution leaders have from the beginning sought solutions on how “to use a variety of the strategies and technologies of the day to help their institutions adapt to dramatically changing social needs” (Miller, [2023](/articles/s41599-024-03526-z#ref-CR50 "Miller GE (2023) eLearning and the Transformation of Higher Education. In: Miller GE, Ives K (eds) Leading the eLearning Transformation of Higher Education. Routledge, pp 3–23. 
                  https://doi.org/10.4324/9781003445623-3
                  
                "), p. 3). Education in the past had always had high hopes for applying the latest technological advances (Reiser, [2001](/articles/s41599-024-03526-z#ref-CR68 "Reiser RA (2001) A history of instructional design and technology: Part I: A history of instructional media. Educ. Technol. Res Dev. 49(1):53–64. 
                  https://doi.org/10.1007/BF02504506
                  
                "); Howard and Mozejko, [2015](/articles/s41599-024-03526-z#ref-CR34 "Howard SK, Mozejko A (2015) Considering the history of digital technologies in education. In: Henderson M, Romeo G (eds) Teaching and digital technologies: Big issues and critical questions. Cambridge University Press, Port Melbourne, Australia, pp 157–168. 
                  https://doi.org/10.1017/cbo9781316091968.017
                  
                ")), including the promise of providing personalised learning or using the latest tools to create and manage courses (Crompton and Burke, [2023](/articles/s41599-024-03526-z#ref-CR18 "Crompton H, Burke D (2023) Artificial intelligence in higher education: the state of the field. Int J. Educ. Technol. High. Educ. 20(1):1–22. 
                  https://doi.org/10.1186/s41239-023-00392-8
                  
                ")).

The most basic (and original) educational settings include three components: the blackboard with chalk, the instructor, and textbooks as elementary “educational technologies” at any level (Reiser, [2001](/articles/s41599-024-03526-z#ref-CR68 "Reiser RA (2001) A history of instructional design and technology: Part I: A history of instructional media. Educ. Technol. Res Dev. 49(1):53–64. 
                  https://doi.org/10.1007/BF02504506
                  
                ")). Beyond these, one may talk about “educational media” which, once digital technology had entered the picture, have progressed from Computer Based Learning to Learning Management Systems to the use of the Internet, and lately to online shared learning environments with various stages in between including intelligent tutoring system, Dialogue-based Tutoring System, and Exploratory Learning Environment and Artificial Intelligence (Paek and Kim, [2021](/articles/s41599-024-03526-z#ref-CR62 "Paek S, Kim N (2021) Analysis of worldwide research trends on the impact of artificial intelligence in education. Sustainability 13(14):7941. 
                  https://doi.org/10.3390/su13147941
                  
                ")). And now the latest craze is about the generative form of AI often called conversational chatbot (Rudolph et al. [2023](/articles/s41599-024-03526-z#ref-CR70 "Rudolph J, Tan S, Tan S (2023) War of the chatbots: Bard, Bing Chat, ChatGPT, Ernie and beyond. The new AI gold rush and its impact on higher education. J. Appl Learn Teach. 6(1):364–389. 
                  https://doi.org/10.37074/jalt.2023.6.1.23
                  
                ")).

The above-mentioned promises appear to be no different in the case of using generative AI tools in education (Baskara, [2023a](/articles/s41599-024-03526-z#ref-CR5 "Baskara FXR (2023a) ChatGPT as a virtual learning environment: multidisciplinary simulations. In: Proceeding of the 3rd International Conference on Innovations in Social Sciences Education and Engineering, Paper 017. 
                  https://conference.loupiasconference.orag/index.php/icoissee3/index
                  
                "); Mhlanga, [2023](/articles/s41599-024-03526-z#ref-CR49 "Mhlanga D (2023) Open AI in Education, the Responsible and Ethical Use of ChatGPT Towards Lifelong Learning. SSRN Electron J 4354422. 
                  https://doi.org/10.2139/ssrn.4354422
                  
                "); Yan et al. [2023](/articles/s41599-024-03526-z#ref-CR97 "Yan L, Sha L, Zhao L et al. (2023) Practical and ethical challenges of large language models in education: A systematic scoping review. Br. J. Educ. Technol. 55(1):90–112. 
                  https://doi.org/10.1111/bjet.13370
                  
                ")). The general claim is that GAI chatbots have transformative potential in HE (Mollick and Mollick, [2022](/articles/s41599-024-03526-z#ref-CR51 "Mollick ER, Mollick L (2022) New modes of learning enabled by AI chatbots: Three methods and assignments. SSRN Electron J 4300783. 
                  https://doi.org/10.2139/ssrn.4300783
                  
                "); Ilieva et al. [2023](/articles/s41599-024-03526-z#ref-CR37 "Ilieva G, Yankova T, Klisarova-Belcheva S et al. (2023) Effects of generative chatbots in higher education. Information 14(9):492. 
                  https://doi.org/10.3390/info14090492
                  
                ")). It is further alleged, that feedback mechanisms supposedly provided by GAI can be used to provide personalised guidance to students (Baskara, [2023b](/articles/s41599-024-03526-z#ref-CR6 "Baskara FXR (2023b) The promises and pitfalls of using ChatGPT for self-determined learning in higher education: An argumentative review. Pros. Semin. Nas. Fakultas Tarb. dan. Ilmu Kegur. IAIM Sinjai 2:95–101. 
                  https://doi.org/10.47435/sentikjar.v2i0.1825
                  
                ")). Some argue, that “AI education should be expanded and improved, especially by presenting realistic use cases and the real limitations of the technology, so that students are able to use AI confidently and responsibly in their professional future” (Almaraz-López et al. [2023](/articles/s41599-024-03526-z#ref-CR3 "Almaraz-López C, Almaraz-Menéndez F, López-Esteban C (2023) Comparative study of the attitudes and perceptions of university students in business administration and management and in education toward Artificial Intelligence. Educ. Sci. 13(6):609. 
                  https://doi.org/10.3390/educsci13060609
                  
                "), p. 1). It is still debated whether the hype is justified, yet the question still remains, how to address the issues arising in the wake of the educational application of GAI tools (Ivanov, [2023](/articles/s41599-024-03526-z#ref-CR40 "Ivanov S (2023) The dark side of artificial intelligence in higher education. Serv. Ind. J. 43(15–16):1055–1082. 
                  https://doi.org/10.1080/02642069.2023.2258799
                  
                "); Memarian and Doleck, [2023](/articles/s41599-024-03526-z#ref-CR48 "Memarian B, Doleck T (2023) Fairness, Accountability, Transparency, and Ethics (FATE) in Artificial Intelligence (AI), and higher education: A systematic review. Comput Educ Artif Intell 100152. 
                  https://doi.org/10.1016/j.caeai.2023.100152
                  
                ")).

Generative AI tools, such as their most-known representative, ChatGPT impact several areas of learning and teaching. From the point of view of students, chatbots may help with so-called Self-Regulated or Self-Determined Learning (Nicol and Macfarlane‐Dick, [2006](/articles/s41599-024-03526-z#ref-CR57 "Nicol DJ, Macfarlane‐Dick D (2006) Formative assessment and self‐regulated learning: A model and seven principles of good feedback practice. Stud. High. Educ. 31(2):199–218.

Indeed, reviews of actual current practices of higher education institutions are rare, and this aspect is not yet the focus of recent HE AI ethics research reports.

As follows from the growing literature and the debate shaping up about the implications of using GAI tools in HE, there was a clear need for a systematic review of how first responses in actual academic policies and guidelines in practice have represented and addressed known ethical principles.

## Research objective and methodology

In order to contribute to the debate on the impact of GAI on HE, this study aimed to review how leading institutions had reacted to the arrival of generative AI (such as ChatGPT) and what policies or institutional guidelines they have put in place shortly after. The research intended to understand whether key ethical principles were reflected in the first policy responses of HE institutions and, if yes, how they were handled.

As potential principles can diverge and could be numerous, as well as early guidelines may cover wide areas, the investigation is intended to be based on a few broad categories instead of trying to manage a large set of ideals and goals. To achieve this objective, the research was executed in three steps:

1. 1.

   It was started with identifying and collecting general ethical ideals, which were then translated and structured for the context of higher education. A thorough content analysis was performed with the intention to put emphasis on *positive values* instead of simply focusing on issues or risks and their mitigation.
2. 2.

   Given those positive ideals, this research collected *actual examples* of university policies and guidelines already available: this step was executed from May to July 2023 to find early responses addressing such norms and principles developed by leading HE institutions.
3. 3.

   The documents identified were then analysed to understand how such norms and principles had been addressed by leading HE institutions.

As a result, this research managed to highlight and contrast differing practical views, and the findings raise awareness about the difficulties of creating relevant institutional policies. The research considered the ethics of using GAI and not expectations towards their development. The next two sections provide details of the two steps.

### Establishing ethical principles for higher education

While the review of relevant ethical and HE literature (as presented above) was not fully conclusive, it highlighted the importance and need for some ideals specific to HE. Therefore, as a first step, this study sought to find highly respected sources of such ethical dimensions by executing a *directed content analysis* of relevant international regulatory and policy recommendations.

In order to establish what key values and ideas drive the formation of future AI regulations in general, Corrêa et al. As the research was looking for key principles and normative attributes that could form a common ground for the comparison of HE policies, this vast set of documents was used to identify internationally recognised bodies that have potential real influence in this arena and decided to consider the guidelines and recommendations they have put forward for the ethical governance of AI.
