## Abstract

The rise of generative AI in higher education has disrupted our traditional understandings of academic integrity, moving our focus from clear-cut infractions to evolving ethical judgment. In this study, a survey of 401 students from major U.S. universities provides insight into how beliefs, behaviors, and policy awareness intersect in shaping how students interact with AI-assisted writing. The findings indicate that students’ ethical beliefs—not institutional policies—are the strongest predictors of perceived misconduct and actual AI use in writing. Policy awareness was found to have no significant effect on ethical judgments or behavior. Instead, students who believe AI writing is cheating were found to be substantially less likely to view it as ethical or engage with it. These findings suggest that many students do not treat AI use in learning activities as an extension of conventional cheating (e.g., plagiarism), but rather as a distinct category of academic conduct/misconduct. Rather than using punitive models to attempt to punish students for using AI, this study suggests that education about AI ethics and the risk of AI overreliance may prove more successful for curbing unethical AI use in higher education.

Keywords: 

[academic integrity](https://www.mdpi.com/search?q=academic+integrity); [AI-assisted writing](https://www.mdpi.com/search?q=AI-assisted+writing); [plagiarism](https://www.mdpi.com/search?q=plagiarism); [AI ethics](https://www.mdpi.com/search?q=AI+ethics); [higher education](https://www.mdpi.com/search?q=higher+education); [generative artificial intelligence](https://www.mdpi.com/search?q=generative+artificial+intelligence)

## 1. Introduction

For students in higher education, the boundaries of academic misconduct have traditionally seemed relatively fixed—cheating, plagiarism, and collusion were clearly defined. But the rise of generative artificial intelligence, particularly large language models (LLMs), has begun to unsettle the map of academic integrity. Unlike plagiarism, which implies a straightforward act of copying without attribution, LLMs produce text that is technically original but procedurally opaque, shaped by probabilistic associations rather than authorship ([White et al., 2023](https://www.mdpi.com/3042-8130/1/1/2#B36-aieduc-01-00002)). As a result, the outputs of these systems sit uneasily between generative tool (e.g., ChatGPT) and coauthor, innovation and infraction—an ambiguous zone where institutional norms have yet to catch up. Research by [Lund et al.](https://www.mdpi.com/3042-8130/1/1/2#B22-aieduc-01-00002) ([2025](https://www.mdpi.com/3042-8130/1/1/2#B22-aieduc-01-00002)) suggests that students are navigating this ambiguity without a clear ethical compass, often uncertain where acceptable use of these tools ends and misconduct begins.

This uncertainty is not simply a matter of policy lagging behind technology. It likely reflects a deeper epistemological shift among students in what it means to write, to know, and to learn. For students, LLMs offer powerful new affordances: instant feedback, tailored content, frictionless summaries of complex material ([Williamson & Murray, 2024](https://www.mdpi.com/3042-8130/1/1/2#B37-aieduc-01-00002)). They expand access to knowledge and scaffold the learning process in ways traditional instruction may not. But with these benefits come ethical frictions—over-reliance, epistemic passivity, and blurred authorship ([Zhai et al., 2024](https://www.mdpi.com/3042-8130/1/1/2#B44-aieduc-01-00002)). More than just technical tools, LLMs are shaping how students conceive of academic labor, creativity, and intellectual ownership ([Darban, 2025](https://www.mdpi.com/3042-8130/1/1/2#B11-aieduc-01-00002)). While institutions scramble to update their honor codes and draft AI integrity policies, students are already making choices in real time, guided as much by perceived fairness and personal values as by formal rules.

Understanding these choices—how students interpret the ethics of AI use, what they believe constitutes “help” versus “cheating,” and how these beliefs vary across contexts—is essential for designing pedagogies and policies that are not only effective, but just. These questions do not have easy answers. They require grappling with the tension between technological possibility and academic responsibility, between efficiency and effort, between the right to use tools and the obligation to learn ([Yue et al., 2025](https://www.mdpi.com/3042-8130/1/1/2#B41-aieduc-01-00002)). In this study, we examine how students position themselves within this evolving landscape, and what their perspectives reveal about the future of academic integrity in an AI-powered world. Our findings highlight the importance of ethical beliefs rather than institutional policies in ensuring appropriate student conduct with AI tools, suggesting the universities invest in a course of ethics instruction to combat AI-powered misconduct.

## 2. Literature Review

### 2.1. Generative AI in Higher Education

Across university campuses, Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) is no longer an emerging novelty. It is here, embedded in the margins of syllabi, lingering in student browsers, shaping drafts before they are even written. Whether higher education institutions choose to formally embrace it or not, the tide of AI adoption is already rising. As [Bearman et al.](https://www.mdpi.com/3042-8130/1/1/2#B5-aieduc-01-00002) ([2022](https://www.mdpi.com/3042-8130/1/1/2#B5-aieduc-01-00002)) suggest, GenAI’s presence is becoming less a matter of policy choice and more an inevitability that demands thoughtful navigation. [McDonald et al.](https://www.mdpi.com/3042-8130/1/1/2#B24-aieduc-01-00002) ([2025](https://www.mdpi.com/3042-8130/1/1/2#B24-aieduc-01-00002)) describe this moment not as an inflection point but as an integration point, one where strategy, ethics, pedagogy, and imagination must converge.

The literature paints an academic landscape that is marked by both promise and peril. On one side, scholars consistently note GenAI’s usefulness as a flexible, scalable, and often responsive assistant for teaching, learning, and administration. [Chiu et al.](https://www.mdpi.com/3042-8130/1/1/2#B7-aieduc-01-00002) ([2023](https://www.mdpi.com/3042-8130/1/1/2#B7-aieduc-01-00002)), [Compton and Burke](https://www.mdpi.com/3042-8130/1/1/2#B8-aieduc-01-00002) ([2023](https://www.mdpi.com/3042-8130/1/1/2#B8-aieduc-01-00002)), and [Kurtz et al.](https://www.mdpi.com/3042-8130/1/1/2#B18-aieduc-01-00002) ([2024](https://www.mdpi.com/3042-8130/1/1/2#B18-aieduc-01-00002)) all highlight its growing role in tutoring, feedback provision, and even lesson planning. These tools are increasingly integrated into how instructors assess student understanding and where administrators forecast enrollment patterns, refine communications, and streamline operational planning ([Zawacki-Richter et al., 2019](https://www.mdpi.com/3042-8130/1/1/2#B43-aieduc-01-00002)). For students—particularly at the undergraduate level—GenAI has been described as a kind of always-on tutor: one that explains, rewrites, rephrases, and even reassures ([Shahzad et al., 2025](https://www.mdpi.com/3042-8130/1/1/2#B29-aieduc-01-00002)). Yet, as [Yusuf et al.](https://www.mdpi.com/3042-8130/1/1/2#B42-aieduc-01-00002) ([2024](https://www.mdpi.com/3042-8130/1/1/2#B42-aieduc-01-00002)) observe, the growing body of research pays comparatively less attention to graduate students, whose needs and challenges may differ substantially.

Despite the enthusiasm around its functionality, the literature repeatedly sounds a cautionary note. Ethical dilemmas prompted by AI are neither small nor theoretical. Scholars such as [Batista et al.](https://www.mdpi.com/3042-8130/1/1/2#B4-aieduc-01-00002) ([2024](https://www.mdpi.com/3042-8130/1/1/2#B4-aieduc-01-00002)) and [Perera and Lankathilaka](https://www.mdpi.com/3042-8130/1/1/2#B26-aieduc-01-00002) ([2023](https://www.mdpi.com/3042-8130/1/1/2#B26-aieduc-01-00002)) point to the blurring line between help and dishonesty, with GenAI enabling new forms of academic misconduct that are difficult to detect. The generation of fabricated citations, a known flaw in some GenAI models, adds another layer of complexity, undermining academic integrity and muddying the waters of authorship and originality ([H. Wang et al., 2024](https://www.mdpi.com/3042-8130/1/1/2#B33-aieduc-01-00002)). [Kurtz et al.](https://www.mdpi.com/3042-8130/1/1/2#B18-aieduc-01-00002) ([2024](https://www.mdpi.com/3042-8130/1/1/2#B18-aieduc-01-00002)) echo these concerns, noting that cheating facilitated by GenAI poses a serious threat to educational integrity.

Beyond ethical concerns lies a deeper pedagogical question: what happens to student learning when artificial machines become too helpful? [Cordero et al.](https://www.mdpi.com/3042-8130/1/1/2#B10-aieduc-01-00002) ([2025](https://www.mdpi.com/3042-8130/1/1/2#B10-aieduc-01-00002)), [D. Lee et al.](https://www.mdpi.com/3042-8130/1/1/2#B20-aieduc-01-00002) ([2024](https://www.mdpi.com/3042-8130/1/1/2#B20-aieduc-01-00002)), and [Zhang and Xu](https://www.mdpi.com/3042-8130/1/1/2#B45-aieduc-01-00002) ([2025](https://www.mdpi.com/3042-8130/1/1/2#B45-aieduc-01-00002)) explore the risk of intellectual atrophy, warning that students may become overly dependent on GenAI tools, sacrificing opportunities to develop creativity, reasoning, and problem-solving skills. [Batista et al.](https://www.mdpi.com/3042-8130/1/1/2#B4-aieduc-01-00002) ([2024](https://www.mdpi.com/3042-8130/1/1/2#B4-aieduc-01-00002)) reinforce this perspective, while also suggesting that without guided instruction, GenAI may ultimately short-circuit meaningful engagement with course content. And yet, across much of this critical discourse, a student’s own perception of GenAI—their understanding, curiosity, trust, or skepticism—is rarely addressed as a factor shaping its misuse.

There is consensus, however, that GenAI’s role in higher education is no longer optional or something that can be prevented. As the literature repeatedly emphasizes, the path forward is not resistance, but regulation—anchored by institutional policies, ethical guidelines, and shared expectations ([Batista et al., 2024](https://www.mdpi.com/3042-8130/1/1/2#B4-aieduc-01-00002); [Cordero et al., 2025](https://www.mdpi.com/3042-8130/1/1/2#B10-aieduc-01-00002); [Kurtz et al., 2024](https://www.mdpi.com/3042-8130/1/1/2#B18-aieduc-01-00002); [D. Lee et al., 2024](https://www.mdpi.com/3042-8130/1/1/2#B20-aieduc-01-00002); [Perera & Lankathilaka, 2023](https://www.mdpi.com/3042-8130/1/1/2#B26-aieduc-01-00002); [H. Wang et al., 2024](https://www.mdpi.com/3042-8130/1/1/2#B33-aieduc-01-00002); [Zhang & Xu, 2025](https://www.mdpi.com/3042-8130/1/1/2#B45-aieduc-01-00002)). Still, any effective policy must reflect the diversity of higher education institutions and their learners. [Yusuf et al.](https://www.mdpi.com/3042-8130/1/1/2#B42-aieduc-01-00002) ([2024](https://www.mdpi.com/3042-8130/1/1/2#B42-aieduc-01-00002)) caution that cultural variability across global institutions makes universal policy frameworks unrealistic. Instead, they argue for context-specific strategies that are sensitive to distinct educational values and ethical frameworks.

Central to this adaptation is GenAI literacy—not only for students but for faculty and staff as well. [Farrelly and Baker](https://www.mdpi.com/3042-8130/1/1/2#B12-aieduc-01-00002) ([2023](https://www.mdpi.com/3042-8130/1/1/2#B12-aieduc-01-00002)) emphasize that GenAI cannot be responsibly integrated without equipping educators with the tools to navigate it critically and creatively. They, along with [McGrath et al.](https://www.mdpi.com/3042-8130/1/1/2#B25-aieduc-01-00002) ([2023](https://www.mdpi.com/3042-8130/1/1/2#B25-aieduc-01-00002)), highlight frameworks like those developed by Ng et al. and Hillier, which provide structured approaches to building GenAI literacy in academic environments. [Zhang and Xu](https://www.mdpi.com/3042-8130/1/1/2#B45-aieduc-01-00002) ([2025](https://www.mdpi.com/3042-8130/1/1/2#B45-aieduc-01-00002)) similarly underline that institutions must invest in upskilling their workforce, not merely to keep pace with technology but to shape its use in pedagogically sound and ethically aligned ways.

### 2.2. Academic Integrity in the Age of AI

Within higher education, academic integrity is a principle that is often considered a core tenet of an institution’s values. An academic institution must be able to uphold academic integrity within its programs; otherwise, the credibility and quality of the programs offered by the institution become questionable ([Balalle & Pannilage, 2025](https://www.mdpi.com/3042-8130/1/1/2#B3-aieduc-01-00002)). The International Center for Academic Integrity [ICAI] (2021) currently describes academic integrity as being the commitment to the values of honesty, trust, fairness, respect, responsibility, and courage within academic communities. Thus, dishonest practices which threaten academic integrity, such as plagiarism and cheating, are largely frowned upon within higher education, especially in higher degree levels ([Șercan & Voicu, 2022](https://www.mdpi.com/3042-8130/1/1/2#B31-aieduc-01-00002)).

Several studies have examined the ethical behavior of higher education students. While some of these studies point to specific attributes like gender and peer networks in influencing students’ ethical behavior ([Joseph & Berry, 2010](https://www.mdpi.com/3042-8130/1/1/2#B15-aieduc-01-00002)), many more studies point to the importance of instruction and discussion of ethical principles as critical in developing ethical behavior ([Armstrong et al., 2003](https://www.mdpi.com/3042-8130/1/1/2#B2-aieduc-01-00002); [Koerber et al., 2005](https://www.mdpi.com/3042-8130/1/1/2#B17-aieduc-01-00002)). Notably, [Susilowati et al.](https://www.mdpi.com/3042-8130/1/1/2#B30-aieduc-01-00002) ([2021](https://www.mdpi.com/3042-8130/1/1/2#B30-aieduc-01-00002)) found that courses on ethical behavior considerably enhanced ethical behavior, whereas a general ethical or policy climate did not influence behavior in meaningful ways.

While threats to the core values of academic integrity are far from being a novel sighting, the rise of generative AI writing tools, such as ChatGPT, have brought reason for concern within academic institutions ([Benke & Szőke, 2024](https://www.mdpi.com/3042-8130/1/1/2#B6-aieduc-01-00002); [Laflamme & Bruneault, 2025](https://www.mdpi.com/3042-8130/1/1/2#B19-aieduc-01-00002); [Sabzalieva & Valentini, 2023](https://www.mdpi.com/3042-8130/1/1/2#B27-aieduc-01-00002)). With LLMs being able to easily provide detailed writing, they have become a prime tool for cheating in academic settings ([Ward et al., 2024](https://www.mdpi.com/3042-8130/1/1/2#B35-aieduc-01-00002)).

When discussing students’ use of LLMs and academic integrity, one of the main concerns presented is that of the development of knowledge and critical thinking skills in students. ([Cong-Lem et al., 2024](https://www.mdpi.com/3042-8130/1/1/2#B9-aieduc-01-00002); [Khatri & Karki, 2023](https://www.mdpi.com/3042-8130/1/1/2#B16-aieduc-01-00002); [Balalle & Pannilage, 2025](https://www.mdpi.com/3042-8130/1/1/2#B3-aieduc-01-00002); [Salehi et al., 2025](https://www.mdpi.com/3042-8130/1/1/2#B28-aieduc-01-00002); [Yeo, 2023](https://www.mdpi.com/3042-8130/1/1/2#B39-aieduc-01-00002)). If a student is overly reliant on AI tools to complete assignments, then there is no guarantee that the student is actually reaping any knowledge from the activity ([Gupta, 2024](https://www.mdpi.com/3042-8130/1/1/2#B13-aieduc-01-00002); [Khatri & Karki, 2023](https://www.mdpi.com/3042-8130/1/1/2#B16-aieduc-01-00002)). This brings concern not only in the context of an academic institution but also in the context of the fields in which these students will work in in the future; this is especially a concern for subject fields in which assessment is heavily based in the quality of a student’s written work, such as the social sciences, arts, and humanities ([Gupta, 2024](https://www.mdpi.com/3042-8130/1/1/2#B13-aieduc-01-00002)).

This concern over the development of critical thinking is also in line with the concern regarding the originality of students’ work. When discussing the use of generative AI for writing content, debates over what constitutes authorship and plagiarism arise ([Lund & Naheem, 2024](https://www.mdpi.com/3042-8130/1/1/2#B23-aieduc-01-00002)). According to Yeo (2023), there are no universally accepted definitions for authorship or for plagiarism; however, there is a general agreement that “authorship” requires that the work be the person’s own original work, and that “plagiarism” involves using someone or something else’s content without credit. While usage of generative AI for essays may not constitute plagiarism, it can reasonably be determined to be “false authorship,” since the student did not write the essay themselves. Functionally, it is almost the same as having a peer write the essay in place of the student.

Additional concerns over the usage of LLMs in education persist as well. The topic of student responsibility is a significant one, especially with it being a core tenet of the idea of academic integrity itself ([Alioğulları et al., 2025](https://www.mdpi.com/3042-8130/1/1/2#B1-aieduc-01-00002); [International Center for Academic Integrity [ICAI], 2021](https://www.mdpi.com/3042-8130/1/1/2#B14-aieduc-01-00002)). The accuracy of LLMs is also a topic of discussion, since LLMs can generate unintentional biases and “hallucinations,” or false facts, and present them as truth ([Alioğulları et al., 2025](https://www.mdpi.com/3042-8130/1/1/2#B1-aieduc-01-00002); [Salehi et al., 2025](https://www.mdpi.com/3042-8130/1/1/2#B28-aieduc-01-00002)). Irresponsibility in students can greatly impact the credibility of an academic program if occurring on a large enough scale, as can the decrease of critical thinking skills and accurate knowledge within a student population.

While the rise of AI-generated writing in academia is of great concern, there are potential uses of AI that would still fit within the ideals of academic integrity. Yeo (2023) discusses the usage of writing assistants, or what might be called “revision tools,” such as Wordtune, which do not generate their own content and instead make subtle changes to text that the user has already provided. If discussing the usage of such tools and the legitimacy of a one’s authorship, it could be reasonably argued that using a tool such as Wordtune would still allow for one to be considered the original author, since they provided the original idea and text simply used Wordtune to revise their work ([Yeo, 2023](https://www.mdpi.com/3042-8130/1/1/2#B39-aieduc-01-00002)). These arguments could apply to other tools such as Grammarly, another revision tool that provides revision and editing services but does not fully generate a written work.

These ongoing debates about authorship, responsibility and the misuse of generative AI in higher education contexts can be further understood from the perspective of classical ethical theory. From a utilitarian perspective, we can view AI use in relation to its consequences for student learning, institutional credibility, and societal outcomes. Because overreliance on AI in academic preparation may result in the erosion of trust in academic standards and limit intellectual growth, the utilitarian perspective suggests that academic integrity policy should limit use of generative AI tools for composing manuscripts. But students are unlikely to use this same utilitarian calculus in making decisions whether to use these tools.

### 2.3. Student Perceptions of AI Use and AI Ethics

As AI applications become increasingly prevalent in educational settings, there has been substantial academic interest in students’ perspectives on their purposes and ethical implications. As these technologies become a routine part of educational practice, learners recognize both the benefits and challenges they present, which informs efforts to promote responsible use and maintain academic integrity. This tension between AI’s educational potential and the complexities it introduces provides a critical foundation for developing informed policies, practices, and pedagogies. One study by [J. E. Lee and Maeng](https://www.mdpi.com/3042-8130/1/1/2#B21-aieduc-01-00002) ([2023](https://www.mdpi.com/3042-8130/1/1/2#B21-aieduc-01-00002)) explored AI systems perception among 30 high school students in South Korea. They found that students valued chatbots for their convenience and efficiency, meaning a rating of 4.33. Students liked that they could find information without temporal or spatial bounds, and they believed that the chatbot was user-friendly, rating it at 3.87 out of 5 for usability. The study also showcased some ethical concerns students had about the chatbot systems, particularly around plagiarism and copyright, with a mean rating of 3.80 for concerns about originality and copyright issues. Students expressed concerns about their personal data being breached, which demonstrates some understanding of privacy risks. Students surveyed with no previous experience using a chatbot were more skeptical about ethical issues and educational concerns, such as the potential for over-dependence on chatbots undermining exploratory learning than students who had previously used chatbots for English language learning. [J. E. Lee and Maeng](https://www.mdpi.com/3042-8130/1/1/2#B21-aieduc-01-00002) ([2023](https://www.mdpi.com/3042-8130/1/1/2#B21-aieduc-01-00002)), recommend that “teachers should provide educational guidance for students to take a critical approach to information provided by the chatbots” ([J. E. Lee & Maeng, 2023, p. 69](https://www.mdpi.com/3042-8130/1/1/2#B21-aieduc-01-00002)). This represented the AI’s duality as a positive educational resource and a source of ethical challenges, especially for younger students.

Another study by [Xiao et al.](https://www.mdpi.com/3042-8130/1/1/2#B38-aieduc-01-00002) ([2023](https://www.mdpi.com/3042-8130/1/1/2#B38-aieduc-01-00002)) showed a mixed method to analyze its effect on academic integrity on learners. Their findings showed that students valued AI as a tool, such as ChatGPT to assist drafting, but had concerns regarding plagiarism and diminished authentic learning experiences. It points out, “some students struggle to put their moral views into words, which reach a path in using assisted writing tools” ([Xiao et al., 2023, p. 45](https://www.mdpi.com/3042-8130/1/1/2#B38-aieduc-01-00002)). They reported that 60% of participants had used these services for academic work, and eventually, 72% responded in the affirmative to ethical matters, for cheating. On one hand, this echoes the complexity and duality of situations when embracing AI, with students seeing its promise as a learning aid. This deep study recommends educational policy to promote responsible ethical use of tools so that organizations develop guidelines that clarify ethical risks while tapping into the benefits of AI.

In addition, other studies analyze student perceptions of AI tools across diverse educational and cultural contexts. They found that cultural context and institutional factors affect attitudes toward AI ethics. For example, participants were generally more concerned about plagiarism and academic dishonesty in a Western context, as opposed to Asian contexts, where privacy ultimately was a bigger concern when deciding to engage with the technology. [Tlili et al.](https://www.mdpi.com/3042-8130/1/1/2#B32-aieduc-01-00002) ([2023](https://www.mdpi.com/3042-8130/1/1/2#B32-aieduc-01-00002)) stated, “Students in Asia expressed more trepidation about any implications regarding data privacy while acknowledging risks, 68% expressed risk of personal information leakage” ([Tlili et al., 2023, p. 12](https://www.mdpi.com/3042-8130/1/1/2#B32-aieduc-01-00002)). The study suggested that globally, 55% of students used AI tools for academic purposes with perceived cognitive advantages of improved writing and problem-solving skills. Yet, ethical concerns were ubiquitous regardless of location, with 70% of participants having diminished critical thinking. Essentially, these showcase the applicability of ethical frameworks of students’ perceptions addressed to responsible engagement with AI technologies.

Moreover, a study by Yu (2023) examined the longer-term ethical use in education by surveying 200 undergraduate students using AI-assisted writing. A significant finding of the study reported that 62% of students ascribed to the use of AI for academic purposes, but 80% said they were concerned that students would lose their sense of independent thought due to overuse or becoming too reliant on AI. Yu (2023) states, “Over reliance on AI might elicit ethical and potentially privacy issues that may lessen authorial ownership” ([Yu, 2023, p. 5](https://www.mdpi.com/3042-8130/1/1/2#B40-aieduc-01-00002)). Students raise concerns about biased outputs and the presence of prejudiced content in AI systems. Despite these issues, many students recognize the value of AI tools for their effectiveness and efficiency, especially given the risk of potential overreliance in educational contexts. Moreover, the study found that three-quarters of students reported that AI improved the quality of writing assignments. Educators of future school leaders will need to employ critical thinking and ethical consideration in their learning as a counterbalance to the negative impacts of AI. Overall, this study stressed the importance of practitioners examining the implications of AI on education in the short term, while also developing ethical implications and academic integrity.

### 2.4. Research Problem and Questions

The rapid adoption of AI tools within higher education has prompted concerns about their ethical use, particularly when used in student writing ([T. Wang et al., 2023](https://www.mdpi.com/3042-8130/1/1/2#B34-aieduc-01-00002)). While many institutions have responded by developing new academic integrity policies related to student AI use, it remains unclear whether students’ awareness of these policies influences their ethical perceptions or their actual use of AI tools. Additionally, the relationship between students’ personal ethical beliefs and their behavior with AI-assisted writing tools is not well understood in the current literature. There is a significant need to explore the ways students interpret and act upon academic integrity standards in the context of AI, and what drives the acceptance or rejection of AI-assisted writing as an ethical academic practice. This problem informs the following research questions:

*   How does students’ awareness of academic integrity policies influence their perceptions of AI-assisted writing? 
*   Do students’ perceptions of AI-assisted writing predict their actual AI tool usage? 
*   How do policy awareness and ethical beliefs influence students’ perceptions of the severity of academic misconduct involving AI-assisted writing? 
*   What are the strongest predictors of whether students perceive AI-assisted writing as an ethically acceptable academic practice? 

## 3. Methods: A Survey of AI and Academic Integrity

This study utilizes an electronic survey/questionnaire method. The questionnaire was created using an online survey platform (Qualtrics) and distributed electronically to participants. Questions were developed by the authors based on the existing literature and then refined through pilot testing with a small group of students at their institution. Eligible participants for the survey were students enrolled in higher education institutions who were at least 18 years old at the time of survey completion. The survey was disseminated via email to students at several major universities across the United States, with recipients encouraged to share the survey link with others to expand participation. It remained open from 1 April to 1 May 2024. During this period, 521 responses were collected, of which 401 were valid and complete. These responses were exported from the survey platform into a CSV file for subsequent statistical analysis using the Python package statsmodels 0.14.4. 

The questionnaire consisted of ten multi-part questions. This includes five questions relating to student demographics—educational status (undergraduate, masters, doctoral), major, residency status (domestic/international), and gender. These questions are followed by five question categories comprising a total of 22 multiple choice and Likert items related to AI use and perceptions of academic integrity. Among the AI and academic integrity questions, students were asked to rate various activities based on their perceived level of academic misconduct (on a scale from “not academic misconduct at all” to “major academic misconduct”), the seriousness of AI use for various academic activities, and a series of statements related to AI rated on a five-point scale from “strongly disagree” to “strongly agree,” including, “Cheating on assignments is unethical,” “Cheating is okay as long as I don’t get caught,” and “Using AI to help write papers is cheating.”

args.summary:
This is a web page for an open-access academic article titled "Student Perceptions of AI-Assisted Writing and Academic Integrity: Ethical Concerns, Academic Misconduct, and Use of Generative AI in Higher Education" published in the journal AI in Education (Volume 1, Issue 1) on September 2, 2025. The study, authored by Brady Lund, Nishith Reddy Mannuru, Zoë Abbie Teel, Tae Hee Lee, Nathanlie Jugan Ortega, Sara Simmons, and Evelyn Ward from the University of North Texas, surveyed 401 students from major U.S. universities to examine how beliefs, behaviors, and policy awareness shape student interactions with AI-assisted writing.

**Key Findings:**
- Students' ethical beliefs—not institutional policies—are the strongest predictors of perceived misconduct and actual AI use in writing.
- Policy awareness was found to have no significant effect on ethical judgments or behavior.
- Students who believe AI writing is cheating are substantially less likely to view it as ethical or engage with it.
- Many students do not treat AI use as an extension of conventional cheating (e.g., plagiarism), but rather as a distinct category of academic conduct/misconduct.
- The study recommends education about AI ethics and the risk of AI overreliance rather than punitive models for curbing unethical AI use.

**Methodology:** An electronic survey distributed via Qualtrics from April 1 to May 1, 2024, with 521 responses collected (401 valid and complete). The questionnaire included questions on demographics, AI use, and perceptions of academic integrity. Regression analyses were performed using Python's statsmodels 0.14.4 package.

The article includes a literature review covering generative AI in higher education, academic integrity in the age of AI, and student perceptions of AI use and AI ethics. The research questions addressed: (1) How policy awareness influences perceptions of AI-assisted writing, (2) Whether perceptions predict actual AI tool usage, (3) How policy awareness and ethical beliefs influence perceptions of misconduct severity, and (4) What are the strongest predictors of perceiving AI-assisted writing as ethically acceptable.

This chapter presents research focused on investigating the dishonest practices of university undergraduate students in the context of the recent massive spread of AI tools. Building upon the Original Academic Dishonesty Scale adapted from McCabe and Trevino's (1993), this study aimed to explore the patterns of academic dishonesty among undergraduate female students in one of the biggest public universities of the United Arab Emirates (UAE). The scale encompasses 12 forms of self-reported academic dishonesty, ranging from cheating on tests to plagiarizing from online sources. Respondents report their experiences in traditional academic dishonesty and e-dishonesty, including the usage of ChatGPT to complete their tasks and exams. This study seeks to enhance understanding of the reasons for e-dishonesty and its prevalence among undergraduate students. The findings serve as the ground to define institutional policies and strategies to promote academic integrity and strong ethics to mitigate both traditional and e-dishonesty practices among undergraduate students.

This chapter discusses academic integrity with a focus on the Artificial Intelligence (AI) application in educational processes. Academic dishonesty remains an important concern in higher education, which was heavily researched in Western countries ([Baran & Jonason, 2020](#EEP_20_YLKF_C020_CIT000007)). However, few studies have been conducted in the Arab world, which motivates us to investigate this subject.

Academic integrity is a fundamental tenet of educational ethos, requiring adherence to honesty and moral discipline, including but not limited to avoiding plagiarism, steering clear of cheating during exams, and refraining from purchasing academic papers ([Currie, 2023](#EEP_20_YLKF_C020_CIT000019)). The definition of academic integrity is based on the culture of honesty and trust within universities, which is linked to the core values of honesty, trust, fairness, respect, responsibility, and courage. These values translate into principles for ethical academic conduct. However, this definition might only partially capture the complexities of the diverse student body perceptions of academic conduct in higher education (Chirikov et al., [2020](#EEP_20_YLKF_C020_CIT000013)).

Studies revealed a need for more consensus on the meaning and importance of academic integrity among students and faculty (Dyer et al., 2020; [Nugroho et al., 2023](#EEP_20_YLKF_C020_CIT000059)). It was shown that subjective interpretations of academic integrity are influenced by academic disciplines, cultural backgrounds, role models, and specific situations ([Cuadrado et al., 2021](#EEP_20_YLKF_C020_CIT000018); [Guerrero-Dib et al., 2020](#EEP_20_YLKF_C020_CIT000030)). This highlights a potential source of misunderstanding and misinterpretation among students. Thus, despite mutual understanding of ideal academic integrity, diverse interpretations and cultural backgrounds within higher education institutions create challenges in establishing a universally understood and meaningful definition for the student population (Zhao et al., [2022](#EEP_20_YLKF_C020_CIT000077)).

The spread of AI tools and their free availability for students create a new threat to higher education. Since the UAE is a country with advanced digitalization in daily life it would be a valuable contribution to current research to look at this country's example of the Arab world region. Therefore, the chapter presents an explorative study on academic integrity and dishonesty among undergraduate students in the UAE, as well as the role of spreading AI tools used by students to complete assignments or cheat in exams. This chapter provides an overview of students’ perceptions and attitudes toward academic dishonesty and the usage of new generative AI (GenAI) tools in their studies. Taking the example of one of the biggest public universities in the p. 334UAE, we are contributing to the international literature and research discussions on academic dishonesty issues from the perspective of the current significant integration of AI technologies into study processes.

## Academic integrity in higher education

Addressing plagiarism remains an important issue in higher education across the globe. Research suggests a correlation between increased individualism and academic misconduct (Lee et al., 2020). The early insights on individual and contextual factors of academic dishonesty came from [McCabe and Trevino's (1997)](#EEP_20_YLKF_C020_CIT000050) and McCabe's ([1999](#EEP_20_YLKF_C020_CIT000049)) cross-cultural study comparing American and French-Canadian students’ perceptions of cheating. Extending this exploration, Whitley Jr. ([1998](#EEP_20_YLKF_C020_CIT000072)) reviewed a group of factors associated with cheating among college students, explaining that both personal and environmental factors played significant roles.

Further research has underscored the role of education in mitigating academic dishonesty. Barnett, Bass, and [Brown (2016)](#EEP_20_YLKF_C020_CIT000008) suggested that exposure to ethical courses positively impacts students’ perceptions of academic integrity. This aligns with the findings of [Yeo and Ang (2011)](#EEP_20_YLKF_C020_CIT000076), who argued that ethical awareness, cultivated through education, could counteract a cheating culture, and with a much earlier study by Baldwin et al. ([1996](#EEP_20_YLKF_C020_CIT000081)) who found that medical students’ exposure to ethical curricula significantly influenced their perceptions of academic misconduct.

Hard, Conway, and [Moran (2006)](#EEP_20_YLKF_C020_CIT000032) provided a complementary perspective, revealing discrepancies between faculty and student beliefs regarding the prevalence of academic misconduct, highlighting the need for coherent communication and educational strategies to bridge this gap. Previous studies have also noted the variance in perceptions of plagiarism across different cultural and linguistic backgrounds. [Rogerson and Basanta (2016)](#EEP_20_YLKF_C020_CIT000063) shed light on how native and non-native English speakers perceive academic writing and plagiarism, underscoring the necessity for culturally sensitive educational approaches. Kuo and Li ([2020](#EEP_20_YLKF_C020_CIT000043)) advanced this discussion by emphasizing the influence of both classroom and individual factors on students’ attitudes toward plagiarism, suggesting that a multilevel approach is required to effectively address this issue. Recent studies contributed to understanding the “code of silence,” where students are reluctant to discuss or report cheating due to varying views on its seriousness ([Adzima, 2020](#EEP_20_YLKF_C020_CIT000001), Gottardello & Karabag, [2022](#EEP_20_YLKF_C020_CIT000027)).

At the intersection of pedagogy and technology, [Gallant (2008)](#EEP_20_YLKF_C020_CIT000082) articulated the imperative of teaching and learning to uphold academic integrity in the modern educational landscape. With AI's increasing role in plagiarism detection, [Gallant and Drinan (2008)](#EEP_20_YLKF_C020_CIT000086) later explored the creation of an academic culture that emphasizes integrity, reinforcing the idea that technology should complement, not substitute, comprehensive educational strategies. Higher education institutions can foster an enduring commitment to academic integrity among students within this interplay of education and technology.p. 335

Summing up, the previous research underlined the significance of integrating ethics education into the curriculum and leveraging technology judiciously to nurture a culture of integrity ([Barnett et al., 2016](#EEP_20_YLKF_C020_CIT000008); [Bertram Gallant, 2008](#EEP_20_YLKF_C020_CIT000082); [Bretag et al., 2011](#EEP_20_YLKF_C020_CIT000010); [Hosseini et al., 2019](#EEP_20_YLKF_C020_CIT000034); [Mahmood & Bretag, 2013](#EEP_20_YLKF_C020_CIT000046)).

## The role of AI in academic integrity

AI's applications in education are enormous, from intelligent tutoring systems for customized individual learning paths ([Xu et al., 2021](#EEP_20_YLKF_C020_CIT000075)) and AI-powered administrative task automation (Khanzode & Sarode, [2020](#EEP_20_YLKF_C020_CIT000039); Stone et al., [2020](#EEP_20_YLKF_C020_CIT000068)) to predictive analytics to forecast student outcomes (Fatima et al., [2020](#EEP_20_YLKF_C020_CIT000087)). However, these AI applications raise questions about their ethical and long-term educational implications ([Alam & Mohanty, 2022](#EEP_20_YLKF_C020_CIT000083)).

AI rapidly transforms the educational landscape, impacting teaching, learning, and assessment practices ([Bearman & Luckin, 2020](#EEP_20_YLKF_C020_CIT000084)). AI has the potential to personalize learning experiences, provide students with immediate feedback, and identify areas where they may need additional support ([Dawson, 2020](#EEP_20_YLKF_C020_CIT000020)). However, alongside these potential benefits, AI also raises concerns regarding academic integrity ([Eaton, 2021](#EEP_20_YLKF_C020_CIT000088); [Mindzak, 2020](#EEP_20_YLKF_C020_CIT000089); [Morrison & Mindzak, 2021](#EEP_20_YLKF_C020_CIT000090)). AI's capabilities in assessment are formidable, including but not limited to validating the authenticity of essays through comprehensive cross-referencing with extant internet sources and scholarly databases ([Holden et al., 2021](#EEP_20_YLKF_C020_CIT000033)). By leveraging machine learning algorithms, AI systems are adept at discerning anomalous patterns in writing styles, potentially unearthing attempts at deception (Nigam et al., [2021](#EEP_20_YLKF_C020_CIT000055)). Ensuring originality in scholarship by preventing plagiarism through technology is crucial for learners ([Perkins, 2023](#EEP_20_YLKF_C020_CIT000061)).

Contemporary students’ reliance on technology is inevitable. However, integrating AI into educational assessment is a double-edged sword. While it reduces the tendency for shortcuts, it also demands a higher level of accountability from students. When used thoughtfully, AI moves beyond being just a deterrent and becomes a force for promoting integrity. This shift from policing to education fosters a scholarly environment where academic integrity is valued above all (Stephens et al., [2021](#EEP_20_YLKF_C020_CIT000067)).

In this context, the responsibilities of educational institutions are manifold. It is important for educational institutions to ensure that the use of AI technology in assessments is conducted in a fair, transparent, and conducive manner for learning. Additionally, institutions must educate students on the ethical use of technology and the value of intellectual property (Sullivan et al., [2023](#EEP_20_YLKF_C020_CIT000069)). It is necessary to evolve assessment practices to test not only knowledge but also the application of learning to reduce cheating ([Crawford et al., 2023](#EEP_20_YLKF_C020_CIT000085)). Moreover, [Ellis et al. (2020)](#EEP_20_YLKF_C020_CIT000023) emphasized the importance of social constructs in upholding academic integrity. They proposed an educational framework that is not solely dependent on AI for enforcement, but rather is supported by a strong value system that students can internalize. This approach creates a self-regulated environment where students are motivated to maintain integrity as an inherent value, rather than just a required standard.p. 336

Plagiarism is a common form of misconduct that is becoming more widespread and is often executed with systematic precision, which is concerning ([Aljurf et al., 2019](#EEP_20_YLKF_C020_CIT000004)). While plagiarism is universally recognized as serious academic misconduct, it paradoxically continues to be a common and increasingly systematic practice among students. This ongoing issue reflects deeper complexities involving cultural, educational, and ethical standards that vary across different academic environments and societal norms. Students who engage in such behavior may not fully understand the long-term consequences, including the potential loss of self-respect and the fear of being exposed, especially if they are future leaders ([Flahive, 2024](#EEP_20_YLKF_C020_CIT000025)).

Importantly, AI is revolutionizing plagiarism detection in academia. Current AI-based software, like Turnitin and SafeAssign, effectively compares student work to vast databases, expediting the process compared to traditional search engine checks by educators ([Wigtil, 2022](#EEP_20_YLKF_C020_CIT000073); [Alua et al., 2023](#EEP_20_YLKF_C020_CIT000006)). However, ethical considerations arise due to the potential for false accusations with highly effective AI ([Alua et al., 2023](#EEP_20_YLKF_C020_CIT000006)). The advancements in AI technology have led to the emergence of more sophisticated plagiarism detection systems that can analyze inconsistencies in writing patterns ([Graf, 2024](#EEP_20_YLKF_C020_CIT000029); [McIntire et al., 2024](#EEP_20_YLKF_C020_CIT000051)). [Tweissi (2022)](#EEP_20_YLKF_C020_CIT000070) reveals a dichotomy in student perceptions: while they generally uphold self-concepts of honesty, relative to their peers, and often harbor regret if caught, the stigma of cheating does not fully dissuade their actions. This suggests a residual ethical framework that educators might leverage to eradicate academic dishonesty. The challenge, as indicated by [Gallant and Pani (2024)](#EEP_20_YLKF_C020_CIT000026), lies in reinforcing this ethical framework to the point where it outweighs the temptation of academic shortcuts.

Furthermore, empirical studies corroborate that higher academic achievement, as indicated by grade-point averages (GPAs), tends to correlate with a lower likelihood of engaging in cheating behaviors. Cheaters in academic settings report lower GPAs, indicating an academic gap between them and their honest counterparts (He et al. 2024). However, the cheaters’ motivations for academic misconduct may be rooted more in a quest for efficiency than a lack of effort (Ncheka et al., [2024](#EEP_20_YLKF_C020_CIT000054)). This insight highlights a common misconception among students: cheating may seem like a shortcut to academic success, but it fails to reflect the true value and long-term benefits of genuine learning and hard work ([Akbar & Picard, 2020](#EEP_20_YLKF_C020_CIT000002)). When students believe that success comes without effort, they tend to use shortcuts ([Alshamsi et al., 2021](#EEP_20_YLKF_C020_CIT000005)).

While AI has been suggested as an effective tool to combat plagiarism, it is much more than that. In fact, AI integration in education should encourage a shift toward more meaningful and authentic learning experiences that prioritize academic integrity ([Facchini et al., 2021](#EEP_20_YLKF_C020_CIT000024)). Therefore, the implementation of AI in academia provides a great opportunity to transform the assessment process. When combined with ethical education, this technological advancement can help create a culture of scholastic integrity that is not just maintained but actively pursued ([Dawson, 2020](#EEP_20_YLKF_C020_CIT000020); [Cotton et al., 2024](#EEP_20_YLKF_C020_CIT000017)).

Although AI provides practical tools for detecting and preventing misconduct, the most effective solution lies in establishing a culture that values honesty and hard work. This culture should prioritize prevention strategies by integrating technological p. 337advancements with a mindset that associates success with integrity and diligence ([Aljurf et al., 2019](#EEP_20_YLKF_C020_CIT000004); [Gallant and Pani, 2024](#EEP_20_YLKF_C020_CIT000026); [Tweissi, 2022](#EEP_20_YLKF_C020_CIT000070)). To sum up, it is the culture of academic integrity and personal attitudes toward AI usage that will define the patterns of misconduct or dishonest behavior among students. In this case, it is important to understand students’ values and attitudes toward using AI tools in their studies.

## Results of a pilot study on academic integrity and AI usage in UAE University

This section of the chapter is dedicated to discussing academic integrity practices among female students at UAE University as an example of an empirical survey on the usage of AI technologies and attitudes to academic dishonesty.

The survey was completed as a pilot test of 109 female students at the biggest public university in the UAE, UAE University (UAEU), in Spring 2024 via online survey data collection with the help of Qualtrics. The vast majority of the student population at UAE university are female (about 75–80%). The federal UAE University is one of the main destinations for Emirati young women to get their university degree, since it still provides segregated education for boys and girls. For many traditional families, it is the only possible solution for their female children to obtain higher education. The targeted sample comprised female students since the study was conducted in the female sections of the CHSS college. Students who participated in the study on a voluntary basis were from different colleges and different years of study. The survey was designed to investigate the current practices of preparation for exams and behavior during exams to explore students’ attitudes toward AI technology and academic integrity. This empirical study allowed us to get a first impression of how much students use tools as ChatGPT or paid help to prepare their assignments and pass exams. The chapter presents the results of this survey to disclose students’ attitudes to academic integrity in general, their AI literacy, and the frequency of usage of AI tools in their daily study practices.

### Academic Integrity Among Students in the UAE

Students demonstrated quite high academic integrity during exams. In general, not many declared direct dishonest practices such as the usage of ChatGPT during exams (1.8%), coping exam questions to share (5.5%), or using paid services to get assignments done (5.5%) ([Table 20.1](#T20.1)). About 6% of the students said they use smart devices to get help during exams. However, other “lighter” misconduct could be found on a larger scale: practices such as using the help of a friend/relative or ChatGPT to complete assignments (38.5%), approaching a professor to influence the grade (44%), or using various information resources such as Chegg and Quizlet sites that provide ready answers to exam questions to prepare for tests (70%).p. 338

These results are in line with the outcomes on students’ attitudes toward dishonest behavior during their assignments and homework. Thus, only 5.5% agreed that it is totally okay to submit a complete paper generated by GenAI tools as their work ([Table 20.2](#T20.2)). About one-third of students said it is better to cite ChatGPT or to paraphrase texts from ChatGPT. The same proportion of students agreed that ChatGPT encourages dishonest behavior.

For exploratory purposes, we tested the collected survey data for correlations between academic dishonesty of students and their year of studies in the university or their grades (GPA). The correlation analysis did not disclose any significant links between academic integrity and current GPA. The same results of no correlations were found between the year of studies and cheating during exams. Only one positive correlation was discovered between the usage of ChatGPT and year of study, but it was rather weak: senior students are more likely to use ChatGPT for their assignments. This outcome might speak to two things: either the sample was too homogeneous or, as previous studies revealed ([Dawson, 2020](#EEP_20_YLKF_C020_CIT000020), [Tweissi, 2022](#EEP_20_YLKF_C020_CIT000070), [Cotton et al., 2024](#EEP_20_YLKF_C020_CIT000017)), it is mainly culture, values, beliefs, and attitudes that predict dishonest behavior. Further, more detailed studies are needed. We understand the limitation of this small exploratory sample and do not generalize the results to the whole student population.p. 339

### Usage of AI Tools among Students and Attitudes to AI

As expected in a highly digitalized society, students are very well aware of AI tool applications in their studies. Only 15.7% of the sample reported not knowing how to use GenAI tools (see [Table 20.3](#T20.3)). Such fast spread of new AI skills might be explained by the fact that younger generations, on average, are more advanced in technology usage than older generations. Thus, only 18.5% said that it is generally difficult for them to learn how to use new applications. More than half of the respondents reported that they can differentiate between non-smart and smart devices, which are internet-connected and capable of autonomous and adaptive functions through advanced computing power, while non-smart devices operate independently with fixed functionalities and without internet connectivity. About one-third p. 340of the students who participated in the survey regularly use ChatGPT in their writing tasks ([Table 20.3](#T20.3)).

## Conclusions

In conclusion, this chapter on academic integrity and the role of AI in the study process connects the empirical findings of a limited explorative UAEU female student sample with the results of existing studies on AI in higher education institutions. Academic integrity is about being honest and trustworthy in schools and colleges. While this concept seems straightforward, previous studies show that not all students and teachers see academic integrity in the same way (Dyer et al., 2020; [Nugroho et al., 2023](#EEP_20_YLKF_C020_CIT000059)), and their views can be influenced by their field of study, cultural background, and other factors ([Cuadrado et al., 2021](#EEP_20_YLKF_C020_CIT000018); [Guerrero-Dib et al., 2020](#EEP_20_YLKF_C020_CIT000030)).

A homogenous sample of undergraduate Arab students allowed us to explore the attitudes and values of academic integrity in one of the federal universities of the p. 342UAE. On the one hand, the students demonstrated quite high academic integrity in terms of low cheating on exams. On the other hand, up to half of the surveyed student population are able to use GenAI for their tasks, and one-third of them are using ChatGPT regularly for writing assignments, including language checks and more. Our preliminary findings did not disclose any correlations between year of study and current GPA and academic integrity indicators. Admitting the need for further studies, this outcome allows us to assume that it is the values, attitudes, and perceptions of students that would define academic dishonesty.

As previous research has shown, cheating in school, such as plagiarism, is linked to certain cultural values and educational environments (Lee et al., 2020). Studies from [McCabe and Trevino (1997)](#EEP_20_YLKF_C020_CIT000050) and Whitley Jr. ([1998](#EEP_20_YLKF_C020_CIT000072)), followed by research like that of [Barnett et al. (2016)](#EEP_20_YLKF_C020_CIT000008), show that teaching students about ethics can help reduce cheating. There is also a recognized difference in how teachers and students view cheating, indicating the need for clear communication and education to reduce misunderstandings ([Hard et al., 2006](#EEP_20_YLKF_C020_CIT000032)). The literature notes differences in how plagiarism is seen by students from different cultures or language backgrounds, pointing to the need for education that considers these differences ([Rogerson & Basanta, 2016](#EEP_20_YLKF_C020_CIT000063); [Kuo & Li, 2020](#EEP_20_YLKF_C020_CIT000043)). The outcomes of the study support the idea that ethical education is key to understanding and preventing academic dishonesty and suggest further studies on ethics, values, and academic integrity in the Arab World context.

AI is becoming more common in education processes, and its impact on cheating and teaching is a growing concern ([Bertram Gallant, 2008](#EEP_20_YLKF_C020_CIT000082); [Gallant & Drinan, 2008](#EEP_20_YLKF_C020_CIT000086)). While AI can help catch plagiarism and personalize learning, it also raises questions about academic honesty ([Eaton, 2021](#EEP_20_YLKF_C020_CIT000088); [Mindzak, 2020](#EEP_20_YLKF_C020_CIT000089); [Morrison & Mindzak, 2021](#EEP_20_YLKF_C020_CIT000090)). AI can detect plagiarism very effectively, which is a step forward in maintaining honest work ([Holden et al., 2021](#EEP_20_YLKF_C020_CIT000033); [Perkins, 2023](#EEP_20_YLKF_C020_CIT000061); [Cotton et al., 2024](#EEP_20_YLKF_C020_CIT000017); Stephens et al., [2021](#EEP_20_YLKF_C020_CIT000067)). We agree with [Sullivan et al. (2023)](#EEP_20_YLKF_C020_CIT000069) and [Crawford et al. (2023) that](#EEP_20_YLKF_C020_CIT000085) higher education institutions and schools have a duty to use AI fairly and teach students about the ethical use of this new technology.

Building upon the insights gained from this study, we can state that artificial intelligence tools are becoming more integrated into academic settings, and their implications on academic integrity are becoming increasingly significant. To address this, higher education institutions should actively develop policies that enforce the transparent use of AI tools. Until now, the UAEU does not have a general policy around the usage of AI in the study process. It is highly recommended that UAEU require students to declare their use of AI in assignments and projects. There should also be also guidelines and regulations produced for faculty members on how to assess those assignments with AI usage.

Additionally, higher educational institutions should develop and implement ethical education programs that not only focus on the responsible use of AI but also tailor these educational programs to the specific needs of the courses to endorse academic integrity via AI usage. As AI technologies evolve, it is crucial for these policies and educational initiatives to be regularly revisited and updated, ensuring they remain effective in fostering an academic environment where honesty and integrity p. 343are upheld. This proactive approach will not only mitigate the risks associated with AI in academic contexts but also prepare students to navigate future technological landscapes ethically and responsibly.

Finally, another important outcome of the explorative study of UAEU students showed that students realize the massive need for AI tools in their future careers for their time-efficiency and up-to-date digital skills. At the same time, the majority understand the challenge of maintaining academic integrity since AI encourages dishonesty with its easy access, availability, and easy usage. We claim that with strong ethics and values, AI can make the learning environment better and more productive. This approach helps higher education institutions create a culture where honesty is practiced sincerely, preparing students to be future leaders who value integrity.

args.summary:
This is a chapter from an academic book examining academic dishonesty among undergraduate students in the context of widespread AI tools, specifically focusing on female students at UAE University (UAEU) in the United Arab Emirates. The study builds upon McCabe and Trevino's (1993) Original Academic Dishonesty Scale and surveyed 109 female students in Spring 2024.

**Key Context:** Few studies on academic dishonesty have been conducted in the Arab world. The UAE presents a unique case due to its advanced digitalization. The chapter explores both traditional academic dishonesty and "e-dishonesty," including ChatGPT usage.

**Key Findings from the Pilot Study:**
- Direct cheating during exams was low (1.8% used ChatGPT during exams, 5.5% paid for assignments, 5.5% copied exam questions)
- However, "lighter" misconduct was widespread: 38.5% used ChatGPT for assignments, 44% approached professors to influence grades, 67.9% used sites like Chegg/Quizlet, and 38.5% used help from friends/relatives
- 34.8% agreed that GenAI tools encourage academic dishonesty
- Only 5.5% thought it was acceptable to submit AI-generated work as their own
- 32.8% regularly use ChatGPT for writing tasks
- 60% believe students must learn AI tools for their careers
- 66.4% use AI to save time; 66.6% use it for new ideas
- No significant correlations were found between GPA or year of study and academic dishonesty (except a weak positive correlation between ChatGPT use and senior year)
- 87% of students were concerned about privacy and information security with AI tools

**Literature Review Highlights:** The chapter reviews extensive research on academic integrity, noting that cultural backgrounds, academic disciplines, and ethical education influence perceptions of dishonesty. AI is described as a "double-edged sword" in education—useful for personalized learning and plagiarism detection, but raising concerns about academic honesty.

**Recommendations:** The authors recommend that UAEU develop policies requiring students to declare AI use, create guidelines for faculty on assessing AI-assisted work, implement ethical education programs, and regularly update policies as AI evolves. The chapter argues that with strong ethics, AI can enhance learning environments.

# New College Board Research: Faculty Express Near-Universal Concern That Student AI Use Undermines Original Writing and Critical Thinking

*Survey of 3,000+ faculty finds widespread student AI use, deep concerns about critical thinking and writing skills, and a call for clearer guidance*

[College Board

* February 25, 2026](/author/college-board-communications)

As generative artificial intelligence becomes prevalent in higher education, the latest entry in College Board’s AI research brief series reveals that college faculty believe AI is already transforming college student learning, often in potentially troubling ways.

According to College Board’s most recent AI research brief, [“College Faculty Perceptions of Generative Artificial Intelligence in Higher Education,”](https://research.collegeboard.org/media/pdf/ai-research-brief-3-vf.pdf) nearly three-quarters (74%) of faculty report that students are using AI to write essays or papers, and 67% say students are using it to paraphrase or rewrite content. Almost half of faculty believe at least half of their students are using AI for writing-related tasks.

“Faculty are navigating this critical transition, as AI rapidly expands in higher education,” said Jessica Howell, PhD, vice president of Research at College Board. “This research shows that faculty have serious concerns about AI’s impact on critical thinking, original writing, and academic integrity. Faculty, especially those in writing-intensive courses, are asking important questions about how to preserve core learning goals while preparing students for a world where AI will be part of the workplace.”

This higher education research builds on two previous briefs examining AI use in high schools. In [October 2025](/new-research-majority-high-school-students-use-generative-ai-schoolwork), College Board reported that 84% of high school students use generative AI for schoolwork tasks such as brainstorming, revising essays, and research, while school leaders and educators are still clarifying policies and guidelines. A [December 2025](/follow-report-ai-high-schools-genai-use-and-policy-varies-academic-achievement-attainment-grade-and) follow-up found AI use and high school policies vary widely by student demographics, academic achievement, grade level, and school context, with disparities in access and official guidance revealing an emerging digital divide.

During summer 2025, College Board surveyed more than 3,000 U.S. college faculty. The research finds that faculty sentiment toward AI skews negative, with 45% reporting an overall negative view of AI use in higher education and 34% reporting a positive view. Despite their concerns, most faculty are experimenting with AI themselves, with 77% saying they have used AI in their professional role.

## Differing Perceptions by Institution Selectivity and Discipline

The findings also emphasize a growing divide within higher education. Faculty at more selective institutions report higher levels of student AI use and greater concern about its academic impact, while faculty at open enrollment colleges are more likely to see AI as a practical instructional tool and report using it themselves.

By discipline, the divide is even sharper. Faculty in writing-intensive fields such as English, history, and humanities are more likely to report student AI use, greater AI use for detecting plagiarism or academic dishonesty, and more negative attitudes toward AI. In contrast, faculty in STEM and business disciplines are generally more likely to report using AI themselves, for research and their own academic writing, and to express more positive views.

Key differences include:

* Negative sentiment toward AI increases with institutional selectivity.
* Faculty at open enrollment colleges are more likely to report using AI themselves to create or revise teaching materials, develop lesson plans, and detect plagiarism.
* Faculty at more selective colleges are more likely to report widespread student AI use, particularly for writing tasks.
* Faculty in English and other writing-intensive disciplines report the highest levels of classroom disruption and challenges related to AI use.
* Writing-based disciplines are more likely to have formal classroom AI policies in place.
* Faculty in STEM and business disciplines are among the most likely to use AI professionally and to view it positively.

## Concerns About Impacts of AI

While some faculty see potential benefits, such as personalized explanations and support for understanding complex concepts, far more agree on the negative impacts of AI use than on its positive impacts. More than 84% agree that AI reduces students’ critical thinking, originality, and deep engagement with course material, while 88% are concerned about overreliance on automation. Regarding academic integrity, 92% of faculty are concerned about plagiarism or dishonesty facilitated by AI.

## Challenges Around Classroom AI Guidance

Nearly three-quarters (72%) of faculty report that they face at least minor challenges managing student AI use. Yet confidence remains low with only 21% reporting feeling very confident guiding AI use in their classrooms and 79% saying they are either just beginning to explore what’s needed or still need guidance. Almost half report having a formal classroom policy on AI use, while many say institutional guidance and support remain inconsistent.

The brief highlights a growing tension in higher education: College student AI use is expanding rapidly, but faculty consensus on how to adjust has not yet formed. The report emphasizes that further research and evidence-based policy development will help institutions balance innovation with academic integrity and student learning.

---

**About College Board**  
College Board reaches more than 7 million students a year, helping them navigate the path from high school to college and career. Our not-for-profit membership organization was founded more than 120 years ago. We pioneered programs like the SAT® and AP® to expand opportunities for students and help them develop the skills they need. Our BigFuture® program helps students plan for college, pay for college, and explore careers. Learn more at cb.org.

The survey of over 3,000 U.S. college faculty found that 74% report students using AI to write essays, and 67% say students use it to paraphrase or rewrite content. Faculty sentiment skews negative, with 45% reporting negative views of AI in higher education versus 34% positive. Over 84% agree AI reduces critical thinking and originality, 88% are concerned about overreliance on automation, and 92% worry about AI-facilitated plagiarism. Only 21% of faculty feel very confident guiding AI use in classrooms, and nearly half have formal AI policies. The research also highlights divides by institutional selectivity and discipline: faculty at selective institutions report more student AI use and concern, while those at open enrollment colleges are more likely to use AI themselves as an instructional tool. Faculty in writing-intensive fields (English, history, humanities) report more negative attitudes and classroom disruption, while STEM and business faculty are more positive and likely to use AI professionally. This brief builds on two prior College Board studies from October and December 2025 examining AI use in high schools.

# Press Release Details

### AI Has Hurt Academic Integrity in College Courses but Can Also Enhance Learning, Say Instructors, Students

*New Wiley survey reveals students far more likely than instructors to use AI in their classes*

**Hoboken, NJ**—College instructors and students have mixed feelings about the use of artificial intelligence (AI) in postsecondary classes, with worries about academic integrity countered by the hope that AI can also be used to enhance learning. But despite their mixed feelings, both instructors and students agree that AI is here to stay.

These findings come from *[The Latest Insights into Academic Integrity: Instructor & Student Experiences, Attitudes, and the Impact of AI 2024 Update](https://www.wiley.com/en-us/network/education/instructors/teaching-strategies/the-latest-insights-into-academic-integrity-instructor-and-student-experiences-attitudes-and-the-impact-of-ai-2024-update?utm_medium=pressrelese&utm_source=wileynewsroom&utm_content=augustpressrelease&utm_term=academicintegrityreport)*, a new report from [Wiley](https://www.wiley.com/en-us) (NYSE: WLY), one of the world’s largest publishers and a global leader in research and learning. The results were gathered in surveys with college instructors and students across North America.

The results of Wiley’s survey show both instructors and students believe cheating is on the rise in college classrooms. Nearly all instructors (96%) say they believe at least some of their students cheated over the past year, a substantial increase from 72% in Wiley’s [2021 survey](https://www.wiley.com/en-us/network/education/instructors/teaching-strategies/new-insights-into-academic-integrity-fall-2021-report). And more than half (53%) of students say there’s more cheating now than last year, with 23% saying significantly more.

The majority of both students and instructors also believe cheating will increase in the next few years, largely because of increased use of AI. And instructors worry that AI could negatively impact student’s critical thinking and writing skills.

On the other hand, both students and instructors believe AI can help generate ideas, save time, and assist learners with understanding difficult content if used appropriately.

“While students and instructors have a general belief that AI will be used in ways that are detrimental to academic integrity, they also seem to sense that AI can benefit learning when used the right way,” said Lyssa Vanderbeek, Wiley group vice president for courseware. “These beliefs will continue to change as instructors and students gain more experience with AI and as the tools that leverage AI continue to evolve.”

“These data drive home the need for faculty to rethink our learning outcomes, teaching strategies and assessments,” said David A. Rettinger, applied professor of psychology at the University of Tulsa and coauthor of the book *Cheating Academic Integrity: Lessons from 30 Years of Research*. “AI will affect every aspect of learning, and faculty must determine whether the impact is positive or negative. AI is disruptive. It is not a fad that we can ignore and hope it goes out of style.”

**Use of AI Limited**

The findings suggest many of the attitudes expressed by students and especially instructors may not be based on actual experience. Use of AI is much more widespread among students than instructors, yet fewer than half (45%) of students say they’ve used AI in the classes the past year. Only 15% of instructors say the same.

Students are most likely to have used generative AI tools to help with writing assignments, to brainstorm and generate ideas, and to help understand difficult concepts.

Students who have not used AI in their classes in the past year say it is because they don’t trust AI tools, they are concerned their instructor would think they were cheating, and/or they’re not familiar with how to use AI tools.

**Deterring Cheating**

Instructors plan to make a variety of changes to help protect academic integrity and avoid misuse of AI. These plans include using different types of assessments, such as more in-person exams, and more communication to students on the negative consequences of cheating and methods used to detect cheating attempts. The findings suggest demonstrating how classes are relevant to students and their career goals could also help.

Instructors clearly express a need for guidance on how to properly use AI and tools to deal with academic misconduct enabled or encouraged by AI.

Wiley includes an academic integrity assignment for students in all of its WileyPLUS, Knewton Alta, and zyBooks courses which gives them feedback on what behaviors are and aren’t appropriate from an academic integrity standpoint. It also employs techniques and enhancements within its courseware to promote academic integrity, including [specific tools](https://www.zybooks.com/why-zybooks/zybooks-academic-integrity/) such as Similarity Checker, Coding Trail, and Playback History.

In addition, Wiley works to educate instructors about teaching strategies proven to reduce academic dishonesty and has conducted research on methods to improve academic integrity, such as [Impact of Several Low-Effort Cheating-Reduction Methods in a CS1 Class](https://www.zybooks.com/research-items/impact-of-several-low-effort-cheating-reduction-methods-in-a-cs1-class/), which found that low-effort actions by instructors can lead to substantial behavior improvements.

**Methodology**

The results of this report are based on surveys completed in March 2024 by 850 college instructors and 2,067 students across the U.S. and Canada.

The full report can be accessed [here](https://www.wiley.com/en-us/network/education/instructors/teaching-strategies/the-latest-insights-into-academic-integrity-instructor-and-student-experiences-attitudes-and-the-impact-of-ai-2024-update?utm_medium=pressrelese&utm_source=wileynewsroom&utm_content=augustpressrelease&utm_term=academicintegrityreport).

**About Wiley**

Wiley (NYSE: WLY) is one of the world’s largest publishers and a trusted leader in research and learning. Our industry-leading content, services, platforms, and knowledge networks are tailored to meet the evolving needs of our customers and partners, including researchers, students, instructors, professionals, institutions, and corporations. We empower knowledge-seekers to transform today’s biggest obstacles into tomorrow’s brightest opportunities. For more than two centuries, Wiley has been delivering on its timeless mission to unlock human potential. Visit us at [Wiley.com](https://www.wiley.com/en-us). Follow us on [Facebook](https://www.facebook.com/JohnWileySons/), [Twitter](https://twitter.com/WileyGlobal), [LinkedIn](https://www.linkedin.com/company/john-wiley-and-sons/) and [Instagram](https://www.instagram.com/wiley_global/).
