### Countries

Most research took place in the USA (N = 8), China (N = 7), Finland (N = 3), Hong Kong (N = 3), Israel (N = 3), Spain (N = 3), Australia (N = 2)and Japan (N=2). Others were conducted in Brazil, Denmark, Greece, Indonesia, New Zealand, Norway,Sweden,Thailand, and the UK. The locations of the remaining six articles are unknown.

### Educational levels

Primary and secondary schools are both the most researched educational levels, each covering 44% of the selected articles, followed by kindergartens (11%) and K-12 education (2%).

These selected studies generally include samples of students of both genders and a wide range of ages, from 3-year-old kindergarten students (Vartiainen et al., [2020](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40692-023-00304-9#ref-CR100)) to 20-year-old Danish high school students (Kaspersen et al., [2021](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40692-023-00304-9#ref-CR41)). It also encompasses participants in science technology engineering mathematics (STEM) classes (Ho et al., [2019](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40692-023-00304-9#ref-CR34)), high-performing students of the Scientists in School program (Heinze et al., [2010](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40692-023-00304-9#ref-CR32)), students with and without an AI background (Yoder et al., [2020](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40692-023-00304-9#ref-CR109)), and students from varying socioeconomic backgrounds (Kaspersen et al., [2021](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40692-023-00304-9#ref-CR41)).

There were three AI-related research studies between 1995 and 2017, mostly adopting unplugged activities and games for AI teaching, which are different from research conducted after 2017. The first article was published by Scherz and Haberman ([1995](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40692-023-00304-9#ref-CR86)), who designed a special AI curriculum with the use of abstract data types and instructional models (e.g., graphs and decision trees) to teach AI concepts such as logic programming and AI systems to high school students in Israel. In another two studies, the use of programming robots (Heinze et al., [2010](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40692-023-00304-9#ref-CR32)) and computer science unplugged activities (Lucas, [2009](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40692-023-00304-9#ref-CR55)) were explored with Australian and New Zealand K-6 students, respectively. Since then, a greater variety of learning tools have been employed and expanded to European and Asian countries across all educational levels in K-12 settings. Appendix [1](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40692-023-00304-9#Sec32) provides an overview of the selected articles.

## Findings

### RQ1: What are the potential learning tools identified in AI K-12 education?

The potential learning tools identified in K-12 contexts were intelligent agents (N=20), software-focused devices (N=19), hardware-focused devices (N=10), and unplugged activities (N=6) (Fig. [4](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40692-023-00304-9#Fig4) and Table [4](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40692-023-00304-9#Tab4)). In this section, intelligent agents, software devices, and hardware devices are discussed.

#### Intelligent agents

Intelligent agents, such as Google Teachable Machine, Learning ML, and Machine Learning for Kids, which make decisions based on environmental inputs by using their sensors and actuators, are the most popular learning tools for enhancing students’ computational thinking skills within K-12 contexts. Teachable Machine is a web-based tool developed by Google and is found to be more effective than are unplugged activities in kindergarten settings (Lucas, [2009](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40692-023-00304-9#ref-CR55); Vartiainen et al., [2020](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40692-023-00304-9#ref-CR100)). In Vartiainen et al. ([2020](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40692-023-00304-9#ref-CR100)), children aged between 3 and 9 autonomously explored the input‒output relationship with Google Teachable Machine, which fostered their intellectual curiosity, developed their computational thinking, and enhanced their understanding of machine learning. In both primary (Toivonen et al., [2020](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40692-023-00304-9#ref-CR95); Melsión et al., [2021](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40692-023-00304-9#ref-CR63)) and secondary schools (Kilhoffer et al., [2023](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40692-023-00304-9#ref-CR43); Martins et al., [2023](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40692-023-00304-9#ref-CR60)), Google Teachable Machine has been employed, allowing students to use their webcams, images, or sounds without coding to develop their own machine learning classification models.

In addition, Learning ML has been employed for primary schools to create AI-driven solutions and models, for example, to teach the supervised machine learning principle (Voulgari et al., [2021](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40692-023-00304-9#ref-CR101); Rodríguez-Garciá et al., [2021](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40692-023-00304-9#ref-CR82)), which simplifies abstract AI algorithms for primary school students. Machine Learning for Kids, which introduces the power of the IBM Watson engine for AI modelling (Fernández-Martínez et al., [2021](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40692-023-00304-9#ref-CR23)), Cognimates (Sabuncuoglu, [2020](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40692-023-00304-9#ref-CR83); Fernández-Martínez et al., [2021](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40692-023-00304-9#ref-CR23)), which allows students to practice coding, and Ecraft2Learn, which contains a deep learning functionality (Kahn et al., [2018](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40692-023-00304-9#ref-CR38)), have also been used in secondary school classrooms. Intelligent agents often offer students hands-on experience to develop datasets and to build customized machine learning systems.

#### Software devices

Software devices are adopted to enable mostly primary and secondary school students to learn about computational thinking, including programming for sequences, rule-based and conditional mechanisms, as well as data science and machine learning using visual language. For example, Scratch, a block-based programming software, is frequently used in both primary (Dai et al., [2023](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40692-023-00304-9#ref-CR19); Li & Song, [2019](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40692-023-00304-9#ref-CR50); Shamir & Levin, [2021](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40692-023-00304-9#ref-CR88)) and secondary schools (Estevez et al., [2019](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40692-023-00304-9#ref-CR22); Fernández-Martínez et al., [2021](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40692-023-00304-9#ref-CR23)). Other software is used for visualizing and scaffolding abstract AI concepts through online games and experiences, such as Quick and Draw (Martins et al., [2023](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40692-023-00304-9#ref-CR60)) and Music Box (Han et al., [2018](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40692-023-00304-9#ref-CR31)). In primary schools, Kitten is used to teach block-based programming (Li & Song, [2019](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40692-023-00304-9#ref-CR50)), whereas C++ and JavaScript are used for logical thinking and simulation (Gong et al., [2020](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40692-023-00304-9#ref-CR27)). In secondary schools, researchers have often employed free online software and tools, such as Snap (Yoder et al., [2020](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40692-023-00304-9#ref-CR109)) and Python (Gong et al., [2018](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40692-023-00304-9#ref-CR28); Norouzi et al., [2020](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40692-023-00304-9#ref-CR70)), for algorithm automation, as well as RapidMiner for no-code data science learning (Sakulkueakulsuk et al., [2018](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40692-023-00304-9#ref-CR84)). To introduce machine learning concepts to secondary school students, other researchers have focused on developing online games such as the Rock Paper Game (Kajiwara et al., [2023](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40692-023-00304-9#ref-CR39)) and the 3D role-player video game Quest (Priya et al., [2022](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40692-023-00304-9#ref-CR77)).

#### Hardware devices

In addition, hardware, such as robotics and physical artifacts, has also been used with built-in software to supplement students’ understanding of AI concepts. Williams et al. ([2019a](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40692-023-00304-9#ref-CR106), [2019b](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40692-023-00304-9#ref-CR107)) introduced a preschool originated programming platform consisting of a social robot (PopBot) and a block-based programming interface. In Williams et al. ([2019a](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40692-023-00304-9#ref-CR106)), 80 prekindergartens to second-grade children (aged four to seven) were asked to build their own LEGO robot characters by using DUPLO block programming. PopBot is used as a learning companion to demonstrate its human-like behavior and to demystify AI concepts to younger students.

The lawn bowling robot (Ho et al., [2019](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40692-023-00304-9#ref-CR34)), Zhorai conversational robot (Lin et al., [2020](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40692-023-00304-9#ref-CR52)), Micro: Bits (Lin et al., [2021](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40692-023-00304-9#ref-CR51)), and Plush toys (Tseng et al., [2021](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40692-023-00304-9#ref-CR97)) have been used in primary schools, while CUHKiCar (Chiu et al., [2021](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40692-023-00304-9#ref-CR16)), the Alpha robot dog (Chai et al., [2020](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40692-023-00304-9#ref-CR11)), Raspberry Pi Raspbian and a four-wheel drive chassis (Gong et al., [2018](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40692-023-00304-9#ref-CR28)) have been used in secondary schools. For example, in Ho et al. ([2019](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40692-023-00304-9#ref-CR34)), grade six students built lawn-bowling robots for games and competitions while learning about the binary search and optimization algorithms of machine learning. Chiu et al. ([2021](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40692-023-00304-9#ref-CR16)) introduced the robotic CUHKiCar to secondary school students so that they could perform face-tracking and line following tasks.

### RQ2: What pedagogical strategies are commonly proposed by studies on AI K-12 learning tools?

As shown in Fig. [5](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40692-023-00304-9#Fig5), the four orientations of pedagogy are summarized as authentic/constructive, reflective, didactic, and unplugged. While a total of 17 potential pedagogical strategies were identified within the four orientations in K-12 contexts (Table [5](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40692-023-00304-9#Tab5)), authentic/constructive methodologies with project-based learning (N=27) were the most popular pedagogy used across kindergartens (Williams et al., [2019a](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40692-023-00304-9#ref-CR106), [2019b](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40692-023-00304-9#ref-CR107)), primary schools (Toivonen et al., [2020](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40692-023-00304-9#ref-CR95); Rodríguez-Garciá et al., [2021](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40692-023-00304-9#ref-CR82)), and secondary schools (Gong et al., [2018](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40692-023-00304-9#ref-CR28); Kilhoffer et al., [2023](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40692-023-00304-9#ref-CR43); Sakulkueakulsuk et al., [2018](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40692-023-00304-9#ref-CR84)). When teaching AI to students with a diverse range of needs, the evidence demonstrates the positive impact of combining multiple pedagogical approaches in K-12 studies (Heinze et al., [2010](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40692-023-00304-9#ref-CR32); Lee et al., [2021](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40692-023-00304-9#ref-CR47); Williams et al., [2019a](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40692-023-00304-9#ref-CR106), [2019b](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40692-023-00304-9#ref-CR107)).

**Fig.5**

![Image 11: Fig. 5](https://media.springernature.com/lw685/springer-static/image/art%3A10.1007%2Fs40692-023-00304-9/MediaObjects/40692_2023_304_Fig5_HTML.png)

[Full size image](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40692-023-00304-9/figures/5)

Four orientations of pedagogical strategies commonly used in AI K-12 education

**Table 5 Four orientations of the pedagogical strategies used in AI K-12 learning tools studies**

[Full size table](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40692-023-00304-9/tables/5)

First, authentic and constructive methodologies, project-based (N=27), human-computer interaction (N=7), and play-based active learning (N=5) approaches have been commonly used in K-12 education. Offering hands-on opportunities to students to learn about real-world applications of AI is an example of project-based learning (Fernández-Martínez et al., [2021](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40692-023-00304-9#ref-CR23); Han et al., [2018](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40692-023-00304-9#ref-CR31); Williams et al., [2019a](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40692-023-00304-9#ref-CR106)). Other researchers have examined whether students can acquire AI knowledge on human-computer interactive experiences and have found that this does not require any prior knowledge of AI models, such as Zohari (Melsión et al., [2021](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40692-023-00304-9#ref-CR63)) and Google Teachable Machine (Lin et al., [2020](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40692-023-00304-9#ref-CR52); Vartiainen et al., [2020](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40692-023-00304-9#ref-CR100)). In addition, child-centered play-based learning can effectively engage students and encourage them to take the initiative to construct knowledge during the process of imaginative play (Heinze et al., [2010](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40692-023-00304-9#ref-CR32)), which involves students adopting the role of AI developer, tester, and AI robot (Henry et al., [2021](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40692-023-00304-9#ref-CR33)).

#### Pedagogical strategies in kindergartens

Researchers have often used project-based approaches (N=3), human-computer interactions (N=3), play-based learning (N=1), and unplugged activities (N=1) to teach younger students AI concepts. In a project-based learning approach, students learn by actively engaging in real-world projects. Williams et al. ([2019a](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40692-023-00304-9#ref-CR106), [2019b](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40692-023-00304-9#ref-CR107)) used a hands-on project allowing prekindergarten and kindergarten students to acquire AI concepts, including knowledge-based systems, supervised machine learning, and AI generative music. Alternatively, Vartiainen et al. ([2020](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40692-023-00304-9#ref-CR100)) studied human-computer interactions that allowed students to freely explore the input‒output relationship with Google Teachable Machine to identify and to evaluate a problem and find a solution to it. Heinze et al. ([2010](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40692-023-00304-9#ref-CR32)) focused on imaginative play, which is relevant to young students, as play is associated with various levels of autonomy and provides an engaging introduction to AI and the formation of scientific concepts. Lucas ([2009](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40692-023-00304-9#ref-CR55)) used unplugged activities to teach the key concepts of computing, including data encoding, data compression, and error detection.

#### Pedagogical strategies in primary schools

Project-based learning is more frequently used in primary schools than in kindergartens: It has been reported as a learning approach in 14 of the 18 studies of primary school settings, compared to only three of the five studies in the kindergarten setting. Similarly, in primary school settings, studies have revealed a strong dependence on play/game-based (N=5) and human-computer interaction learning approaches (N=3).

Projects that demonstrate students’ improved AI knowledge have been conducted. Machine learning projects (Toivonen et al., [2020](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40692-023-00304-9#ref-CR95)), LearningML projects (Rodríguez-Garciá et al., [2021](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40692-023-00304-9#ref-CR82)), and “AI+” projects (Han et al., [2018](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40692-023-00304-9#ref-CR31)) have been designed to demystify AI knowledge. Henry et al. ([2021](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40692-023-00304-9#ref-CR33)) integrated machine learning in role-playing games, while Shamir and Levin ([2021](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40692-023-00304-9#ref-CR88)) allowed students to play with AI chatbots to develop AI models and to construct a rule-based machine-learning system. Some researchers have designed learning programs that offer human-computer interaction activities to educate students about gender bias (Melsión et al., [2021](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40692-023-00304-9#ref-CR63)) and the social impact of mistakes made by AI models in training datasets (Lin et al., [2020](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40692-023-00304-9#ref-CR52)).

#### Pedagogical strategies in secondary schools

The project-based learning approach (N=10) is also the most dominant in secondary schools, followed by collaborative learning (N=5). First, project-based learning is used to engage students by applying their AI knowledge to solve real-world problems. Teachers have reported that AI projects and hands-on activities are effective in keeping students focused on tasks (Kilhoffer et al., [2023](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40692-023-00304-9#ref-CR43)). For example, a smart car-themed AI project (Gong et al., [2018](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40692-023-00304-9#ref-CR28)), the Redesign YouTube project (Fernández-Martínez et al., [2021](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40692-023-00304-9#ref-CR23)), and the agriculture-based AI Challenge project (Sakulkueakulsuk et al., [2018](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40692-023-00304-9#ref-CR84)) have been introduced to provide hands-on experience for students to connect their knowledge to their day-to-day lives. Through active exploration, such projects prompt secondary school students to contemplate the personal, social, economic, and ethical consequences of AI technologies (Kaspersen et al., [2021](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40692-023-00304-9#ref-CR41)).

Second, collaborative learning allows students to work in groups to promote cognitive knowledge, as it engages them in scientific inquiry with the help of smart devices (Wan et al., [2020](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40692-023-00304-9#ref-CR102)). Kaspersen et al. ([2021](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40692-023-00304-9#ref-CR41)) designed a collaborative learning tool, VotestratesML, together with a voting project allowing students to build machine learning models based on real-world voting data to predict results.

### RQ3: What learning outcomes have been demonstrated in studies on AI K-12 learning tools?

Of the 46 articles, 31 reported potential learning outcomes: (1) cognitive outcomes, (2) affective and behavioral outcomes, and (3) the level of course satisfaction and soft skills acquisition.

#### Cognitive outcomes

Thirty-one studies documented various degrees of positive cognitive outcomes. Students generally showed a basic understanding of AI, including AI rule-based systems (Ho et al., [2019](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40692-023-00304-9#ref-CR34)), machine learning principles and applications (Han et al., [2018](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40692-023-00304-9#ref-CR31); Shamir & Levin, [2021](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40692-023-00304-9#ref-CR88)), AI ethics (Melsión et al., [2021](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40692-023-00304-9#ref-CR63)), and AI limitations (Lin et al., [2020](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40692-023-00304-9#ref-CR52)). In Williams et al. ([2019a](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40692-023-00304-9#ref-CR106)), 70% of prekindergarten and kindergarten students understood knowledge-based systems, whereas Vartiainen et al. ([2020](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40692-023-00304-9#ref-CR100)) found that, through AI learning tools, younger students developed their computational thinking and their understanding of machine-learning principles and applications. Then, Dai et al. ([2023](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40692-023-00304-9#ref-CR19)) reported that primary school students taught with analogy-based pedagogy (i.e., using humans as a reference to teach and learn AI) significantly outperformed primary school students taught with the conventional direct instructional approach in terms of developing their conceptual understanding and increasing their AI technical knowledge proficiency as well as their ethical awareness of AI. Other researchers have argued that primary school students have demonstrated their understanding of AI by constructing and applying machine-learning algorithms with the help of digital role-playing games (Voulgari et al., [2021](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40692-023-00304-9#ref-CR101)) and project-based pedagogy (Shamir & Levin, [2021](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40692-023-00304-9#ref-CR88)). Through designing and programming a robot, students increased their understanding of AI biases (Melsión et al., [2021](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40692-023-00304-9#ref-CR63)). In secondary schools, researchers have also reported an increase in students’ knowledge of AI algorithms (Yoder et al., [2020](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40692-023-00304-9#ref-CR109)) and machine learning concepts (Sakulkueakulsuk et al., [2018](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40692-023-00304-9#ref-CR84)), as well as their recognition of AI patterns (Wan et al., [2020](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40692-023-00304-9#ref-CR102)). For example, students understood the fundamental neural networks of machine learning concepts by developing a classification model of recycling images (Martins et al., [2023](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40692-023-00304-9#ref-CR60)).

#### Affective and behavioral outcomes

Affective and behavioral outcomes have been identified in AI learning tool studies within K-12 contexts. In general, students’ motivation to learn AI (Han et al., [2018](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40692-023-00304-9#ref-CR31); Shamir & Levin, [2021](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40692-023-00304-9#ref-CR88), [2022](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40692-023-00304-9#ref-CR89)) and their interest in the course (Mariescu-Istodor & Jormanainen, [2019](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40692-023-00304-9#ref-CR58); Martins et al., [2023](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40692-023-00304-9#ref-CR60)) were enhanced as a result of AI learning activities. Students’ perceptions of the relevance of AI to their life also increased (Kajiwara et al., [2023](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40692-023-00304-9#ref-CR39); Lin et al., [2021](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40692-023-00304-9#ref-CR51)). Students scored high on self-efficacy (Kajiwara et al., [2023](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40692-023-00304-9#ref-CR39); Shamir & Levin, [2022](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40692-023-00304-9#ref-CR89)) and confidence (Shamir & Levin, [2021](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40692-023-00304-9#ref-CR88)) in training and validating an AI system. In Martins et al. ([2023](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40692-023-00304-9#ref-CR60)), over 45% of 108 secondary school student participants in the introductory course “Machine Learning for all” reported that they perceived AI learning as an enjoyable experience, and 63% of them hoped to learn more about machine learning in the future.

Moreover, students reported that they were highly motivated to explore the Teachable Machine (Vartiainen et al., [2020](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40692-023-00304-9#ref-CR100)), to design the robotic arm and computer source codes (Ho et al., [2019](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40692-023-00304-9#ref-CR34)), to draw animals and sea creatures for the machine learning project (Mariescu-Istodor & Jormanainen, [2019](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40692-023-00304-9#ref-CR58)), and to predict the sweetness of mangoes by using machine learning models (Sakulkueakulsuk et al., [2018](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40692-023-00304-9#ref-CR84)).

From the behavioral perspective, high student engagement was reported in project-based (Kaspersen et al., [2021](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40692-023-00304-9#ref-CR41); Shamir & Levin, [2021](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40692-023-00304-9#ref-CR88); Wan et al., [2020](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40692-023-00304-9#ref-CR102)) and play/game-based (Heinze et al., [2010](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40692-023-00304-9#ref-CR32); Voulgari et al., [2021](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40692-023-00304-9#ref-CR101)) settings. Primary students attended all sessions and expressed a desire to join an upcoming AI contingency course (Shamir & Levin, [2021](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40692-023-00304-9#ref-CR88)), while secondary students were actively engaged in scientific inquiry (Wan et al., [2020](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40692-023-00304-9#ref-CR102)). Students were also keen on recommending AI games to their friends (Voulgari et al., [2021](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40692-023-00304-9#ref-CR101)). Therefore, a combination of play/game-based and project-based approaches may consolidate AI concepts through gameplay while enhancing students’ engagement in AI projects (Han et al., [2018](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40692-023-00304-9#ref-CR31)).

args.key_excerpts: The investigation reveals that the promotion of AI literacy education has seen significant progress in the past two decades.,Intelligent agents, including Google's Teachable Machine, Learning ML, and Machine Learning for Kids, are age-appropriate tools for AI literacy education in K-12 contexts.,Project-based, human–computer collaborative learning and play- and game-based approaches, with constructivist methodologies, have been applied frequently in AI literacy education.,Cognitive, affective, and behavioral learning outcomes, course satisfaction and soft skills acquisition have been reported.,One challenge is delivering AI content in an age-appropriate and effective manner.
args.summary:
This open-access article, "Artificial intelligence (AI) learning tools in K-12 education: A scoping review," published on January 6, 2024, in the Journal of Computers in Education (Volume 12, pages 93–131, 2025), reviews 46 studies from academic conferences and journals to investigate pedagogical strategies, learning tools, assessment methods, and student learning outcomes in AI literacy education for K-12 contexts.

**Key Findings:**
- **Learning Tools:** Intelligent agents (e.g., Google's Teachable Machine, Learning ML, Machine Learning for Kids) are the most popular (N=20), followed by software devices like Scratch and Python (N=19), hardware devices like PopBots and robotics (N=10), and unplugged activities (N=6). Kindergarten students benefit from tools like PopBots, while Scratch and Python are introduced in primary and secondary schools.
- **Pedagogical Strategies:** Project-based learning (N=27) is the most common approach across all levels, followed by human-computer collaborative learning and play/game-based approaches. Constructivist methodologies are applied frequently.
- **Learning Outcomes:** 31 studies reported positive outcomes including cognitive (understanding of AI concepts, machine learning, ethics), affective (increased motivation, interest, self-efficacy), and behavioral (high engagement) outcomes, as well as course satisfaction and soft skills acquisition.
- **Publication Trends:** 39 out of 46 articles were published in the past 5 years, peaking in 2021. Most research was conducted in the USA (N=8), China (N=7), Finland (N=3), Hong Kong (N=3), Israel (N=3), and Spain (N=3).
- **Educational Levels:** Primary and secondary schools each cover 44% of studies, kindergartens 11%, and K-12 overall 2%.
- **Research Methods:** The study followed PRISMA guidelines and used a modified technology-based learning model by Hsu et al. (2012) to frame the research questions.

The paper informs educators of appropriate learning tools, pedagogical strategies, and assessment methodologies for AI literacy education in K-12 contexts, and discusses research implications and future directions.

## Abstract

Artificial intelligence (AI) has become increasingly integral to second language learning due to its outstanding advantages, such as [personalized learning](https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/social-sciences/personalized-learning) experiences, real-time feedback, and increased engagement. Despite the growing popularity of AI-powered platforms like Duolingo and ChatGPT, there is limited empirical research comparing their effectiveness in fostering key educational outcomes. This study addressed this gap by investigating the impact of Duolingo and ChatGPT on the motivation, enjoyment, critical thinking (CT), and [autonomy](https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/social-sciences/autonomy) of English as a Foreign Language (EFL) learners in China. Employing a true-experimental design, the study involved three groups: two experimental groups (EGs) using Duolingo (n = 81) and ChatGPT (n = 81) and a control group (CG) (n = 82). The outcomes of a one-way [MANOVA](https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/social-sciences/multivariate-analysis) indicated that both experimental groups significantly outperformed the control group in terms of motivation, enjoyment, CT, and [autonomy](https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/social-sciences/autonomy). Furthermore, the results demonstrated no significant differences between the Duolingo and ChatGPT groups, suggesting both platforms are equally effective in the constructs under investigation in this study. These findings indicated the potential of AI-driven platforms to transform second language education by providing engaging, personalized, and cognitively enriching experiences.

## Introduction

With the rise of positive psychology in language education, numerous L2 researchers (e.g., Chen et al., 2021; Dewaele & MacIntyre, 2014; Lee & Lee, 2021; Li & Wei, 2021; MacIntyre & Gregersen, 2012; Wang et al., 2021; Zhang et al., 2022) have recently explored the role of positive emotions and their effects in language classrooms. Many of these studies have affirmed the positive impact emotions have on language learning. Inspired by positive psychology, the focus has shifted from negative to positive emotions, fueling an increase in research on constructs such as enjoyment and motivation (Dewaele and Dewaele, 2018, Dewaele and Dewaele, 2020, Dewaele and Li, 2020, Liem and Chong, 2017). However, positive emotions like enjoyment are not entirely new in L2 research. Krashen (1982), in his affective filter theory, highlighted the importance of emotions that either facilitate or impede learning. According to Lee and Lee (2021), experiencing enjoyment as a positive emotion lowers the affective filter, which aids language acquisition. Brantmeier (2005) defined enjoyment as the happiness or cheerfulness that arises from a specific experience or context.

Enjoyment in second language learning refers to the positive emotions learners experience after overcoming challenges, completing tasks, and meeting their psychological needs (Dewaele et al., 2016). As a dynamic construct, enjoyment varies due to social, psychological, and situational factors (Dewaele and Dewaele, 2017, Shirvan and Talebzadeh, 2018) and differs in intensity among learners (Pavelescu & Petri´c, 2018). This variability necessitates effective regulation through strategies such as planning, monitoring, and evaluation, particularly in collaborative EFL settings (Zhang et al., 2021). Importantly, enjoyment significantly influences academic performance, with higher levels linked to improved outcomes (Jin and Zhang, 2021, Zhao and Wang, 2023). Beyond academic performance, enjoyment shapes emotional factors such as attitude and motivation; learners with higher enjoyment exhibit more positive attitudes towards foreign languages (Dewaele et al., 2017, Wu and Chen, 2024). In a longitudinal study, Dewaele et al. (2022) revealed that enjoyment sustains motivation across diverse linguistic contexts, while a study involving 360 learners of English, German, French, and Spanish in Kuwait demonstrated that enjoyment moderately influences motivation, particularly for highly motivated learners. Similarly, Dewaele and Meftah (2024) highlighted a reciprocal relationship between enjoyment and motivation, especially for proficient learners. Moreover, enjoyment has been shown to directly impact learners’ willingness to communicate (L2WTC), underscoring its role in fostering effective language use (Yu & Ma, 2024).

Motivation is a fundamental driving force behind educational success, serving as “individual students’ primary impetus for initiating learning and continuing the often long and challenging process of education” (Ushioda, 2008, p. 14). Academic motivation, as defined by Hsu (2010), reflects the degree of interest and desire students exhibit toward learning. Ryan and Deci (2020) categorize academic motivation into two primary types: intrinsic and extrinsic motivation. Intrinsic motivation involves “activities undertaken for their own sake or due to inherent interest and enjoyment” (Ryan & Deci, 2020, p. 10), while extrinsic motivation pertains to “behaviors performed for reasons other than inherent satisfaction” (Cao, 2022, p. 7). For instance, students may engage in academic tasks driven by personal curiosity (intrinsic motivation) or external rewards provided by instructors (extrinsic motivation) (Ma, 2024).

As a critical factor, academic motivation fosters meaningful engagement with educational activities, encouraging active participation (Wang, 2022). According to self-determination theory (SDT), motivational resources are essential for enhancing classroom engagement, as they provide the energy and emotional drive necessary for students to become more involved (Jin, 2024). Numerous studies highlight the strong relationship between academic motivation and educational outcomes, suggesting that progress, growth, and success in learning environments are closely tied to students’ motivational levels (Fan and Wang, 2022, Wang and Hemchua, 2022, Wu et al., 2023). Recognizing its significance, researchers have extensively examined the potential outcomes of academic motivation in classroom contexts (e.g., Akter, 2021; Kong et al., 2021; Lee et al., 2020; Teng, 2021; Xu et al., 2021). Notably, highly motivated learners are often more autonomous in EFL classrooms, demonstrating greater initiative and self-regulation in their learning processes.

This study also examined autonomy, a construct closely tied to motivation and learner success. Nakata (2011) emphasized that personal autonomy fosters motivation, which in turn drives creative output. Motivation and autonomy share a reciprocal relationship in education, with each reinforcing the other to promote deeper learning and self-regulation (Yu, 2006, Han, 2021). According to Deci and Ryan’s (2000) SDT, autonomy is one of three core psychological needs, alongside competence and relatedness, that fuel motivation. When students are granted autonomy—such as choosing topics, strategies, or assessments—they are more likely to develop self-determined, enduring motivation (Deci & Ryan, 2017). Autonomy-supportive environments, where learners perceive instructor support and engage actively, enrich psychological well-being, motivation, and achievement (Jang et al., 2016). Research (e.g., Brown, 2007; Dickinson, 1995; Little, 2007; Ushioda, 2006) highlights the strong link between autonomy and attributes like high motivation, willingness to communicate, self-efficacy, and critical thinking (CT). In such classrooms, teachers encourage inquiry, exploration of personal interests, and open-ended tasks that require CT, fostering curiosity, open-mindedness, and the ability to challenge ideas—skills essential for CT development (Alrabai, 2021).

CT, another construct examined in this study, is an essential cognitive skill enabling individuals to analyze situations carefully and make thoughtful decisions, rather than acting impulsively (Gever et al., 2021). CT benefits individuals, society, and meaningful social change, as it equips citizens to critically evaluate information and respond constructively (Pescatore, 2007, Zou’bi, 2021, Moore and Parker, 2009). Developing CT is most effective during childhood, as acquiring these skills becomes more challenging in adulthood (Polat & Aydin, 2020). Schools play a pivotal role in fostering CT, with modern curricula increasingly designed to stimulate these skills through problem-solving, questioning, and decision-making activities (Florea and Hurjui, 2015, Gilmanshina et al., 2021, Hayes and Devitt, 2008). Group activities, active participation, and tools like mind mapping have also been shown to enhance CT in children (Polat and Aydin, 2020, Nappi, 2017).

The above-reviewed constructs can be significantly affected by Artificial Intelligence (AI). AI has emerged as a transformative force in education, significantly influencing key constructs such as teacher competence, personalized learning, and student engagement. By leveraging its ability to perceive, understand, learn, and reason, AI can process vast amounts of complex data, offering innovative solutions for educational challenges (Holmes et al., 2023). In particular, AI technologies enhance teacher competence by enabling emotion recognition, personalized instruction, and learning pattern analysis, thereby improving teaching effectiveness and enriching students' learning experiences (Dave and Patel, 2023, King and ChatGPT., 2023). The use of AI to support personalized learning in classrooms has also gained traction, with AI chatbots, such as ChatGPT, playing a pivotal role (Hwang & Chang, 2023). ChatGPT, an advanced pre-trained language model developed by OpenAI, has become a widely adopted tool for facilitating dynamic discussions, answering inquiries, and aiding educators in lesson planning (Flanagin et al., 2023, Lo et al., 2024). Its integration into pedagogical practices has reshaped teaching and learning, reflecting the growing significance of AI tools in education (Al-khresheh, 2024, Rezai et al., 2024a). However, scholars have raised concerns about potential inaccuracies in ChatGPT’s outputs and their implications for academic integrity (Zhang & Tur, 2023). Over-reliance on AI tools like ChatGPT may also reduce opportunities for students to engage in CT and independent problem-solving (Sallam, 2023, Vargas-Murillo et al., 2023). A balanced and informed approach to integrating ChatGPT into educational settings is essential to optimize its benefits while addressing its limitations. This nuanced perspective will guide future research on AI-mediated learning and foster its effective application in diverse educational contexts (Ahmed and Sab, 2023, Vargas-Murillo et al., 2023).

Empirical investigations into ChatGPT’s pedagogical implications have yielded insightful findings. For instance, Meniado (2023) examined the utility of ChatGPT in English language instruction, learning, and assessment. The study demonstrated that ChatGPT enhances language acquisition by providing meaning-oriented input, scaffolding output production, offering corrective feedback on linguistic accuracy, and facilitating extensive practice to promote fluency. Additionally, the research underscored ChatGPT’s capacity to support educators by enabling the creation of innovative lesson plans, fostering both in-class and out-of-class language learning, developing personalized instructional resources, assessing second language acquisition, and delivering prompt, individualized feedback. In a related study, Urban et al. (2024) investigated the impact of ChatGPT on performance in a complex creative problem-solving task among university students. Their results indicated that ChatGPT significantly enhanced students’ self-efficacy in completing the task and improved the quality, elaboration, and originality of their solutions. Moreover, the students who employed ChatGPT perceived the task as less cognitively demanding and reported reduced mental effort.

Duolingo, a widely used AI tool in English language learning and teaching, is available as a website and mobile app, offering free lessons in 40 languages to over 500 million users (Blanco, 2021, Jašková, 2014). It allows learners to practice listening, speaking, reading, writing, and even engage in conversations with intelligent chatbots. Reflecting the vast interest in language learning, Duolingo has become the most downloaded educational app globally (Blanco, 2021, Kessler, 2023, Sendurur et al., 2017). However, compared to traditional classroom settings, using technology like Duolingo outside the classroom poses challenges due to the lack of instructors and guidance (Brophy, 2010), requiring learners to have a high level of self-directed learning (SDL) skills to succeed. Research indicates that learners must exhibit strong independence, autonomy, and control to effectively manage their learning in a distance language learning context (Benson and Voller, 2014, Namaziandost et al., 2024).

Several studies have assessed Duolingo’s effectiveness in second language acquisition. For example, Rachels and Rockinson-Szapkiw (2018) compared L2 Spanish classroom learning with Duolingo usage and found no significant differences in post-test performance on grammar and vocabulary. Similarly, Loewen et al. (2019) discovered that L2 Turkish learners using Duolingo made only modest gains, although there was a moderate correlation between time spent on the app and learning improvements. Additionally, Li and Bonk (2023) explored self-directed language learning experiences, benefits, motivations, and challenges among online language learners using tools like Duolingo in non-classroom settings. Through in-depth, semi-structured interviews with 10 Duolingo users, the study revealed that learners manage various resources to achieve their goals and self-monitor their learning progress through judgments of information adequacy and resource evaluation. In another study, Vinni and Sitti (2023) investigated how the Duolingo program influenced the motivation and vocabulary growth of 10th-grade students at SMKN 1 Padang. The researchers found that Duolingo significantly enhanced the students' motivation to study English and their vocabulary acquisition during the learning process.

In recent years, the integration of AI in education has transformed traditional learning environments, offering dynamic platforms such as Duolingo and ChatGPT to enhance learners' experiences. Despite the growing popularity of AI tools in language learning, there remains a gap in understanding how these platforms impact key educational outcomes, particularly motivation, enjoyment, CT, and autonomy. While Duolingo offers structured, gamified language learning, ChatGPT provides interactive, open-ended responses, each potentially influencing learners' cognitive and emotional engagement in different ways (Yu, 2023). However, limited empirical evidence exists comparing the effects of these AI-driven platforms on students’ motivation, enjoyment, CT, and autonomy, which are crucial for effective language acquisition and self-regulated learning. Given the increasing reliance on AI tools in language education, it is critical to explore how these platforms support or hinder the development of these key factors, particularly in comparison to each other. This research problem addresses the need to uncover the distinctive impacts of AI-integrated education platforms like Duolingo and ChatGPT on fostering motivation, enjoyment, CT, and autonomy among language learners, thereby providing insights into optimizing AI usage for more effective learning experiences. The main purposes of this study were to investigate and compare the impact of AI-based language learning tools (Duolingo and ChatGPT) on various aspects of EFL learners' experiences, specifically focusing on motivation, enjoyment, CT, and autonomy. For these objectives, the following research questions (RQs) were formulated:

RQ1: Do ChatGPT and Duolingo significantly improve motivation in EFL learners?

RQ2: Do ChatGPT and Duolingo significantly foster enjoyment in EFL learners?

RQ3: Do ChatGPT and Duolingo significantly promote critical thinking in EFL learners?

RQ4: Do ChatGPT and Duolingo significantly increase autonomy in EFL learners?

args.summary:
This is a research article published in *Learning and Motivation* (Volume 89, February 2025) by Jia Xu and Qianwen Liu, titled "Uncurtaining windows of motivation, enjoyment, critical thinking, and autonomy in AI-integrated education: Duolingo Vs. ChatGPT." The study investigates the comparative impact of two AI-powered language learning platforms—Duolingo and ChatGPT—on four key educational outcomes among Chinese EFL learners: motivation, enjoyment, critical thinking (CT), and autonomy.

**Methodology:** The study employed a true-experimental design with three groups: two experimental groups using Duolingo (n=81) and ChatGPT (n=81), and a control group (n=82). A one-way MANOVA was used for analysis.

**Key Findings:**
- Both experimental groups significantly outperformed the control group across all four measures (motivation, enjoyment, critical thinking, and autonomy).
- No significant differences were found between the Duolingo and ChatGPT groups, suggesting both platforms are equally effective in fostering these outcomes.
- The findings indicate that AI-driven platforms have strong potential to transform second language education by providing engaging, personalized, and cognitively enriching experiences.

**Context:** The study is part of a special issue on "Learning and Motivation Beyond the Classroom: Pitfalls and Potentials." The article provides extensive background on the constructs of enjoyment, motivation, autonomy, and critical thinking in second language acquisition, and reviews existing literature on ChatGPT and Duolingo's applications in education. The study has been cited by 22 other works as of the page's publication.

**Limitations:** The study acknowledges its narrow focus on only two AI tools, assessment of general constructs, and other limitations that temper broader implications.

**Funding:** The work was supported by Inner Mongolia Medical University Undergraduate Teaching Reform Research and Practice Project (Project NYJXGGSJ2024038).

# Duolingo AI Customer Research Strategy 2026: How a Public Edtech Giant Listens at Billion-User Scale

Perspective AI Team··11 min read

![Duolingo AI Customer Research Strategy 2026: How a Public Edtech Giant Listens at Billion-User Scale](/_next/image?url=%2Fcontent-images%2Fimages%2Fblog%2Fduolingo-ai-customer-research-strategy-2026-hero.png&w=3840&q=75&dpl=dpl_GTAwHkvZGdTTvXDca7rha5DtP4Ya)

## TL;DR[#](#tldr)

Duolingo runs one of the most disciplined customer research operations in consumer software, and based on the company's public engineering blog, investor letters, and conference talks, that operation has shifted from periodic survey panels toward continuous, AI-assisted discovery in 2025–2026. The company reported 116.7 million monthly active users in Q1 2025 and continues to ship multiple A/B tests per week per team, which means traditional moderated interviews and quarterly NPS panels cannot keep up with the decision cadence. Publicly Duolingo has discussed leaning on large-language-model tooling for content generation, evaluation, and learner feedback synthesis, with executives Luis von Ahn and Severin Hacker repeatedly framing the product roadmap as "AI-first." For other product-led growth companies running ai customer interviews, the takeaway is clear: at billion-event scale you cannot rely on surveys to explain behavior, and the next-best-thing is conversational research that runs continuously alongside the experiment system. This post unpacks what Duolingo has said publicly, why traditional research broke at their scale, and what other PLG operators should copy. For a sister case study, see the [Notion AI customer research breakdown](/blog/notion-ai-customer-research-how-a-10b-company-decides-what-to-build).

## Why a 100M-MAU Edtech Outgrew Traditional Surveys[#](#why-a-100m-mau-edtech-outgrew-traditional-surveys)

A 100M-MAU consumer app outgrows traditional surveys because the survey panel cannot match the experiment cadence. Duolingo publicly disclosed in its 2024 shareholder letter that the company runs hundreds of A/B tests at any given moment, with the experimentation platform integrated directly into the learner application. When a team ships ten variants per quarter, the bottleneck is not "what's the result?" — that's a quantitative question the warehouse answers. The bottleneck is *why* did the cohort churn at 2.3x the control rate? Surveys cannot answer at that speed. By the time a panel returns, the team has shipped the next iteration.

This is the same scaling wall every PLG company hits. We covered the mechanics in [the sample-size problem in customer research at scale](/blog/customer-research-at-scale-why-the-sample-size-problem-is-finally-solvable) — once your DAU base crosses 1M, traditional moderated interviews capture ~0.0001% of behavior, and unmoderated surveys top out at 5–15% response rates. Duolingo's public engineering writing suggests they hit this wall around 2022–2023, when MAUs climbed 50%+ year-over-year. The math forces a redesign: either accept that 99.99% of behavior is unexamined narrative, or run conversational research continuously alongside the experiment platform. That second path is what we mean by [continuous discovery operationalized with AI conversations](/blog/continuous-discovery-habits-in-2026-operationalizing-teresa-torres-s-framework-with-ai-conversations).

## What Duolingo Publicly Says About Its Research Practice[#](#what-duolingo-publicly-says-about-its-research-practice)

Duolingo's public-facing posture on research has three consistent themes across CEO Luis von Ahn's interviews, investor letters, and the company's [engineering blog](https://blog.duolingo.com/).

Theme 1: Experimentation is the primary product-decision mechanism. Von Ahn has repeated in earnings calls and in his 2024 [New York Times interview](https://www.nytimes.com/2024/02/02/business/media/duolingo-luis-von-ahn.html) that almost everything Duolingo ships is A/B tested first, and that the company's moat comes from running tests faster than competitors. The corollary: qualitative understanding must keep pace with the quantitative test cadence, which traditional research cannot do.

Theme 2: The 2023–24 contractor reduction signaled an AI-content pivot. Duolingo confirmed in early 2024 it had reduced its translator and writer contractor base because LLMs could handle the bulk of content generation. As reported in *Bloomberg* and *The Verge*, leadership framed the change as freeing the remaining team for higher-leverage work — including the synthesis tasks (interview tagging, thematic analysis, transcript summarization) that LLMs do well. Same shift powers [AI qualitative research as the new default](/blog/ai-qualitative-research-how-conversational-ai-makes-qualitative-the-default-not-the-luxury).

Theme 3: Conversational AI is woven into the product itself, not just R&D. Duolingo Max launched in 2023 with the Roleplay and Explain My Answer features — both explicitly conversational. Publicly Duolingo has discussed using these to gather a second-order data stream (what learners ask the AI tutor) that surfaces curriculum gaps no survey could find. Same instrumentation logic behind [AI moderated interviews as a research method](/blog/ai-moderated-interviews-how-they-work-when-to-use-them-and-what-they-replace).

The *pattern* — moving from survey-panel research to always-on conversational data collection — is now the public posture of one of the largest consumer apps in the world. That is meaningful tailwind for any team defending budget for [ai customer interviews](/blog/the-state-of-ai-customer-interviews-in-2026-adoption-patterns-and-what-s-coming-next) inside their own org.

## The Continuous-Discovery Loop in Action[#](#the-continuous-discovery-loop-in-action)

Duolingo's continuous-discovery loop, as inferable from public sources, runs in four overlapping cycles rather than the traditional research-quarter rhythm.

Cycle 1: Behavior signal from the experiment platform. Every shipped variant is instrumented for retention, lesson completion, streak length, and revenue per user. When a metric moves, the variant is flagged for qualitative follow-up.

Cycle 2: Targeted qualitative on the cohort that moved. Where smaller companies email a survey, Duolingo's scale makes that a non-starter — even a 10% response rate on a 500K-learner cohort yields 50,000 free-text responses no human team can read. This is where conversational AI takes over the synthesis layer; it's the architecture we describe in [the customer feedback analysis AI-first workflow](/blog/customer-feedback-analysis-the-ai-first-workflow-that-cuts-synthesis-from-weeks-to-hours).

Cycle 3: In-product conversation as standing research instrument. Duolingo Max's Roleplay and Explain My Answer surfaces are also research instruments — every learner question signals curriculum gaps or comprehension breakdowns. That's conversational research embedded inside the product surface, the pattern we cover in [conversational data collection as a research method](/blog/conversational-data-collection-the-method-that-replaces-forms-for-good-customer-data).

Cycle 4: Roadmap loop with the executive team. Von Ahn has discussed in podcast appearances reviewing learner feedback summaries weekly. At Duolingo's scale, that summary must be an LLM-generated synthesis of thousands of conversations, ranked by frequency and severity — the same workflow product leaders at smaller PLG companies now stand up with off-the-shelf tooling, including [the AI-first jobs-to-be-done interview pattern](/blog/jobs-to-be-done-interviews-the-ai-first-approach-to-running-jtbd-research-at-scale).

The loop collapses the gap between "we noticed something" and "we understand why" from 6 weeks to closer to 6 days. For PLG companies competing on iteration speed, that is the ballgame.

## What This Means for Other PLG Operators[#](#what-this-means-for-other-plg-operators)

For PLG operators below the 100M-MAU mark, the takeaway is not "build what Duolingo built." Most teams cannot justify a dedicated research-engineering function. The takeaway is *adopt the pattern with off-the-shelf tooling*, which is now possible in 2026 in a way it wasn't in 2022.

Three concrete moves a 50–500-person PLG company can copy from the public playbook:

1. Pair every meaningful experiment with a conversational follow-up. Route the affected cohort into a 5-minute AI-moderated interview rather than a survey. The completion-rate gap is 2–4x in published benchmarks — see [the conversion gap between forms and conversations](/blog/the-conversion-gap-between-forms-and-conversations-hit-4x-in-2026) — so the same outreach budget yields 2–4x more "why" data.
2. Treat the in-product help / chat surface as a research instrument. Pipe whatever conversational AI you have through the same synthesis layer your formal research uses. This is the mechanic behind [why product-led companies killed their lead forms first](/blog/why-product-led-companies-killed-their-lead-forms-first).
3. Stand up a weekly synthesis ritual at the executive level. Without an executive consumer of the synthesis, the loop atrophies. The operating cadence is detailed in [the voice of customer program 2026 blueprint](/blog/voice-of-customer-program-the-2026-blueprint-for-cx-leaders-running-real-voc).

The continuous-discovery layer can be stood up in a week with modern conversational research tooling — see the [user interview software 2026 vendor comparison](/blog/user-interview-software-2026-vendor-comparison-by-interview-mode-and-team-size) for the current vendor map.

## Lessons for Product, Research, and CX Teams[#](#lessons-for-product-research-and-cx-teams)

For product, research, and CX teams, the Duolingo case yields three role-specific lessons.

Product managers: Stop treating the experimentation platform and the research stack as separate systems. Duolingo's effective research velocity comes from the qualitative loop being wired *to* the experiment system, not parked next to it. The lightest-weight version is auto-routing affected cohorts to an AI interview when an experiment crosses a metric threshold — a workflow detailed in [feature prioritization with AI customer research](/blog/feature-prioritization-framework-using-ai-customer-research-to-rank-the-roadmap).

UX and product researchers: Your research-to-decisions ratio is broken. A team running 12 studies per quarter against 200+ shipped changes covers 6% of decisions. Duolingo's solution — the one available to you in 2026 — is to delegate first-pass synthesis to LLMs and use human researchers on the strategic 10–20%. Mechanics in [UX research at scale: the 2026 playbook](/blog/ux-research-at-scale-the-2026-playbook-for-research-leaders-running-100-studies-per-quarter).

CX and CS teams: Your churn signals arrive 60+ days late because your detection system is built on quarterly NPS rather than continuous conversation. Duolingo doesn't run an NPS panel — they let conversation surfaces carry the early-warning load. For a CX adaptation, see [how to identify at-risk customers before they churn](/blog/how-to-identify-at-risk-customers-before-they-churn-a-2026-playbook).

The deeper lesson: *Duolingo's research advantage is a cadence, not a tool.* AI enables the cadence; it doesn't invent it. Teams that copy the cadence — even with simpler tooling — compound learning faster than teams running quarterly studies on the most expensive enterprise tier.

## The Edtech Context: Why This Matters Beyond Duolingo[#](#the-edtech-context-why-this-matters-beyond-duolingo)

In edtech specifically, learner feedback has historically been the worst-instrumented part of the product — survey fatigue is acute among kids and students, and NPS scoring breaks for products used in 5-minute sessions. Duolingo's pivot to conversational, in-product research is now the de facto reference architecture for the category. The same pattern appears in [AI in education: how conversational feedback is replacing static surveys](/blog/ai-in-education-how-conversational-feedback-is-replacing-static-surveys) and in higher-ed deployments documented in [AI in higher education in 2026](/blog/ai-in-higher-education-in-2026-admissions-student-success-and-the-voice-of-student-layer).

For consumer-app operators outside edtech, the lesson generalizes: when sessions are short, voluntary, and high-frequency, surveys tax the relationship and conversational micro-interviews don't. That structural shift is what Duolingo's research org is built around.

## Frequently Asked Questions[#](#frequently-asked-questions)

### Does Duolingo use Perspective AI for customer research?[#](#does-duolingo-use-perspective-ai-for-customer-research)

There is no public confirmation that Duolingo uses Perspective AI; based on public engineering posts, the company runs significant in-house research and ML infrastructure. Duolingo handles survey fatigue at scale primarily by running fewer formal surveys and instrumenting in-product behavior more heavily. # Best AI for Learning in 2026

Stanford's Tutor CoPilot study found students gained up to 9 percentage points in topic mastery when AI assisted their tutors. Specialized tools outperform general chatbots at specific learning tasks. Eight tools tested across tutoring, language learning, coding, and professional development, with strengths, limitations, and pricing for each.

![AI interface analyzing and organizing documents for study and research](/_astro/best-ai-for-learning-2026-hero.DYTaYFZ9_r95TH.webp)

## How we picked these 8 tools

Stanford researchers built an AI coaching tool called Tutor CoPilot and tested it with 900 tutors and 1,800 students. Students assigned to lower-rated tutors who used AI assistance gained up to 9 percentage points in topic mastery compared to those without it. The finding points to a pattern that shows up across every category in this list: AI tools designed around a specific learning task outperform general-purpose chatbots at that task.

We tested each tool below against four criteria.

**Does it teach or just answer?**

Tools that guide you through a problem with questions produce better retention than tools that hand you the answer.

**Is the free tier usable?**

A free plan that gates every useful feature behind a paywall does not count.

**Does it adapt?**

The best tools adjust difficulty, pacing, and feedback based on your performance.

**Is it focused?**

A tool built specifically for language learning will beat a general chatbot at language learning.

Here are all 8 picks with pricing at a glance:

1. Khanmigo, guided tutoring for math and science, $4 per month
2. Duolingo Max, AI-powered language practice, free or $14 per month
3. NotebookLM, source-grounded study assistant, free
4. ChatGPT, general-purpose learning across any subject, free or $20 per month
5. Replit, learn-by-building code editor, free
6. DataCamp, data science and AI skills, free or $14 per month
7. LinkedIn Learning, career-aligned professional courses, $30 per month
8. Fastio, intelligent workspace for organizing learning materials, free

## Best AI tutors for structured subjects

Structured subjects like math and languages share a pattern: you need guided practice with immediate feedback, not just explanations. These two tools score highest on pedagogical design and adaptivity. Both use different approaches to the same idea: guiding you through problems instead of handing you answers.

### 1. Khanmigo

Khan Academy's AI tutor, built on GPT-4 and integrated directly into Khan Academy's curriculum. Instead of giving answers, Khanmigo asks guiding questions to help you work through problems yourself. Research on this Socratic approach consistently shows it produces better retention than direct answer-giving.

**Strengths:**

* Guides you to answers through questions, backed by Khan Academy's full course library
* Covers math, science, coding, history, and humanities
* Teachers get free access through a Microsoft partnership

**Limitations:**

* Limited to subjects within Khan Academy's catalog
* Available only in English

**Best for:** K-12 students and adult learners working through math, science, or coding fundamentals.

**Pricing:** $4 per month or $44 per year. Free for teachers.

### 2. Duolingo Max

Duolingo reached 56.5 million daily active users in Q1 2026, making it the largest AI-powered learning app by active usage. The Max tier adds two AI features that matter for serious language learners: Video Call with Lily, a live AI conversation partner who asks follow-up questions and remembers previous sessions, and Roleplay, which drops you into scenarios like ordering coffee in Paris and grades your accuracy, vocabulary range, and sentence complexity.

As of January 2026, Duolingo made its AI grammar explanation feature free for all users, so the main reason to pay for Max is the speaking practice.

**Strengths:**

* Video Call provides real spoken conversation practice with an AI partner
* Roleplay creates scenario-based exercises with detailed performance feedback
* Gamified daily structure keeps practice consistent

**Limitations:**

* Max features available for only 7 languages learning from English
* At $168 per year, it costs more than practicing conversation with ChatGPT's voice mode

**Best for:** language learners who need structured daily practice with spoken feedback.

**Pricing:** Free (basic), Super at roughly $7 per month, Max at $14 per month billed annually.

## Best AI tools for self-directed study

Self-directed learners, whether preparing for exams, exploring a new field, or working through research papers, need tools that adapt to whatever material they bring. These two handle the widest range of unstructured learning tasks. One grounds answers in your own documents, the other covers nearly every subject with no setup.

 ![AI chat interface showing a conversational response to a research question](/_astro/ripley-chat-response.DpD5YxlX_ZhrcKR.webp) 

### 3. NotebookLM

Google's source-grounded research assistant. Upload your notes, papers, slides, or readings, and NotebookLM answers questions based only on your materials. Every response includes citation chips that link to the exact passage in your documents. In 2026, Google added flashcard generation, quizzes, mind maps, and Audio Overviews that transform dense text into listenable podcast-style summaries you can join mid-conversation.

**Strengths:**

* Completely free with full feature access
* Grounds every response to your uploaded sources, minimizing hallucination
* Audio Overviews let you study by listening while commuting or exercising

**Limitations:**

* Cannot search the open web, only answers from materials you upload
* Requires a Google account

**Best for:** exam prep, literature reviews, and studying from your own course materials.

**Pricing:** Free.

### 4. ChatGPT

The general-purpose default. ChatGPT handles concept explanations, step-by-step math walkthroughs, essay brainstorming, coding help, and language practice across every subject. The free tier runs on GPT-4o mini. Plus adds GPT-4o, voice mode for conversational practice, and higher usage limits.

**Strengths:**

* Covers every subject area with reasonable competence
* Voice mode doubles as an informal language practice partner
* Custom GPTs let you build subject-specific study aids

**Limitations:**

* Does not cite sources, so you need to verify factual claims independently
* Can confidently state incorrect information

**Best for:** general-purpose learning when no specialized tool covers your subject.

**Pricing:** Free (GPT-4o mini) or $20 per month for ChatGPT Plus.

## Best AI tools for learning technical skills

Learning to code or build with data requires doing, not reading. These tools provide interactive environments where you write real code, get instant feedback, and build projects from the first lesson. One focuses on general programming, the other on data science and AI engineering specifically.

### 5. Replit

A browser-based development environment with a built-in AI agent that explains its reasoning as it builds. Replit supports every major programming language and lets you go from an idea to a deployed, shareable project without installing anything. The AI does not just generate code. It narrates what it is doing and why, which turns code generation into instruction.

**Strengths:**

* Runs entirely in the browser with no local setup
* AI agent explains each step as it builds, teaching through demonstration
* Instant deployment lets you share working projects immediately

**Limitations:**

* Free tier has compute limits that can interrupt longer sessions
* Professional developers will outgrow it as project complexity increases

**Best for:** beginners learning to code and students building their first web applications.

**Pricing:** Free (with compute limits). Paid plans start at $25 per month.

### 6. DataCamp

Interactive platform for data science, machine learning, and AI engineering. DataCamp launched AI-native courses in early 2026 with adaptive tutoring that adjusts difficulty based on your performance in real time. Courses cover Python, SQL, R, Tableau, Power BI, and a full AI Engineering track. Unlike video-based platforms, every lesson includes an interactive coding environment where you practice inside the lesson itself.

**Strengths:**

* AI-native courses adapt difficulty and provide personalized feedback
* Interactive coding environments let you practice within each lesson
* Career tracks map courses directly to specific job roles

**Limitations:**

* Premium AI-native courses consume credits that refresh only on yearly plans
* Focused on data and AI skills, not general programming

**Best for:** professionals building data science, machine learning, or AI engineering skills.

**Pricing:** Free (limited courses) or $14 per month billed annually.

## Best AI tools for career development

Career development looks different from academic study. You are usually learning around a full-time job, targeting skills tied to specific roles, and you need credentials employers actually recognize. These two tools approach that problem differently: one through structured courses with certificates, the other through organized workspaces where you collect and search across everything you are learning.

### 7. LinkedIn Learning

AI-powered course recommendations tied directly to your LinkedIn profile and career goals. The platform analyzes what skills employers in your industry are hiring for and recommends courses that close the gap between your current role and where you want to be. With over 16,000 courses taught by industry professionals, the catalog covers business, technology, and creative skills.

**Strengths:**

* Course recommendations adapt based on your LinkedIn profile and target role
* Certificates display directly on your LinkedIn profile where recruiters see them
* Broad catalog spanning technical, business, and creative topics

**Limitations:**

* Courses are pre-recorded video, not adaptive at the lesson level
* $30 per month is expensive for individual learners

**Best for:** professionals who want career-aligned courses with credentials that show up where hiring managers look.

**Pricing:** Free trial, then $30 per month or $240 per year.

### 8. Fastio

Not a learning tool itself. [Fastio](https://fast.io) is an intelligent workspace for organizing and searching across all the materials your other learning tools generate. Upload course notes, research papers, project files, and reference documents from any source. Intelligence Mode auto-indexes everything so you can ask questions about your files and get answers with citations, similar to NotebookLM but designed for shared workspaces and larger collections.

**Strengths:**

* generous storage with 5 workspaces, no credit card required
* Intelligence Mode enables semantic search and AI-powered Q&A across uploaded files
* Shared workspaces let study groups or project teams collaborate on materials

**Limitations:**

* Does not teach or tutor. It organizes and searches your learning content
* Smaller user base than Google Drive or Dropbox

**Best for:** organizing learning materials across tools and sharing resources with study groups or teams.

**Pricing:** Free (50GB storage, 5 workspaces, [included credits per month](/pricing/)).

## Which tool to pick based on what you are learning

You do not need all 8 tools. Pick one specialized tool for your primary goal and pair it with a general-purpose assistant for everything else.

**If you are learning a language:** Start with Duolingo's free tier for daily practice. Upgrade to Max when you are ready for spoken conversation with Lily. Use ChatGPT voice mode for unstructured conversation in languages Duolingo Max does not cover.

**If you are preparing for exams:** NotebookLM is free and grounds answers to your own study materials. Upload your notes and let it generate flashcards, quizzes, and audio summaries.

**If you are learning to code:** Replit gives you a complete development environment in the browser with an AI that teaches as it builds. Move to a professional IDE once you are building more complex projects.

**If you are building data or AI skills:** DataCamp's adaptive courses teach through hands-on coding exercises tied to specific career tracks.

**If you need career credentials:** LinkedIn Learning ties course recommendations to your professional profile and puts certificates where hiring managers look.

**If you want a general-purpose tutor:** ChatGPT's free tier covers most subjects. Khanmigo at $4 per month adds guided math and science practice with Socratic questioning.

The strongest combination for most people is one specialized tool (Duolingo for language, Replit for code, DataCamp for data skills) plus NotebookLM for studying your own materials and ChatGPT for everything else. What is the best AI for learning new skills? 

It depends on the skill. For languages, Duolingo Max provides structured daily practice with AI conversation partners. For coding, Replit offers a browser-based IDE with an AI agent that explains what it builds. For math and science, Khanmigo guides you through problems with Socratic questioning at $4 per month. For general-purpose learning across any subject, ChatGPT covers the widest range of topics on its free tier.

  Can AI help me learn faster? 

Yes, when matched to the right task. Stanford research on Tutor CoPilot found that students gained up to 9 percentage points in topic mastery when AI assisted their tutors. The gains came from specialized AI coaching, not from general chatbot use. NotebookLM generates flashcards and quizzes from your actual study materials. DataCamp adapts lesson difficulty based on your performance. These targeted approaches outperform generic Q&A for specific learning goals.

  What is the best AI tutor? 

Khanmigo is the strongest dedicated AI tutor for K-12 math and science. It uses Socratic questioning instead of giving direct answers and works alongside Khan Academy's full curriculum. For language tutoring, Duolingo Max's Video Call feature provides live conversation practice with AI feedback. ChatGPT works as a general tutor but lacks the structured pedagogy of purpose-built tools.

  Which AI is best for language learning? 

Duolingo Max is the leading AI-powered language learning tool, offering Video Call for spoken practice and Roleplay for scenario-based exercises in 7 languages. ChatGPT's voice mode is a free alternative for open-ended conversation practice in dozens of languages, though it lacks Duolingo's structured progression, gamification, and detailed performance feedback.

  Are AI learning tools free? 

Several of the best ones are. NotebookLM is completely free with full features. ChatGPT, Duolingo, and Replit all have usable free tiers. Khanmigo costs $4 per month, but teachers get free access. You are tasked with summarizing the raw content of a webpage retrieved from a web search. Your goal is to create a summary that preserves the most important information from the original web page.
