<webpage_content>
[Xiangying Jiang, Ph.D.](/author/xiangying/)

# 4 learnings from Duolingo efficacy studies

At Duolingo, we take learning seriously! Here’s how we test our efficacy.

[Xiangying Jiang, Ph.D.](/author/xiangying/)[Audrey Kittredge, Ph.D.](/author/audrey/)[Elise Hopman, Ph.D.](/author/elise-hopman/)

![A green image with a white silhouette of Duo the owl next and white text reading ](https://storage.ghost.io/c/7a/33/7a33d0f4-927d-4fe8-a6bf-96131b5e76d4/content/images/2024/09/cover_efficacy-lab.png)

Duolingo courses are fun and easy to use, but we also want to help our learners achieve their goals. That’s why we hold ourselves accountable with rigorous efficacy research, and—in case you were wondering—the research shows that Duolingo really works!

Our [Efficacy Research Lab](https://duolingo.com/efficacy/studies?ref=blog.duolingo.com) brings together learning experts with PhDs in applied linguistics, assessment science, and cognitive psychology to conduct learning research with new and existing users around the globe. We ensure that Duolingo learners acquire real-life communication skills by applying our [comprehensive learning framework](https://blog.duolingo.com/duolingo-efficacy-research-framework/) and the [Common European Framework of Reference for Languages](https://www.coe.int/en/web/common-european-framework-reference-languages?ref=blog.duolingo.com) (CEFR), an international proficiency standard, to our courses.

Here are 4 things we know about learning with Duolingo:

* [Duolingo learners improve all language skills](#duolingo-learners-improve-all-language-skills)
* [Duolingo is as effective as classroom learning](#duolingo-is-as-effective-as-classroom-learning)
* [Duolingo courses are evolving to teach better](#duolingo-courses-are-evolving-to-teach-better)
* [Learners who use Duolingo’s AI tools build confidence](#learners-who-use-duolingos-ai-tools-build-confidence)

Here’s how we hold ourselves accountable to our learners.

## Duolingo learners improve all language skills

Our research program evaluates learning across the four skills needed for communication—reading, writing, speaking, and listening—and at different levels of proficiency.

A recent study found that university students learning Spanish with Duolingo [significantly improved in all four language skills](https://scholarspace.manoa.hawaii.edu/server/api/core/bitstreams/ea47a53e-da6e-4419-bd55-e72b458294f4/content?ref=blog.duolingo.com) after just three months. In fact, after just 4-6 weeks of using Duolingo, [beginners achieved 90% accuracy](https://duolingo-papers.s3.amazonaws.com/reports/Duolingo_whitepaper_language_conversation_2024.pdf?ref=blog.duolingo.com) in a test of short spoken and written conversation!

These results also extend to our English courses. In [one study](https://journal.equinoxpub.com/Calico/article/view/26704?ref=blog.duolingo.com), learners who had completed the A2 CEFR level of Duolingo’s English content scored *above* A2 in reading and listening on an independent standardized test.

## Duolingo is as effective as classroom learning

Formal courses at universities have long been the gold standard of language education, but they aren’t accessible or affordable for all learners. Luckily, Duolingo courses make the grade! After completing five sections of Duolingo—half of intermediate-level [B1 content](https://blog.duolingo.com/goldilocks-and-the-cefr-levels-which-proficiency-level-is-just-right/)—French and Spanish learners [knew as much as university students](https://duolingo-papers.s3.amazonaws.com/reports/Duolingo_whitepaper_language_read_listen_2021.pdf?ref=blog.duolingo.com) who took five semesters of language classes.

In some cases, Duolingo learners outperform their university peers. In an [independent study](https://duolingo-papers.s3.amazonaws.com/reports/RodriguezFuentes_etal_whitepaper_language_proficiency_Columbia_2023.pdf?ref=blog.duolingo.com) of English learners in Colombia, learners who used Duolingo for one semester significantly improved in speaking, writing, reading, and listening, while university English students did not.

Teachers also [recognize Duolingo’s effectiveness](https://duolingo-papers.s3.amazonaws.com/reports/Duolingo_whitepaper_language_educator_perception_2024.pdf?ref=blog.duolingo.com). In a survey of language teachers in North America, the vast majority thought Duolingo was effective (97%) and efficient (96%) for language learning, and 96% said they would recommend Duolingo to learners!

## Duolingo courses are evolving to teach better

In 2022, we introduced our new “path” design, and to test the impact of the change on learning outcomes, we compared learners who studied with the old design with those who used the new path. Learners in the new system had improved learning outcomes, including higher reading and listening scores.

## Learners who use Duolingo’s AI tools build confidence

At Duolingo, we started using AI to improve learning long before ChatGPT hit the scene. For example, our courses have long used a proprietary machine learning model ([Birdbrain](https://blog.duolingo.com/learning-how-to-help-you-learn-introducing-birdbrain/)) to tailor the difficulty of lessons to each learner.

Today we also offer learners [AI-powered features](https://blog.duolingo.com/duolingo-max/) to practice conversation and get personalized grammar information. [A recent study](https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/education/articles/10.3389/feduc.2025.1499497/full?ref=blog.duolingo.com) found that over 90% of learners who used these AI tools in their courses for a month felt prepared to use their new language in real-life situations. Even more impressive is that over 60% of learners said they used what they learned on Duolingo outside the app, for instance to ask for directions or order food while traveling.

## The evidence speaks for itself: Duolingo works!

Our efficacy research program shows that Duolingo helps learners achieve meaningful language goals. As we continue to expand and improve our courses, our research team will keep evaluating and testing how well we’re serving our learners—because they deserve the best education in the world.

--- SOURCE 2: University AI Academic Integrity Policy — CASRAI ---
URL: https://casrai.org/guides/university-ai-academic-integrity-policy-trends

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This CASRAI guide (last updated 23 July 2026) documents how universities have shifted from blanket bans on generative AI tools toward tiered permission frameworks and disclosure requirements. Between 2023 and 2026, most institutions moved through a common arc: initial prohibition, then a shift toward conditional, task-specific frameworks. Blanket bans proved difficult to enforce due to AI-detection false positives and didn't account for how AI tools are used differently across disciplines.

Tiered policies, exemplified by Carnegie Mellon University's Eberly Center (which offers six sample policy statements ranging from full prohibition to conditional use), specify permission by tool, task, assignment, or course stage. The University of Chicago uses a four-tier system (prohibited, permitted with authorization, permitted with citation, broadly allowed), and UCLA treats unauthorized AI use like unauthorized human assistance.

The AI Assessment Scale (AIAS), developed by Leon Furze and Mike Perkins, provides a shared five-level framework from "no AI" to "full AI" for assignment-level communication. Disclosure requirements mirror research-integrity norms: students must report which tool (including version), what task it was used for, and sometimes the prompts and outputs. Data privacy has emerged as a separate but related policy axis, with institutions restricting sensitive data from consumer AI tools and offering institutionally licensed alternatives.

AI-detection tools remain part of enforcement but are treated cautiously due to false-positive problems, particularly for non-native English writers. Institutional guidance now treats detector results as one input requiring corroboration, not standalone proof. For research administrators, key takeaways include: design tiered frameworks with disclosure and oversight, consider data privacy as a distinct compliance concern, and recognize that AI-detection tools have limitations that should be reflected in policy language.
</summary>

<summary>
The University of North America (UoNA) has established a comprehensive Student AI Policy governing the use of Artificial Intelligence tools in academic work. **Core Principles:**
- Academic integrity is paramount; using AI to complete assignments or exams without permission is considered cheating
- Instructors have final authority to set AI rules for their courses; if not explicitly allowed, AI use is prohibited by default

**Prohibited Uses:** Submitting AI-generated work as one's own, using AI on exams or restricted assessments, automating programming assignments, failing to disclose AI use, and violating copyright via AI.

**Consequences of Violations:** Range from failing grade on an assignment to course failure, probation, suspension, or expulsion for serious or repeated offenses.

**Support Resources:** The University provides workshops, writing center support, library guides, and consultations to help students use AI appropriately. The policy is reviewed at least annually and updated as technology evolves.

The webpage from the Learn & Work Ecosystem Library provides a comprehensive overview of two interrelated European Union initiatives: the European Digital Education Hub and the EU Digital Education Action Plan (2021-2027), last updated January 16, 2025.

**European Digital Education Hub:** Launched in June 2022, this is an online collaborative community connecting digital education stakeholders across Europe. It offers a voluntary platform for sharing best practices, peer learning, and cross-sector collaboration. Membership includes school educators, teacher trainers, policymakers, and school representatives. By January 2025, the Hub had grown to over 5,500 members, with more than 100 publications and 200 activities. Most activities occur online, primarily in English.

**EU Digital Education Action Plan:** Adopted September 2020, this strategic framework (2021-2027) supports the sustainable digital transformation of education and training systems across Europe. It is part of the broader European Education Area initiative. Key areas of activity include:

- **Enhance digital skills and competencies** – basic digital literacy, advanced digital skills (AI, cybersecurity), and teacher training.
- **Build a high-performing digital education ecosystem** – strengthen digital infrastructure and access to secure tools.
- **Develop robust digital infrastructure** – address gaps in remote/rural areas, foster public-private partnerships.
- **Promote digital inclusion** – reduce the digital divide for disadvantaged groups.
- **Enhance collaboration** – cross-border cooperation among EU Member States.
- **Drive innovation and research** – support initiatives like the Hub, fund pilot projects.

Work focuses on developing a European Digital Education Content Framework, introducing self-assessment tools for digital competencies, and promoting open educational resources (OER). The plan is a key enabler for achieving a European Education Area by 2025, originally endorsed at a 2017 Social Summit in Sweden. It also contributes to the European Skills Agenda, European Social Pillar Action Plan, and the 2030 Digital Compass. The plan is supported by EU funding programs including Erasmus+, Horizon Europe, and the Digital Europe Programme.

--- SOURCE 22: Assessment reform for the age of artificial intelligence ---
URL: https://www.teqsa.gov.au/sites/default/files/2023-09/assessment-reform-age-artificial-intelligence-discussion-paper.pdf

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This document, "Assessment Reform for the Age of Artificial Intelligence," authored by Jason M. Lodge and colleagues, was commissioned by TEQSA in November 2023 to guide Australian higher education institutions in reforming assessment practices in response to generative AI. It argues that bans on AI are oversimplified and that assessment must evolve to address both risks (academic integrity) and opportunities (preparing students for an AI-ubiquitous world). The document builds on the foundational "Assessment 2020" propositions and aligns with the Higher Education Standards Framework.

**Guiding Principles:**
1. Assessment should equip students to participate ethically in an AI-ubiquitous society.
2. Trustworthy judgements require multiple, inclusive, and contextualised approaches to assessment.

**Five Key Propositions for Assessment Reform:**
1. **Appropriate, authentic engagement with AI** – Assessment should foster critical, ethical, and productive use of AI aligned with disciplinary values.
2. **Systemic program-level approach** – Assessment design should span entire programs (not just individual units) to allow multiple methods and integrated tasks.
3. **Emphasis on the process of learning** – Assessment should reveal thinking, judgement, and decision-making processes that AI cannot easily simulate.
4. **Collaboration with peers and AI** – Students should work appropriately with each other and AI, with clear boundaries articulated.
5. **Security at meaningful points across a program** – Key assessment moments (e.g., capstones) should be secured to assure learning outcomes, rather than attempting to secure all tasks.

The document emphasizes that reform is not prescriptive but offers a "compass" for direction. It calls for inclusive stakeholder discussions (students, educators, accreditors, First Nations peoples) and acknowledges challenges including workload, capability building, and accreditation barriers. The report was developed through expert collaboration at a TEQSA-hosted forum in August 2023, with additional public consultation.
</summary>

--- SOURCE 3: Generation Ready: Building the Foundations for AI-Proficient Education in England’s Schools ---
URL: https://institute.global/insights/public-services/generation-ready-building-the-foundations-for-ai-proficient-education-in-englands-schools

SUMMARY:
<summary>
# Generation Ready: Building the Foundations for AI-Proficient Education in England's Schools

## Overview
This report by the Tony Blair Institute for Global Change (TBI), published 1st September 2025, argues that England's education system is not preparing pupils for an AI-driven future. Without urgent reform across four key pillars—curriculum, teacher training, family engagement, and digital infrastructure—young people will leave school unready for an AI-driven labour market, undermining national competitiveness and deepening inequality.

## Key Findings

**The Economic Stakes:** Up to 3 million existing UK jobs could be displaced by AI, while job postings requiring AI skills have grown 3.6 times faster than all UK jobs over the past decade. Conversely, embracing AI could raise national income by 11%.

**The Skills Framework:** Pupils need three sets of skills: (1) AI literacy (understanding and using AI), (2) human-centred capabilities (critical thinking, communication, creativity, ethical reasoning), and (3) AI technical skills (designing and building AI systems for technical career paths).

**The AI-Literacy Gap:** Only 1 in 5 teachers say their school teaches pupils how AI works; just 1 in 10 reports AI being integrated into subject teaching. Almost 1 in 5 secondary pupils uses AI to do all their schoolwork. 43% of teachers rate their AI confidence at just 3 out of 10, and 91% of those using AI are self-taught.

**The Human-Centred Capabilities Gap:** 59% of all UK job vacancies list critical thinking as a key requirement, yet employers consistently report shortages.

**The AI-Technical-Skills Gap:** 52% of UK technology leaders report AI-related skills shortages. A fifth of non-selective state schools do not offer GCSE computer science; only 13% of Key Stage 4 pupils take it.

**The New Disadvantage Divide:** Schools with larger disadvantaged cohorts are less likely to teach AI or offer GCSE computer science. Independent schools are three times more likely than state schools to have a school-wide AI strategy. A third of pupils lack continuous access to a device at home for online schoolwork.

## Four Policy Pillars

**Pillar 1 – Pupils:** Embed AI literacy from Key Stage 2, require a Year 7 AI-literacy module, revise the computing curriculum, introduce a Certificate in Applied Computing, reform GCSE computer science, treat AI as a cross-curricular competency, and create an independent body for curriculum reform.

**Pillar 2 – Teachers and Leaders:** Create a national network of AI hubs, introduce government-funded AI lead teachers in every school, launch an AI-mastery pedagogical framework, update Teachers' Standards to include AI competence, and introduce a new NPQ in Leading AI and Digital Innovation.

<summary>
# U.S. Department of Education Report: Artificial Intelligence and the Future of Teaching and Learning (May 2023)

## Overview
This report from the U.S. Department of Education's Office of Educational Technology addresses the need for policy development around AI in education. It defines AI as "automation based on associations" and examines opportunities, risks, and recommendations for integrating AI into teaching and learning.

## Key Definitions
- **AI**: "Automation based on associations" - computers automate reasoning based on patterns in data
- **Two fundamental shifts**: (1) from capturing data to detecting patterns, (2) from providing access to resources to automating instructional decisions

## Three Reasons to Address AI Now
1. **Opportunities**: AI may enable achieving educational priorities at scale (adaptivity, teacher support, customizable resources)
2. **Risks**: Algorithmic bias, surveillance, privacy concerns, potential replacement of teachers (which the Department rejects)
3. **Unintended consequences**: At scale, AI could widen achievement gaps if based on poor data or biased assumptions

## Four Foundations for Ethical AI Policy
1. **Center People** - Keep humans in the loop; AI should augment human decision-making, not replace it
2. **Advance Equity** - Address algorithmic bias and ensure AI doesn't discriminate against underserved communities
3. **Ensure Safety, Ethics, and Effectiveness** - Maintain data privacy/security and require evidence of effectiveness (aligned with ESEA standards)
4. **Promote Transparency** - AI models must be inspectable, explainable, and overridable by educators

## Key Insights by Domain

### Learning
- AI enables adaptivity through intelligent tutoring systems
- Need dual focus: learning *with* AI and learning *about* AI
- Recommendation: Seek AI models aligned to a shared vision for learning

### Teaching
- Always center educators in instructional loops
- AI can improve teaching jobs through automated assistants but must avoid surveillance
- Recommendation: AI must be inspectable, explainable, and overridable by teachers

### Formative Assessment
- AI can enhance feedback loops
- Automated essay scoring is an example application
- Recommendation: Harness assessment expertise to reduce bias

### Research & Development
- Focus on addressing context and the "long tail" of learner variability
- Use design-based research partnerships
- Recommendation: R&D must account for context of teaching and learning

## Seven Recommendations
1. **Emphasize Humans in the Loop** - Require human oversight in educational AI
2. **Align AI Models to a Shared Vision for Education** - Ensure AI supports educational goals
3. **Design Using Modern Learning Principles** - Base AI on sound pedagogy
4. **Prioritize Strengthening Trust** - Build trustworthy systems
5. **Inform and Involve Educators** - Engage teachers in AI adoption
6. **Focus R&D on Addressing Context and Enhancing Trust and Safety** - Research real-world applications
7. **Develop Education-Specific Guidelines and Guardrails** - Create policies for safe AI use

## Key Principles
- "AI in education can only grow at the speed of trust" (Dr. Dale Allen)
- Three perspectives on AI: Human-like reasoning, algorithmic goal pursuit, and intelligence augmentation
- The Department "firmly rejects the idea that AI could replace teachers"
- Policies must address algorithmic discrimination, data privacy, and the need for human checks and balances

--- SOURCE 18: Artificial Intelligence in Technical and Vocational Education and Training: Empirical Evidence, Implementation Challenges, and Future Directions ---
URL: https://www.preprints.org/manuscript/202504.2173

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This preprint (version 1, submitted April 25, 2025, posted April 27, 2025) by Adam Zary and Nabil Zary is a systematic literature review examining the empirical evidence on AI in Technical and Vocational Education and Training (TVET). The review searched databases including IEEE Xplore, Scopus, ERIC, and Google Scholar, plus grey literature, identifying 11 studies published between 2021-2025 that met inclusion criteria (TVET settings with measurable outcomes).

**Key Findings:**
- **AI Technologies in TVET**: Five categories identified: AI-augmented simulators/XR systems (e.g., Lee et al. 2021 found AI-guided welding trainer improved accuracy and learning rate), AI Teaching Factories (e.g., Wahjusaputri et al. 2024 found AI teaching factory boosted technical proficiency and industry readiness), adaptive learning systems, generative AI applications (ChatGPT), and AI-enhanced LMS.
- **Geographic Concentration**: Research clustered in Malaysia (5 studies), China (3), Germany (2), and Indonesia (1). No research from Africa, Latin America, or much of North America.
- **Methodological Imbalance**: 46% survey/observational studies, 18% case studies, 18% analytical/framework studies, 9% controlled experiments, 9% mixed-methods. Only two studies used quantitative skill assessments.
- **Barriers**: Teacher capacity/lack of AI literacy (most common), infrastructure limitations, cost of implementation, technical complexity, curriculum integration difficulties, and insufficient institutional support.
- **Student vs. Teacher Perceptions**: Students generally positive about AI tools; teachers showed more complex views with concerns about preparedness.

**Conclusions**: AI shows promise for enhancing vocational skill acquisition, especially in hands-on/physical trades with sensor-rich feedback systems. However, the evidence base is limited by short-term pilots, perception-based research, and lack of longitudinal studies tracking employment outcomes. The paper recommends future research priorities including longitudinal studies, standardized assessment frameworks, multi-context replication studies, teacher professional development evaluations, and comparative studies across vocational domains.
</summary>

URL: https://ojs.aaai.org/index.php/AIES/article/download/36697/38835

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This academic paper by Evani Radiya-Dixit and Angèle Christin (Stanford University), presented at the AAAI/ACM Conference on AI, Ethics, and Society (AIES 2025), investigates how the term "Global South" is conceptualized and used within AI ethics. The authors conducted semi-structured interviews with 20 AI ethics scholars and practitioners who engage with global politics, alongside content analysis of their published materials.

Key findings reveal four major limitations of the term "Global South": (1) it homogenizes countries with diverse political power and technological development, (2) it serves as a proxy for underdeveloped in AI innovation and regulation, (3) it implies technological illiteracy, and (4) it suggests unidirectional influence with AI technology marketed from centers to peripheries. The authors argue the term can perpetuate an imperial gaze, similar to the earlier terms "Third World" and "developing countries."

Despite these limitations, many participants feel pressured to use the term "Global South" due to research and funding structures that reinforce the United States as a center of resources and knowledge production. Participants described how academic publishing, grant funding, and conference structures require them to frame their work using this terminology to be legible to audiences at the center.

The paper recommends three interventions: (a) grounding work in specific regions and communities rather than using broad generalizations, (b) leveraging particular analytical frameworks (such as anti-caste theories) when drawing connections across communities, and (c) making deeper structural changes to build alternative funding structures and foster solidarity among countries at the peripheries.
</summary>

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a scoping review published in Education Sciences (2024) by Schei, Møgelvang, and Ludvigsen from Western Norway University of Applied Sciences. The review analyzes 24 empirical articles published between 1 January 2022 and 5 September 2023 on students' perceptions and use of AI chatbots (like ChatGPT, Copilot, Gemini, Claude) in higher education. **Key Findings:**

**Geographic & Disciplinary Distribution:** Research is concentrated in Asia, with STEM disciplines (computer science, programming, engineering) being predominant. Mixed methods were the most common research approach.

**Positive Perceptions:** Students perceive AI chatbots as highly useful, motivating, and easy to use—serving as personal task assistants, providing immediate feedback, and helping with writing, coding, and academic tasks. **Concerns:** Students worry about accuracy and reliability of AI responses, potential negative impacts on learning, critical thinking, creativity, academic integrity, and plagiarism. There is a recognized tension between surface-level use (shortcuts) and deep learning approaches.

**Learning Processes:** Students use AI chatbots for diverse, purpose-driven tasks including brainstorming, summarizing, coding, problem-solving, writing support, and language learning. The review concludes that while positive attitudes and critical use prevail, addressing students' concerns is crucial for responsible AI integration in higher education.
</summary>

<summary>
**Summary: AI Productivity in Education — Real Gains, Costs, and What to Do Next**

This article by Professor Keith Lee of SIAI examines the current state of AI productivity in education, arguing that while AI tools produce real efficiency gains, the benefits are uneven, adoption is shallow, and achieving net improvements requires workflow redesign, training, and guardrails.

**Key Findings:**

- **Modest but real gains:** Late 2024 surveys show U.S. workers using generative AI saved ~5.4% of weekly hours, translating to ~1.1% workforce-wide productivity. For a 40-hour week, this is roughly 2 hours saved.
- **Uneven benefits:** AI productivity gains are strongest for novice/less-experienced workers (e.g., ~14-15% improvement in customer support, largest for juniors). Benefits are significant on well-defined tasks but weaker or adverse on complex, judgment-heavy problems.
- **Shallow adoption:** Only 23% of employed U.S. adults used AI for work in the past week; ~30% of ChatGPT usage is work-related. Deep, regular use remains low.
- **Requirements beyond tools:** Gains require high-quality data, redesigned workflows, training, and robust safeguards. Integration costs, oversight, and change management consume resources. Hallucination risks, privacy regulations, and curriculum alignment remain challenges.
- **Macro context:** U.S. labor productivity grew ~2.3% in 2024 and 1.5% year-over-year by Q2 2025 — an uptick, but not a dramatic AI-driven shift.

**Practical 18-Month Agenda:**

1. Identify 3 workflows where AI can improve time and quality (e.g., formative feedback on drafts, generating aligned practice items, triaging student services).
2. Establish "gold standard" baselines without AI, then insert AI for repetitive tasks — not to replace human judgment.
3. Use retrieval-augmented generation for course content; require human review for high-stakes decisions (final grades, progression).
4. Procure complementary tools (training, prompt libraries, LMS integration, safe retrieval APIs).
5. Run small cross-functional pilots as mini-randomized controlled trials: define metrics, gather baselines, run for a term, publish methods.
6. Measure net costs (computing, licensing, hidden labor for redesign/review).
7. Track outcomes: hours returned to instruction, grading variability reduction, student support response times, error rates in AI-assisted outputs.

**Conclusion:** The 1.1% productivity boost is modest but sufficient if reinvested into feedback, course clarity, and student support. The key is targeting "upper-junior" levels, routine tasks that free expert time, and aligning incentives for deep use in impactful workflows.

--- SOURCE 2: Who wrote this? Evaluating the reliability of AI detection tools in higher education ---
URL: https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40979-026-00226-w

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is an open-access research article published on June 29, 2026, in the International Journal for Educational Integrity (Volume 22, Article 16). The study, conducted by researchers Marijke Van Vlasselaer, Filip Van Droogenbroeck, and Bram Spruyt from a Belgian university, evaluates the reliability of four AI detection tools—GPTZero, Pangram, Copyleaks, and Turnitin—in higher education contexts.

**Methodology**: The researchers created a synthetic dataset of 160 academic papers with known ground truth across four categories: (1) fully human-written, (2) fully AI-generated (using GPT-4o Deep Research), (3) hybrid (human text with AI-inserted passages), and (4) humanised AI text (AI-generated text rewritten to resemble student writing). All AI text was generated in May 2025. In the second part of the study, the best-performing tool (Pangram) was applied to 1,163 real master's theses submitted in the 2024-2025 academic year.

**Key Findings**:
- Pangram consistently outperformed the other tools, achieving high accuracy in detecting fully AI-generated, hybrid, and humanised texts.
- Other tools significantly underestimated GenAI content, particularly for texts generated with the most advanced model (GPT-4o Deep Research).
- All tools correctly identified fully human-written texts (false positives were rare, suggesting improvement over earlier studies).
- When applied to real master's theses, Pangram flagged 45.5% of cases, typically indicating low to moderate levels of AI-associated text.

**Context**: The study notes that student GenAI use has risen dramatically—from 66% in 2024 to 92% in 2025, with 88% using it for academic assignments and 18% directly copying GenAI text. The authors conclude that while detection tools can provide useful initial flags, they should not be used as sole evidence in high-stakes decision-making but should be part of a broader evaluation strategy.

**Background on Detection Tools**: The article explains how GenAI detectors work (linguistics-based, statistical-based, and learning-based methods) and provides detailed descriptions of each tool's approach. Turnitin uses perplexity, burstiness, repetition, and generic writing analysis. Pangram uses a "mirror prompt" technique and "hard negative mining" trained on ~28 million human-authored documents. Copyleaks analyses frequency ratios, syllable dispersion, and grammatical structures. GPTZero primarily uses perplexity and burstiness metrics.

--- SOURCE 3: Can AI-Driven Plagiarism Detection Tools Uphold Academic Integrity Without Ethical Compromises? A Comprehensive Analysis of False Positives, Contextual Misunderstandings, and Dependency Issues ---
URL: https://www.preprints.org/manuscript/202412.1683

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This preprint (Version 1, submitted December 19, 2024) by Edgar Eslit investigates the role of AI-driven plagiarism detection tools in higher education, examining whether they can uphold academic integrity without ethical compromises. The study analyzes tools like Turnitin, PlagScan, GPTZero, Copyleaks, and QuillBot, finding that they often struggle with context interpretation, resulting in false positives and missed instances of nuanced plagiarism. 

The research employs a qualitative methodology, using thematic and comparative analysis of existing scholarly literature from databases such as Google Scholar, Web of Science, and Scopus. It is grounded in three theoretical frameworks: Technological Determinism, Socio-Technical Systems Theory (STS), and Actor-Network Theory (ANT).

Key findings include:
- AI tools contribute to academic integrity by quickly identifying potential plagiarism, but their limitations are significant.
- False positives occur when legitimate work is flagged, particularly for non-native speakers who may use language structures that unintentionally mirror existing texts.
- The tools struggle with paraphrasing, contextual understanding, and distinguishing between human-written and AI-generated content.
- There is a growing overreliance on AI, which may encourage a "checklist mentality" among educators and reduce the role of human judgment.
- Major universities (e.g., UC, Oxford, Harvard) have been hesitant to rely solely on AI tools for plagiarism detection.

The study concludes that AI-driven tools should be used as supplementary aids rather than definitive arbiters of originality. Human judgment remains essential for upholding academic integrity. The answer to whether these tools can uphold academic integrity without ethical compromises is nuanced: they cannot be used as the ultimate arbitral judge in determining if a paper is AI-generated or plagiarized.
</summary>

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is an open-access review article published in the journal *Information* (Vol. 16, Issue 10, 2025) authored by Promethi Das Deep, William D. Edgington, Nitu Ghosh, and Md. Shiblur Rahaman from Sam Houston State University (USA) and Noakhali Science and Technology University (Bangladesh). The paper evaluates the effectiveness, limitations, and ethical implications of AI detection tools (e.g., Turnitin AI, GPTZero, Copyleaks, ZeroGPT) in higher education, based on a qualitative evidence synthesis of 24 peer-reviewed articles published between 2021 and 2024.

**Key Findings:**

- **Institutional Implementation:** Universities are revising academic integrity policies to address AI-generated content, but many lack comprehensive, AI-specific guidelines. The review recommends proactive frameworks like Situational Crime Prevention (SCP) models rather than purely punitive approaches.

- **Detection Tool Effectiveness:** AI detectors show inconsistent accuracy. They frequently produce false positives, particularly misclassifying human-written content (especially from non-native English speakers) as AI-generated. Tools trained on older models (e.g., GPT-2) perform poorly on advanced outputs (e.g., GPT-4). One study found Quillbot achieved 95.59% accuracy, while others showed rates ranging from 0% to 100%. A paraphrasing model (DIPPER) reduced detection accuracy of DetectGPT from 70.3% to 4.6%.

- **Ethical Concerns:** Key issues include surveillance, lack of transparency, due process violations, and bias against multilingual/non-native English speakers. The unilateral deployment of detection software risks eroding trust between instructors and students.

- **Emerging Innovations:** Researchers are exploring watermarking (inference-time embedding), hybrid detection systems, and machine learning approaches (e.g., TF-IDF with logistic regression achieving 99.82% accuracy). However, implementation challenges persist.

- **Recommendations:** The paper calls for a shift from punitive approaches toward AI-integrated pedagogies that emphasize ethical use, student support, inclusive assessment design (e.g., in-class tasks, oral presentations, portfolio-based evaluations), and faculty training. Students often lack clarity on acceptable AI usage, with 87% showing inadequate comprehension of implications.

The article concludes that while AI detection tools have a role in preserving academic standards, institutions must adopt balanced, transparent, and student-centered strategies that uphold academic integrity without compromising equity or student rights.

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This study, published in Cogent Education (Volume 12, 2025) and authored by Said Abubakar, Abdulkadir Jeilani, and Mohamed Yusuf of Mogadishu University, investigates the impact of over-reliance on AI on student learning outcomes, examining the moderating effects of ethical concerns and institutional policies.

**Methodology:** A quantitative cross-sectional survey of 226 participants (192 undergraduate, 34 postgraduate; 89 female, 137 male) from major universities in Mogadishu, Somalia. The sample was determined using G*Power (minimum 129 needed) with α=0.05, effect size 0.15, power 0.95. Data was analyzed using SPSS and JAMOVI. Reliability was strong (Cronbach's α = 0.895 overall).

**Key Findings:**
- **Over-reliance on AI** had a moderate mean score (3.0162). Students recognized AI's negative impact on critical thinking and motivation.
- **Ethical concerns** yielded a moderate mean (3.2072), with students aware of academic dishonesty, privacy, and transparency issues.
- **Institutional policies** had a moderate perception (3.1342), with students seeing existing policies as moderately effective but needing improvement.
- **Negative consequences** scored high (3.4655), with strong concerns about technology dependency, content accuracy, bias in assessments, and reduced teacher roles.

**Regression Results:** The model explained 38.9% of variance (R²=0.389, F=47.133, p<0.001). Ethical concerns had the strongest effect (β=0.429, p<0.001), followed by reliance on AI (β=0.207) and institutional factors (β=0.136, p=0.022). All three hypotheses were supported:
- **H1:** Significant positive relationship between over-reliance on AI and negative learning consequences.
- **H2:** Ethical concerns significantly moderate (reduce) the negative effect of over-reliance (interaction estimate = −0.0978, p=0.031).
- **H3:** Institutional policies significantly moderate (reduce) the negative effect of over-reliance (interaction estimate = −0.115, p=0.035).

**Conclusion:** While AI can enhance education, over-reliance poses risks to critical thinking and academic integrity. Robust ethical frameworks and well-communicated institutional policies can alleviate adverse impacts. The study offers novel empirical evidence from a post-conflict higher education context (Somalia) where AI policy infrastructure is still developing. Recommendations include promoting balanced AI integration, enhancing ethical awareness through workshops, and establishing clear institutional policies.

<summary>
This webpage presents a systematic review published in npj Science of Learning (Volume 10, Article 29, May 2025) examining AI-driven Intelligent Tutoring Systems (ITS) in K-12 education. Authored by Létourneau et al., the review analyzed 28 studies involving 4,597 students to determine the effects of ITSs on learning outcomes and the experimental designs used to evaluate them.

The introduction highlights the global educational crisis and UNESCO's call to leverage AI for sustainable development. ITSs are defined as software programs equipped with AI that monitor progress, identify difficulties, and adapt instruction to individual learners. Notable prior work includes Kulik & Fletcher's (2016) meta-analysis of 50 controlled assessments, which found no scientific consensus on ITS effectiveness but showed they can be highly effective instructional tools.

- Roughly half (54%) of studies compared school levels and subjects to assess differences.
- None of the included articles mentioned AI ethics considerations, highlighting a gap in addressing ethical implications.
- The review calls for additional research with longer interventions, larger and more diverse sample sizes, and investigation into ethical implications of AI in teaching.

The authors note that ITS effectiveness depends on sound pedagogical features (immediate feedback, guided practice, adaptivity) applied under the right conditions, consistent with Honebein and Reigeluth's (2021) thesis that ITS must be well-aligned with instructional theory to produce positive outcomes.

This is a meta-analysis study published in Behavioral Sciences (2026) by Ren, Stephens, and Lee from the University of Auckland, examining the impact of AI on learners' self-efficacy in educational contexts. The study analyzed 23 empirical studies published between January 2005 and February 2025, indexed in Web of Science, Scopus, and ERIC databases.

**Key Findings:**
- AI had a significant positive impact on self-efficacy in learning contexts, with a medium effect size of 0.758 (Hedges' g).

**Methodology:** The study used a random-effects model due to high heterogeneity (I² = 89.677). Hedges' g was used for effect size calculations. Publication bias was assessed via funnel plot, classic fail-safe N, and Egger's test, all indicating no substantial bias. Sensitivity analysis confirmed robustness of results.

**Conclusion:** AI effectively promotes learners' self-efficacy, particularly in natural sciences and medicine, and when used as an intelligent learning tool. The study recommends integrating AI in classrooms and designing activities that promote student-AI interaction, while noting the need for more experimental research in this domain.

# U.S. Department of Education Report: Artificial Intelligence and the Future of Teaching and Learning (May 2023)

## Overview
This report from the U.S. Department of Education's Office of Educational Technology addresses the need for policy development around AI in education. It defines AI as "automation based on associations" and examines opportunities, risks, and recommendations for integrating AI into teaching and learning.

## Key Definitions
- **AI**: "Automation based on associations" - computers automate reasoning based on patterns in data
- **Two fundamental shifts**: (1) from capturing data to detecting patterns, (2) from providing access to resources to automating instructional decisions

## Three Reasons to Address AI Now
1. **Opportunities**: AI may enable achieving educational priorities at scale (adaptivity, teacher support, customizable resources)
2. **Risks**: Algorithmic bias, surveillance, privacy concerns, potential replacement of teachers (which the Department rejects)
3. **Unintended consequences**: At scale, AI could widen achievement gaps if based on poor data or biased assumptions

## Four Foundations for Ethical AI Policy
1. **Center People** - Keep humans in the loop; AI should augment human decision-making, not replace it
2. **Advance Equity** - Address algorithmic bias and ensure AI doesn't discriminate against underserved communities
3. **Ensure Safety, Ethics, and Effectiveness** - Maintain data privacy/security and require evidence of effectiveness (aligned with ESEA standards)
4. **Promote Transparency** - AI models must be inspectable, explainable, and overridable by educators

## Key Insights by Domain

### Learning
- AI enables adaptivity through intelligent tutoring systems
- Need dual focus: learning *with* AI and learning *about* AI
- Recommendation: Seek AI models aligned to a shared vision for learning

### Teaching
- Always center educators in instructional loops
- AI can improve teaching jobs through automated assistants but must avoid surveillance
- Recommendation: AI must be inspectable, explainable, and overridable by teachers

### Formative Assessment
- AI can enhance feedback loops
- Automated essay scoring is an example application
- Recommendation: Harness assessment expertise to reduce bias

### Research & Development
- Focus on addressing context and the "long tail" of learner variability
- Use design-based research partnerships
- Recommendation: R&D must account for context of teaching and learning

## Seven Recommendations
1. **Emphasize Humans in the Loop** - Require human oversight in educational AI
2. **Align AI Models to a Shared Vision for Education** - Ensure AI supports educational goals
3. **Design Using Modern Learning Principles** - Base AI on sound pedagogy
4. **Prioritize Strengthening Trust** - Build trustworthy systems
5. **Inform and Involve Educators** - Engage teachers in AI adoption
6. **Focus R&D on Addressing Context and Enhancing Trust and Safety** - Research real-world applications
7. **Develop Education-Specific Guidelines and Guardrails** - Create policies for safe AI use

## Key Principles
- "AI in education can only grow at the speed of trust" (Dr. Dale Allen)
- Three perspectives on AI: Human-like reasoning, algorithmic goal pursuit, and intelligence augmentation
- The Department "firmly rejects the idea that AI could replace teachers"
- Policies must address algorithmic discrimination, data privacy, and the need for human checks and balances

SUMMARY:
<summary>
Khan Academy published findings from six months of rigorous product testing (October 2025 to April 2026) aimed at improving Khanmigo, its generative AI tutor for students and assistant for teachers. The improvements yielded a cumulative 6.1% improvement in next-item correctness across more than 15 million tutoring threads.

**Core metrics tracked:** Response latency (speed of replies), next-item correctness (independent student performance on the next problem after tutoring), and cognitive engagement quality (measured as passive/active/constructive). Guardrail metrics such as answer-giving, math error rates, and interaction counts were also monitored.

**Key findings on reducing latency:** Switching to a faster AI model reduced response time by 0.3 seconds (1.35M threads). Instructing the math agent to produce more concise responses cut mean response time by 3 seconds (352K threads) and limiting focus to already-completed math reduced latency another 400ms while reducing answer-giving by 50%. Adding a pre-check to determine whether math verification was needed cut unnecessary calls by 0.3 seconds (1.04M threads). Math accuracy held steady across all tests.

**Key findings on improving tutoring with student history:** Providing a summary of the student's recent problem-solving history improved next-item correctness by +3.4% (608K threads, 97.5% confidence). Surfacing prerequisite skills the student hadn't yet mastered improved next-item correctness by +2.7% (1.36M threads, 98.5% confidence). Providing the full in-session conversation log in plain text (instead of JSON) plus all threads from the previous 24 hours yielded a 5.09% increase in cognitive engagement (99.4% confidence). Adding examples of different problem types and providing more relevant follow-up content links showed no statistically significant effect.

**Conclusion:** No single improvement produced a dramatic leap, but collectively the work meaningfully improved Khanmigo's effectiveness while identifying less expensive and faster ways to run it at scale. A full paper will be published at the 27th International Conference in AI for Education.
</summary>

--- SOURCE 1: AI Tutoring Equity Gap: Why Access Alone Won't Close It ---
URL: https://www.valere.io/ai-tutoring-equity-gap

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This article by Guy Pistone (CEO of Valere) examines the equity problem surrounding AI tutoring in K-12 education. While AI tutoring shows real promise—with a 2020 meta-analysis finding effect sizes equivalent to one-on-one human tutoring in controlled settings—the author warns that the technology risks following the same pattern as other democratizing technologies: benefiting the already-advantaged first and widening the gap before narrowing it.

Key issues identified include:
- **The access gap**: ~15% of U.S. children (9 million students) still lack reliable home broadband, concentrated in low-income, rural, and Tribal communities. As of early 2026, districts report 1 in 5 low-income families still lack reliable home internet.
- **The readiness gap**: The harder problem than access. Schools with the most to gain are often least positioned to close the feedback loop between AI-generated insights and changed instruction, due to fewer teachers per student, less planning time, and less administrative bandwidth.
- **Market failure**: The business incentives point toward well-resourced early adopters. Vendor-funded studies (e.g., Carnegie Learning's own 2022 efficacy study showing 30% improvement on algebra assessments) paint a more optimistic picture than independent research.
- **Teacher training deficit**: A 2022 study found teachers with >10 hours of platform-specific PD were significantly more effective at acting on AI data than those with standard 2-hour onboarding.

The article cites widely deployed platforms including Carnegie Learning's MATHia (3,000+ schools), Khan Academy's Khanmigo (free through OpenAI partnership), DreamBox Learning (5 million+ active students), and Synthesis. District licensing typically runs $15–$30 per student per year.

The author argues that closing the gap requires treating connectivity as infrastructure, designing offline/low-bandwidth AI tools, investing in sustained teacher professional development, and using equity-centered procurement frameworks. State-level AI education policy remains fragmented, with California (AB 2876), Virginia, and North Carolina leading, while most meaningful policy happens at the district level.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"The readiness gap. It is the distance between having access to an AI tool and being able to use it effectively.", "The technology does not distribute itself equitably by default. It never has, nor will.", "The one-size-fits-all classroom is a real problem. A third grader interested in horses who gets a math lesson framed around horses is more engaged, more likely to retain the concept, and more likely to stay curious.", "The companies that get the most out of AI are not necessarily the ones with the most sophisticated models. They are the ones who invested in helping their people understand what the tools are doing and what to do with what they surface.", "The promise is real. So is the gap. And both deserve to be taken seriously."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 2: Frontiers | AI and the digital divide in education ---
URL: https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/computer-science/articles/10.3389/fcomp.2026.1759027/full

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This review article (published February 5, 2026, in Frontiers in Computer Science) by Matjie, Nethavhani, and Matlakala from the University of Limpopo, South Africa, examines how artificial intelligence (AI) contributes to the digital divide in education, focusing on language barriers, cultural mismatches, and algorithmic bias as key factors that create inequities even when access to AI tools exists.

The authors conducted a focused narrative and comparative review of case studies from countries with similar socio-economic statuses and visible urban-rural divides, including South Africa, China, Brazil, Kenya, Mali, and others. Case studies analyzed include: AI4D Maseno University (Kenya) on sign language translation; RobotsMali producing children's books in Bambara; the GPE KIX STEPS project in Benin, Cameroon, and DRC for culturally relevant STEM materials; primary education in urban vs. rural China (revealing a "TPACK divide"); higher education in Latin America during COVID-19; and STEM education in BRICS countries.

The conceptual framework identifies three interconnected digital divides: linguistic divide (limited engagement), cultural divide (reduced relevance), and algorithmic divide (biased feedback and unequal outcomes). The authors argue that even when learners have equal access to AI tools, the tools remain discriminatory due to language dominance (predominantly English), cultural insensitivity, and algorithmic bias from non-representative training datasets.

The article proposes three practical solutions:
1. **Development of AI tools with multilingual and culturally relevant content** (e.g., multilingual intelligent tutoring systems, local-language AI writing assistants, culturally contextualized AI chatbots)
2. **Use of diverse, representative datasets to mitigate algorithmic bias** (e.g., fair adaptive learning algorithms, bias-aware language models, participatory dataset curation)
3. **Capacity-building for educators and learners** (e.g., teacher professional development in AI pedagogy, learner AI literacy workshops, community-based train-the-trainer models)

Key contradictions identified include: participatory vs. top-down AI design approaches; short-term efficiency gains vs. long-term equity outcomes; and the inconsistent emphasis on teacher capacity-building across interventions. The authors conclude that AI's contribution to educational equity depends on participatory design, comprehensive teacher training, and multilingual support, rather than merely providing access to technology.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"AI should change learning for all learners across the globe; however, that is not always the case. AI in higher education brings some concerns with it, specifically the issues of access and such as the algorithmic bias and discrimination.", "According to Van Dijk (2017), the digital divide is the gap between people who do and do not have access to forms of information and communication. This gap appears to be wider for learners from rich countries and regions and those from poor countries and regions in terms of access to AI technologies that enable learning.", "Without deliberate commitments to inclusive design, transparency, and governance, AI risks reproducing and intensifying existing social hierarchies. Algorithmic bias thus constitutes a structural threat to educational equity, requiring systemic intervention if AI is to function as a tool for inclusion rather than exclusion.", "The cases reveal a tension between short-term efficiency gains and long-term equity outcomes. RobotsMali shows that AI-assisted content creation can reduce costs and production time while preserving cultural relevance. However, the BRICS STEM education case demonstrates that policy-driven AI and STEM expansion without parallel investment in access and training leads to skills shortages and labour market exclusion.", "AI does not inherently reduce digital divides. Instead, equitable outcomes depend on participatory design, sustained capacity-building, and institutional readiness."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 3: AI Access Is Creating a New Digital Divide ---
URL: https://edcircuit.com/ai-access-is-creating-a-new-digital-divide

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This article from edCircuit (published in 2026) argues that AI access in K–12 schools is creating a new digital divide, beyond the traditional gaps in internet connectivity and devices. It contrasts "AI-forward" districts, where students learn prompt engineering, AI ethics, and personalized tutoring, with districts that have no AI literacy initiatives, guidance, or professional development. Wealthier suburban districts with dedicated technology coaches, cybersecurity teams, and strong funding can adopt AI quickly, while rural and underfunded districts—often relying on a single tech administrator—struggle to keep pace. The article cites the 2026 State of EdTech District Leadership report by CoSN, which identifies AI, cybersecurity, and staffing as key challenges. Teachers in AI-ready districts receive training on AI-enhanced lesson planning and ethical integration, while others get no guidance, creating instructional and professional inequities. The article acknowledges legitimate concerns about data privacy, cybersecurity, bias, and academic integrity but warns that avoiding AI entirely leaves students unprepared for a workforce increasingly reliant on AI. The author calls for state-level AI guidance, regional collaboration, expanded professional development, public-private partnerships, and AI governance frameworks to ensure equitable access. The central thesis is that the next digital divide will be measured not by devices or bandwidth, but by which students were prepared to shape an AI-driven future and which were left behind.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"AI access in K–12 schools is rapidly creating a new digital divide that could determine which students are prepared for the future, and which students are left behind.", "That gap may become one of the defining educational equity issues of this decade.", "The next digital divide may be defined by access to artificial intelligence.", "The districts most capable of preparing students for an AI-driven future are often the districts that already possess significant technological advantages.", "The AI divide will not simply be measured by devices or bandwidth. It may ultimately be measured by which students were prepared to shape the future—and which students were left trying to catch up to it."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 4: AI and the next digital divide in education | Brookings ---
URL: https://www.brookings.edu/articles/ai-and-the-next-digital-divide-in-education

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This Brookings Institution commentary by Michael Trucano (July 10, 2023) examines the evolution of the digital divide in education in the context of emerging AI technologies. The article traces the progression: the first digital divide (rich have technology, poor do not), the second digital divide (rich have technology and skills, poor have technology but lack skills), and a potential third digital divide where the rich have access to both AI technology and human teachers/tutors, while the poor only have access to the technology.

Key context includes the global learning crisis: 70% of 10-year-olds in low- and middle-income countries cannot read basic texts, 244 million children are out of school, and a projected shortage of 70 million teachers by 2030. The article discusses the promise of AI-enabled personalized learning tools like Khan Academy's Khanmigo, while noting that historical efforts at personalized learning technology have had mixed results.

The author raises a critical question: As AI becomes more prevalent in education, could a new divide emerge where wealthy students have access to both AI tools and human support (teachers, tutors, engaged parents), while disadvantaged students only have access to the AI technology? Evidence from COVID-19 remote learning showed that even where technology access was equitable, parental and tutor involvement significantly impacted outcomes. The article concludes that education is fundamentally a human endeavor, and asks what society should do if access to people becomes the new dividing line.
</summary>

--- SOURCE 6: Ensuring Fairness in AI: Addressing Algorithmic Bias in Education and Hiring | YIP Institute ---
URL: https://yipinstitute.org/capstone/ensuring-fairness-in-ai-addressing-algorithmic-bias

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This webpage is a policy capstone titled "Ensuring Fairness in AI: Addressing Algorithmic Bias in Education and Hiring," published by the Institute for Youth in Policy. Authored by Aarush Tahiliani (2025 Winter Fellow), the piece examines how AI systems in college admissions, financial aid, and hiring processes reinforce systemic biases against marginalized communities. Key points include:

- **Problem**: AI-powered tools in hiring and education replicate societal biases (e.g., a 2019 NBER study found AI resume-screening disproportionately filtered out Black candidates; AI admissions models favor wealthier students).
- **Current Stance**: The U.S. lacks comprehensive AI regulation. The White House's 2022 Blueprint for an AI Bill of Rights outlines principles but lacks enforcement. The EU's AI Act requires audits for high-risk AI systems, but the U.S. has no equivalent.
- **Stakeholders**: Students, job seekers, marginalized communities, educational institutions, employers, policymakers, and AI developers.
- **Tried Policies**: NYC's Local Law 144 (2023) mandates bias audits for hiring AI; Illinois' AI Video Interview Act (2020) requires disclosure but no auditing. No federal regulations govern AI in education.

<summary>
# Bias in AI: Examples and 6 Ways to Fix it in 2026

This article from AIMultiple (updated August 6, 2026) provides a comprehensive overview of AI bias, including real-world examples, categories, causes, legal frameworks, and mitigation strategies.

## AI Bias Benchmark Results
The author benchmarked 14 leading LLMs on 66 bias evaluation questions across gender, race, age, disability, socioeconomic status, and sexual orientation. Key findings:
- Open-ended questions showed less bias than multiple-choice formats
- GPT-4o cited statistical crime rates for specific races when asked to identify perpetrators
- Gemini 2.5 Pro identified male names as doctors and female names as nurses despite being told answers could be "cannot be determined"
- Claude 4.5 Sonnet notably avoided most errors

## Recent Real-Life Examples of AI Bias

**Racism:**
- Facial recognition systems misidentified darker-skinned women at rates up to 35%, while lighter-skinned men had error rates below 1% (MIT Media Lab, 2018)
- A healthcare risk-prediction algorithm used on 200+ million U.S. citizens showed racial bias by using healthcare spending as a proxy for need
- Facebook allowed advertisers to target by gender, race, and religion (2019)

**Sexism:**
- A 2024 UNESCO study found LLMs associate women with "home" and "family" four times more often than men
- A 2024 University of Washington study found resume-screening AI favored white male names
- Amazon's 2014 recruiting tool penalized resumes mentioning "women's" and was scrapped in 2015
- Image generators (Stable Diffusion, DALL-E 2) produced 75-100% male images for STEM professions

**Ageism:**
- iTutorGroup's AI recruitment software automatically rejected female applicants 55+ and male applicants 60+ (settled for $365,000)
- A 2025 federal class action lawsuit against Workday alleged AI screening tools disproportionately disadvantaged applicants over 40

**Ableism:**
- A 2025 University of Melbourne study found AI hiring tools struggled with speech disabilities and non-native accents
- HireVue's AI interview platform raised concerns about fairness for candidates with mobility or communication impairments
- Generative AI depicted autistic individuals using stereotypical imagery

## Types of AI Bias
- **Historical bias**: Training data reflects past prejudices
- **Sample bias**: Training data doesn't represent real-world populations
- **Ontological bias**: Western-centric worldview embedded in AI's fundamental concepts
- **Amplification bias**: AI not only learns but exacerbates human biases
- **Label bias**: Inconsistent or biased data labeling
- **Aggregation bias**: Hiding important differences through data aggregation
- **Confirmation bias**: Favoring information that confirms existing beliefs
- **Cultural & geographic bias**: LLMs trained mostly on Western data
- **Evaluation bias**: Testing on unrepresentative data
- **Politeness bias**: LLMs more likely to comply with harmful requests if asked politely

## Legal Frameworks
- **EU AI Act**: Classifies AI by risk; mandates data governance and bias mitigation for high-risk systems
- **GDPR**: Limits processing of sensitive data; Article 22 grants right to explanation of automated decisions
- **EEOC/U.S. law**: AI vendors can be treated as employers' agents and sued under Title VII, ADA, ADEA
- **South Korea**: AI Framework Act effective January 2026, with fines up to ~$21,000
- **Japan**: AI Basic Act passed May 2025, emphasizing risk-based governance
- **Singapore**: Voluntary, light-touch approach with AI Verify testing tool
- **China**: Binding interim regulations on generative AI since 2023

## Steps to Fix AI Bias
1. **Fathom the algorithm and data**: Examine training datasets, conduct subpopulation analysis, monitor over time
2. **Establish a debiasing strategy**: Technical tools, operational strategies (red teams, third-party auditors), organizational transparency
3. **Improve human-driven processes**: Use model building to identify and address long-standing biases through training and cultural change

The article concludes that while AI can theoretically be unbiased if training data is perfectly clean, in practice AI is unlikely to ever be completely unbiased as it relies on human-created data.

--- SOURCE 13: Bloom's 2 Sigma Problem Debunked: One-to-One Tutoring Isn’t Going to Save Education (Here’s Why) ---
URL: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=IaTk7lHC470

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This video and article by Dr. Luke Rowe (PhD in learning sciences) debunks Benjamin Bloom's famous 1984 '2 Sigma Problem'—the claim that one-to-one tutoring can lift student achievement by two standard deviations (from the 50th to the 98th percentile). 

**Key Arguments & Evidence:**
- Bloom's claim rested heavily on two very small, unpublished studies by his doctoral students (Anania and Burke) in the early 1980s, plus a selectively cherry-picked table of effect sizes from secondary sources.
- Paul von Hippel's (2024) data sleuthing revealed major problems: the famous graph was a hand-drawn caricature, not actual data; Bloom rounded up and fabricated numbers from Walberg's (1984) work; and the doctoral students themselves did not go on to build careers around tutoring research.
- The tutoring condition was heavily confounded: tutors received extra training and coaching, students got frequent formative testing (retrieval practice effect ~0.5 SD), individual feedback, worked examples, Socratic questioning, praise, and extra time on task. These confounds likely inflated the effect.
- The mastery learning condition (which included testing and feedback but no tutoring) already showed over 1 SD gain, meaning about half the 2 sigma effect came from testing and feedback alone.
- Large-scale meta-analyses (Nickow et al., 2020, 2024) show tutoring effects are real but typically around 0.3 to 0.4 standard deviations (moving from 50th to ~64th percentile), not 2.0 SD. Matthew Kraft (2020) found most educational interventions produce effects of about 0.1 SD.
- Replacing classroom instruction with tutoring (as in Bloom's studies) produces inflated effects compared to tutoring as a supplement (the more common real-world scenario).
- Despite the debunking, the 2 sigma claim has become sticky in education and AI circles (e.g., Sal Khan's Khan Academy/Khanmigo citing it as a benchmark for AI tutors).

**Conclusion:** Tutoring is effective but modestly so (~0.3 SD). The 2 sigma claim is highly exaggerated, unreplicable science that has misled educational policy, parental spending on tutoring, and AI tutoring development goals.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"Bloom's two sigma claim had some basis in fact but it also contained elements of fiction like some science fiction" (von Hippel). "The idea that tutoring consistently raises achievement by two standard deviations is exaggerated and oversimplified. About 1/3 of a standard deviation seems to be the typical effect of an intense, well-designed program evaluated against broad tests" (von Hippel). "The two sigma problem is more like a 0.33 problem" (Dr. Luke Rowe). "Most educational interventions produce effect sizes of 0.1 standard deviation... you have a big impact through the aggregation of many small impacts" (Matthew Kraft). "Anania and Burke mixed a potent cocktail of interventions that included tutoring, training, and coaching in effective instructional practices, extra time, and frequent testing, feedback, and retesting" (von Hippel).

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This article from the Network Law Review, authored by Thibault Schrepel (Vrije Universiteit Amsterdam) and published in Winter 2026, examines how generative AI is reshaping academic publishing through the lens of network theory. The central argument is that AI's reduction of the marginal cost of academic writing will paradoxically amplify the Matthew Effect (cumulative advantage), concentrating reputational gains among established scholars rather than democratizing scientific influence.

Key arguments:
1. **Output Explosion**: AI is dramatically increasing submission volumes. Studies show AI-assisted writing has surged across disciplines since 2023, with LLM adoption associated with substantial increases in manuscript output among already-active researchers.

2. **Journals as Attention Allocators**: Contrary to predictions that AI will kill traditional journals, the author argues journals become more valuable as filtering institutions. In an environment of content abundance, credible certification of quality becomes more scarce and valuable.

3. **Amplified Matthew Effect**: AI amplifies cumulative advantage through two channels: (a) quality-correlated productivity, where researchers with strong foundations produce better work faster, widening the gap; and (b) reputational priors, where editors under increasing submission pressure rely more heavily on author reputation. Studies cited show LLM peer review models exhibited bias toward well-known authors and prominent institutions.

4. **Stratification**: The result is a bifurcated publication market—top journals increasingly publish established names, while secondary outlets (growing from 2% to 30% of global publications, 2003-2022) serve emerging scholars. This creates parallel tracks that rarely intersect.

The article concludes that the practical question for junior researchers is not how to produce more, but how to be read. It suggests two escape routes: genuine intellectual originality and academic writing that achieves literary quality, making the reading experience itself valuable.
</summary>

High-reputation authors attract editorial attention. Editorial attention produces acceptances. Acceptances produce citations. Citations reinforce reputation. --- SOURCE 1: [PDF] Tutor CoPilot: A Human-AI Approach for Scaling Real-Time Expertise ---
URL: https://edworkingpapers.com/sites/default/files/ai24_1054_v2.pdf

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This paper presents Tutor CoPilot, a Human-AI system that uses Large Language Models (LLMs) to provide real-time expert guidance to tutors during live K-12 math tutoring sessions. The study conducted a randomized controlled trial with over 700 tutors and 1,000 students from underserved communities in a U.S. Southern school district, partnered with FEV Tutor (a chat-based virtual tutoring provider), from March 27 to May 17, 2024.

**Key Findings:**
- Students with tutors using Tutor CoPilot were 4 percentage points more likely to master math topics (p<0.01), with exit ticket pass rates increasing from 62% to 66%.
- Gains were highest for students of lower-rated tutors (+9 p.p., from 56% to 65%) and less experienced tutors (+7 p.p., from 61% to 68%), helping less-effective tutors achieve outcomes comparable to their more-effective peers.
- The tool is low-cost at approximately $20 per tutor per year.
- Analysis of over 350,000 messages showed Tutor CoPilot promoted effective pedagogy: treatment tutors were more likely to use probing questions (e.g., "prompt the student to explain" used ~10% more) and less likely to use generic praise (used ~10% less by control tutors).

**Methodology:** The study used intent-to-treat (ITT) regression analysis, controlling for student-level covariates (baseline MAP math scores, demographics), school and grade fixed effects, and clustering at the student-tutor pair level. This review article (published February 5, 2026, in Frontiers in Computer Science) by Matjie, Nethavhani, and Matlakala from the University of Limpopo, South Africa, examines how artificial intelligence (AI) contributes to the digital divide in education, focusing on language barriers, cultural mismatches, and algorithmic bias as key factors that create inequities even when access to AI tools exists.

The authors conducted a focused narrative and comparative review of case studies from countries with similar socio-economic statuses and visible urban-rural divides, including South Africa, China, Brazil, Kenya, Mali, and others. The conceptual framework identifies three interconnected digital divides: linguistic divide (limited engagement), cultural divide (reduced relevance), and algorithmic divide (biased feedback and unequal outcomes). The authors argue that even when learners have equal access to AI tools, the tools remain discriminatory due to language dominance (predominantly English), cultural insensitivity, and algorithmic bias from non-representative training datasets.

The article proposes three practical solutions:
1. **Development of AI tools with multilingual and culturally relevant content** (e.g., multilingual intelligent tutoring systems, local-language AI writing assistants, culturally contextualized AI chatbots)
2. **Use of diverse, representative datasets to mitigate algorithmic bias** (e.g., fair adaptive learning algorithms, bias-aware language models, participatory dataset curation)
3. **Capacity-building for educators and learners** (e.g., teacher professional development in AI pedagogy, learner AI literacy workshops, community-based train-the-trainer models)

Key contradictions identified include: participatory vs. top-down AI design approaches; short-term efficiency gains vs. long-term equity outcomes; and the inconsistent emphasis on teacher capacity-building across interventions. The authors conclude that AI's contribution to educational equity depends on participatory design, comprehensive teacher training, and multilingual support, rather than merely providing access to technology.

- **How AI may exacerbate disparities:** AI algorithms can replicate historical biases. Admissions algorithms using race-neutral data (like SAT scores) can still produce disparate racial impacts, potentially allocating more scholarship funding to White and Asian students over Black and Latino students.

- **Ethical considerations:** Wealthier schools may afford better AI tools, potentially widening achievement gaps. The article poses a critical question: "What if AI does improve academic results for low-income Black students but further boosts results for wealthy White students, widening the academic achievement gap?" Student privacy and data collection also raise concerns.

- **Digital divide and AI literacy:** 72% of White teens had heard of ChatGPT vs. 56% of Black teens. 35% of low-income California households lacked reliable internet access in 2021. 38% of Black residents in the rural south lack broadband access. Without AI literacy, underserved students may use AI tools less effectively than wealthier counterparts.

- **Regulation:** Congress has not passed AI legislation. Colorado enacted the Artificial Intelligence Act (May 2024). California advanced ~30 AI bills. The White House released the Blueprint for an AI Bill of Rights (October 2022), and President Biden issued an Executive Order on AI (October 2023). The article questions whether profit-driven tech companies can be trusted to self-regulate.

- **Recommendations:** Stakeholders should make AI tools more accessible to underserved communities. AI developers should include teachers, students, and families in development. The article concludes that government, civil society, and tech companies share responsibility for safe and ethical AI implementation in education.
</summary>

This is because race is included as a risk factor in the algorithms and treated as an indicator of success or failure based on the historical performance of students with those identities.", "In a scenario where wealthy students have access to better AI tools, what if AI does improve academic results for low-income Black students but further boosts results for wealthy White students, widening the academic achievement gap? Should we embrace that outcome because academic results for Black students are nonetheless improving?", "Wisconsin's Dropout Early Warning System generated false alarms about Black and Latino students 'at a significantly greater rate than it did for their White classmates.'", "72% of White teens had heard about ChatGPT compared to 56% of Black teens.", "Teacher Victoria Salas Salcedo described Project Topeka as 'almost like having an extra teacher in the room, coaching [students] through the writing process.'"

--- SOURCE 13: AI Tutors Support 16 Percent of Learning. What About the Other 84 Percent? – Social Science Space ---
URL: https://www.socialsciencespace.com/2026/02/ai-tutors-support-16-percent-of-learning-what-about-the-other-84-percent

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This article by Rose Luckin (Professor of Learner-Centered Design at UCL) argues that AI tutoring addresses only a small fraction of genuine human learning and intelligence. While AI tutors can effectively deliver personalized academic content, practice procedures, and drill factual knowledge — representing about 16 percent of learning — they miss the other 84 percent that encompasses the full breadth of human intelligence.

Luckin critiques the frequent invocation of Benjamin Bloom's 1984 "2 sigma" finding (that one-to-one tutoring lifts students two standard deviations above peers) to justify AI tutoring, noting the original study had limited conditions and mixed replication results.

She presents a seven-element model of human intelligence: (1) knowledge about the world (where AI tutors operate), (2) personal epistemology, (3) social intelligence, (4) metacognitive awareness, (5) metasubjective intelligence (emotions and motivation), (6) metacontextual awareness, and (7) accurate perceived self-efficacy.

Drawing on the CAPITAL framework, which identified 19 distinct acts of learning, the article notes AI tutors primarily handle rehearsal, exposition, and partial tutorial interaction — but cannot support social learning acts, scenarioed acts requiring real-world transfer, or deeper personal acts like reflection and construction.

The article warns of risks including "metacognitive laziness" — reduced self-monitoring, increased procrastination, and gains that evaporate when AI is removed. It recommends: (1) welcome AI tutors for what they do well (academic content delivery), (2) invest in developing pedagogical approaches for the other six elements of intelligence, (3) reform assessment systems to value metacognition, collaboration, and self-regulation rather than just knowledge recall.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
AI tutors support perhaps 16 percent of what it means to develop an intelligent human being, and a handful of the 19 acts through which real learning happens., An AI tutor cannot model what it means to wrestle with the provisional nature of knowledge. It cannot teach a student to debate conflicting evidence, because it does not understand what evidence is., AI-assisted learners demonstrate reduced self-monitoring, increased procrastination, and what has been described as 'metacognitive laziness.', The human fundamentals of learning, including metacognition, social sense-making, and cognitive load management, should drive our approach to technology rather than the other way around., If we get this balance right, AI could be the catalyst that finally compels education to value what makes us distinctively human. If we get it wrong, we will have built the most sophisticated system ever devised for teaching people the things that matter least.
</key_excerpts>
