Many European universities may have to “change everything” about how they use artificial intelligence once landmark European Union regulations come into force, an expert has warned.

Thomas Jørgensen, director of policy coordination and foresight at the European University Association, singled out the growing practice of academics using tools such as ChatGPT to assess student work as a particular concern. Such informal uses of AI could potentially fall foul of the EU Artificial Intelligence Act, he said.

“If you do assessment with AI, according to the AI act, there’s a whole range of requirements that you need to meet, both as a user and as a provider,” Jørgensen told *Times Higher Education*. “And I think it’s fair to say that the big large language models [LLMs] do not fulfil the criteria because it has to do with transparency and the data that’s being trained on it.”

[Academics sometimes use AI tools](https://www.timeshighereducation.com/news/one-four-uk-lecturers-now-using-ai-tools-teaching) to grade students without any institutional oversight, but the compliance challenges would also affect universities that have set up their own formal AI tools, he added.

ADVERTISEMENT

“For teachers using ChatGPT for assessment, there is a risk that it is illegal; but we do not know yet as we do not have the guidelines from the European Commission’s AI Office,” he said, referring to the body that oversees the implementation of the act.

The EU AI act, a sweeping piece of legislation that covers a wide range of sectors, came into force in August 2024. Its remaining provisions are set to take effect over the next six to 36 months.

ADVERTISEMENT

In March, the European Parliament voted to [delay key provisions](https://www.europarl.europa.eu/news/en/press-room/20260323IPR38829/artificial-intelligence-act-delayed-application-ban-on-nudifier-apps) of the legislation to give companies and regulators more time to prepare for the changes. These provisions relate to high-risk artificial intelligence systems and were originally set to come into force in August this year. Under the act, AI used for student assessment is classified as high-risk – it falls into the same category as AI used for hiring decisions and credit scoring.

Jørgensen pointed out that universities had responded to the arrival of generative AI tools in 2022 and 2023 with task forces and guidelines and had developed reasonably [clear strategies](https://www.timeshighereducation.com/news/universities-and-industry-need-common-language-around-ai) for responsible use in learning and teaching.

But a regulatory reckoning was now approaching. “The next step will be when the AI act really comes into force and the guidelines from the AI Office land. That’s going to be a big challenge.”

Once the provisions fully come into force, he said, the biggest risk will be that universities have to “change everything” and revisit a lot of the practices they have implemented with regards to AI in order to comply with the act.

ADVERTISEMENT

Jorgensen said AI use in research was already substantial, particularly in STEM fields where researchers often worked with large and complex datasets. He was cautiously optimistic about what this could mean for the speed of scientific progress, which he said had been slow in recent years, but there were questions around data privacy.

“Typically, in the health space, we need to have policies on this because otherwise there is a risk that we don’t comply. But that is a conversation that’s just starting,” he said.

In January, [the EUA published a report](https://eua.eu/publications/reports/adopting-ai-that-serves-the-needs-and-values-of-universities.html), spearheaded by Jørgensen, that examined the use of AI across European universities. Pointing out that the main source of data for training many models comes from the English-speaking world, and overwhelmingly from the US, it stressed that there was a need for European AI models.

Jørgensen warned that universities across Europe using the same US-trained commercial models risked eroding the intellectual diversity that made collaboration worthwhile. “Things become bland and uniform,” he said. “The idea of cooperation, because you come up with something different, goes away, because you ask the same model, trained on American data.”

ADVERTISEMENT

He pointed to the emergence of European large language models, including EuroLLM, as a potentially more suitable alternative for universities. “The big US models don’t really cut it for us. They’re very US-centric,” he said. “If you speak a [different] language, they may not be as good for you.”

#### Mike Perkins

##### Head of the Centre for Research & Innovation

Dr Mike Perkins heads the Centre for Research & Innovation at British University Vietnam, Hanoi. He is an Associate Professor and leads GenAI policy integration and trains Vietnamese educators and policymakers on this topic. Mike is one of the authors of the AI Assessment Scale, which has been adopted across more than 250 schools and universities worldwide, and translated into 16 languages. His research focuses on GenAI’s impact on education, and has explored various areas within this field. This has included AI text detectors, attitudes to AI technologies, and the ethical integration of AI in assessments through the AI Assessment Scale. His work bridges technology, education, and academic integrity.

![](https://images.coachingforleaders.com/cb:ztCJ~31fd5/w:150/h:150/q:mauto/rt:fill/g:ce/f:best/ig:avif/https://teachinginhighered.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/04/1711606869065.jpeg)

#### Jasper Roe

Jasper is an Assistant Professor in Digital Literacies and Pedagogies at Durham University, UK. Prior to joining Durham, Jasper held senior leadership positions as the Head of Pre-University at British University Vietnam and Head of the Language School at James Cook University Singapore. Aside from academic leadership, Jasper has taught a wide variety of subjects, including educational research methods, sociology and anthropology, English language education, and training in-service teachers on technology use. Jasper's early studies in corpus linguistics and discourse analysis, along with his experience as an English for Academic Purposes (EAP) teacher, led to a natural interest in language applications such as Automated Paraphrasing Tools (APTs) and Digital Writing Assistants (DWAs). Since 2022, he has focused more fully on the implications of Generative AI (GenAI) in educational settings and new methods of fostering AI literacy in higher education.

#### Bonni Stachowiak

Bonni Stachowiak is dean of teaching and learning and professor of business and management at Vanguard University. She hosts Teaching in Higher Ed, a weekly podcast on the art and science of teaching with over five million downloads. Bonni holds a doctorate in Organizational Leadership and speaks widely on teaching, curiosity, digital pedagogy, and leadership. She often joins her husband, Dave, on his Coaching for Leaders podcast.

This is a transcript and show notes page for Episode 569 of the "Teaching in Higher Ed" podcast, featuring Dr. Mike Perkins and Jasper Roe discussing a practical framework for ethical AI integration in assessment. The episode introduces the AI Assessment Scale (AIAS), a five-level framework designed to help educators move beyond binary thinking (ban vs. allow AI) toward nuanced, context-appropriate integration of generative AI in assessments.

The scale includes: Level 1 (No AI - under controlled circumstances), Level 2 (AI for planning and idea generation), Level 3 (AI collaboration - co-writing with AI), Level 4 (Full AI integration - tasks designed to require AI use), and Level 5 (AI exploration - using AI to solve new problems). The AIAS has been adopted by over 250 institutions worldwide and translated into 26 languages.

Key themes discussed include: shifting from a punitive "catch and punish" approach to transparent conversations about appropriate AI use; addressing equity concerns around differential access to AI tools; fostering critical AI literacy rather than just allowing or banning AI; the tension between creative writing development and AI assistance (illustrated by a story about a second grader's story ending); and the importance of distinguishing criticality from pessimism when evaluating AI capabilities.

Mike Perkins is Head of the Centre for Research & Innovation at British University Vietnam. Jasper Roe is an Assistant Professor in Digital Literacies and Pedagogies at Durham University, UK. The episode also includes recommendations: the SIFT Toolbox for fact-checking with AI (by Mike Caulfield), the Bend app for stretching, Strava, Garmin devices, and the Netflix series "The Residence."

# The AI Assessment Scale (AIAS)

A five-level framework that helps educators decide what role AI should play in an assessment task, and redesign the task so that decision holds up in practice.

[Explore the levels](#levels) [Redesign a task →](https://chatgpt.com/g/g-6a6411ff3b1c8191825395a9e5c439af-ai-assessment-scale-aias-advisor)

![The AI Assessment Scale v2.1, showing its five levels: No AI, AI Planning, AI Collaboration, Full AI, and AI Exploration](https://aiassessmentscale.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/ai-assessment-scale-2-1-titled-large.png)

## About the AIAS

The AI Assessment Scale (AIAS) was originally developed by Mike Perkins, Jasper Roe, Leon Furze and Jason MacVaugh in response to the rapid emergence of generative AI in education. The project began from a concern that students and educators needed a clearer, fairer and more practical basis for understanding when and how AI could be used in formative and summative tasks, and how these could be designed to account for the new GenAI reality. The AIAS has since been further developed through research, institutional implementation, sector feedback and international use.

First published in 2023 and revised through Version 2 and AIAS 2.1, the Scale gives students, educators, and institutions a shared vocabulary for AI in assessment. It supports academic integrity, but its main job is assessment redesign: lining up learning outcomes, task design, validity, marking criteria, and AI use so that a grade still means what it claims to mean.

The AIAS is used in more than 350 institutions worldwide, has been translated into more than 30 languages, and is noted by the Australian Tertiary Education Quality and Standards Agency (TEQSA) in its [2024 paper](https://www.teqsa.gov.au/sites/default/files/2024-08/evolving-risk-to-academic-integrity-posed-by-generative-artificial-intelligence.pdf) as an option to assist with implementing GenAI into assessment.

The AIAS is owned and maintained by [Learning Innovation Practice Ltd](https://learninginnovationpractice.com), a research-informed consultancy set up to hold, develop and support the framework and to help institutions redesign assessment for the GenAI era. It is free to use on a non-commercial basis.

[Download the grid](https://aiassessmentscale.com/resources/) as a PDF, PowerPoint or image, or open the [editable template](https://aiassessmentscale.com/resources/)

The framework

## Understanding the levels

Each level describes a different kind of task, not a degree of permission. No level is better than another; the right one depends on what the task is meant to assess. Any level can be run under secure, supervised conditions if the task calls for it. Level 1 is the only level where those conditions are compulsory, and the padlock marks that.

1 No AI

This task is completed in a controlled environment designed to exclude AI. Knowledge, understanding, and skills are demonstrated and assessed independently.

2 AI Planning

This task focuses on planning activities such as topic exploration, outlining, and initial research. AI may be used to support this process, and the quality of planning and idea development is assessed whether or not AI was used.

3 AI Collaboration

AI may be used to help complete this task, including idea generation, drafting, feedback, and refinement. It is designed so that AI alone will not reach the required standard. Assessment covers both the work itself and how AI outputs are evaluated, modified, and integrated.

4 Full AI

There is an expectation of AI involvement in this task. The goal cannot be reached by AI or by a person working alone in the time available. Assessment focuses on the critical thinking and subject knowledge shown in directing AI.

5 AI Exploration

This task is designed for creative AI use to solve problems, generate novel insights, or develop innovative solutions in the discipline. Approaches may be co-designed by students and instructors.

## An alternative view of the AIAS

No one level of the AIAS is better or worse than another and any level can be used to support learning outcomes. Our [assets](https://aiassessmentscale.com/resources/) also include the AIAS in a circular, non-hierarchical representation to emphasise that the levels are different kinds of task, not steps from worse to better.

![The AI Assessment Scale 2.1 shown as five circular representations, one per level](https://aiassessmentscale.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/aias-2-1-circular.png)

What changed in AIAS 2.1?

## One clear statement per level

The five levels of the scale are unchanged. Each level now has a single statement explaining how the task has been designed and what is expected of students. If you already use Version 2, your existing level choices remain applicable, but consider whether the revised wording suggests any changes to the design of the task.

[See what changed at each level →](https://aiassessmentscale.com/faqs/#v2-to-v21)

Working on a specific task? New

The AIAS Custom GPT asks about your context, learning objectives, task, and constraints, then helps you pick a level, reword the brief, decide what evidence students should produce, and sketch rubric criteria.

[Open the AIAS Custom GPT](https://chatgpt.com/g/g-6a6411ff3b1c8191825395a9e5c439af-ai-assessment-scale-aias-advisor)

Limited ChatGPT access? [Use the Poe version](https://poe.com/AIAS-Advisor).

![QS Reimagine Education Awards 2025 Bronze Winner badge](https://aiassessmentscale.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/qs-reimagine-badge.png)

**QS Reimagine Education Awards 2025 · Bronze Winner**  
Learning Assessment category

Implement the AIAS

## Using the AIAS for task redesign

Choosing a level is only the start. The real work is redesigning the task so students know what evidence they need to produce, what AI use is expected or constrained, and how their work will be judged.

1

Start with learning

Clarify the learning outcomes, skills, and evidence the task should generate.

2

Choose the AI role

Decide whether AI should be excluded, used for planning, used collaboratively, integrated throughout, or explored creatively.

3

Redesign the evidence

Build in the process, artefacts, reflection, demonstration, or live elements needed to support valid assessment.

4

Align the rubric

Make the marking criteria reflect the intended AI use, student judgement, critical evaluation, and disciplinary standards.

Want guided support for this process?

The AIAS Custom GPT walks you through these steps for your own task, from choosing a level through to rubric ideas. Or read the full [Implementation guide](https://aiassessmentscale.com/implementation-guide/).

[Start with the Custom GPT](https://chatgpt.com/g/g-6a6411ff3b1c8191825395a9e5c439af-ai-assessment-scale-aias-advisor)

If your institution wants support with this work, [Learning Innovation Practice](https://learninginnovationpractice.com) runs assessment reviews, policy development, and staff workshops built around the AIAS. [Get in touch](https://learninginnovationpractice.com/contact.html).

Evidence base

## Research papers

The AIAS research base covers the original framework, the revised assessment-redesign model, implementation studies, and language-context adaptations.

args.summary:
The AI Assessment Scale (AIAS) is a five-level framework designed to help educators determine the appropriate role of AI in assessment tasks and redesign those tasks accordingly. Developed by Mike Perkins, Jasper Roe, Leon Furze, and Jason MacVaugh, the AIAS addresses the need for clearer, fairer practices for AI use in formative and summative assessments. 

First published in 2023 and now updated to AIAS 2.1, the framework provides a shared vocabulary for AI in assessment, supporting academic integrity and assessment redesign. It is used in over 350 institutions worldwide, translated into 30+ languages, and referenced by the Australian Tertiary Education Quality and Standards Agency (TEQSA) in its 2024 paper.

The five levels are:
1. **No AI** – Completed in a controlled environment excluding AI.
2. **AI Planning** – AI supports planning activities like topic exploration and outlining.
3. **AI Collaboration** – AI assists with idea generation, drafting, and refinement, but alone cannot reach the required standard.
4. **Full AI** – AI involvement is expected; the goal cannot be reached by AI or a person alone.
5. **AI Exploration** – Creative AI use for problem-solving and innovation.

No level is superior; each represents a different task type. The framework includes an AIAS Custom GPT for guided task redesign, and an implementation process: start with learning outcomes, choose the AI role, redesign evidence, and align the rubric.

The AIAS is owned by Learning Innovation Practice Ltd and is free for non-commercial use. It has won a QS Reimagine Education Awards 2025 Bronze in the Learning Assessment category. Research papers supporting the framework are published in journals such as JUTLP, TESOL Journal, AJET, and Emerald.

<webpage_content>
 

[![](/media/gfbdiih2/tesol_connections_masthead_basic-logo.png)  TESOL Connections | TESOL International Association](/tesol-connections/ "TESOL Connections | TESOL International Association")



**KEEPING ENGLISH LANGUAGE PROFESSIONALS CONNECTED**

# The AI Assessment Scale: A Practical Framework for TESOL Educators in the Age of ChatGPT

by Jasper Roe, Leon Furze, Mike Perkins, Christina Kitson | 17 Mar 2025

Recent advances in generative artificial intelligence (AI) have transformed education globally, with a significant impact on English language teaching. Since the release of ChatGPT in late 2022, TESOL educators have grappled with questions regarding academic integrity, assessment design, and the role of AI in language learning. Although some institutions initially attempted to ban these technologies, there is growing recognition that AI tools will be an integral part of students' academic and professional lives (Perkins, Furze, et al., 2024).

Against this backdrop, the AI Assessment Scale (AIAS) was developed as a practical framework to help educators structure and guide students’ use of AI tools in assessments. Originally developed to address urgent concerns about academic integrity, the AIAS has evolved into a flexible tool that supports transparent dialogue between teachers and students about appropriate AI use (Perkins, Roe, & Furze, 2024).

Before diving into how TESOL educators can use the AIAS to help manage their students’ use of AI tools, we present the story of how we developed the scale and outline its basic structure.

#### Understanding the AI Assessment Scale

The AIAS was designed to provide educators with a structured approach to integrating AI into assessment and instruction while maintaining transparency, academic integrity, and pedagogical soundness. The first version, outlined in the *Journal of University Teaching and Learning Practice*, introduced a five-level framework, from no AI use to the full integration of AI tools (Perkins, Furze, et al., 2024).

However, as generative AI capabilities rapidly evolved, it became clear that the framework needed to be more flexible. The revised version, currently published as a preprint (Perkins, Roe, & Furze, 2024), incorporates feedback from global educators, including those from the disciplines of TESOL and English language education. This version also expands the scope to reflect increasingly capable generative AI applications.

Notably, the revised version of the AIAS introduced *AI Exploration* as a new category, recognizing that AI is no longer just a writing tool but a fundamental component of digital literacy in language learning. *AI Exploration* refers to tasks in which AI must be used to address a task.

The AIAS consists of five levels (see Figure 1). For any assessment activity, teachers can specify (in the task instructions, e.g.) which level of the AIAS is allowed. The levels of engagement with AI are as follows:

**Level 1 *(No AI)*** asks students to complete assessments without AI assistance and in controlled environments.

**Level 2 *(AI Planning)*** allows the use of AI for pretask activities, such as brainstorming and research.

**Level 3 *(AI Collaboration)*** permits AI assistance for specific tasks under careful guidance.

**Level 4 *(Full AI)*** enables extensive AI use throughout the assessment process.

**Level 5 *(AI Exploration)*** encourages the creative application of AI technologies to solve new problems.

[![The AI Assessment Scale](/media/3q4g5zuh/2025-03_ai-assessment-scale.jpg?rmode=max&width=500)](/media/3q4g5zuh/2025-03_ai-assessment-scale.jpg "2025 03 AI Assessment Scale")  
Figure 1. The AI Assessment Scale. 

#### Practical Applications in TESOL

In the English language classroom, the AIAS is not only relevant to assessment, but also can be used as a framework to structure different types of language learning activities and assignments. This approach recognises that—rather than banning AI tools altogether—educators and students can find productive ways to use these tools. The AIAS enables English language teachers to communicate their expectations clearly to students, administrators, and colleagues.

The application of the AIAS in classroom contexts, including English as a foreign language (EFL) and English for academic purposes (EAP), has demonstrated key benefits and challenges of the scale.

In practice, we have observed notable differences between the two contexts:

**English as a Foreign Language**

In this context, AI tools have been found particularly useful for enhancing fluency and accuracy, helping learners at various proficiency levels to structure their writing. Research indicates that AI-assisted planning and editing activities (AIAS Levels 2 and 3) have allowed students to refine their writing skills while maintaining their voice. Additionally, AI collaboration (Level 4) encourages critical engagement with AI-generated content, supporting learners in evaluating coherence, lexical appropriateness, and cultural relevance (Roe et al., 2025).

**English for Academic Purposes**

In this context, the AIAS framework has been adapted to address academic writing conventions, research synthesis, and source integration. AI-assisted feedback mechanisms (Level 3) have supported self-regulation in the writing process by reducing dependence on instructor feedback while increasing engagement with revision strategies. AI exploration (Level 5) introduces students to multimodal academic tasks, allowing them to work with AI-generated summaries, research insights, and structured outlines to build complex academic arguments (Roe et al., 2024).

![](/media/irqpu3qt/2025-03_aias_quote.png?rmode=max&width=450&height=375)A major takeaway from both contexts is that using the AIAS fosters metacognitive awareness, helping learners transition from passive AI consumers to active AI collaborators. Although AI offers efficiency, students still require explicit instruction on how to evaluate AI output, refine responses, and ensure ethical AI use in their writing. This aligns with the growing call for critical AI literacy to become an integral part of TESOL pedagogy.

Ultimately, our research shows that the AIAS can be particularly valuable in EFL and EAP contexts. For example, for assessments and assignments at AIAS Level 2, students might use AI tools to

* + generate vocabulary lists for specific academic contexts,
  + brainstorm ideas for writing tasks, and
  + understand complex reading passages.

At AIAS Level 3, common applications include

* + getting feedback on draft writing,
  + practicing dialogue with AI conversation partners, and
  + analyzing academic text structures.

#### Adapting the Scale for Your Classroom

A key benefit of the AIAS is its flexibility. Language teachers can adapt the framework to suit their specific teaching contexts, whether working with beginners or advanced learners. For instance, a Level 2 task might involve using AI to help plan a presentation, whereas a Level 4 activity could include using AI tools to create and analyze academic writing samples.

Roe, Perkins, and Tregubova (2024) demonstrated how the AIAS can be modified for EAP settings, where tasks often focus on developing both language proficiency and academic skills (see Figure 2).

[![The AI Assessment Scale, adapted for English for Academic Purposes](/media/tdcddcvj/2025-03_aias-for-eap.png?rmode=max&width=500)](/media/tdcddcvj/2025-03_aias-for-eap.png "2025 03 AIAS For EAP")  
Figure 2. The AI Assessment Scale adapted for English for academic purposes (EAP). 

A significant advantage of the AIAS is that it provides structured opportunities for students to interact with AI in ways that prioritize learning objectives, relieving students’ uncertainty about permitted AI use. The scale's adaptable design offers instructors considerable flexibility to customize its language according to their specific teaching context and students' proficiency levels. [Teachers can tailor the framework](https://www.canva.com/design/DAGPfnleXV8/E2oTbyjScUiJ9JaT56Clvw/view?utm_content=DAGPfnleXV8&utm_campaign=designshare&utm_medium=link&utm_source=publishsharelink&mode=preview "Edit the AIAS with Canva.com") to specify eligible assignments, authorized AI tools, and additional requirements, such as submitting AI interactions for assessment purposes.

#### Key Takeaways

The future of assessment in English language teaching will likely involve the increasing integration of AI tools. However, this integration must be carefully and systematically planned. The AIAS provides a practical framework for managing this transition, helping teachers design assessments that acknowledge the presence of AI while maintaining pedagogical validity—a key challenge facing educators (Dawson et al., 2024).

For TESOL educators considering implementing the AIAS, here are six key takeaways:

1. 1. Start gradually, perhaps beginning with Level 2 activities.
   2. Don’t limit the AIAS to just assessment tasks; try using it to structure different learning activities.
   3. Be explicit about expectations for AI use in different tasks.
   4. Focus on developing students' critical evaluation skills.
   5. Consider how AI tools can support, rather than replace, language learning.
   6. Ensure that AI use reflects student proficiency level and language understanding.

#### Conclusion

AI is here to stay, and the TESOL community must find ways to understand its potential while maintaining pedagogical integrity. The AIAS offers a structured approach to AI integration and helps educators understand the implications of this technology. By using AI for planning, editing, and collaboration while also fostering critical literacy, TESOL professionals can prepare students for these increasingly ubiquitous and capable technologies without compromising authentic language learning.

The AIAS also offers TESOL educators a practical way to address the challenges and opportunities presented by AI in language teaching. By providing clear guidelines for AI use, academic integrity can be maintained while acknowledging the reality of these tools in students' lives. The scale can act as a conversation starter between students and faculty about appropriate, transparent AI use. As these technologies continue to develop, frameworks such as the AIAS will become increasingly valuable for structuring effective language teaching and assessment.

[Anna Mills](https://www.linkedin.com/in/anna-mills-oer?trk=public_post_comment-text) it’s a blurry line! As Leon says, in general level 2 is for prep work. However I would say that what you might be talking about is a level 2 task, followed by a level 1 task, if you actually want to assure that the student has used their own words…because how do you know otherwise? The issue here is that the AIAS isn’t supposed to be a restricting tool for students to say “you can do this, but you can’t do that”. As is clear now, students will use GenAI however they want to achieve the task, and you aren’t going to be able to stop them or “catch” “illicit” use of the tools. But this is where the AIAS can help, as the purpose of the scale is firstly to help instructors design their assessments with a consideration of how this technology may or may not align with their leaning objectives. Secondly, it can help the discussions you have with students to say “using GenAI tools like THIS is how I would like you to use it”, but being aware that students might just ignore you is something that you have to really plan for and build into your tasks.

In my online grad course I taught in this summer, I extensively integrated AIAS into many assignments. I think singling out the levels from one another doesn’t work well in terms of instructional consistency. Here is how my design and pedagogy flow (completing a study on this and more to come soon). I let my students to use genAI tools to learn about the topic of the module. It is a L4 task. They will engage in the resources I curated and take their notes. Next: I used L2 for discussions of what they have learned. I allow teachers to prepare their initial post with genAI tools. That’s parallel with what [Leon Furze](https://au.linkedin.com/in/leonfurze?trk=public_post_comment-text) is telling us about. They must write an AI use statement for each task, as well. So I see AIAS levels as integrated “elements” that guide my efforts to incorporate AI into my course design and pedagogy. I just submitted a proposal of my study to AERA26 and will work on a full study this fall. See some prelim results in my posts.

URL: https://www.nature.com/articles/s41539-025-00320-7

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This webpage presents a systematic review published in npj Science of Learning (Volume 10, Article 29, May 2025) examining AI-driven Intelligent Tutoring Systems (ITS) in K-12 education. Authored by Létourneau et al., the review analyzed 28 studies involving 4,597 students to determine the effects of ITSs on learning outcomes and the experimental designs used to evaluate them.

The introduction highlights the global educational crisis and UNESCO's call to leverage AI for sustainable development. ITSs are defined as software programs equipped with AI that monitor progress, identify difficulties, and adapt instruction to individual learners. Notable prior work includes Kulik & Fletcher's (2016) meta-analysis of 50 controlled assessments, which found no scientific consensus on ITS effectiveness but showed they can be highly effective instructional tools.

Key findings:
- The effects of ITSs on K-12 learning are generally positive but mitigated when compared to non-intelligent tutoring systems.
- 96% of articles were authored by individuals from educational science, computer science, or both; only one article was from an ITS company.
- 54% of studies originated from the USA, 27% from Asia, and 15% from Europe.
- Roughly half (54%) of studies compared school levels and subjects to assess differences.
- None of the included articles mentioned AI ethics considerations, highlighting a gap in addressing ethical implications.
- The review calls for additional research with longer interventions, larger and more diverse sample sizes, and investigation into ethical implications of AI in teaching.

The authors note that ITS effectiveness depends on sound pedagogical features (immediate feedback, guided practice, adaptivity) applied under the right conditions, consistent with Honebein and Reigeluth's (2021) thesis that ITS must be well-aligned with instructional theory to produce positive outcomes.
</summary>

SUMMARY:

This is a meta-analysis study published in Behavioral Sciences (2026) by Ren, Stephens, and Lee from the University of Auckland, examining the impact of AI on learners' self-efficacy in educational contexts. The study analyzed 23 empirical studies published between January 2005 and February 2025, indexed in Web of Science, Scopus, and ERIC databases.

**Key Findings:**
- AI had a significant positive impact on self-efficacy in learning contexts, with a medium effect size of 0.758 (Hedges' g).
- Two moderating variables were significant: discipline (Q = 10.348, p < 0.05) and the role played by AI (Q = 3.991, p < 0.05).
- AI had the highest effect on self-efficacy in natural sciences (1.310) and medicine (1.013), while the effect was not significant for engineering.
- AI as an intelligent learning tool produced the highest effect on self-efficacy (0.883), while mixed roles (tool + tutor) had lower effects (0.450).
- No significant moderating effects were found for learner levels, research settings, type of AI utilized, or duration of studies.

**Methodology:** The study used a random-effects model due to high heterogeneity (I² = 89.677). Hedges' g was used for effect size calculations. Publication bias was assessed via funnel plot, classic fail-safe N, and Egger's test, all indicating no substantial bias. Sensitivity analysis confirmed robustness of results.

**Conclusion:** AI effectively promotes learners' self-efficacy, particularly in natural sciences and medicine, and when used as an intelligent learning tool. The study recommends integrating AI in classrooms and designing activities that promote student-AI interaction, while noting the need for more experimental research in this domain.
</summary>

# U.S. Department of Education Report: Artificial Intelligence and the Future of Teaching and Learning (May 2023)

## Overview
This report from the U.S. Department of Education's Office of Educational Technology addresses the need for policy development around AI in education. It defines AI as "automation based on associations" and examines opportunities, risks, and recommendations for integrating AI into teaching and learning.

## Key Definitions
- **AI**: "Automation based on associations" - computers automate reasoning based on patterns in data
- **Two fundamental shifts**: (1) from capturing data to detecting patterns, (2) from providing access to resources to automating instructional decisions

## Three Reasons to Address AI Now
1. **Opportunities**: AI may enable achieving educational priorities at scale (adaptivity, teacher support, customizable resources)
2. **Risks**: Algorithmic bias, surveillance, privacy concerns, potential replacement of teachers (which the Department rejects)
3. **Unintended consequences**: At scale, AI could widen achievement gaps if based on poor data or biased assumptions

## Four Foundations for Ethical AI Policy
1. **Center People** - Keep humans in the loop; AI should augment human decision-making, not replace it
2. **Advance Equity** - Address algorithmic bias and ensure AI doesn't discriminate against underserved communities
3. **Ensure Safety, Ethics, and Effectiveness** - Maintain data privacy/security and require evidence of effectiveness (aligned with ESEA standards)
4. **Promote Transparency** - AI models must be inspectable, explainable, and overridable by educators

## Key Insights by Domain

### Learning
- AI enables adaptivity through intelligent tutoring systems
- Need dual focus: learning *with* AI and learning *about* AI
- Recommendation: Seek AI models aligned to a shared vision for learning

### Teaching
- Always center educators in instructional loops
- AI can improve teaching jobs through automated assistants but must avoid surveillance
- Recommendation: AI must be inspectable, explainable, and overridable by teachers

### Formative Assessment
- AI can enhance feedback loops
- Automated essay scoring is an example application
- Recommendation: Harness assessment expertise to reduce bias

### Research & Development
- Focus on addressing context and the "long tail" of learner variability
- Use design-based research partnerships
- Recommendation: R&D must account for context of teaching and learning

## Seven Recommendations
1. **Emphasize Humans in the Loop** - Require human oversight in educational AI
2. **Align AI Models to a Shared Vision for Education** - Ensure AI supports educational goals
3. **Design Using Modern Learning Principles** - Base AI on sound pedagogy
4. **Prioritize Strengthening Trust** - Build trustworthy systems
5. **Inform and Involve Educators** - Engage teachers in AI adoption
6. **Focus R&D on Addressing Context and Enhancing Trust and Safety** - Research real-world applications
7. **Develop Education-Specific Guidelines and Guardrails** - Create policies for safe AI use

## Key Principles
- "AI in education can only grow at the speed of trust" (Dr. Dale Allen)
- Three perspectives on AI: Human-like reasoning, algorithmic goal pursuit, and intelligence augmentation
- The Department "firmly rejects the idea that AI could replace teachers"
- Policies must address algorithmic discrimination, data privacy, and the need for human checks and balances
</summary>

--- SOURCE 1: AI Tutoring Equity Gap: Why Access Alone Won't Close It ---
URL: https://www.valere.io/ai-tutoring-equity-gap

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This article by Guy Pistone (CEO of Valere) examines the equity problem surrounding AI tutoring in K-12 education. While AI tutoring shows real promise—with a 2020 meta-analysis finding effect sizes equivalent to one-on-one human tutoring in controlled settings—the author warns that the technology risks following the same pattern as other democratizing technologies: benefiting the already-advantaged first and widening the gap before narrowing it.

Key issues identified include:
- **The access gap**: ~15% of U.S. children (9 million students) still lack reliable home broadband, concentrated in low-income, rural, and Tribal communities. As of early 2026, districts report 1 in 5 low-income families still lack reliable home internet.
- **The readiness gap**: The harder problem than access. Schools with the most to gain are often least positioned to close the feedback loop between AI-generated insights and changed instruction, due to fewer teachers per student, less planning time, and less administrative bandwidth.
- **Market failure**: The business incentives point toward well-resourced early adopters. Vendor-funded studies (e.g., Carnegie Learning's own 2022 efficacy study showing 30% improvement on algebra assessments) paint a more optimistic picture than independent research.
- **Teacher training deficit**: A 2022 study found teachers with >10 hours of platform-specific PD were significantly more effective at acting on AI data than those with standard 2-hour onboarding.

The article cites widely deployed platforms including Carnegie Learning's MATHia (3,000+ schools), Khan Academy's Khanmigo (free through OpenAI partnership), DreamBox Learning (5 million+ active students), and Synthesis. District licensing typically runs $15–$30 per student per year.

The author argues that closing the gap requires treating connectivity as infrastructure, designing offline/low-bandwidth AI tools, investing in sustained teacher professional development, and using equity-centered procurement frameworks. State-level AI education policy remains fragmented, with California (AB 2876), Virginia, and North Carolina leading, while most meaningful policy happens at the district level.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"The readiness gap. It is the distance between having access to an AI tool and being able to use it effectively.", "The technology does not distribute itself equitably by default. It never has, nor will.", "The one-size-fits-all classroom is a real problem. A third grader interested in horses who gets a math lesson framed around horses is more engaged, more likely to retain the concept, and more likely to stay curious.", "The companies that get the most out of AI are not necessarily the ones with the most sophisticated models. They are the ones who invested in helping their people understand what the tools are doing and what to do with what they surface.", "The promise is real. So is the gap. And both deserve to be taken seriously."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 2: Frontiers | AI and the digital divide in education ---
URL: https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/computer-science/articles/10.3389/fcomp.2026.1759027/full

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This review article (published February 5, 2026, in Frontiers in Computer Science) by Matjie, Nethavhani, and Matlakala from the University of Limpopo, South Africa, examines how artificial intelligence (AI) contributes to the digital divide in education, focusing on language barriers, cultural mismatches, and algorithmic bias as key factors that create inequities even when access to AI tools exists.

The authors conducted a focused narrative and comparative review of case studies from countries with similar socio-economic statuses and visible urban-rural divides, including South Africa, China, Brazil, Kenya, Mali, and others. Case studies analyzed include: AI4D Maseno University (Kenya) on sign language translation; RobotsMali producing children's books in Bambara; the GPE KIX STEPS project in Benin, Cameroon, and DRC for culturally relevant STEM materials; primary education in urban vs. rural China (revealing a "TPACK divide"); higher education in Latin America during COVID-19; and STEM education in BRICS countries.

The conceptual framework identifies three interconnected digital divides: linguistic divide (limited engagement), cultural divide (reduced relevance), and algorithmic divide (biased feedback and unequal outcomes). The authors argue that even when learners have equal access to AI tools, the tools remain discriminatory due to language dominance (predominantly English), cultural insensitivity, and algorithmic bias from non-representative training datasets.

The article proposes three practical solutions:
1. **Development of AI tools with multilingual and culturally relevant content** (e.g., multilingual intelligent tutoring systems, local-language AI writing assistants, culturally contextualized AI chatbots)
2. **Use of diverse, representative datasets to mitigate algorithmic bias** (e.g., fair adaptive learning algorithms, bias-aware language models, participatory dataset curation)
3. **Capacity-building for educators and learners** (e.g., teacher professional development in AI pedagogy, learner AI literacy workshops, community-based train-the-trainer models)

Key contradictions identified include: participatory vs. top-down AI design approaches; short-term efficiency gains vs. long-term equity outcomes; and the inconsistent emphasis on teacher capacity-building across interventions. The authors conclude that AI's contribution to educational equity depends on participatory design, comprehensive teacher training, and multilingual support, rather than merely providing access to technology.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"AI should change learning for all learners across the globe; however, that is not always the case. --- SOURCE 13: Bloom's 2 Sigma Problem Debunked: One-to-One Tutoring Isn’t Going to Save Education (Here’s Why) ---
URL: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=IaTk7lHC470

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This video and article by Dr. Luke Rowe (PhD in learning sciences) debunks Benjamin Bloom's famous 1984 '2 Sigma Problem'—the claim that one-to-one tutoring can lift student achievement by two standard deviations (from the 50th to the 98th percentile). 

**Key Arguments & Evidence:**
- Bloom's claim rested heavily on two very small, unpublished studies by his doctoral students (Anania and Burke) in the early 1980s, plus a selectively cherry-picked table of effect sizes from secondary sources.
- Paul von Hippel's (2024) data sleuthing revealed major problems: the famous graph was a hand-drawn caricature, not actual data; Bloom rounded up and fabricated numbers from Walberg's (1984) work; and the doctoral students themselves did not go on to build careers around tutoring research.
- The tutoring condition was heavily confounded: tutors received extra training and coaching, students got frequent formative testing (retrieval practice effect ~0.5 SD), individual feedback, worked examples, Socratic questioning, praise, and extra time on task. These confounds likely inflated the effect.
- The mastery learning condition (which included testing and feedback but no tutoring) already showed over 1 SD gain, meaning about half the 2 sigma effect came from testing and feedback alone.
- Large-scale meta-analyses (Nickow et al., 2020, 2024) show tutoring effects are real but typically around 0.3 to 0.4 standard deviations (moving from 50th to ~64th percentile), not 2.0 SD. Matthew Kraft (2020) found most educational interventions produce effects of about 0.1 SD.
- Replacing classroom instruction with tutoring (as in Bloom's studies) produces inflated effects compared to tutoring as a supplement (the more common real-world scenario).
- Despite the debunking, the 2 sigma claim has become sticky in education and AI circles (e.g., Sal Khan's Khan Academy/Khanmigo citing it as a benchmark for AI tutors).

**Conclusion:** Tutoring is effective but modestly so (~0.3 SD). The 2 sigma claim is highly exaggerated, unreplicable science that has misled educational policy, parental spending on tutoring, and AI tutoring development goals.
</summary>

Published in 1984, Benjamin Bloom's research showed that students receiving one-on-one tutoring performed two standard deviations (2 sigma) better than those in traditional classrooms, with the average tutored student outperforming 98% of conventional classroom students. However, scaling personalized tutoring was impractical due to cost. Lecturio's AI tools attempt to replicate this effectiveness at scale through several features:

1. **AI Tutor**: Provides 24/7 on-demand personalized guidance, answering natural language questions and adapting responses based on each student's knowledge level and learning context, delivering formative feedback in real-time.

2. **Spaced Repetition**: Uses evidence-based algorithms to enhance long-term retention and mastery learning through repeated practice, leveraging the testing effect.

3. **Adaptive Review**: Gives feedback on performance and directs learners toward mastery by analyzing quiz and Qbank performance, providing just-in-time suggestions for additional resources on areas of weakness.

4. **Faculty Insights and Adaptive Dashboards**: Provides analytics on student performance, engagement, and common misunderstandings, enabling educators to identify at-risk students and tailor instruction.

The article concludes that by embedding individualized instruction, timely feedback, and mastery learning into a scalable platform, Lecturio is helping democratize high-quality medical education.
</summary>

This article from Structural Learning (updated July 1, 2026) examines how AI tools can support special educational needs and disabilities (SEND) in classrooms. **Key benefits identified:**
- Personalised learning pathways: AI adapts content difficulty, pace, reading format, and response options for individual learners.

Education-specific products (ChatGPT Edu, Microsoft Copilot for Education, Claude for Education) offer enhanced protections. Schools must avoid inputting learner names, diagnoses, or IEPs into public AI tools.

**Personalisation caveats:** Research warns that adaptive systems can misinterpret neurodivergent behaviours (autistic communication, ADHD attention shifts, self-regulation) as poor engagement. 1. Adaptive systems may confuse measurable behaviour with real learning; neurodivergent self-regulation may be misread as disengagement.
2. Algorithmic bias can encode ableist norms, especially for Black, bilingual, working-class, and culturally minoritised learners.
3. Much research comes from higher education or small pilots, not crowded primary classrooms or EHCP reviews.
4. AI can weaken skill development if it provides answers before learners have planned, recalled, or self-corrected.

--- SOURCE 11: The Matthew Effect at Scale: Attention Scarcity and the AI Output Explosion - Network Law Review ---
URL: https://www.networklawreview.org/matthew-effect

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This article from the Network Law Review, authored by Thibault Schrepel (Vrije Universiteit Amsterdam) and published in Winter 2026, examines how generative AI is reshaping academic publishing through the lens of network theory. The central argument is that AI's reduction of the marginal cost of academic writing will paradoxically amplify the Matthew Effect (cumulative advantage), concentrating reputational gains among established scholars rather than democratizing scientific influence.

Key arguments:
1. **Output Explosion**: AI is dramatically increasing submission volumes. Studies show AI-assisted writing has surged across disciplines since 2023, with LLM adoption associated with substantial increases in manuscript output among already-active researchers.

2. **Journals as Attention Allocators**: Contrary to predictions that AI will kill traditional journals, the author argues journals become more valuable as filtering institutions. In an environment of content abundance, credible certification of quality becomes more scarce and valuable.

3. **Amplified Matthew Effect**: AI amplifies cumulative advantage through two channels: (a) quality-correlated productivity, where researchers with strong foundations produce better work faster, widening the gap; and (b) reputational priors, where editors under increasing submission pressure rely more heavily on author reputation. Studies cited show LLM peer review models exhibited bias toward well-known authors and prominent institutions.

4. **Stratification**: The result is a bifurcated publication market—top journals increasingly publish established names, while secondary outlets (growing from 2% to 30% of global publications, 2003-2022) serve emerging scholars. This creates parallel tracks that rarely intersect.

The article concludes that the practical question for junior researchers is not how to produce more, but how to be read. It suggests two escape routes: genuine intellectual originality and academic writing that achieves literary quality, making the reading experience itself valuable.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
Generative AI is lowering the marginal cost of academic writing. A natural prediction is that this will allow more researchers to exercise scientific influence. This article argues that the effects are more complex. An output explosion amplifies the Matthew effect, concentrates reputational gains among established scholars, and contributes to the emergence of increasingly stratified publication tracks that rarely intersect., AI publications have experienced near-exponential growth, with AI conferences such as NeurIPS seeing surges in submissions in 2023 and 2024, and a large-scale PNAS study finds strong evidence of a sharp increase in AI-assisted academic writing across disciplines since 2023, with no significant difference between journals with and without AI policies., Herbert Simon observed that a wealth of information creates a poverty of attention. Journals are attention brokers. Their role is to certify that a paper is worth reading before a reader invests the time to read it., The mechanism economists describe as preferential attachment, in which nodes with high connectivity attract new connections at a higher rate, applies here directly. High-reputation authors attract editorial attention. Editorial attention produces acceptances. Acceptances produce citations. Citations reinforce reputation. The network feeds itself., The long-run consequence is a publication market that looks less like a single competitive field and more like a set of parallel tracks. Track one: high-reputation authors publishing in high-visibility journals, producing the ideas that get cited, taught, and applied. Track two: a large volume of work circulating in secondary outlets, contributing to the literature in technical terms but rarely crossing into track one's citation networks.
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 1: [PDF] Tutor CoPilot: A Human-AI Approach for Scaling Real-Time Expertise ---
URL: https://edworkingpapers.com/sites/default/files/ai24_1054_v2.pdf

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This paper presents Tutor CoPilot, a Human-AI system that uses Large Language Models (LLMs) to provide real-time expert guidance to tutors during live K-12 math tutoring sessions. The study conducted a randomized controlled trial with over 700 tutors and 1,000 students from underserved communities in a U.S. Southern school district, partnered with FEV Tutor (a chat-based virtual tutoring provider), from March 27 to May 17, 2024.

**Key Findings:**
- Students with tutors using Tutor CoPilot were 4 percentage points more likely to master math topics (p<0.01), with exit ticket pass rates increasing from 62% to 66%.
- Gains were highest for students of lower-rated tutors (+9 p.p., from 56% to 65%) and less experienced tutors (+7 p.p., from 61% to 68%), helping less-effective tutors achieve outcomes comparable to their more-effective peers.
- The tool is low-cost at approximately $20 per tutor per year.
- Analysis of over 350,000 messages showed Tutor CoPilot promoted effective pedagogy: treatment tutors were more likely to use probing questions (e.g., "prompt the student to explain" used ~10% more) and less likely to use generic praise (used ~10% less by control tutors).
- Tutor interviews (n=18) indicated the tool was helpful for providing well-phrased explanations but sometimes generated suggestions misaligned with students' grade levels.

**Methodology:** The study used intent-to-treat (ITT) regression analysis, controlling for student-level covariates (baseline MAP math scores, demographics), school and grade fixed effects, and clustering at the student-tutor pair level. Machine learning classifiers (RoBERTa models) were trained to identify pedagogical strategies in tutor messages, achieving F1 scores between 0.65 and 0.90.

**Design:** Tutor CoPilot is a tutor-facing tool that provides multiple pedagogical suggestions tutors can choose from, edit, or regenerate, preserving tutor agency. It uses the Bridge method to capture expert decision-making from think-aloud protocols of experienced educators. The tool automatically de-identifies names and limits user information sent to external language model services.

**Limitations noted:** The study was conducted with novice tutors teaching young students from underserved communities (majority Hispanic) in one U.S. Southern district. No statistically significant improvements were found in end-of-year MAP test scores, likely due to short implementation duration (2 months) and inconsistent student-tutor matching. The study measures the impact of offering the tool rather than specific strategy use.
</summary>

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This webpage from J-PAL (Abdul Latif Jameel Poverty Action Lab) describes a randomized evaluation studying "Tutor CoPilot," a human-AI tool designed to improve tutoring quality in mathematics for K-12 students in the United States.

**Context:** The study took place across grades 3-6 in a large Southern school district serving over 30,000 students, primarily from economically disadvantaged and minority backgrounds (80% Hispanic, two-thirds economically disadvantaged). Researchers partnered with FEV Tutor, a virtual tutoring provider.

**Intervention:** Tutor CoPilot is an AI language model that provides real-time expert-like guidance to tutors during live tutoring sessions. It analyzes chat content and offers tailored suggestions for responses, which tutors can edit, regenerate, or customize.

**Methodology:** 783 full-time tutors were randomly assigned to either the Tutor CoPilot group (388 tutors) or the comparison group (395 tutors). The evaluation ran from March to May 2024.

- **Cost:** Estimated annual cost of about US$20 per tutor (API costs only, excluding salaries).

**Outcome:** FEV Tutor incorporated Tutor CoPilot into all sessions following the study. Other companies like Eedi have also adapted the concept. The research demonstrates that AI-generated guidance based on expert thinking can improve tutor quality at low cost with potential to scale.

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This Brookings Institution commentary by Mary Burns, published January 27, 2026, examines the research on generative AI in tutoring systems. It traces the evolution from traditional Intelligent Tutoring Systems (ITSs) to those enhanced by generative AI, noting that meta-reviews have shown ITSs can "match the success" of human tutoring. The article summarizes four recent randomized controlled trials demonstrating that generative AI-enhanced tutoring platforms deliver substantial learning gains, greater knowledge transfer, improved motivation, and efficiency.

Key value additions of generative AI to tutoring platforms include: naturalistic dialogue generation, dynamic question formulation, psychologically safe learning environments where students can seek help without judgment, and versatile accessibility (in-school, at-home, self-paced, or collaborative). System-level benefits include increased teacher productivity (especially for novice teachers in under-resourced schools), the potential for flipped classroom models that free up in-class time for higher-order tasks, and dynamic content creation that reduces development costs.

The article emphasizes that design matters—successful platforms employ pedagogically sound approaches (Socratic methods, scaffolding, step-by-step solutions) rather than simply providing direct answers. It identifies three areas for improvement: (1) many platforms individualize rather than truly personalize learning; (2) feedback should include both verification and elaboration at the answer and step levels; and (3) the optimal model is human-AI hybrid vigor, where teachers monitor and guide AI use rather than being replaced.
</summary>

URL: https://ieg.worldbankgroup.org/evaluations/confronting-learning-crisis/chapter-2-world-banks-global-and-regional-analytics-and

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This chapter from the Independent Evaluation Group's (IEG) "Confronting the Learning Crisis" evaluation examines the World Bank's global and regional analytics, programs, and partnerships in basic education. The World Bank has recognized the learning crisis and produced substantial knowledge products (145 ASA products, including 88 advisory services and 57 impact evaluations) as global public goods focused on education system strengthening, learning measurement, and teaching practices. The SABER initiative (Systems Approach for Better Education Results, 2011-2020) was applied in 100 countries across 13 policy areas, providing comparative data on education policies, though it measured policy intent at the central level without assessing implementation. The Learning Poverty initiative (launched in 2019 with UNESCO) successfully unified global partners around a common metric—the share of children unable to read by age 10—and created a single message across development partners. The COVID-19 pandemic response involved heightened partnerships, including the Global Education Coalition, joint work with GPE, UNESCO, UNICEF, and WHO. The Accelerator Program (launched 2020 with UNICEF and partners) aims to demonstrate that committed governments can improve foundational learning outcomes within a few years. However, the evaluation finds that the World Bank has not systematically evaluated the country-level influence of its global and regional work, lacking a critical feedback loop. Key gaps include: insufficient attention to adaptations for children with disabilities, absence of a focus on Education Management Information Systems (EMIS), limited outcome measures in trust fund results frameworks, and a general lack of rigorous evaluation of whether global products lead to sustainable improvements in education systems, teaching, and learning measurement.
</summary>

This tendency to concentrate on the central policy level without strong supplemental attention to implementation and delivery across the system is a feature of the approach at the country level.", "The World Bank's internal reporting of outputs lacks systematic and rigorous evaluation of the influence and impact of its ASA and sometimes lacks outcome measures to support assessment.", "Clients who use the World Bank's ASA find it most effective when it customizes 'best practice to local conditions' and formulates 'actionable recommendations that fit local administrative and political economy constraints.'"

--- SOURCE 11: AI and the digital divide in education ---
URL: https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/computer-science/articles/10.3389/fcomp.2026.1759027/full

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This review article (published February 5, 2026, in Frontiers in Computer Science) by Matjie, Nethavhani, and Matlakala from the University of Limpopo, South Africa, examines how artificial intelligence (AI) contributes to the digital divide in education, focusing on language barriers, cultural mismatches, and algorithmic bias as key factors that create inequities even when access to AI tools exists.

The authors conducted a focused narrative and comparative review of case studies from countries with similar socio-economic statuses and visible urban-rural divides, including South Africa, China, Brazil, Kenya, Mali, and others. Case studies analyzed include: AI4D Maseno University (Kenya) on sign language translation; RobotsMali producing children's books in Bambara; the GPE KIX STEPS project in Benin, Cameroon, and DRC for culturally relevant STEM materials; primary education in urban vs. rural China (revealing a "TPACK divide"); higher education in Latin America during COVID-19; and STEM education in BRICS countries.

The conceptual framework identifies three interconnected digital divides: linguistic divide (limited engagement), cultural divide (reduced relevance), and algorithmic divide (biased feedback and unequal outcomes). The authors argue that even when learners have equal access to AI tools, the tools remain discriminatory due to language dominance (predominantly English), cultural insensitivity, and algorithmic bias from non-representative training datasets.

The article proposes three practical solutions:
1. **Development of AI tools with multilingual and culturally relevant content** (e.g., multilingual intelligent tutoring systems, local-language AI writing assistants, culturally contextualized AI chatbots)
2. **Use of diverse, representative datasets to mitigate algorithmic bias** (e.g., fair adaptive learning algorithms, bias-aware language models, participatory dataset curation)
3. **Capacity-building for educators and learners** (e.g., teacher professional development in AI pedagogy, learner AI literacy workshops, community-based train-the-trainer models)

Key contradictions identified include: participatory vs. top-down AI design approaches; short-term efficiency gains vs. long-term equity outcomes; and the inconsistent emphasis on teacher capacity-building across interventions. The authors conclude that AI's contribution to educational equity depends on participatory design, comprehensive teacher training, and multilingual support, rather than merely providing access to technology.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>

AI in higher education brings some concerns with it, specifically the issues of access and such as the algorithmic bias and discrimination.", "According to Van Dijk (2017), the digital divide is the gap between people who do and do not have access to forms of information and communication. This gap appears to be wider for learners from rich countries and regions and those from poor countries and regions in terms of access to AI technologies that enable learning.", "Without deliberate commitments to inclusive design, transparency, and governance, AI risks reproducing and intensifying existing social hierarchies. Algorithmic bias thus constitutes a structural threat to educational equity, requiring systemic intervention if AI is to function as a tool for inclusion rather than exclusion.", "The cases reveal a tension between short-term efficiency gains and long-term equity outcomes. RobotsMali shows that AI-assisted content creation can reduce costs and production time while preserving cultural relevance. However, the BRICS STEM education case demonstrates that policy-driven AI and STEM expansion without parallel investment in access and training leads to skills shortages and labour market exclusion.", "AI does not inherently reduce digital divides. Instead, equitable outcomes depend on participatory design, sustained capacity-building, and institutional readiness."

--- SOURCE 12: How will AI Impact Racial Disparities in Education? - Stanford Center for Racial Justice - Stanford Law School ---
URL: https://law.stanford.edu/2024/06/29/how-will-ai-impact-racial-disparities-in-education

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This article from the Stanford Center for Racial Justice examines how AI will impact racial disparities in education, analyzing both potential benefits and significant risks. 

**Key sections include:**

- **What is AI in education?** AI refers to machine simulation of human intelligence. Traditional "narrow AI" (like Siri) handles specific tasks, while generative AI (like ChatGPT, Google Gemini) creates new content. AI in education dates back to 1970 with Carbonell's SCHOLAR model. Current tools include adaptive learning platforms (DreamBox), AI tutoring (MATHia, Khanmigo), and writing assistants (Grammarly).

- **Potential benefits for racial equity:** AI can personalize learning for marginalized students disproportionately impacted by COVID learning loss. The PL² program in Pittsburgh showed nearly double the gains on standardized math assessments for marginalized students. AI tools like Project Topeka help multilingual learners by providing real-time feedback, described by teacher Victoria Salas Salcedo as "almost like having an extra teacher in the room." AI also assists students with disabilities through speech-to-text and text-to-speech tools.

- **How AI may exacerbate disparities:** AI algorithms can replicate historical biases. Predictive analytics tools often rate racial minorities as less likely to succeed - Wisconsin's Dropout Early Warning System generated false alarms for Black students at a 42% higher rate than for White students. Admissions algorithms using race-neutral data (like SAT scores) can still produce disparate racial impacts, potentially allocating more scholarship funding to White and Asian students over Black and Latino students.

- **Ethical considerations:** Wealthier schools may afford better AI tools, potentially widening achievement gaps. The article poses a critical question: "What if AI does improve academic results for low-income Black students but further boosts results for wealthy White students, widening the academic achievement gap?" Student privacy and data collection also raise concerns.

- **Digital divide and AI literacy:** 72% of White teens had heard of ChatGPT vs. 56% of Black teens. 35% of low-income California households lacked reliable internet access in 2021. 38% of Black residents in the rural south lack broadband access. Without AI literacy, underserved students may use AI tools less effectively than wealthier counterparts.

- **Regulation:** Congress has not passed AI legislation. Colorado enacted the Artificial Intelligence Act (May 2024). California advanced ~30 AI bills. The White House released the Blueprint for an AI Bill of Rights (October 2022), and President Biden issued an Executive Order on AI (October 2023). The article questions whether profit-driven tech companies can be trusted to self-regulate.

- **Recommendations:** Stakeholders should make AI tools more accessible to underserved communities. AI developers should include teachers, students, and families in development. The article concludes that government, civil society, and tech companies share responsibility for safe and ethical AI implementation in education.
</summary>

Should we embrace that outcome because academic results for Black students are nonetheless improving?", "Wisconsin's Dropout Early Warning System generated false alarms about Black and Latino students 'at a significantly greater rate than it did for their White classmates.'", "72% of White teens had heard about ChatGPT compared to 56% of Black teens.", "Teacher Victoria Salas Salcedo described Project Topeka as 'almost like having an extra teacher in the room, coaching [students] through the writing process.'"

--- SOURCE 13: AI Tutors Support 16 Percent of Learning. What About the Other 84 Percent? – Social Science Space ---
URL: https://www.socialsciencespace.com/2026/02/ai-tutors-support-16-percent-of-learning-what-about-the-other-84-percent

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This article by Rose Luckin (Professor of Learner-Centered Design at UCL) argues that AI tutoring addresses only a small fraction of genuine human learning and intelligence. While AI tutors can effectively deliver personalized academic content, practice procedures, and drill factual knowledge — representing about 16 percent of learning — they miss the other 84 percent that encompasses the full breadth of human intelligence.

Luckin critiques the frequent invocation of Benjamin Bloom's 1984 "2 sigma" finding (that one-to-one tutoring lifts students two standard deviations above peers) to justify AI tutoring, noting the original study had limited conditions and mixed replication results.

She presents a seven-element model of human intelligence: (1) knowledge about the world (where AI tutors operate), (2) personal epistemology, (3) social intelligence, (4) metacognitive awareness, (5) metasubjective intelligence (emotions and motivation), (6) metacontextual awareness, and (7) accurate perceived self-efficacy.

Drawing on the CAPITAL framework, which identified 19 distinct acts of learning, the article notes AI tutors primarily handle rehearsal, exposition, and partial tutorial interaction — but cannot support social learning acts, scenarioed acts requiring real-world transfer, or deeper personal acts like reflection and construction.

The article warns of risks including "metacognitive laziness" — reduced self-monitoring, increased procrastination, and gains that evaporate when AI is removed. It recommends: (1) welcome AI tutors for what they do well (academic content delivery), (2) invest in developing pedagogical approaches for the other six elements of intelligence, (3) reform assessment systems to value metacognition, collaboration, and self-regulation rather than just knowledge recall.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
AI tutors support perhaps 16 percent of what it means to develop an intelligent human being, and a handful of the 19 acts through which real learning happens., An AI tutor cannot model what it means to wrestle with the provisional nature of knowledge. It cannot teach a student to debate conflicting evidence, because it does not understand what evidence is., AI-assisted learners demonstrate reduced self-monitoring, increased procrastination, and what has been described as 'metacognitive laziness.', The human fundamentals of learning, including metacognition, social sense-making, and cognitive load management, should drive our approach to technology rather than the other way around., If we get this balance right, AI could be the catalyst that finally compels education to value what makes us distinctively human. If we get it wrong, we will have built the most sophisticated system ever devised for teaching people the things that matter least.
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 14: Stanford AI tutor bias study reveals risks in personalized learning | ETIH EdTech News — EdTech Innovation Hub ---
URL: https://www.edtechinnovationhub.com/news/ai-tutor-bias-study-finds-unequal-feedback-for-students-across-race-gender-and-ability

SUMMARY:
<summary>
A Stanford University study (published as a preprint on arXiv) has found that AI tutors produce unequal feedback depending on students' perceived race, gender, academic ability, and language background. The research introduces "marked pedagogies," where AI tutors adopt different instructional approaches based on inferred student characteristics. High-achieving or White students received more detailed, development-focused feedback (critique of argumentation, reasoning suggestions). Hispanic students or English language learners received feedback focused more on grammar, spelling, and formality rather than higher-order thinking. Students labeled as low-achieving or with learning disabilities experienced "feedback withholding bias," receiving positive reinforcement with limited critical input. The study also found that AI outputs sometimes referenced cultural or gender stereotypes, particularly for non-White or female students. These patterns emerged even when prompts were held constant and only student descriptors changed. The findings raise concerns about AI tutors being integrated into K-12, higher education, and workforce training, and suggest that EdTech providers need stronger guardrails, evaluation frameworks, and monitoring to ensure consistent, fair feedback aligned with pedagogical goals.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"The research introduces the concept of 'marked pedagogies,' where AI tutors adopt different instructional approaches based on inferred student characteristics.", "Students identified as high-achieving or White were more likely to receive detailed, development-focused feedback.", "For students labeled as low-achieving or having learning disabilities, the study found a pattern of what it describes as feedback withholding bias.", "The study does not conclude that AI tutors should be removed from classrooms. But it does highlight a gap between how these systems are positioned and how they currently behave."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 15: FairAIED: Navigating Fairness, Bias, and Ethics in Educational AI Applications ---
URL: https://arxiv.org/html/2407.18745v2

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a comprehensive survey paper (arXiv:2407.18745) titled "FairAIED: Navigating Fairness, Bias, and Ethics in Educational AI Applications." The paper provides a systematic review of algorithmic fairness within educational AI, bridging the gap between technical fairness research and educational applications. 

The paper's key contributions include: (1) Proposing a novel taxonomy categorizing biases into individual-level, group-level, and a newly introduced multi-level dimension that captures fairness issues simultaneously affecting both individual students and student groups; (2) Integrating bias sources, fairness definitions, mitigation strategies, evaluation resources, and ethical considerations into a coherent education-centered framework; (3) Highlighting practical challenges such as censored or partially observed learning outcomes and the fairness-utility trade-off.

The paper identifies multiple biases in educational AI: **Group-level biases** (Historical Bias, Mapping Bias, Representation Bias, Exclusion Bias), **Individual-level biases** (Measurement Bias, Confirmation Bias), and **Multi-level biases** (Algorithm Bias, Learning Bias, Interaction Bias, Stereotyping Bias, Censored Outcome Bias). 

The paper formalizes fairness definitions in educational settings, including **Group Fairness** metrics (Statistical Parity, Equal Opportunity, Predictive Parity, Predictive Equality, Concordance Imparity) and **Individual Fairness** metrics (Distance-Based Individual Fairness, Ranking-Based Individual Fairness). 

The survey discusses real-world case studies, analytical tools, datasets, ethical considerations, and policy guidelines. It concludes with open challenges and future directions, including balancing personalization with data privacy, addressing the digital divide, and improving teacher/student adoption through targeted training.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
AI systems can unintentionally perpetuate biases inherent in their training data, disproportionately impacting historically marginalized student groups, AI-based early-warning systems intended to identify at-risk students often overpredict risk for certain demographic groups, such as students of lower socioeconomic backgrounds, because of historical bias embedded in attendance or disciplinary data, We propose a novel taxonomy categorizing biases into individual-level, group-level, and the newly introduced multi-level dimension, forming a harmonized analytical framework, We highlight and analyze key practical challenges in educational AI, including handling censored or partially observed outcomes such as incomplete student records..., We discuss open challenges and outline future research directions, including balancing personalization with data privacy, addressing the digital divide in AI access and infrastructure, and improving teacher and student adoption through targeted training and support
</key_excerpts>

SUMMARY:
<summary>
MATHia is an intelligent math tutoring software from Carnegie Learning that uses AI to provide personalized one-on-one coaching to students.
