## D) Regional/Country Case Studies

### European Union

**Digital Education Action Plan (2021-2027):** Adopted on 30 September 2020, this is an EU initiative promoting high-quality, inclusive, and accessible digital education. [50][51] The plan has two strategic priorities: "Fostering the development of a high-performing digital education system" and "Enhancing digital skills and competences for the digital transformation." [50] It defines 14 actions to achieve these priorities, targeting education/training systems to make them fit for the digital age, ensuring all citizens can participate in and benefit from digital transformation, and promoting investments in connectivity and equipment. [50] Ethical aspects and protection of personal rights and data are fundamental considerations. [50] Key figures: Fewer than 40% of EU educators felt ready to use digital technologies in teaching (OECD, 2018). Over 40% of 13-14-year-olds in the EU lack basic digital skills, falling short of the EU's 2030 goal of reducing this below 15% (ICILS, 2023). 20% of low-income households lack access to computers and broadband (Eurostat, 2020). 95% of public consultation respondents said COVID-19 marked a turning point in educational technology use (2020). [51][52] Up to 90% of future jobs may require digital skills, yet at least one in five young people and over a third of EU workers lack basic digital skills. Only 39% of teachers feel well prepared to use digital technologies on a daily basis. [53] Key actions include launching a strategic dialogue with Member States, proposing a Council Recommendation on online/distance learning, developing a European Digital Education Content Framework, updating the Digital Competence Framework to include AI and data skills, creating a European Digital Skills Certificate, and establishing a European Digital Education Hub as a think-tank and monitoring body. [53]

**European Digital Education Hub:** Launched in June 2022, this is an online collaborative community connecting digital education stakeholders across Europe. By January 2025, the Hub had grown to over 5,500 members, with more than 100 publications and 200 activities. [54] The DEAP Ethical Guidelines on AI and Data in Teaching and Learning (2022) focuses on transparency, data protection, and ethical practices, with practical examples for AI use in education. [17]

**EU AI Act (2024):** The EU AI Act categorizes AI systems by risk, placing those used in "education and vocational training" in the high-risk category because of their potential impact on learners' rights and opportunities. [46][18]

**EUA Report on AI in Higher Education (2023):** The only European document specifically for Higher Education, advocating for responsible, ethical, and transparent AI use, arguing against banning AI tools in favor of institutional adaptation. [17] A dedicated EU policy on AI in Higher Education is urgently needed, as existing frameworks either generalize across sectors or focus on school-level education, overlooking the unique pedagogical models, governance structures, research dimensions, and ethical challenges of universities. [17]

### United Kingdom

The Department for Education published a policy paper on Generative Artificial Intelligence in Education (2025) outlining the opportunities and challenges of generative AI in education, emphasizing its potential to enhance teaching and reduce administrative burdens. [55] The document advocates for careful implementation and ongoing collaboration with the education sector to maximize benefits while ensuring safety and compliance with legal obligations. [55] The DfE guidance (published 29 March 2023, last updated 12 August 2025) sets out the government's position on generative AI in education, with a focus on compulsory education in schools and colleges. [56]

### United States

The U.S. Department of Education's Office of Educational Technology published "Artificial Intelligence and the Future of Teaching and Learning" (May 2023). [42] The report defines AI as "automation based on associations" and identifies two fundamental shifts: (1) from capturing data to detecting patterns in data, and (2) from providing access to instructional resources to automating decisions about instruction and other educational processes. [42] The report provides seven recommendations and emphasizes that "AI in education can only grow at the speed of trust." [42]

The Pennsylvania Advisory Committee to the U.S. Commission on Civil Rights adopted a proposal in December 2023 to study the rising use of AI in K-12 education, examining how AI algorithms are developed and their impact on reducing or exacerbating disparities in K-12 classrooms based on federally protected classes. [57]

### Asia

**Singapore:** Singapore's "Smart Nation" strategy aims to position the country as a world leader in AI by 2030 by bringing together researchers, government and industry. [26][27] AI-enabled companions provide customized feedback, automated grading, and machine learning to identify student responses. A national initiative to build AI literacy among students and teachers is underway, with training for all teachers by 2026. [26][27]

**South Korea:** As detailed in Section B, Korea will become the first nation to introduce AI digital textbooks nationwide (March 2025 for grades 3, 4, 7, and 10, full implementation by 2028). [25] The government has allocated approximately $0.74 billion for three years (2024–2026) for teacher training. [25] The 2022 Revised National Curriculum established AI literacy as a core competency. [28]

**China:** As detailed in Section B, China launched a national "AI+Education Action Plan" in April 2026 mandating AI across its education system from kindergarten through lifelong learning, with the goal of deep integration by 2030. [33][34] Starting September 2025, AI education is mandatory nationwide for students from age 6, with at least 8 hours per year. [35] The plan is guided by Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era. [34]

**Japan:** As detailed in Sections A and B, Japan's AI Strategy 2019 established three core principles: human dignity, diversity, and sustainability. [19] MEXT published guidelines on generative AI in schools (December 2024, ver. 2.0) [38] and guidance for universities (July 2023). [19] Japan has been developing "sovereign AI" through the NII's LLM-JP model. [19] The AI Safety Institute (AISI) launched in February 2024. [58] Japan led the Hiroshima AI Process following the G7 Hiroshima Summit (May 2023). [58]

### Australia

As detailed in Section A, TEQSA launched a nationwide RFI in 2024 with 100% response rate from higher education providers. [13] The TEQSA Assessment Reform paper (2023) provides five key propositions for assessment reform. [14] The ACSES Australian Framework for AI in Higher Education (December 2025) centers on equity. [15]

### Global South

**Overview:** The Brookings Institution (Chinasa T. Okolo, November 2023) examines AI adoption in the Global South. [59] Key Opportunities: AI is being applied to traditional development challenges in agriculture (banana disease identification, cassava disease detection in East Africa, precision agriculture in Brazil), healthcare (predictive models for maternal health in India, antimicrobial resistance tools in Ghana, fetal ultrasound interpretation in Zambia), and education (at-risk student identification in Colombia, English learning for Thai students, AI teaching assistants in West Africa). [59] Grassroots organizations like Masakhane, Ghana NLP, Deep Learning Indaba, and Khipu are democratizing AI and expanding access to low-resource African languages. Big tech companies (IBM, Microsoft, Google) have established research labs in India, Kenya, Ghana, Nigeria, Brazil, and South Africa. [59] Key Challenges: Infrastructure gaps - Internet penetration in Africa was only 36% in 2021 (up from 8% in 2011). Rural Sub-Saharan Africa has only 30.4% electricity connectivity vs. 98.3% in rural South Asia and 96.5% in rural Latin America. [59] Concerns about "algorithmic colonization" and exploitation of data workers in East Africa and South Asia for content moderation and data labeling. The Global South risks being excluded from global AI governance conversations despite holding a majority of the world's population. PwC estimates AI could contribute $15.7 trillion to the global economy by 2030, but only $1.7 trillion (excluding China) is expected to impact the Global South. [59] Recommendations: Invest in independent cloud computing infrastructure and data centers. Build local AI research capacity and integrate digital skills training into K-12 curricula. Ensure equitable inclusion of Global South stakeholders in international AI governance bodies. [59]

**Africa:** The African Union developed a Continental Strategy on AI, expected for endorsement at the February 2024 AU Summit. The strategy will articulate "the African approach to AI governance," addressing challenges like limited use of African datasets, overreliance on foreign algorithms, and algorithmic biases (including racial and gender bias). [60] Currently fewer than 10 African countries have national AI strategies (Rwanda, Benin, Egypt, Morocco, Mauritius, Tunisia, Sierra Leone, Senegal). Namibia and South Africa are expected to advance AI governance within SADC, while Côte D'Ivoire, Nigeria, Kenya, and Ethiopia are also progressing. [60] Senegal aims to train 90,000 in data science by 2028. South Africa has launched pilot AI/coding programs in schools. [60] "If 2023 was the year in which discussions around AI governance took global centre stage, then 2024 is poised to witness the translation of these deliberations into concrete actionable policy measures." [60] "African voices and perspectives are important in policy dialogues around artificial intelligence (AI)." [60]

**India:** Ed tech company Embibe uses AI to clarify complex math and science concepts via smartphone scanning of textbooks with 3-D visualization. AI is also used to predict student performance for early intervention. [26][27]

**South-South Cooperation:** The UNOSSC initiative on "South-South and triangular cooperation for sustainable AI" examines how countries in the Global South can move from an emerging AI divide towards a shared AI dividend over the next 10-15 years. [61] "The Global South is not a 'follower.' Countries and communities across this group are already leading the way. AI could mark the next chapter in this story." [61] Kenya rolled out mobile phone-delivered payments years before higher-income countries and cities. Mobile money was responsible for US$2 trillion in transactions across the Global South in 2025. India has developed a universal digital ID solution that has built a digital economy which may contribute up to 20% of the country's GDP by the end of this decade. [61] "AI can support sustainable development only if countries act collectively and deliberately to build the capacities, partnerships and guardrails needed to ensure that AI systems are inclusive, trusted, rights-respecting, environmentally sustainable and responsive to the needs of people and communities." [61]

## E) Pedagogical Models

### AI Assessment Scale (AIAS)

The AI Assessment Scale (AIAS) is a five-level framework designed to help educators determine the appropriate role of AI in assessment tasks and redesign those tasks accordingly. [3] Developed by Mike Perkins, Jasper Roe, Leon Furze, and Jason MacVaugh, the AIAS addresses the need for clearer, fairer practices for AI use in formative and summative assessments. First published in 2023 and now updated to AIAS 2.1, the framework provides a shared vocabulary for AI in assessment, supporting academic integrity and assessment redesign. [3] The AIAS is used in more than 350 institutions worldwide, has been translated into more than 30 languages, and is noted by the Australian Tertiary Education Quality and Standards Agency (TEQSA) in its 2024 paper as an option to assist with implementing GenAI into assessment. [3] It won a QS Reimagine Education Awards 2025 Bronze in the Learning Assessment category. [3]

The five levels are:
1. **No AI** – Completed in a controlled environment excluding AI.
2. **AI Planning** – AI supports planning activities like topic exploration and outlining.
3. **AI Collaboration** – AI assists with idea generation, drafting, and refinement, but alone cannot reach the required standard.
4. **Full AI** – AI involvement is expected; the goal cannot be reached by AI or a person alone.
5. **AI Exploration** – Creative AI use for problem-solving and innovation.

"No level is superior; each represents a different task type. Choosing a level is only the start. The real work is redesigning the task so students know what evidence they need to produce, what AI use is expected or constrained, and how their work will be judged." [3]

The AIAS fosters metacognitive awareness, helping learners transition from passive AI consumers to active AI collaborators. [62] "We wanted to be flexible and have some opportunities for students and faculty to really have open conversations about how AI might be suitably used given the individual circumstances and the cultural context." - Mike Perkins. [63] "Let's move away from this idea that if you paraphrase slightly incorrectly, then it's a punishable offense." - Jasper Roe. [63]

### Carnegie Mellon University's Six Policy Options

CMU's Eberly Center provides six sample policies ranging from complete prohibition to full encouragement: [2]
- Example 1 (No AI allowed): Students must complete all graded assignments without any generative AI.
- Example 2 (No AI allowed): Specifically forbids use of ChatGPT or any generative AI at all stages of work, including brainstorming.
- Example 3 (Full AI use encouraged): Students are encouraged to use AI tools but must cite the tool and version used, include the exact prompt and AI's full response in an appendix.
- Example 4 (Full AI use encouraged): Welcomes use of AI tools but emphasizes ethical responsibilities; cutting and pasting or paraphrasing AI content without citation is plagiarism.
- Example 5 (Conditional AI use): AI use is permitted only when explicitly stated in assignment prompts; otherwise, it is disallowed.
- Example 6 (Conditional AI use): AI tools may be used during some class sessions for learning exercises, but NOT for graded assignments.

### ASCCC Syllabus Language Continuum

The ASCCC framework provides four categories of AI use: [6]
- **Open**: Full allowance with citation
- **Conditional**: AI allowed with specific conditions
- **Restricted**: AI only allowed for specific tasks
- **Closed**: Complete prohibition

### Georgia's Traffic Light System

Georgia's framework (January 2025, updated June 2025) uses a "Traffic Light" system: [39]
- **Red**: AI not allowed (academic dishonesty)
- **Yellow**: AI allowed for content creation assistance
- **Green**: AI encouraged with proper citation

### Pedagogical Models for AI in Education

**AI as Tutor:** AI systems provide personalized instruction, feedback, and adaptivity through intelligent tutoring systems. Examples include South Korea's personalized AI tutor for each child [25][26] and AI-enabled companions providing customized feedback in Singapore. [26][27]

**AI as Co-Pilot/Collaborator:** The AIAS Level 3 (AI Collaboration) models this approach, where AI assists with idea generation, drafting, and refinement. The Estonian AI Leap learning app is designed to act "more like a teacher, guiding students to find answers and formulate their own conclusions" rather than giving direct answers. [30]

**AI as Assessment Tool:** The EU AI Act classifies AI used for student assessment as "high-risk." [18] Automated essay scoring is an example application identified by the U.S. Department of Education. [42] However, concerns about AI detection tools producing false positives, particularly for non-native English writers, have led to cautious institutional guidance. [1]

**AI as Simulator:** AI-augmented simulators and Extended Reality (XR) systems equipped with sensor-rich elements deliver real-time feedback on practical abilities, particularly in vocational training. The strongest empirical evidence arises from research on these systems, such as the multisensor AI-assisted welding trainer studied by Lee et al. (2021). [47]

**AI for Planning and Idea Generation:** The AIAS Level 2 (AI Planning) models AI use for brainstorming, topic exploration, and outlining. [3]

**Full AI Integration:** Tasks designed to require AI use, where the goal cannot be reached by AI or a person alone (AIAS Level 4). [3]

**AI Exploration:** Creative AI use for problem-solving and innovation (AIAS Level 5), recognizing AI as a fundamental component of digital literacy. [3][62]

### Maturity Model: From Banning to Acceptance to Integration

The CASRAI guide documents that between 2023 and 2026, most universities moved through the same arc on generative AI: an initial instinct toward blanket prohibition, followed by a shift toward permission-based frameworks that specify when and how AI assistance is allowed rather than banning it outright. [1]

Michigan's three-stage maturity framework provides a structured model: [39]
1. **Investigating** - Exploring AI tools and their implications
2. **Implementing** - Putting AI policies and practices into place
3. **Innovating** - Full integration and creative use of AI

The ASCCC framework emphasizes that "Embrace the uncertainty of the moment. Be curious, not fearful – for only the curious discover." [6]

### Evidence on Effective Strategies

**What Works:**
- Tiered permission frameworks specifying when and how AI is allowed, rather than blanket bans [1]
- Clear communication of AI use expectations in course syllabi [12]
- Assessment redesign focusing on process, thinking, and judgement (TEQSA propositions) [14]
- Authentic engagement with AI aligned with disciplinary values [14]
- Program-level assessment design spanning entire programs [14]
- Teacher training and professional development (South Korea's $0.74 billion investment, UNESCO's AI Competency Framework for Teachers) [22][25]

**What Doesn't Work:**
- Blanket bans on AI tools, which are "oversimplified solutions to a complex set of problems" [14]
- AI detection tools as sole basis for integrity findings, due to false positives and bias [1]
- "Reactive claims of 'don't worry, we've got it covered'" which risk unnuanced legislation [13]

**Key Principles Across Sources:**
- "AI in education can only grow at the speed of trust" [42]
- "Meaningful digital transformation in schools depends not on technology adoption alone but on aligning AI integration with clearly defined educational challenges" [28]
- "Teaching is fundamentally relational—built on interpretation, judgment, emotional understanding, and the ability to guide learners as developing individuals. These dimensions cannot be automated or delegated to AI systems" [23]
- "The core question is not whether AI should enter education but how it should be used, who benefits from it, and what values guide its integration" [23]

You are a research supervisor. Your job is to conduct research by calling the "ConductResearch" tool. For context, today's date is Mon Aug 24, 2026.

<Task>
Your focus is to call the "ConductResearch" tool to conduct research against the overall research question passed in by the user. 
When you are completely satisfied with the research findings returned from the tool calls, then you should call the "ResearchComplete" tool to indicate that you are done with your research.
</Task>

<Available Tools>
You have access to three main tools:
1. **ConductResearch**: Delegate research tasks to specialized sub-agents
2. **ResearchComplete**: Indicate that research is complete
3. **think_tool**: For reflection and strategic planning during research

**CRITICAL: Use think_tool before calling ConductResearch to plan your approach, and after each ConductResearch to assess progress. Do not call think_tool with any other tools in parallel.**
</Available Tools>

<Instructions>
Think like a research manager with limited time and resources. Follow these steps:

1. **Read the question carefully** - What specific information does the user need?
2. **Decide how to delegate the research** - Carefully consider the question and decide how to delegate the research. Are there multiple independent directions that can be explored simultaneously?
3. **After each call to ConductResearch, pause and assess** - Do I have enough to answer? What's still missing?
</Instructions>

<Hard Limits>
**Task Delegation Budgets** (Prevent excessive delegation):
- **Bias towards single agent** - Use single agent for simplicity unless the user request has clear opportunity for parallelization
- **Stop when you can answer confidently** - Don't keep delegating research for perfection
- **Limit tool calls** - Always stop after 3 tool calls to ConductResearch and think_tool if you cannot find the right sources

**Maximum 3 parallel agents per iteration**
</Hard Limits>

<Show Your Thinking>
Before you call ConductResearch tool call, use think_tool to plan your approach:
- Can the task be broken down into smaller sub-tasks?

After each ConductResearch tool call, use think_tool to analyze the results:
- What key information did I find?
- What's missing?
- Do I have enough to answer the question comprehensively?
- Should I delegate more research or call ResearchComplete?
</Show Your Thinking>

<Scaling Rules>
**Simple fact-finding, lists, and rankings** can use a single sub-agent:
- *Example*: List the top 10 coffee shops in San Francisco → Use 1 sub-agent

**Comparisons presented in the user request** can use a sub-agent for each element of the comparison:
- *Example*: Compare OpenAI vs. Anthropic vs. DeepMind approaches to AI safety → Use 3 sub-agents
- Delegate clear, distinct, non-overlapping subtopics

**Important Reminders:**
- Each ConductResearch call spawns a dedicated research agent for that specific topic
- A separate agent will write the final report - you just need to gather information
- When calling ConductResearch, provide complete standalone instructions - sub-agents can't see other agents' work
- Do NOT use acronyms or abbreviations in your research questions, be very clear and specific
</Scaling Rules>

As someone working in education, I need a comprehensive analysis of whether artificial intelligence will fundamentally transform how we teach and assess student learning, or if it is merely another passing educational technology trend. My research should cover three key dimensions:

1. **Popular AI Tools and Their Impact on Student Processes**: Identify the most widely used AI tools in education (e.g., ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, Copilot, Grammarly, Perplexity, etc.) and analyze how they are changing student research workflows, writing practices, and problem-solving approaches. Include evidence on both productivity gains and concerns about over-reliance, critical thinking erosion, or academic integrity.

2. **Effectiveness and Equity of AI-Driven Personalized Learning**: Examine whether research (from 2022 onwards) shows that personalized AI tutoring systems and adaptive learning platforms can improve educational outcomes (e.g., test scores, retention, engagement, skill mastery) compared to traditional human instruction alone. Also investigate whether these technologies are creating or exacerbating new forms of educational inequality (e.g., access gaps, digital divides, algorithmic bias, differential outcomes by socioeconomic status or language background).

3. **Global Institutional Adaptation Strategies**: Analyze how different educational institutions (K-12, higher education, vocational training) across various countries and regions are adapting their curricula, honor codes, academic integrity policies, and teaching methods to integrate AI tools rather than ban them. Look for concrete case studies, policy frameworks, and pedagogical models that have been implemented since 2022.

The report should be global in scope with no restriction to a specific country or region. All evidence and data should be from 2022 onwards. I prefer sources that are peer-reviewed research, official institutional reports, government education policy documents, and credible education technology analyses. For academic claims, link directly to original studies or official journal publications. The report should be in English.

args.research_topic:
Dimension 1: Popular AI Tools and Their Impact on Student Learning Processes (2022-2026)

Research Question: How are the most widely used AI tools (ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, Microsoft Copilot, Grammarly, Perplexity, and other major AI writing/research assistants) transforming student research workflows, writing practices, and problem-solving approaches in educational settings?

Please conduct a comprehensive investigation covering:

A) For each major tool, find evidence on how students are using them:
- ChatGPT for research assistance, essay drafting, brainstorming, and problem-solving
- Claude for analytical writing, document analysis, and research synthesis
- Google Gemini for multimodal learning and research
- Microsoft Copilot integrated into Office/education workflows
- Grammarly for writing enhancement and editing
- Perplexity for AI-powered research and source discovery
- Any other notable AI education tools (e.g., Khanmigo, Quizlet Q-Chat, etc.)

B) Productivity Gains: Find data/studies showing:
- Time savings for students in research and writing tasks
- Improvements in writing quality, organization, and clarity
- Enhanced ability to understand complex concepts through AI explanations
- Accessibility benefits for students with disabilities or language barriers

C) Concerns and Risks: Find evidence on:
- Over-reliance on AI tools and erosion of critical thinking skills
- Academic integrity violations and plagiarism concerns
- Students using AI as a substitute rather than supplement for learning
- Evidence of skill atrophy in writing, research, or problem-solving

D) Academic Integrity: Find research on:
- How AI is changing definitions of plagiarism and academic dishonesty
- Detection tools and their effectiveness/limitations
- Studies on student attitudes toward AI use in academic work

Search for peer-reviewed studies from 2022-2026, higher education research reports, surveys of student usage patterns, and credible education technology analyses. Provide specific citations and links to original studies where possible.

Dimension 2: Effectiveness and Equity of AI-Driven Personalized Learning (2022-2026)

Research Question: Does research from 2022 onwards show that personalized AI tutoring systems and adaptive learning platforms can improve educational outcomes compared to traditional human instruction alone, and are these technologies creating or exacerbating educational inequalities?

Please conduct a comprehensive investigation covering:

A) Effectiveness Evidence:
- Find peer-reviewed studies and meta-analyses comparing AI tutoring systems (e.g., Khan Academy's Khanmigo, Carnegie Learning's MATHia, Duolingo's AI tutor, Squirrel AI, Century Tech, ALEKS, etc.) to traditional instruction
- Evidence on impact on: test scores, knowledge retention, student engagement, skill mastery, learning speed, and motivation
- Any large-scale randomized controlled trials (RCTs) or quasi-experimental studies
- Research on the "2 sigma problem" (Bloom, 1984) and whether AI tutoring is closing the gap between group and one-on-one instruction
- Studies on AI's effectiveness for specific subjects (math, reading, science, writing, languages)

B) Mechanism Analysis:
- How adaptive learning algorithms adjust difficulty, pacing, and content
- Effectiveness of real-time feedback, hints, and scaffolding
- Impact of AI on metacognition, self-regulated learning, and study habits
- Comparison of AI tutoring vs. human tutoring vs. blended approaches

C) Equity Concerns:
- Access gaps: Who has access to premium AI tutoring tools? (cost, internet, device requirements)
- Digital divide: Evidence on disparities by income level, geography (urban/rural), and country
- Language barriers: How well do AI tutors serve non-English speakers and multilingual learners?
- Algorithmic bias: Evidence of AI tutoring systems performing differently for different demographic groups (race, gender, socioeconomic status)
- Differential outcomes: Do AI tools help all students equally, or do they widen achievement gaps (the "Matthew effect")?
- Accessibility for students with disabilities and special educational needs

D) Policy Implications:
- What do education researchers recommend regarding equitable deployment of AI tutoring?
- Models for ensuring equal access (e.g., government-funded programs, public-private partnerships)

Search for peer-reviewed journal articles, meta-analyses, large-scale education studies, OECD/UNESCO/World Bank reports, and government education department evaluations from 2022-2026. Provide specific citations and links to original studies.

Dimension 3: Global Institutional Adaptation Strategies for AI in Education (2022-2026)

Research Question: How are educational institutions across different countries and regions (K-12, higher education, vocational training) adapting their curricula, honor codes, academic integrity policies, and teaching methods to integrate AI tools rather than ban them?

Please conduct a comprehensive investigation covering:

A) Higher Education Adaptation:
- Case studies of universities that have explicitly revised their academic integrity policies to address AI (e.g., Harvard, MIT, Stanford, Oxford, University of Tokyo, University of Melbourne, etc.)
- Universities that have developed AI literacy programs or required AI coursework
- Institutions that have redesigned assessments (e.g., oral exams, in-person proctored writing, process-based assessment, portfolio evaluation)
- Honor code revisions: How are universities defining acceptable vs. unacceptable AI use?
- Examples of AI-integrated curricula and pedagogy in higher education
- Specific policy frameworks (e.g., Australia's universities framework on AI, European University Association guidelines)

B) K-12 Adaptation:
- How school districts and education ministries are adapting to AI
- Case studies of countries that have integrated AI into national curricula (e.g., Singapore, Finland, South Korea, Estonia, Japan)
- UNESCO's recommendations on AI in K-12 education
- Examples of AI literacy curricula for primary and secondary students
- Policies on AI use in homework, classroom assignments, and assessments
- Professional development programs for teachers on AI integration

C) Vocational and Adult Education:
- How vocational training institutions are adapting to AI
- Integration of AI tools in skills training and competency-based education
- Industry partnerships for AI-ready workforce development

D) Regional/Country Case Studies:
- EU: European Commission's AI in Education initiatives, Digital Education Action Plan
- UK: Department for Education's approach to generative AI in education
- USA: Department of Education reports, state-level policies, institutional approaches
- Asia: Singapore's Smart Nation initiative, South Korea's AI education plans, China's AI in education strategy, Japan's approach
- Australia: TEQSA's framework on AI in higher education
- Global South: How developing countries are approaching AI in education (e.g., India, Kenya, Brazil, Rwanda)

E) Pedagogical Models:
- Different pedagogical approaches: AI as tutor, AI as co-pilot, AI as assessment tool, AI as simulator
- The "AI in Education" maturity model from banning to acceptance to integration
- Evidence on which adaptation strategies are most effective

Search for official institutional policy documents, government education ministry white papers, UNESCO/OECD reports, university senate decisions, accreditation body guidelines, education technology analyses, and peer-reviewed research on educational policy. Provide specific links to policy documents and case studies. All evidence from 2022-2026.

**List of Queries and Tool Calls Made**

1. Search: "student use of ChatGPT Claude Gemini in higher education 2022-2026 peer-reviewed study"
2. Search: "AI tools impact student learning processes research 2023 2024"
3. Search: "productivity gains AI writing tools students time savings research study"
4. Search: "AI academic integrity plagiarism detection tools effectiveness 2024 2025 study"
5. Search: "student attitudes toward AI use academic dishonesty higher education research"
6. Search: "Grammarly Perplexity Khanmigo education student use research study"
7. Search: "AI over-reliance critical thinking skills erosion students research 2024 2025"

---

**Fully Comprehensive Findings**

---

## Dimension A: Popular AI Tools and Their Impact on Student Learning Processes

### A1) ChatGPT Usage in Education

**Scoping Review of 24 Empirical Articles (Schei, Møgelvang, & Ludvigsen, 2024):** A scoping review published in *Education Sciences* (2024) analyzed 24 empirical articles published between January 1, 2022 and September 5, 2023 on students' perceptions and use of AI chatbots (including ChatGPT, Copilot, Gemini, Claude) in higher education. The review found that research is concentrated in Asia, with STEM disciplines (computer science, programming, engineering) being predominant. Students perceive AI chatbots as "highly useful and motivating as personal task assistants and for getting immediate feedback and help with writing, coding, and academic tasks." Students use AI chatbots for diverse, purpose-driven tasks including brainstorming, summarizing, coding, problem-solving, writing support, and language learning. The review concludes that "while positive attitudes, perceptions, and critical use prevail, addressing students' concerns is crucial for responsible AI integration in higher education." [1]

**University of Phoenix Doctoral Student Study (Veera, Bennett, & Rice, 2026):** A quantitative study published in the *International Journal of AI in Pedagogy, Innovation, and Learning Futures* (2026) surveyed 54 doctoral students at a private online U.S. university. Key findings: students with more favorable perceptions of AI chatbot use reported more frequent ChatGPT usage; students who viewed chatbot-generated responses as superior also reported higher levels of chatbot use; significant differences in attitudes toward AI chatbots were identified across academic disciplines; no statistically significant gender differences were observed. The study supports the need for "discipline-sensitive institutional guidance on ethical AI use in higher education." DOI: https://doi.org/10.5070/P8I2314143 [2]

**EU-JER Study on ChatGPT Perceptions (Uppal & Hajian, 2025):** A study published in the *European Journal of Educational Research* (January 2025) conducted a correlational analysis with 44 students. Students who viewed ChatGPT as reliable and efficient tended to report higher grades, improved understanding of the material, and greater confidence in their knowledge. The study found a statistically significant relationship between dependency on ChatGPT and procrastination (r = 0.546, p < .001), indicating that higher reliance on AI tools may contribute to increased procrastination. No statistically significant association was found between ChatGPT dependency and the risk of plagiarism. [3]

**UC Irvine Study on How Students Adopt AI for Writing and Research (Spring 2023):** This study examined how 277 undergraduate students used AI in a large General Education course on sustainability and technology at UC Irvine in Spring 2023 (just months after ChatGPT's release). Of 277 students, 39 documented their AI use in their final project. Through iterative qualitative coding, the researchers identified 38 codes across 6 thematic categories. Key findings: higher-order writing tasks — students used AI for understanding complex topics (24 instances) and finding evidence/examples (11 instances); lower-order writing tasks — the most common use was revising and editing (47 instances), with students primarily using AI to improve communication of their original ideas; ghostwriting — 24 instances reported, with varying degrees of reliance ranging from overcoming writer's block to heavy dependence; efficiency and independence — 14 instances of efficiency, with students emphasizing maintaining their own ideas and independent writing; skepticism — 12 instances of critical perspectives, including concerns about AI accuracy, fabricated facts, and invented references. The study's theoretical framework draws on Vygotsky's zone of proximal development, viewing AI as a "more expert other." Students demonstrated sophisticated strategies, actively distinguishing between AI-assisted editing and their original thinking. [4]

**Polish University Study (National University of Science and Technology POLITEHNICA Bucharest, 2025):** A study published in *Education Sciences* (2025) involving 85 second-year students from Aerospace and Medical Engineering programs found that 95.6% of students use AI in academic activities, with virtual assistants (88.2%) being the most popular (e.g., ChatGPT, Siri, Google Assistant), followed by AI-based educational platforms (42.4%). Most students use AI weekly (57.6%) and believe it enhances learning efficiency (83.5%) and academic performance (82.4%). However, concerns include incorrect or imprecise answers (48.2%), negative impacts on critical thinking (16.5%), and over-dependence on technology (16.5%). Thematic analysis of open-ended responses revealed that AI improves learning through time-saving, comprehension optimization, and information structuring. [5]

### A2) Claude for Analytical Writing, Document Analysis, and Research Synthesis

**Vallejo-Blanxart & Sans Study Comparing ChatGPT, Claude, and Gemini (2025):** Published in the *Journal of Technology and Science Education*, Vol 15, No 3 (2025), this study examined how generative AI chatbots (ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini) are reshaping higher education. A pilot study with 300 undergraduate students and 120 faculty members from five European universities found that "ChatGPT and Claude achieved the best balance between pedagogical clarity and privacy compliance, while Gemini excelled in technical capacity but showed weaker ethical safeguards." Student satisfaction was "strongly associated with transparency in data policies and pedagogical usefulness rather than raw technical performance." [6]

**AI Study Modes Comparison (Glasp Deep Dive Podcast, 2025-2026):** A podcast episode compared three AI study modes (ChatGPT Study Mode, Gemini Guided Learning, and Claude Learning Mode) released between April 2025 and July 2025. Scoring out of 15: Claude Learning Mode scored 11 (strongest on pedagogy, designed to be annoying/refuse direct answers, backed by institutional campus deals with Northeastern, LSE, Syracuse, etc.), ChatGPT Study Mode scored 9 (free on all plans, best memory and tracking, but folds under pressure), Gemini Guided Learning scored 6 (best explainer with YouTube integration, but the free student offer expired March 2026 and became $9.99/month; pedagogically weak because it presents more than it retrieves). The hosts noted: "Claude wins on pedagogy, because the thing students complain about, the refusal to just answer, is the active ingredient." Key events: In April 2026, ChatGPT Study Mode vanished overnight without announcement, was publicly criticized by Ethan Mollick, and returned upgraded—revealing modes as removable behavior layers. Google's free student offer expired March 11, 2026. Critical research cited: Roediger & Karpicke (2006) testing-effect study; Bjork's desirable difficulties; Gerlich's 2025 study linking heavy AI use to lower critical thinking; MIT EEG study showing "cognitive debt" in AI-assisted essay writing. Key finding: "None of the three products do spacing—they don't bring Tuesday's confusion back on Friday." [7]

### A3) Google Gemini for Multimodal Learning and Research

### C1) Over-Reliance on AI Tools and Erosion of Critical Thinking Skills

**Duke University CTL (AI Ethics Learning Toolkit):** The Duke University Center for Teaching and Learning cites research showing that "university students who use Large Language Models (LLMs) to complete writing and research tasks experienced reduced cognitive load but demonstrated poorer reasoning and argumentation skills compared to those students using traditional search methods." Another study found that "students using LLMs focused on a narrower set of ideas, resulting in more biased and superficial analyses." The page quotes Matteo Wong from The Atlantic: "[AI] could completely reorient our relationship to knowledge, prioritizing rapid, detailed, abridged answers over a deep understanding and the consideration of varied sources and viewpoints." [23]

**NSTA Blog (Royce & Bennett, March 2025):** Citing a 2025 Microsoft study of knowledge workers, the authors found "an inverse correlation between confidence in AI and critical thinking, and a direct correlation between user self-confidence and critical thinking." Studies indicate that "when individuals rely heavily on AI for information retrieval and decision making, their ability to engage in reflective problem solving and independent analysis may decline." Importantly, "younger participants (ages 17–25) showed higher dependence on AI tools and lower thinking scores than older age groups did." [24]

**The Cognitive Paradox of AI in Education (Frontiers in Psychology, April 2025):** This article examines the dual role of AI as both a cognitive amplifier and inhibitor. Key findings: cognitive offloading — AI-powered tools reduce opportunities for active recall and problem-solving, essential for cognitive development; memory retention — a study by Bai, Liu, and Su found that excessive reliance on AI (e.g., ChatGPT) reduces cognitive engagement and long-term retention; Akgun and Toker's study showed pretesting before AI use improved retention, but prolonged AI exposure led to memory decline; problem-solving and critical thinking — Ododo et al. found AI poses threats to critical thinking, with students passively accepting AI-provided information; creativity — Habib et al. found AI-supported students scored better on fluency and flexibility but experienced cognitive fixation and lower creative confidence due to over-reliance. The Stanford research found a 15% increase in test scores from AI tutoring, but University of Pennsylvania research showed ChatGPT users scored 17% lower on concept understanding despite answering 48% more problems correctly. "AI has the potential to maximize the extraneous load through the elimination of redundant work, allowing the student to focus on more important cognitive operations. However, over-reliance on AI has the potential to reduce the germane load, which is needed for deep learning and the development of higher-order thinking skills." [25]

**Systematic Review on Over-Reliance (Zhai, Wibowo, & Li, Smart Learning Environments, June 2024):** This systematic review of 14 articles examined how over-reliance on AI dialogue systems affects students' cognitive abilities. Key findings: over-reliance on AI occurs when users accept AI-generated recommendations without question, leading to errors in task performance; ethical issues with AI (hallucinations, algorithmic biases, plagiarism, privacy concerns, transparency issues) contribute to over-reliance; this over-reliance negatively impacts critical cognitive capabilities including decision-making, critical thinking, and analytical reasoning; users increasingly favor fast, optimal solutions over slow, practical ones; regular utilization of AI dialogue systems is linked to decline in cognitive abilities, diminished information retention, and increased dependence on these systems; over-reliance may reduce motivation for independent thinking and analysis, weakening essential cognitive skills and fostering automation bias. Regarding AI hallucinations, Athaluri et al. (2023) found that among 178 reference sources produced by AI dialogue systems, 69 lacked a Digital Object Identifier (DOI), and 28 could not be found through a Google search. [26]

**Cogent Education Study on Over-Reliance (Abubakar, Jeilani, & Yusuf, 2025):** A quantitative cross-sectional survey of 226 participants from major universities in Mogadishu, Somalia. The regression model explained 38.9% of variance (R²=0.389, F=47.133, p<0.001). Key findings: significant positive relationship between over-reliance on AI and negative learning consequences (H1 supported); ethical concerns significantly moderate (reduce) the negative effect of over-reliance (interaction estimate = −0.0978, p=0.031) (H2 supported); institutional policies significantly moderate (reduce) the negative effect of over-reliance (interaction estimate = −0.115, p=0.035) (H3 supported). The study concludes that "robust ethical frameworks and comprehensive policies can alleviate some adverse impacts of AI reliance." [27]

**College Board Research (February 2026):** A survey of over 3,000 U.S. college faculty found: 74% report students using AI to write essays; 67% say students use it to paraphrase or rewrite content; 45% report negative views of AI in higher education versus 34% positive; over 84% agree AI reduces critical thinking, originality, and deep engagement with course material; 88% are concerned about overreliance on automation; 92% worry about AI-facilitated plagiarism; only 21% feel very confident guiding AI use in classrooms; nearly half have formal AI policies. Faculty in writing-intensive fields (English, history, humanities) report more negative attitudes, while STEM and business faculty are more positive. [28]

## Dimension D: Academic Integrity

### D1) How AI Is Changing Definitions of Plagiarism and Academic Dishonesty

**Adler University White Paper (Halbert et al., 2025):** Adler University created a GPT Taskforce of 13 faculty members across three campuses (Chicago, Vancouver, and Online) to evaluate and update their Academic Honesty Policy to address AI-generated content. The policy was approved by all three faculty councils and implemented in Spring 2024. The policy explicitly includes "material retrieved from or generated by artificial intelligence tools, including but not limited to ChatGPT" as plagiarism. The definition of plagiarism now includes: "Copying material and/or using ideas from an article, book, unpublished paper, or any material or source found on the Internet without proper documentation of references and citations, or without properly enclosing quoted material in quotation marks. This includes material retrieved from or generated by artificial intelligence tools, including but not limited to ChatGPT." And: "Substantial utilization of the published or unpublished work of others without permission, citation, or credit—also known as 'cut and paste' or 'patch writing'—and including works retrieved from or generated by artificial intelligence tools such as but not limited to ChatGPT." The paper discusses two real-world cases: (1) a student whose paper was 100% flagged as AI after using a tool that reworked their paper, and (2) a student who wrote in Mandarin and used AI to translate to English. [11]

**Student Perceptions of AI-Assisted Writing Study (Lund et al., 2025):** Published in *AI in Education* (Volume 1, Issue 1, September 2025), this study surveyed 401 students from major U.S. universities. Key findings: students' ethical beliefs — not institutional policies — are the strongest predictors of perceived misconduct and actual AI use in writing. Policy awareness was found to have no significant effect on ethical judgments or behavior. Students who believe AI writing is cheating are substantially less likely to view it as ethical or engage with it. Many students do not treat AI use as an extension of conventional cheating (e.g., plagiarism), but rather as a distinct category of academic conduct/misconduct. The study recommends education about AI ethics and the risk of AI overreliance rather than punitive models for curbing unethical AI use. [32]

**UAE University Study (2024):** Only 5.5% of students thought it was acceptable to submit AI-generated work as their own. 34.8% agreed that GenAI tools encourage academic dishonesty. The chapter recommends that institutions develop policies requiring students to declare AI use, create guidelines for faculty on assessing AI-assisted work, implement ethical education programs, and regularly update policies as AI evolves. The authors argue that "with strong ethics and values, AI can make the learning environment better and more productive." [17]

**Coursiv (2026):** By 2026, most universities have replaced AI bans with more relaxed regulations — using AI to explain concepts is generally acceptable, but submitting AI-generated work as your own is considered plagiarism. [12]

### D2) Detection Tools and Their Effectiveness/Limitations

**Van Vlasselaer, Van Droogenbroeck, & Spruyt Study (International Journal for Educational Integrity, June 2026):** This study evaluated the reliability of four AI detection tools — GPTZero, Pangram, Copyleaks, and Turnitin — in higher education contexts. The researchers created a synthetic dataset of 160 academic papers with known ground truth across four categories: (1) fully human-written, (2) fully AI-generated (using GPT-4o Deep Research), (3) hybrid (human text with AI-inserted passages), and (4) humanised AI text (AI-generated text rewritten to resemble student writing). Key findings: Pangram consistently outperformed the other tools, achieving high accuracy in detecting fully AI-generated, hybrid, and humanised texts. Other tools significantly underestimated GenAI content, particularly for texts generated with the most advanced model (GPT-4o Deep Research). All tools correctly identified fully human-written texts (false positives were rare, suggesting improvement over earlier studies). When applied to 1,163 real master's theses submitted in the 2024-2025 academic year, Pangram flagged 45.5% of cases, typically indicating low to moderate levels of AI-associated text. The study notes that student GenAI use has risen dramatically — from 66% in 2024 to 92% in 2025, with 88% using it for academic assignments and 18% directly copying GenAI text. The authors conclude that "while detection tools can provide useful initial flags, they should not be used as sole evidence in high-stakes decision-making but should be implemented in a broader evaluation strategy." [33]

**Eslit Preprint (2024):** This preprint analyzes tools like Turnitin, PlagScan, GPTZero, Copyleaks, and QuillBot, finding that they often struggle with context interpretation, resulting in false positives and missed instances of nuanced plagiarism. False positives occur when legitimate work is flagged, particularly for non-native speakers who may use language structures that unintentionally mirror existing texts. The tools struggle with paraphrasing, contextual understanding, and distinguishing between human-written and AI-generated content. There is a growing overreliance on AI, which may encourage a "checklist mentality" among educators. Major universities (e.g., UC, Oxford, Harvard) have been hesitant to rely solely on AI tools for plagiarism detection. The study concludes that AI-driven tools should be used as supplementary aids rather than definitive arbiters of originality. [34]

**Deep, Edgington, Ghosh, & Rahaman Review (Information, 2025):** This review evaluated AI detection tools (e.g., Turnitin AI, GPTZero, Copyleaks, ZeroGPT) based on a qualitative evidence synthesis of 24 peer-reviewed articles (2021-2024). Key findings: AI detectors show inconsistent accuracy, frequently producing false positives, particularly misclassifying human-written content (especially from non-native English speakers) as AI-generated. Tools trained on older models (e.g., GPT-2) perform poorly on advanced outputs (e.g., GPT-4). One study found Quillbot achieved 95.59% accuracy, while others showed rates ranging from 0% to 100%. A paraphrasing model (DIPPER) reduced detection accuracy of DetectGPT from 70.3% to 4.6%. Ethical concerns include surveillance, lack of transparency, due process violations, and bias against multilingual/non-native English speakers. The review notes that "non-native English students are most at risk for such mistakes because of the similarities in syntax and structure with AI-written language." The paper calls for a shift from punitive approaches toward AI-integrated pedagogies that emphasize ethical use, student support, inclusive assessment design (e.g., in-class tasks, oral presentations, portfolio-based evaluations), and faculty training. Students often lack clarity on acceptable AI usage, with 87% showing inadequate comprehension of implications. [35]

**Adler University White Paper (2025):** Turnitin is described as the gold standard for plagiarism detection, but institutions need better training initiatives for students. Perkins et al. (2023) indicated that AI tools like Turnitin are very reliable in capturing AI-generated content — "while the software is not perfect, the errors do not seem to be labeling something incorrectly as AI content; rather, they are not labeling them at all." AI detection tools like Turnitin are reliable for GPT-3.5 but less precise for GPT-4.0. GrammarlyGo (the generative AI feature) can trigger Turnitin AI flags, though most institutions turn this feature off. Best practices established at Adler University include: a Turnitin similarity threshold of 20% and an AI score threshold of 30% (anything above requires investigation), and a four-step response plan for plagiarism (zero, meeting, redo option for first offense, tracking for repeat offenses). [11]

**Systematic Review on Over-Reliance (Zhai, Wibowo, & Li, 2024):** Khalil and Er (2023) reported that popular plagiarism detection tools such as Turnitin and iThenticate show a significant limitation in identifying plagiarism in essays based on existing literature — these tools could only detect plagiarism in less than 15% of cases. [26]

**UIC Student Attitudes Report (2025):** Approximately 50% expressed concerns about AI and academic dishonesty. Around 40% acknowledged using AI for research and writing assistance. Over 30% called for more education on AI tool usage. About 45% view AI as a beneficial learning tool if used properly. [31]

**Wiley 2024 Survey:** Only 45% of students and 15% of instructors have actually used AI in classes. Students who avoid AI cite distrust, fear of being accused of cheating, or unfamiliarity. Both groups acknowledge AI's potential benefits for generating ideas, saving time, and helping with difficult content when used appropriately. [30]

**UAE University Study (2024):** 60% of students believe students must learn AI tools for their careers. 66.4% use AI to save time; 66.6% use it for new ideas. 87% were concerned about privacy and information security. Only 5.5% thought it was acceptable to submit AI-generated work as their own. [17]

**Scoping Review (Schei et al., 2024):** Students are "concerned about the accuracy and reliability of the responses from the chatbots, as well as potential negative impacts on their learning processes, critical thinking, discipline, and creativity." [1]

**Polish University Study (2025):** 48.2% of students expressed concern about the possibility of receiving incorrect or imprecise answers. [5]

**Vallejo-Blanxart & Sans Study (2025):** Student satisfaction was "strongly associated with transparency in data policies and pedagogical usefulness rather than raw technical performance." [6]

**College Board Research (2026):** Faculty sentiment skews negative, with 45% reporting negative views of AI in higher education versus 34% positive. Only 21% of faculty feel very confident guiding AI use in their classrooms. [28]

**Michigan Virtual Khanmigo Pilot (2024-2025):** Teachers noted that "students struggled to ask Khanmigo the correct question. They didn't know what they didn't know—where to start or what to ask." One teacher emphasized: "We have to teach kids how to use it and how not to use it—and be clear about the intended purpose." Another noted: "Students don't want to use it how we would like them to. We have to model appropriate usage for them consistently." The article recommends that "AI may need to be taught progressively, with different levels of understanding increased gradually from year to year in school." [15]

- 92% of higher education students now use generative AI (up from 66% in 2024)
- The global AI in education market was valued at $7.05 billion in 2025, projected to reach $136.79 billion by 2035 (35% CAGR)
- 86% of education organizations use generative AI — the highest adoption rate of any industry
- Only 20% of universities have a formal AI policy, though 56% believe their institution is unprepared
- Students in low-income and rural areas are the least likely to report that their schools allow or integrate AI use, highlighting an equity gap [19]

---

**Fully Comprehensive Findings**

---

## A) EFFECTIVENESS EVIDENCE

### A1) Meta-Analyses and Systematic Reviews

**Systematic Review of AI-Driven Intelligent Tutoring Systems (Létourneau et al., 2025)**
Published in npj Science of Learning (Volume 10, Article 29, May 2025), this systematic review analyzed 28 studies involving 4,597 students examining AI-driven Intelligent Tutoring Systems (ITS) in K-12 education. Key findings: "The effects of ITSs on learning and performance in K-12 education are generally positive but are found to be mitigated when compared to non-intelligent tutoring systems." 96% of articles were authored by individuals from educational science, computer science, or both; only one article was from an ITS company. 54% of studies originated from the USA, 27% from Asia, and 15% from Europe. Roughly half (54%) of studies compared school levels and subjects to assess differences. None of the included articles mentioned AI ethics considerations. The review calls for additional research with longer interventions, larger and more diverse sample sizes, and investigation into ethical implications of AI in teaching. ITS effectiveness depends on sound pedagogical features (immediate feedback, guided practice, adaptivity) applied under the right conditions. [1]

**Meta-Analysis: AI's Impact on Learners' Self-Efficacy (Ren, Stephens, and Lee, 2026)**
Published in Behavioral Sciences (2026) by researchers from the University of Auckland, this meta-analysis examined 23 empirical studies published between January 2005 and February 2025. Key findings: AI had a significant positive impact on self-efficacy in learning contexts, with a medium effect size of 0.758 (Hedges' g). Two moderating variables were significant: discipline (Q = 10.348, p < 0.05) and the role played by AI (Q = 3.991, p < 0.05). AI had the highest effect on self-efficacy in natural sciences (1.310) and medicine (1.013), while the effect was not significant for engineering. AI as an intelligent learning tool produced the highest effect on self-efficacy (0.883), while mixed roles (tool + tutor) had lower effects (0.450). No significant moderating effects were found for learner levels, research settings, type of AI utilized, or duration of studies. The study used a random-effects model due to high heterogeneity (I² = 89.677). [2]

**Systematic Review: Personalized Learning Trends and Future Directions (Frontiers in Education, 2026)**
Published on March 13, 2026, this systematic review employed the PRISMA review protocol alongside a meta-literature review, analyzing 31 relevant articles from the Scopus database spanning 2013 to 2025. Methodological distribution: 45% qualitative, 42% quantitative, 13% mixed methods. Geographic distribution: China leads with 6 papers, followed by India (4), USA, Saudi Arabia, Colombia, and Kazakhstan (2 each), with 14 other countries contributing 1 paper each. Top author: Chiappe, A. with 3 contributions. Major themes discussed include: personalized learning pathways and student engagement via AI; predictive analytics, assessment, and early intervention; teacher training, digital competence, and pedagogical innovation; ethical, governance, and data privacy concerns; generative AI and Education 5.0 transformation; equity, inclusivity, and socio-cultural impact. The review highlights the need for professional development in pedagogical integration and digital literacy for educators, and urges policymakers to develop ethical frameworks for AI implementation addressing data privacy, algorithmic bias, and unequal access. The findings reveal that "the swift expansion of AI, combined with persistent concerns about educational standards in developing countries, may create additional institutional pressures that influence the effectiveness of education." [3]

**Systematic Review: AI vs. Traditional Teaching Methods (Onyefu and Toedat, 2026)**
Published in the International Journal of Applied Resilience and Sustainability (IJARS), Vol. 2 No. 3 (July 2026), this PRISMA-based systematic literature review compares AI-based teaching methods with traditional teaching approaches on student performance in higher education, K-12, and STEM settings. Key findings: "AI-based learning systems tend to be more effective in enhancing academic motivation, self-regulated learning, adaptive learning, and personalized learning results than conventional teaching strategies." However, "the conventional approaches to teaching are more efficient in promoting collaborative learning, emotional intelligence, critical thinking, and teacher-student relationship." The review identifies significant challenges including ethical AI concerns, algorithmic bias, data privacy, academic integrity, teacher preparedness, and the digital divide. Future educational models (Education 4.0 and 5.0) are expected to integrate blended learning approaches that combine AI-facilitated personalization with human pedagogical skills to maximize student performance and equity. [4]

**Review: Personalized Learning through AI (Vorobyeva et al., 2025)**
Published in Contemporary Educational Technology (April 2025), this review examined AI-supported personalized learning (PL) systems with emphasis on pedagogical approaches and implementation challenges. The authors searched Web of Science and Scopus databases, reviewing 30 publications in detail. Key findings: ChatGPT and machine learning are the most commonly utilized AI tools in education. General education and language learning account for the majority of AI applications. AI's educational roles primarily involve automated feedback systems and adaptive content distribution, supported by learning approaches emphasizing student characteristics and expectations. The study identifies major challenges in three areas: (1) technical constraints and data privacy concerns; (2) educational and pragmatic barriers; and (3) pedagogical challenges (which rank above technology integration). Curriculum integration and teacher preparation are considered major concerns. The authors conclude that "the efficient application of AI-enabled PL requires a comprehensive strategy addressing technological, pedagogical, and ethical issues all at once." [5]

### A2) Large-Scale Randomized Controlled Trials (RCTs) and Quasi-Experimental Studies

**Harvard RCT: AI Tutoring vs. In-Class Active Learning (Kestin et al., 2025)**
Published in Scientific Reports (2025), this randomized controlled trial conducted at Harvard University in Fall 2023 involved 194 undergraduate physics students. The study compared learning outcomes between AI tutoring (using GPT-4 with carefully engineered prompts) and in-class active learning instruction. Key findings: Students using the AI tutor demonstrated significantly higher learning gains (median post-test score 4.5 vs 3.5 for in-class active learning), with gains over double those of the in-class group. The result was statistically significant (p < 10⁻⁸) with a large effect size (0.73 to 1.3 standard deviations). 70% of AI-tutored students spent less than 60 minutes on task (median 49 minutes), compared to the fixed 60-minute in-class lesson. AI-tutored students reported significantly higher engagement and motivation, with comparable enjoyment and growth mindset. The AI tutor was designed following pedagogical best practices: facilitating active learning, managing cognitive load, promoting growth mindset, scaffolding content, ensuring accuracy (via pre-written step-by-step solutions), providing timely personalized feedback, and allowing self-pacing. The authors note that previous AI education studies showed mixed results because they lacked such structured pedagogical design. They argue that AI tutoring is particularly effective for initial content engagement (understanding/applying/analyzing levels of Bloom's Taxonomy) and should complement rather than replace in-person instruction, which can focus on higher-order skills. [6]

**NBER Randomized Trial: Khanmigo (Oreopoulos and Low, 2024-2026)**
A two-year NBER randomized trial (w35620) across 18 middle schools in Hamilton County, Tennessee found that Khan Academy's AI tutor Khanmigo raised maths achievement by 1.26 national percentile ranks per term (0.040 SD) during the 2024-25 and 2025-26 school years. The study, conducted by Philip Oreopoulos (University of Toronto) and Nina Low (Charles River Associates), analyzed 6,902 student-term observations across 53 grade-within-school clusters. Effects were larger in year two (0.084 SD) than year one (0.020 SD, not distinguishable from zero). Programme cost was roughly $15 per student per year. Usage data revealed that while 96% of students messaged Khanmigo at least once, the median student only messaged it on 33% of practice days and in 14% of exercise sessions. Only 14.5% of student messages contained a mathematical question or reasoning step, with most being bare answers (39.4%), suggested prompt clicks (24.2%), or low-effort responses (12.6%). The authors note the study "cannot isolate the tutor's marginal contribution" and that the gain "resembles those from Khan Academy practice without AI assistance." The paper was one of three tutoring trials released simultaneously by NBER. The second (w35621) tested AI plus mastery progression in a one-week classroom experiment with 6,000+ students, finding a marginal positive effect (3.1 percentage points, p=0.065) only when AI was combined with mastery requirements. The third (w35622) examined home virtual tutoring in Toronto, where take-up rose from 45.3% to 82.5% after redesigning the invitation, but results were not distinguishable from zero. Across all three trials, the consistent finding is that student engagement—not AI capability—is the binding constraint on AI tutoring effectiveness. Oreopoulos told The Hechinger Report: "I don't want to jump out and say we've demonstrated that AI is going to be the game changer that we hope it is." [7]

**Tutor CoPilot RCT (Wang et al., 2024)**
This study, published as an EdWorkingPaper and summarized by multiple sources, is a randomized controlled trial involving over 700 tutors and 1,000 K-12 students from underserved communities in a U.S. Southern school district, partnered with FEV Tutor (a chat-based virtual tutoring provider), conducted from March 27 to May 17, 2024. Key findings: Students with tutors using Tutor CoPilot were 4 percentage points more likely to master math topics (p<0.01), with exit ticket pass rates increasing from 62% to 66%. Gains were highest for students of lower-rated tutors (+9 p.p., from 56% to 65%) and less experienced tutors (+7 p.p., from 61% to 68%), helping less-effective tutors achieve outcomes comparable to their more-effective peers. The tool is low-cost at approximately $20 per tutor per year. Analysis of over 350,000 messages showed Tutor CoPilot promoted effective pedagogy: treatment tutors were more likely to use probing questions (e.g., "prompt the student to explain" used ~10% more) and less likely to use generic praise (used ~10% less by control tutors). Tutor interviews (n=18) indicated the tool was helpful for providing well-phrased explanations but sometimes generated suggestions misaligned with students' grade levels. No statistically significant improvements were found in end-of-year MAP test scores, likely due to short implementation duration (2 months) and inconsistent student-tutor matching. The tutoring provider FEV Tutor incorporated Tutor CoPilot into all of its sessions following this study. World Bank teams replicated positive effects in Nigerian secondary English classes (0.31 standard deviation growth within six weeks). [8][9][10][11]

**Quasi-Experimental Study: AI-Integrated Learning Platform in 3D Modeling Course (Frontiers in Education, 2026)**
Published in Frontiers in Education (March 2026), this quasi-experimental study evaluated the impact of an AI-integrated learning platform on student performance in a university-level 3D modeling course at Astana IT University, Kazakhstan. The study involved 120 second-year undergraduate students (experimental group: n=62, control group: n=58) over an 8-week intervention period. The AI-integrated platform incorporated GPT-3.5/GPT-4 for generating formative questions and feedback, and the Gemini model for rubric-based assessment and grading. Key findings: The experimental group showed statistically significant improvements in post-test performance compared to the control group (p < 0.05). Post-test results showed the experimental group had 8.06% high-level, 27.42% above average, 38.71% average, 19.35% low, and 6.45% very low proficiency, compared to the control group's 3.45% high, 12.07% above average, 24.14% average, 43.10% low, and 17.24% very low. 74% of students reported increased motivation and active engagement. The platform supported development of goal-setting, progress monitoring, and metacognitive awareness through learning analytics dashboards and continuous feedback. 87% found the interface intuitive, 82% rated content accessibility positively, 76% appreciated adaptability, 79% valued AI feedback, and 85% expressed overall satisfaction. The study concludes that AI-integrated platforms can function as metacognitive scaffolds, enhancing strategic learning behaviors and cognitive engagement in applied digital skills education. [12]

**Quasi-Experimental Study: AI-Assisted College English Instruction (Li and Long, 2025)**
Published in the journal Information (MDPI, 2025, Volume 16, Issue 10, Article 895), this study investigated the impact of integrating Generative AI (ChatGPT 4.0 and DeepSeek 3.2) into college English instruction in China. A six-week quasi-experiment was conducted with 150 non-English major undergraduates randomly assigned to an AI-assisted group and a traditional teaching group (75 each). The AI group used a structured "draft → feedback → revision" loop with prompt templates and responsible-use guidelines. Key findings: AI-supported learning improved overall English proficiency, especially in writing skills and among lower- and intermediate-level learners. The quality of AI interaction—meaningful feedback adoption and autonomous revision—was more influential than mere usage frequency. AI-enhanced teaching stimulated motivation and self-efficacy but raised concerns about potential overreliance and shallow engagement. The study proposes a Three-Tiered Human–AI Collaboration Model (Tool Layer, Process Layer, Cognitive Layer) and a Four-Stage Evolutionary Pathway. [13]

**Khanmigo Study: Undergraduate Physics (Slijepcevic and Yaylali, 2025)**
Published in the Journal of Teaching and Learning (Vol. 19, No. 4, 2025), this mixed-methods study involved 69 undergraduate students divided into two groups (Khanmigo AI tutor vs. Google search engine), with a third Paper-only group emerging during the experiment. Participants completed pre- and post-tests using the Lunar Phases Concept Inventory (LPCI). Quantitative analysis revealed significant learning gains across all conditions but found no statistically significant differences between groups in terms of learning outcomes. Qualitative findings indicated that students perceived Khanmigo positively, appreciating its step-by-step guidance, practice problems, and personalized interactions. However, students viewed it as a supplementary tool rather than a replacement for traditional instruction. The study noted that the short duration of exposure to the AI tutor and the quality of printed materials may have affected results. [14]

**Quasi-Experimental Study: AI-Based Adaptive Learning in Higher Education (Suleiman and Ibrahim)**
This quantitative exploratory study involved 500 undergraduate students from five institutions using platforms such as Knewton, Coursera's adaptive models, and Smart Sparrow. Key findings: 74% of respondents agreed/strongly agreed that students using adaptive learning systems achieved better academic results than those in traditional environments. 76% agreed/strongly agreed that students appeared more engaged with adaptive platforms; 78% agreed that interactive features encouraged active participation; 77% agreed that immediate feedback increased interest in learning tasks. 75% agreed that adaptive systems help students remain committed to completing programs; 74% agreed that students using adaptive technologies are less likely to drop out; 75% agreed that personalized learning support encourages persistence. Challenges identified include technical barriers, initial implementation costs, resistance to change among educators and students, data privacy concerns, algorithmic bias risks, and disparities in digital access/literacy. [15]

**Duolingo Efficacy Studies (2020-2026)**
Duolingo's Efficacy Research Lab has conducted rigorous research demonstrating effectiveness across multiple dimensions. Key findings: Duolingo learners' communication skills are comparable to or better than classroom learners. Duolingo improves speaking, reading, writing, and listening skills. Learners can start basic conversations after 4-6 weeks. Duolingo French/Spanish learners score as well as university students after 4-5 semesters of language classes, after learning on Duolingo for half that time. Older adults who learned a language on Duolingo showed improved brain health. Duolingo ABC improved children's literacy skills comparable to 2 months of kindergarten. Studies also show that doing more lessons (not just time spent) leads to better outcomes. Using Duolingo Max with generative AI increased learners' self-efficacy. 97% of surveyed language teachers considered Duolingo effective, and 96% said they would recommend it. Over 90% of learners who used AI-powered features (including conversation practice and personalized grammar info) for a month felt prepared to use their new language in real-life situations. Over 60% used what they learned outside the app. [16][17][18]

**Study: Duolingo vs. ChatGPT on Motivation, Enjoyment, Critical Thinking, and Autonomy (Xu and Liu, 2025)**
Published in Learning and Motivation (Volume 89, February 2025), this study investigated the comparative impact of two AI-powered language learning platforms—Duolingo and ChatGPT—on four key educational outcomes among Chinese EFL learners: motivation, enjoyment, critical thinking (CT), and autonomy. The study employed a true-experimental design with three groups: two experimental groups using Duolingo (n=81) and ChatGPT (n=81), and a control group (n=82). Key findings: Both experimental groups significantly outperformed the control group across all four measures (motivation, enjoyment, critical thinking, and autonomy). No significant differences were found between the Duolingo and ChatGPT groups, suggesting both platforms are equally effective in fostering these outcomes. [19]

### A4) The "2 Sigma Problem" and AI Tutoring

Benjamin Bloom's 1984 research found that students taught one-to-one with mastery-based methods performed approximately two standard deviations better than those in conventional classrooms—the average tutored student outperformed 98% of conventionally taught students. Mastery learning alone (without one-on-one) produced a one sigma improvement—the average mastery learning student outperformed about 84% of conventionally taught students. [29][30]

**Critical Perspectives on the 2 Sigma Claim:**
Dr. Luke Rowe (PhD in learning sciences) has debunked aspects of the 2 sigma claim. Key arguments: Bloom's claim rested heavily on two very small, unpublished studies by his doctoral students (Anania and Burke) in the early 1980s, plus a selectively cherry-picked table of effect sizes from secondary sources. Paul von Hippel's (2024) data sleuthing revealed major problems: the famous graph was a hand-drawn caricature, not actual data; Bloom rounded up and fabricated numbers from Walberg's (1984) work. The tutoring condition was heavily confounded: tutors received extra training and coaching, students got frequent formative testing (retrieval practice effect ~0.5 SD), individual feedback, worked examples, Socratic questioning, praise, and extra time on task. Large-scale meta-analyses (Nickow et al., 2020, 2024) show tutoring effects are typically around 0.3 to 0.4 standard deviations (moving from 50th to ~64th percentile), not 2.0 SD. Matthew Kraft (2020) found most educational interventions produce effects of about 0.1 SD. Despite the debunking, the 2 sigma claim has become sticky in education and AI circles (e.g., Sal Khan's Khan Academy/Khanmigo citing it as a benchmark for AI tutors). [31]

**Current AI Tutoring Effect Sizes Relative to 2 Sigma:**
The Harvard RCT (Kestin et al., 2025) found effect sizes of 0.73 to 1.3 standard deviations for AI tutoring compared to active learning. However, the article by Dr. Kola Tytler (2026) notes that AI tutoring is "a promising supplement, not a proven replacement for expert teaching and mentorship" and that "the honest goal is to close part of the gap for many learners, not to pretend the gap has been closed." [29][6]

The Top 10 AI Tutoring Systems analysis found that well-designed AI tutoring systems do improve learning outcomes, with effect sizes (0.25-0.45) comparable to human tutoring. Students typically gain 1-3 months of additional learning. However, effectiveness varies by implementation quality, student engagement (3-5 hours weekly optimal), subject domain, and platform quality. [20]
